events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1309, King Denis of Portugal granted the Magna Charta Privilegioum, establishing the charter for Portugal's first university, now known as the University of Coimbra. This marked a significant step in the development of higher education in Portugal.
events.name: Granting of Magna Charta Privilegioum

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1309, King Ferdinand IV of Castile agreed to assist King Jaume II of Aragon in a military campaign against the Islamic Emirate of Granada. This collaboration aimed to strengthen Christian control in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Agreement to Assist Aragon against Granada

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1309, Pope Clement V officially moved the papal headquarters from Rome to Avignon, initiating the period known as the Avignon Papacy. This decision was influenced by the violence in Rome and marked a significant shift in the Catholic Church's governance.
events.name: Transfer of Papacy to Avignon

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1309, Sultan Muhammad III was deposed during a palace coup and replaced by his half-brother Abu al-Juyush Nasr in the Emirate of Granada. Muhammad was allowed to live in Almuñécar, while his vizier was executed.
events.name: Deposition of Sultan Muhammad III

events.enhanced_description: In April 1309, after ascending to the throne, Emir Nasr ad-Din Muhammad of Granada sent envoys to the Marinid court in Fez, Morocco, seeking support and alliances against the Christian kingdoms.
events.name: Envoys to Marinid court

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1309, Spanish kings James II of Aragon and Ferdinand IV of Castile persuaded Pope Clement V to issue the papal bull Indesinentis cure, authorizing a crusade against Islam in the Iberian Peninsula and the conquest of Corsica and Sardinia.
events.name: Papal Bull Indesinentis cure

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1309, Pope Clement V issued the papal bull Prioribus decanis, granting King Ferdinand IV of Castile a portion of clergy taxes to finance the ongoing war against Granada. This financial support was crucial for the Christian campaign.
events.name: Papal Bull Prioribus decanis

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1309, Robert the Wise ascended to the throne as King of Naples following the death of his father, Charles the Lame. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize and strengthen the kingdom.
events.name: Robert the Wise becomes King of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1309, Marinid Sultan Abu al-Rabi Sulayman launched an attack on Ceuta, seeking to strengthen his position in North Africa. This military action was part of a broader strategy to consolidate power in the region.
events.name: Marinid attack on Ceuta

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1309, Charles I of Hungary was coronated for the second time in Székesfehérvár, after his initial coronation attempt in 1301 was not recognized. This event solidified his claim to the throne.
events.name: Second Coronation of Charles I of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1309, Portugal allied with the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon to launch an attack on Gibraltar. This military collaboration aimed to strengthen Christian control over the strategically important territory.
events.name: Portugal joins forces against Gibraltar

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1309, Aragonese forces under King James II landed on the coast of Almería and began a blockade of the city. Despite multiple assaults, the siege faced challenges, leading to a truce in December due to supply shortages.
events.name: Siege of Almería

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1309, a fleet from the Kingdom of Aragon, led by Eimeric de Bellveí, successfully conquered the north African territory of Ceuta, which was under the control of the Emirate of Granada. This victory marked a significant expansion of Aragonese influence.
events.name: Conquest of Ceuta

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1310, Castilian forces abandoned the siege of Algeciras after signing a seven-year peace treaty with Abu al-Juyush Nasr, the Sultan of Granada. This treaty included significant financial and territorial concessions, marking a pivotal moment in the relations between Castile and Granada.

image.caption: Aerial view of part of Algeciras and its port.
image.credit: Adam Cli — Own work
image.date_qualification: A modern aerial view of the city and port, not a depiction of the medieval siege. The original image date is 2023-12-30.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Siege of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1309, the Byzantine garrison of Rhodes surrendered to the Crusader forces of the Knights Hospitaller, led by Grand Master Foulques de Villaret. This event marked the completion of the Knights' conquest of Rhodes, establishing their headquarters on the island.
events.name: Conquest of Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1309, a relief force from the Emirate of Granada attempted to drive out the Kingdom of Aragon forces besieging Almeria. The effort resulted in heavy losses for the Granadan forces, with thousands of men killed in the confrontation.
events.name: Relief force from the Emirate of Granada at Almeria

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1309, Castilian forces led by Juan Núñez II de Lara and Alonso Pérez de Guzmán besieged and conquered the Saracen fortress at Gibraltar, which had been under Muslim control since 711. The siege involved a blockade of the port and was ordered by Ferdinand IV of Castile to repair the city's defenses.
events.name: Siege of Gibraltar

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1309, Archbishop Cassone della Torre of Milan was imprisoned by troops sent by his cousin Guido della Torre, who attacked the archbishop's palace. This event marked a significant power struggle within the ruling families of Milan.
events.name: Imprisonment of Archbishop Cassone della Torre

events.enhanced_description: In October 1309, approximately 500 knights led by John of Castile deserted the Castilian encampment during the Siege of Algeciras. Their departure was prompted by unpaid wages and the cession of one-sixth of Granada to the Kingdom of Aragon, which caused discontent among the troops.
events.name: Desertion during the Siege of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: In 1309, King Edward II summoned a council to meet at York, but several nobles, including the earls of Lancaster, Lincoln, Warwick, Oxford, and Arundel, refused to attend due to the presence of Piers Gaveston. This refusal highlighted the growing tensions between the king and the nobility.
events.name: King Edward II summons council at York

events.enhanced_description: In 1309, Alnwick Castle in Northumberland was purchased by the House of Percy, which would later become the Earls of Northumberland. This acquisition marked a significant moment in the history of the Percy family and their influence in northern England.

locations.name: Alnwick Castle, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Purchase of Alnwick Castle by the House of Percy

events.enhanced_description: In 1309, the village of Lukáčovce in Slovakia first appeared in historical records. This marks an important point in the documentation of local history and settlement patterns in the region.
events.name: First historical record of Lukáčovce

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1309, Pope Clement V signed a mandate allowing for the posthumous trial of Boniface VIII for heresy. This decision was sent to the Bishop of Paris, reflecting the ongoing conflicts within the Church and the legacy of Boniface VIII.
events.name: Pope Clement V's mandate on Boniface VIII

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1309, Pope Clement V signed a mandate allowing for the posthumous trial of Boniface VIII for heresy. This decision was sent to the Bishop of Paris, reflecting the ongoing conflicts within the Church and the legacy of Boniface VIII.
events.name: Pope Clement V's mandate on Boniface VIII (duplicate)

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1309, Thihathu was crowned as the monarch of the Myinsaing Kingdom in central Myanmar. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the region as it established Thihathu's rule.
events.name: Coronation of Thihathu

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1309, the trial of the Knights Templar arrested in England commenced, which would last for five months. This trial was part of a broader crackdown on the Templars across Europe, initiated by King Philip IV of France.
events.name: Trial of the Knights Templar in England

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1309, Archbishop Cassone della Torre was exiled to Bologna by his cousin Guido, who had previously imprisoned him. This exile was part of the ongoing conflict between the two factions in Milan.
events.name: Exile of Archbishop Cassone della Torre

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1309, Alauddin Khalji, the Sultan of Delhi, ordered General Malik Kafur to invade the Kakatiya kingdom, ruled by Prataparudra, and to besiege its capital, Warangal. This marked a significant military campaign in the expansion of the Delhi Sultanate.
events.name: Alauddin Khalji's order to invade Kakatiya kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1309, Pope Clement V declared that the Knights Hospitaller would not be sent to the Holy Land and Jerusalem, limiting their role to defending the Mediterranean Sea, including Cyprus and Rhodes. This decision reflected the changing dynamics of the Crusades and the Church's military orders.
events.name: Pope Clement V's declaration on Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1309, General Malik Kafur of the Delhi Sultanate resumed his march toward Warangal after a layover in Masudspur. The army made several stops along the way, indicating the logistical challenges of the campaign against the Kakatiya kingdom.
events.name: Delhi Sultanate Army's march toward Warangal

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1309, Pope Clement V reversed the excommunication of Flemish hero Willem van Saeftinghe and granted him absolution. However, he required Willem to join the Knights Hospitaller in their crusade at the island of Rhodes, reflecting the intertwining of personal and political motives in papal decisions.
events.name: Pope Clement V's absolution of Willem van Saeftinghe

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1309, Fernando Ponce de León was appointed as the new ruler of Marchena, along with several other towns, by King Ferdinand IV of Castile. This appointment came three months after the death of Alonso Pérez de Guzmán, indicating a shift in local power dynamics.
events.name: Fernando Ponce de León becomes ruler of Marchena

events.enhanced_description: In 1310, the first purpose-built accommodation for students, known as the Mob Quad, was completed at Merton College, Oxford. This development marked a significant advancement in the provision of student housing in medieval England.
events.name: Completion of Mob Quad at Merton College

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1310, General Malik Kafur of the Delhi Sultanate began the siege of Warangal, the capital of the Kakatiya kingdom. This military campaign was part of Alauddin Khalji's broader strategy to expand his empire in southern India.
events.name: Siege of Warangal by Malik Kafur

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1310, James II of Aragon ended the siege of Almeria after five months without capturing the city. This decision reflected the challenges faced by Aragonese forces in their attempts to reclaim territory from the Emirate of Granada.
events.name: End of the Siege of Almeria

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1310, the English Parliament opened at Westminster after being summoned on October 26 of the previous year. This session would continue until April 12, addressing various political issues of the time.
events.name: Opening of the English Parliament at Westminster

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1310, King Edward II of England opened the first session of the Parliament of Ireland in Dublin, acting in his capacity as Lord of Ireland. This Parliament would hold 14 sessions before being dismissed in 1326.

image.caption: The Great Parliament of Ireland, a retrospective illustration associated with the Parliament of Ireland.
image.credit: Henry Barraud, John Hayter — [1]
image.date_qualification: 18th century; depicts no verified date for the 1310 session.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First session of the Parliament of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1310, a group of 12 Scottish Catholic bishops, including William Sinclair, Bishop of Dunkeld, swore fealty to Robert the Bruce, King of Scotland. This act of allegiance was significant in consolidating Bruce's power during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Scottish bishops swear fealty to Robert the Bruce

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1310, Konrad I of Oleśnica and his brother Boleslaw renounced their rights to Gdańsk Pomerania in exchange for payment from the principality of Brandenburg, ruled by Margrave Heinrich I. This transaction reflected the complex feudal relationships in medieval Europe.
events.name: Renunciation of rights to Gdańsk Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1310, Baybars II, Sultan of the Mamluks in Egypt, was driven from office by an angry mob of supporters of his predecessor, An-Nasir Muhammad. This event highlighted the instability and factionalism within Mamluk politics.
events.name: Baybars II driven from office

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1310, General Malik Kafur of the Delhi Sultanate began his return journey to Delhi after securing the surrender of King Prataparudra of Kakatiya during the siege of Warangal. His successful campaign marked a significant expansion of the Sultanate's influence in southern India.
events.name: Malik Kafur's return journey to Delhi

events.enhanced_description: In spring 1310, Castilian forces abandoned the siege of Algeciras after six months, leading to negotiations with Granada. The eventual peace treaty signed on May 26 marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between Castile and Granada.
events.name: Abandonment of the Siege of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1323, Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq dispatched an expeditionary army led by his son Muhammad bin Tughluq to besiege Warangal after its ruler Prataparudra refused to pay tribute, culminating in the city's surrender on November 9.
events.name: Siege of Warangal

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1310, a significant political negotiation took place in Szeged, Hungary, where Thomas II, Archbishop of Esztergom, successfully negotiated the return of the Crown of Saint Stephen from Ladislaus III Kán, the Voivode of Transylvania. This event was crucial for the legitimacy of the Hungarian monarchy, as the crown was a symbol of royal authority.
events.name: Return of the Crown of Saint Stephen

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1310, Athinkhaya, one of the three regents of the Kingdom of Myinsaing in present-day Myanmar, passed away at the age of 49. His death left his brothers, Thihathu and Yazathingyan, in control, with Thihathu soon to become the sole ruler of Burma.
events.name: Death of Athinkhaya

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1310, Sultan An-Nasir Muhammad of Egypt ordered the execution of his predecessor, Baybars II. This act marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the Mamluk Sultanate, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the time.
events.name: Execution of Baybars II

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1310, Nephon I was elected as the new Patriarch of the Eastern Orthodox Church in Constantinople, succeeding the elderly Athanasius I, who was forced to retire. Nephon's election was significant for the Orthodox community during a period of political and religious turmoil.
events.name: Nephon I becomes Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1310, in Paris, 54 members of the Knights Templar were burned at the stake for heresy on the orders of King Philip IV of France. This brutal act was part of a larger campaign against the Templars, which involved Pope Clement V attempting to assert the Church's authority over the situation.
events.name: Burning of Knights Templar

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1310, Otto III, Duke of Carinthia, died and was succeeded by his younger brother, Henry of Bohemia. This transition marked a significant shift in the leadership of the region during a time of political instability.
events.name: Death of Otto III, Duke of Carinthia

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1310, the Tiepolo conspiracy unfolded in Venice, where leading nobles, including Bajamonte Tiepolo, organized a failed plot against Doge Pietro Gradenigo. The rebellion was suppressed, leading to significant political changes, including the establishment of the Council of Ten.
events.name: Tiepolo Conspiracy

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1310, General Malik Kafur arrived in Delhi, presenting treasures captured from the fortress of Warrangal to Sultan Alauddin Khilji. This event highlighted the military successes of the Delhi Sultanate during its expansion in southern India.
events.name: Malik Kafur arrives at Delhi

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1310, the Citadel of Erbil, which served as the headquarters for a rebellion by Eastern Christians, was captured by the Mongol Ilkhanate after a prolonged siege. The event resulted in a massacre of the defenders, marking a brutal chapter in the Mongol conquests.
events.name: Capture of the Citadel of Erbil

events.enhanced_description: In summer 1310, Count Charles of Valois founded the Diocese of Corfu, Zakynthos, and Cephalonia, with its seat in Corfu. This establishment was significant for the Christian community in the Ionian Islands.
events.name: Foundation of the Diocese of Corfu

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1310, the Council of Ten was established in Venice by decree of Doge Pietro Gradenigo. This council was created in response to the Tiepolo conspiracy and became a powerful governing body within the Venetian Republic.
events.name: Creation of the Council of Ten

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1310, Károly Róbert I was crowned for the third time as King of Hungary in Székesfehérvár, following the successful negotiation for the return of the Crown of Saint Stephen by Thomas II, Archbishop of Esztergom. This event solidified Károly's claim to the throne and reinforced the importance of the crown in Hungarian royal legitimacy.
events.name: Coronation of Károly Róbert I

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1310, John of Luxembourg, the younger brother of King Henry of Bohemia, married Princess Elizabeth, the daughter of the late King Wenceslaus II. This marriage was significant in strengthening political alliances within the region.
events.name: Marriage of John of Luxembourg

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1310, King Edward II of England reached Roxburgh as part of his invasion of Scotland. Despite the initial advance, the campaign proved fruitless, with English forces unable to achieve significant territorial gains.
events.name: Edward II's Invasion of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1310, King Robert the Bruce of Scotland wrote from Kildrum, attempting to initiate peace talks with King Edward II, who was encamped in Scotland at Biggar. However, Edward refused to negotiate, highlighting the ongoing tensions between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Robert the Bruce's Peace Talks

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1310, Abu Sa'id Uthman II ascended to the throne as the new Sultan of Morocco following the death of his nephew, Sultan Abu al-Rabi Sulayman. This transition marked a significant moment in Moroccan history.
events.name: Abu Sa'id Uthman II becomes Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1310, Prague, the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia, was captured by John of Luxembourg, who deposed his brother, Henry of Bohemia. This event marked a significant shift in power within the region.
events.name: Capture of Prague

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1310, Stephen I, Duke of Bavaria, died, leaving his older brothers Otto III and Louis III as the dual rulers of the southern German duchy. This transition was significant in the political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Death of Stephen I, Duke of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1310, Henry IV, known as Henry the Faithful, became the new duke of Silesia and much of Greater Poland following the death of his father, Henry III, Duke of Głogów. This succession was part of a broader division of territories among Henry III's sons.
events.name: Henry IV becomes Duke of Silesia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Woplauken was fought between the Teutonic Knights and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, resulting in a victory for the Knights. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region during the early 14th century.
events.name: Battle of Woplauken

events.enhanced_description: On an unspecified date in 1311, Matthew III Csák was excommunicated by Gentile Portino da Montefiore, a Roman Catholic Cardinal sent by Pope Clement V, shortly after beginning his siege of Buda. This act reflected the intertwining of religious authority and political power during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Excommunication of Matthew III Csák

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1311, Henry VII, the future Holy Roman Emperor, was crowned King of Italy in Milan using a mock-up of the Iron Crown of Lombardy. This event was met with resistance from the Tuscan Guelphs, who opposed Henry's rule.
events.name: Coronation of Henry VII of Italy

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1311, German forces under Baldwin of Luxembourg crushed the Italian Guelph troops led by Guido della Torre during the Milan Uprising. The swift cavalry charge by the Teutonic Knights resulted in a decisive victory for the German forces.
events.name: Milan Uprising

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Halmyros, fought on March 15, 1311, marked a significant victory for the mercenaries of the Catalan Company against the Latin forces led by Walter V. Following this battle, the Catalans took control of the Duchy of Athens, establishing their rule over Attica and Boeotia until the 1380s.
events.name: The Battle of Halmyros

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1311, King Ferdinand IV of Castile granted new privileges to the Catholic Church during an assembly in Palencia. This event was part of Ferdinand's broader efforts to consolidate power and maintain the support of the Church amidst political challenges.
events.name: Privileges granted to the Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1311, Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan was proclaimed as the Mongol Emperor Renzong of the Yuan Dynasty in China, following the death of his brother Külüg Khan. This transition marked a significant moment in the Mongol Empire's history, influencing the political landscape of Asia.
events.name: Proclamation of Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, the siege of Cremona was lifted after the arrival of Scaramuccia da Forlì, ending the conflict between the condottieri troops led by Francesco Piccinino and Luigi dal Verme. This event reflected the volatile nature of Italian city-states during the Renaissance.
events.name: Siege of Cremona

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1311, Pope Clement V officially excused King Philip IV of France from any condemnation related to the late Pope Boniface VIII's alleged heresies. This decision was made in the context of the Council of Vienne, which sought to address various ecclesiastical issues.
events.name: Papal Excusal of King Philip IV

events.enhanced_description: The Ocho era began in Japan on May 17, 1311, marking a new period in the historical timeline of the country. This era is characterized by significant cultural and political developments.
events.name: Beginning of the Ocho Era

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1311, Sancho the Peaceful ascended to the throne as the King of Majorca following the death of his father, King Jaume II. His reign marked a continuation of the dynastic rule over the Balearic Islands.
events.name: Sancho the Peaceful becomes King of Majorca

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1311, the painting Maestà, a masterwork by the Italian artist Duccio di Buoninsegna, was unveiled at the Siena Cathedral. This artwork is considered a pivotal piece in the history of Italian art, showcasing the transition to the Renaissance style.
events.name: Unveiling of Maestà

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1311, Boleslaw III the Wasteful, Duke of Wrocław, renounced his claims to the throne of the Kingdom of Poland. This decision was part of the ongoing political struggles within the region.
events.name: Boleslaw III the Wasteful renounces claims

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1311, Matthew III Csák, the Palatine of Hungary, attempted to expand his territory by pillaging the area around Buda, which is now part of Budapest. This act of aggression was part of the broader conflicts within the kingdom.
events.name: Matthew III Csák's pillaging near Buda

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1311, Bolad, who had served as the Mongol Empire's representative in the Middle East, was appointed as the Duke of Ze by the Mongol Emperor Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan. This appointment highlighted the Mongol Empire's administrative structure and its influence across regions.
events.name: Bolad appointed Duke of Ze

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1311, Matteo I Visconti was restored to rule over the Duchy of Milan after purchasing the title of imperial vicar from King Henry VII. This event marked a significant moment in the power dynamics of northern Italy.
events.name: Matteo I Visconti restored to rule

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1311, a fleet of Marinid ships arrived at Algeciras, sent by Sultan Abu Sa'id Uthman II of Morocco. This mission aimed to restore the Muslim presence in the region, reflecting the ongoing conflicts between Christian and Muslim powers in medieval Spain.
events.name: Marinid fleet arrives at Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1311, Pietro Gradenigo, the Doge of the Republic of Venice, died after a 22-year reign. Following his death, Marino Zorzi was elected by the Venetian nobles to succeed him, marking a transition in the leadership of the republic.
events.name: Death of Pietro Gradenigo

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1311, the Parliament of England presented the Ordinances of 1311 to King Edward II, which effectively substituted the 21 Lord Ordainers for the King as the governing body of the country. This marked a significant shift in the balance of power within the English monarchy.
events.name: Presentation of the Ordinances of 1311

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1311, Amadeus Aba, an oligarch in the northeastern part of the Kingdom of Hungary, was assassinated by rebels at the south gate of Košice. This event underscored the political turmoil and power struggles within the region.
events.name: Assassination of Amadeus Aba

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1311, after a four-month siege, Guelph rebels in the Italian city of Brescia surrendered to Cangrande I della Scala, who was an officer of King Henry VII. This event was part of the broader conflicts between Guelphs and Ghibellines in Italy.
events.name: Surrender of Guelph rebels in Brescia

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1311, peace was restored in northeastern Hungary as envoys of King Charles I mediated an agreement between the rebels at Košice and the two sons of the late Amadeus Aba. This resolution was crucial for stabilizing the region after a period of unrest.
events.name: Peace restored in northeastern Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1311, the Ordinances of 1311 were published in England by King Edward II, which restricted the powers of the monarchy. This event was a significant step towards the development of parliamentary governance in England.

image.caption: Heraldic coat of arms of the English kings.
image.credit: Sodacan — Own work
image.date_qualification: A modern heraldic depiction associated with English kings, not an image of the 1311 publication. The saved image date is 2010-08-26.

events.name: Publication of the Ordinances of 1311

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1311, Pope Clement V convened the 15th Ecumenical Council at Vienne, France, attended by numerous cardinals and bishops. The council's agenda included the dissolution of the Knights Templar, marking a pivotal moment in church history.
events.name: Council of Vienne

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1311, King Ferdinand IV of Castile signed the Concord of Palencia with the principal magnates of his kingdom, promising to respect their customs and privileges. This agreement was crucial for maintaining stability and support among the nobility.
events.name: Concord of Palencia

events.enhanced_description: Eight days after the signing of the Concord of Palencia, John of Castile breaks his promise to his nephew Ferdinand IV by forming an alliance with Juan Núñez II de Lara, which escalates tensions within the region.
events.name: John of Castile violates promise to Ferdinand IV

events.enhanced_description: Munenobu Hojo is appointed as the regent for the Kamakura Shogunate, marking a significant moment in the political landscape of feudal Japan as the Hojo clan continues to exert influence over the shogunate.
events.name: Munenobu Hojo becomes regent for the Kamakura Shogunate

events.enhanced_description: Pope Clement V appoints Jens Grand, the Danish-born Prince-Archbishop of Bremen, to mediate a dispute between the Archbishopric of Riga and the Teutonic Prussia, reflecting the Pope's influence in regional conflicts.
events.name: Pope Clement V appoints Jens Grand as arbiter

events.enhanced_description: Alboino I della Scala, the Lord of Verona, passes away, leading to his brother Cangrande taking over the lordship, which significantly impacts the political dynamics of the region.
events.name: Death of Alboino I della Scala

events.enhanced_description: Al-Mahdi Muhammad bin al-Mutahhar leads the Zaidi troops to victory against the Sunni Rasulid sultanate in the Sheref district of Yemen, resulting in a ten-year ceasefire agreement.
events.name: Victory of Al-Mahdi Muhammad in Yemen

events.enhanced_description: In early 1312, King Ferdinand IV of Castile left his palace in Ávila for the last time, placing his son, Prince Alfonso, in charge. He traveled to Toledo and then to the province of Jaén to join his younger brother, marking the final journey of his reign.
events.name: King Ferdinand IV of Castile's Last Journey

events.enhanced_description: Piers Gaveston secretly returns from exile and reunites with King Edward II at Knaresborough Castle, where they plan to seek assistance from King Robert the Bruce of Scotland.
events.name: Piers Gaveston reunites with Edward II

events.enhanced_description: Dungal MacDouall surrenders Dumfries Castle to the forces of King Robert the Bruce, despite his previous involvement in the murder of Bruce's brothers, and is allowed to go into exile.

locations.name: Dumfries Castle, Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland

events.name: Dungal MacDouall surrenders Dumfries Castle

events.enhanced_description: Öljaitü, the ruler of the Ilkhanate, conducts a purge of corrupt officials, resulting in the arrest and execution of his vizier Sa'd al-Din Savaji, reflecting the internal strife within the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Öljaitü's purge of corrupt officials

events.enhanced_description: The division of Greater Poland is executed by the sons of Henry III, Duke of Silesia-Glogau, resulting in a split of territories among the heirs, which shapes the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Division of Greater Poland

events.enhanced_description: Beatrice, Countess of Montfort, passes away, and her daughter Yolande of Dreux succeeds her, continuing the lineage of noble rule in Montfort.
events.name: Death of Beatrice, Countess of Montfort

events.enhanced_description: Under pressure from King Philip IV of France, Pope Clement V officially disbands the Knights Templar during the Council of Vienne, redistributing their assets to the Knights Hospitaller and marking a significant shift in medieval power dynamics.
events.name: Pope Clement V disbands the Knights Templar

events.enhanced_description: During the Council of Vienne, a future Christian Crusade against a Muslim nation is approved, although disagreements arise over its target, ultimately leading to the crusade never materializing.
events.name: Council of Vienne approves future Crusade

events.enhanced_description: Archbishop Pierre de Savoie signs a treaty with King Philip IV of France, effectively ending the threat of a takeover of the sovereign Archdiocese of Lyon, granting Philip authority over local courts.
events.name: Treaty signed by Archbishop Pierre de Savoie

events.enhanced_description: Frederick I, Margrave of Meissen, signs the Treaty of Tangermünde after being captured by Waldemar the Great of Brandenburg, ceding territory and paying a substantial sum, reshaping regional power dynamics.
events.name: Treaty of Tangermünde signed

events.enhanced_description: Mladen II Šubić of Bribir ascends to the position of Ban of Croatia following the death of his father, Paul I Šubić, continuing the family's influence in Croatian politics.
events.name: Mladen II Šubić becomes Ban of Croatia

events.enhanced_description: Pope Clement V issues the papal bull Ad providam, ordering the confiscation of all property belonging to the Knights Templar, further consolidating the Church's power and diminishing the Templars' influence.
events.name: Pope Clement V orders confiscation of Knights Templar property

events.enhanced_description: While in Newcastle upon Tyne, Edward II and Piers Gaveston receive news of an approaching English force led by Henry Percy and Robert Clifford, prompting their escape to Scarborough Castle.

locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, Tyne and Wear, England

events.name: Edward II and Piers Gaveston alerted to approaching forces

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Vienne, convened by Pope Clement V, concludes after nearly seven months, during which significant decisions regarding the Knights Templar and a future crusade were made.
events.name: Council of Vienne closes

events.enhanced_description: Frederick IV ascends to the title of Duke of Lorraine following the death of his father, Theobald II, marking a continuation of the ducal lineage in the region.
events.name: Frederick IV becomes Duke of Lorraine

events.enhanced_description: Scarborough Castle is captured by English forces led by Aymer de Valence after a two-week siege, resulting in the surrender of Piers Gaveston, who is promised safety.
events.name: Capture of Scarborough Castle

events.enhanced_description: King Ferdinand IV of Castile's forces, led by Peter of Castile, defeat the rebel Granadan Governor Abu Said Faraj in a battle, allowing Faraj to retain his position while resuming tribute payments.
events.name: Battle against rebel Granadan Governor

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Rozgony, Hungarian forces led by King Charles I defeat the family of Palatine Amadeus Aba, securing Charles' power base in Hungary and diminishing resistance to his rule.
events.name: Battle of Rozgony

events.enhanced_description: Piers Gaveston is executed at Blacklow Hill after being taken hostage by Guy de Beauchamp, 10th Earl of Warwick, following a tumultuous period of political strife in England.
events.name: Execution of Piers Gaveston

events.enhanced_description: Henry VII is crowned emperor of the Holy Roman Empire in the Lateran Palace, as St. Peter's Basilica is occupied by hostile Romans, highlighting the political tensions of the era.
events.name: Henry VII crowned emperor of the Holy Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Hirotoki Hojo is appointed as the regent for the Kamakura Shogunate, continuing the legacy of the Hojo clan in the governance of feudal Japan.
events.name: Hirotoki Hojo becomes regent for the Kamakura Shogunate

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1312, Francesco I Pico, Lord of Mirandola, was captured by Guelph rebels in Baggiovara while returning home after being invested as imperial vicar by Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII. Pico was imprisoned for nine months before being released to resume his lordship.
events.name: Capture of Francesco I Pico

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1312, Giovanni Soranzo was elected as the new Doge of Venice, just ten days after the death of his predecessor, Marino Zorzi. Soranzo would go on to serve as Doge for the next 18 years, influencing the Republic's political landscape.
events.name: Election of Giovanni Soranzo as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1312, Jean III, known as 'John the Good', ascended to the title of Duke of Brittany following the death of his father, Arthur II. His reign would be marked by efforts to strengthen the duchy's independence.
events.name: Jean III becomes Duke of Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1312, King Ferdinand IV of Castile died after a 17-year reign. He was succeeded by his one-year-old son, Alfonso XI, with his mother, Queen Constance, serving as regent during his minority.
events.name: Death of King Ferdinand IV of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1312, the Charter of Kortenberg was signed, which is considered one of the earliest constitutions in Europe, allowing for democratic decision-making within the feudal system. This document marked a significant step towards governance reform in the region.
events.name: Signing of the Charter of Kortenberg

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1312, Özbeg Khan, the Mongol ruler of much of Russia, demanded that Öljaitü, the Middle Eastern Mongol ruler, cede the territory of Azerbaijan, which is part of modern-day Iran. This demand highlighted the ongoing power struggles within the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Özbeg Khan's Demand for Azerbaijan

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1312, Henry VII, Holy Roman Emperor, abandoned his campaign against Florence, a significant event in the context of the political struggles in Italy during this period. His withdrawal marked a turning point in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Henry VII Abandons Campaign Against Florence

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1312, Otto III, Duke of Lower Bavaria and former King of Hungary, died in his capital of Landshut. His death left behind minor heirs, creating a power vacuum in the region.
events.name: Death of Otto III, Duke of Lower Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1312, Prince Edward, the future King Edward III of England, was born at Windsor Castle, four years after the marriage of his parents, King Edward II and Queen Isabella. He would later ascend to the throne at the age of 14 after his father's death.
events.name: Birth of Edward III of England

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1312, Michael II, the Syrian Orthodox patriarch of Antioch, passed away after serving for 20 years. His death marked a significant transition in the leadership of the Syrian Orthodox Church.
events.name: Death of Michael II, Patriarch of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1312, John Hotham was appointed as the new Chancellor of the Exchequer in England by King Edward II. He would serve in this capacity for three and a half years, overseeing the kingdom's finances during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Appointment of John Hotham as Chancellor of the Exchequer

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1312, Henry II the Lion, ruler of Mecklenburg, successfully conquered the Lordship of Rostock, which was then a protectorate of King Eric VI Menved of Denmark. This conquest solidified Henry's power in the region.
events.name: Conquest of the Lordship of Rostock

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1312, Pope Clement V elevated nine French bishops to the position of Roman Catholic cardinals in Avignon. This act was significant in the context of the papacy's influence in France and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Elevation of Bishops to Cardinals by Pope Clement V

events.enhanced_description: In 1313, Tran Anh Tong, the emperor of Annam (Northern Vietnam), occupied Champa (Southern Vietnam) and established the Cham royal dynasty as puppet rulers. This event marked a significant expansion of Annam's influence over the region.
events.name: Tran Anh Tong Occupies Champa

events.enhanced_description: In 1313, Wang Zhen, a Chinese agronomist and government official, published the 'Nong Shu' (Book of Agriculture), which detailed agricultural practices and innovations. This work is significant for its contributions to agricultural science and technology in China.
events.name: Wang Zhen Publishes the Nong Shu

events.enhanced_description: In 1313, King Stefan Milutin, one of the most powerful rulers of Serbia, founded the Banjska Monastery, which became an important religious and cultural site in the region. The monastery reflects the architectural and artistic achievements of the Serbian medieval period.
events.name: Foundation of Banjska Monastery

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1313, King Robert the Bruce of Scotland recaptured Perth Castle from the English and ordered its destruction to prevent it from being used as a garrison again. This act was part of his broader campaign to secure Scottish independence.
events.name: Recapture of Perth Castle by Robert the Bruce

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1313, William de Sancto Claro, the Bishop of Dunkeld, was issued a safe conduct pass by King Edward II of England to return to Scotland from Rome. This reflects the complex political relations between England and Scotland during this period.
events.name: Safe Conduct Pass for William de Sancto Claro

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1313, King Thihathu proclaimed the establishment of the Pinya Kingdom in what is now the Mandalay Region of Myanmar, separating it from the Myinsaing Kingdom. This marked a significant political shift in the region.
events.name: Proclamation of the Pinya Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1313, Francesco da Barberino of Tuscany received a doctorate in both civil law and canonical law through a papal bull issued by Pope Clement V. This recognition highlighted the importance of legal scholarship during this period.
events.name: Francesco da Barberino Receives Doctorate

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1313, the Duchy of Masovia was divided among the three sons of Boleslaw II upon his death. Siemowit II established the Duchy of Rawa with its capital at Rawa Mazowiecka, while Trojden received Czersk and Wenceslaus received Płock.
events.name: Division of the Duchy of Masovia

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1313, the French ship Ste Marie was shipwrecked at Chale Bay on the Isle of Wight. Local residents looted the ship's cargo, leading to the construction of St Catherine's Oratory by the Lord of Chale as an act of penance.
events.name: Shipwreck of the Ste Marie

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1313, Pope Celestine V was canonized as a Roman Catholic saint, seventeen years after his death in prison in Ferentino. His canonization reflected the Church's recognition of his spiritual legacy.
events.name: Canonization of Pope Celestine V

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1313, Veera Virupaksha Ballala, the son and heir of Emperor Veera Ballala III of the Hoysala Empire, returned to Halebidu after two years as a hostage in Delhi. His return marked a significant moment in the Hoysala dynasty's history.
events.name: Return of Veera Virupaksha Ballala to Halebidu

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1313, Bolko II of Opole and his brother Albert of Strzelce became the new rulers of Opole and Upper Silesia following the death of their father, Bolko I. This transition marked a continuation of their family's influence in the region.
events.name: New Rulers of Opole and Upper Silesia

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1313, King Robert the Bruce of Scotland led an invasion of the Isle of Man, landing at Ramsey with a fleet of ships. He captured the island within five days, facing minimal resistance from the local lord.
events.name: Robert the Bruce's Invasion of the Isle of Man

events.enhanced_description: In 1313, Thomas Cobham was elected Archbishop of Canterbury by his peers, but King Edward II intervened, seeking to overturn the election by appealing to Pope Clement V. The Pope ultimately sided with the king, installing Walter Reynolds as the new archbishop on October 1, 1313.
events.name: Election of Thomas Cobham as Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: Castle Rushen, located on the Isle of Man, surrendered to King Robert the Bruce of Scotland after a three-week siege in June 1313. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between Scotland and England during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Surrender of Castle Rushen

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1313, Pope Clement V declared Naples to be under papal protection, recognizing King Robert the Wise of Naples as the 'Senator of Rome.' This declaration solidified the Pope's influence in Italian politics during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Papal Protection of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1313, a peace agreement was reached in Bavaria between Rudolf I, Duke of Bavaria, and his brother Louis the Bavarian. Rudolf retained control of the Electoral Palatinate while supporting Louis's election as the next Holy Roman Emperor.
events.name: Peace between Rudolf I and Louis the Bavarian

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1313, Sir Philip Mowbray from the English garrison at Stirling Castle proposed a truce to Edward Bruce, brother of King Robert the Bruce of Scotland, after a prolonged siege. The truce was controversial and ultimately angered Robert the Bruce, who felt it undermined Scottish efforts for independence.
events.name: Truce Proposal at Stirling Castle

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1313, Catherine of Valois-Courtenay, the Latin Empress of Constantinople, broke her engagement to Hugh V, Duke of Burgundy, to marry Philip I, Prince of Taranto. This complex marital arrangement involved significant political maneuvering among European nobility.
events.name: Marital Pact of Catherine of Valois-Courtenay

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1313, Emperor Henry VII initiated a military campaign against King Robert of Naples, known as 'Robert the Wise.' Despite having a sizable army, Henry's allies were reluctant to support him, complicating his efforts.
events.name: Henry VII's Campaign Against Robert of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1313, in Horsens, Denmark, Eric of Jutland reached a settlement with King Eric VI Menved, receiving the Duchy of Schleswig in exchange for renouncing claims to Langeland. This agreement was significant in the context of Danish territorial politics.
events.name: Settlement in Horsens, Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1313, Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII died of malaria in Buonconvento, Tuscany, shortly after contracting the disease during a siege of Siena. His death led to a power struggle among his relatives, particularly between Louis of Bavaria and Frederick the Fair.
events.name: Death of Henry VII

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1313, the English Parliament was convened for the fourth time in less than a year, following three unsuccessful attempts to gather members. King Edward II successfully persuaded Parliament to pass a tax bill to fund military campaigns against Scotland.
events.name: English Parliament Session

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1313, King Robert the Bruce delivered an ultimatum to Scottish nobles in Dundee, demanding that those who had not yet sworn fealty to him do so within a year or risk losing their estates. This move was part of Bruce's efforts to consolidate power in Scotland.
events.name: Robert the Bruce's Ultimatum

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1313, the Battle of Gammelsdorf took place, where Louis IV the Bavarian's forces defeated his cousin Frederick the Fair, who was supported by Leopold I of Austria. Despite the victory, Louis chose not to pursue Frederick's retreating army, which had significant implications for the power dynamics within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Gammelsdorf

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1313, Queen Constance of Portugal, the mother of the young King Alfonso XI, passed away. Following her death, a regency was established, with her mother-in-law and other relatives taking charge of the young king's affairs.
events.name: Death of Queen Constance of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1313, King Edward II of England issued a summons for eight earls and 87 barons to muster their troops at Berwick-upon-Tweed by June 10, 1314, in preparation for an invasion of Scotland. This call to arms was part of Edward's ongoing efforts to regain control over Scotland.
events.name: Edward II's Summons for Invasion of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In March 1314, following revelations of adultery involving his sons' wives, King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of Margaret of Burgundy and others implicated in the scandal. This event, known as the Tour de Nesle Affair, had significant political ramifications for the French royal family.
events.name: Tour de Nesle Affair

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1314, Queen Oljath of Georgia married Qara Sonqur, the Governor of Maragheh, in a politically motivated union that included a substantial dowry. This marriage was part of the intricate alliances among the ruling families of the region.
events.name: Marriage of Queen Oljath

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1314, Muhammad III of Granada was murdered by drowning on the orders of his brother, Sultan Nasr. This act of fratricide led to a swift power shift within the Emirate of Granada.
events.name: Murder of Muhammad III of Granada

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1314, in what is now Spain, Nasr ibn Muhammad was forced to abdicate as the ruler of the Emirate of Granada by his nephew, Abu'l-Walid Ismail I. The proclamation took place at the Alhambra, a significant cultural and historical site.
events.name: Abdication of Nasr ibn Muhammad

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1314, Walter de Godeton, Lord of Chale, was convicted of theft related to the plundering of wine from a shipwreck on the Isle of Wight. He was fined 287 marks, reflecting the legal and social issues of the time.
events.name: Conviction of Walter de Godeton

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1314, Jacques de Molay, the Grand Master of the Knights Templar, was executed by burning at the stake on the orders of King Philip IV of France. As he faced his death, he proclaimed the innocence of the Templar Order and foretold the demise of both Philip and Pope Clement V within the year.

locations.name: Île de la Cité, Paris, France

events.name: Execution of Jacques de Molay

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1314, Exeter College was founded in Oxford by Bishop Walter de Stapledon as a school to educate clergy. This institution has since become one of the prominent colleges within the University of Oxford.
events.name: Foundation of Exeter College

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1314, Philip and Walter de Aunay were executed for their involvement in the adultery scandal with the daughters-in-law of King Philip IV of France. Their brutal execution followed torture at the Place du Grand Martroy in Pontoise, highlighting the severe consequences of political intrigue in the royal court.
events.name: Execution of Philip and Walter de Aunay

events.enhanced_description: Pope Clement V, the first pope to reside in Avignon, France, died in Roquemaure after a pontificate marked by the centralization of the Catholic Church's administration. His death led to a significant power vacuum and the subsequent papal conclave to elect his successor.
events.name: Pope Clement V dies after a 9-year pontificate at Roquemaure

events.enhanced_description: The papal conclave to elect a successor to Pope Clement V commenced at Carpentras Cathedral, attended by 23 cardinals. The conclave was marked by factional divisions and would ultimately lead to a prolonged vacancy of the papacy.
events.name: The papal conclave to elect a successor to Pope Clement V begins

events.enhanced_description: In a significant religious event, over 50 Fraticelli spiritualists of the Franciscan order were excommunicated by the Archbishop of Genoa for their refusal to return to obedience to the Pope. This act highlighted the tensions within the Church during this period.
events.name: Excommunication of Fraticelli spiritualists in Italy

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1314, King Edward II of England led his forces from Berwick-upon-Tweed towards Stirling Castle, crossing the River Tweed and navigating through the Merse of Berwickshire. This movement was part of the lead-up to the pivotal Battle of Bannockburn.

image.caption: A manuscript depiction of the Battle of Bannockburn from Walter Bower’s Scotichronicon.
