image.date_qualification: Retrospective depiction made in the 1440s, about 130 years after the battle; it does not depict Edward II’s departure from Berwick as a contemporary event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: English forces led by King Edward II leave Berwick-upon-Tweed

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1314, English forces, under King Edward II, advanced towards Edinburgh, waiting for a substantial supply train to catch up. This strategic pause was crucial before their planned march to Stirling Castle.
events.name: English forces march to the environs of Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1314, English forces approached Scottish positions at Torwood, where they faced fierce resistance. Notably, King Robert the Bruce killed Henry de Bohun in a duel, showcasing the intense personal and military stakes of the conflict.
events.name: English forces approach Scottish positions at Torwood

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Bannockburn, fought on June 24, 1314, saw Scottish forces led by Robert the Bruce decisively defeat the English army. The Scottish schiltrons effectively repulsed English cavalry, leading to a rout of Edward II's forces.
events.name: Battle of Bannockburn

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1314, after the defeat at Bannockburn, Edward II arrived at Dunbar Castle and took a ship to Bamburgh in Northumberland. This marked his retreat following a catastrophic loss in the Scottish campaign.
events.name: Edward II arrives at Dunbar Castle

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1314, the Italian cardinals participating in the papal conclave walked out after enduring harassment from supporters of a French candidate. This event led to a significant disruption in the election of the new pope.
events.name: Italian cardinals walk out of the papal conclave

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1314, Scottish raiders under Edward Bruce plundered the northeastern counties in the Pennines but were confronted by English forces led by Andrew Harclay at Stainmore. This skirmish was part of the ongoing conflicts between Scotland and England.
events.name: Scottish raiders led by Edward Bruce plunder the Pennines

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1314, King Haakon V Magnusson moved his capital from Bergen to Oslo, where he initiated the construction of Akershus Fortress. This strategic relocation marked a significant shift in the governance of Norway.
events.name: King Haakon V Magnusson of Norway moves his capital

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1314, King Edward II of England released Elizabeth de Burgh, wife of Robert the Bruce, along with his sister and daughter, in exchange for captured English nobles. This exchange was part of the ongoing political maneuvering during the Scottish Wars of Independence.
events.name: Edward II releases Elizabeth de Burgh and others

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1314, Frederick the Fair of the House of Habsburg was elected King of the Romans at Sachsenhausen and subsequently crowned at Bonn Minster. His election was part of the ongoing power struggles within the Holy Roman Empire.

locations.name: Sachsenhausen, Frankfurt am Main, Hesse, Germany
Bonn Minster, Bonn, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany

events.name: Frederick the Fair elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1314, Louis X ascended to the throne of France following the death of his father, King Philip IV, in a hunting accident at Fontainebleau. His reign began amidst significant political challenges.
events.name: Louis X becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: The state funeral and burial of King Philip IV took place on December 3, 1314, at the Basilica of Saint-Denis, marking the end of a significant reign characterized by territorial expansion and conflict.

image.caption: Miniature of Philip IV, based on an image engraved on the king’s great seal.
image.credit: anonymous — Not necessary, PD by age.
image.date_qualification: Sixteenth-century retrospective depiction based on an image engraved on Philip IV’s great seal; not a contemporary image of his funeral or burial.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: State funeral and burial of King Philip IV

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1314, the Margraviate of Brandenburg renounced all claims to the region around Loitz in favor of the Principality of Rügen in Denmark, resolving a long-standing territorial dispute.
events.name: Brandenburg–Pomeranian conflict resolution

events.enhanced_description: Enguerrand de Marigny, the former Chief Minister of France, is executed at the Gibbet of Montfaucon on the orders of King Louis X. His death signifies the volatile nature of political power in France during this era.
events.name: Death of Enguerrand de Marigny

events.enhanced_description: In early 1315, Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy arrived in Mecca with an Egyptian army, planning to oust Emir Humaydah ibn Abi Numayy. This military campaign involved looting Humaydah's castle and capturing his son, although Humaydah managed to escape.
events.name: Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy arrives at Mecca

events.enhanced_description: In a significant power struggle, Humaydah ibn Abi Numayy defeats his brother Abu al-Ghayth in a battle near Mecca. Following his defeat, Abu al-Ghayth is captured and executed on the orders of Humaydah, marking a pivotal moment in the leadership of the Emirate of Mecca.
events.name: Battle of Mecca

events.enhanced_description: The Al-Shamah Mosque is completed in Gaza City, commissioned by the Mamluk Sultanate Governor Sanjar al-Jawli. This mosque stands as a testament to the architectural and cultural achievements of the Mamluk period in the region.
events.name: Completion of Al-Shamah Mosque

events.enhanced_description: In a significant religious appointment, Kunga Lotro Gyaltsen is installed as the Imperial Preceptor of Tibetan Buddhists by the Mongol Emperor Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan. This event underscores the Mongol Empire's influence over Tibetan Buddhism and its integration into the broader imperial structure.
events.name: Installation of Kunga Lotro Gyaltsen

events.enhanced_description: The Scottish parliament convenes in Ayr, where Edward Bruce is proclaimed the legal heir to the throne, ensuring the continuity of the Bruce lineage should his brother, King Robert the Bruce, die. This event solidifies the political landscape of Scotland during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Proclamation of Edward Bruce as Heir

events.enhanced_description: The Mamluk Sultanate army invades the Christian outpost of Malatya, looting the city and asserting their military dominance in the region. This invasion reflects the ongoing conflicts between Muslim and Christian territories during the period.
events.name: Invasion of Malatya

events.enhanced_description: Margaret of Burgundy, the Queen consort of France, dies in Château Gaillard prison after being convicted of adultery. Her death marks a tragic end to her tumultuous life and highlights the political intrigues of the French monarchy during this period.
events.name: Death of Margaret of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: Odo IV ascends to the title of Duke of Burgundy following the death of his brother, Hugh V. This transition in leadership is significant for the political landscape of France, particularly in the context of regional power dynamics.
events.name: Odo IV Becomes Duke of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: King Edward II of England lands at Larne with over 6,000 troops to counter the Scottish invasion led by Edward Bruce. This military action is part of the larger conflict between England and Scotland during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Edward II Lands in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: King James II of Aragon is married by proxy to Marie of Lusignan in a ceremony held in Nicosia. This strategic marriage is significant for the political alliances between Aragon and Cyprus during the medieval period.
events.name: Proxy Marriage of James II of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: King Louis X of France abolishes serfdom in the Kingdom of France, a landmark decision that impacts the feudal structure of French society. This act is seen as a progressive move towards greater social equality.
events.name: Abolition of Serfdom in France

events.enhanced_description: Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg, marries Anna of Saxe-Wittenberg, strengthening ties between noble families in Germany. This marriage is significant for the future political landscape of the region.
events.name: Marriage of Henry II of Mecklenburg

events.enhanced_description: Scottish forces led by King Robert the Bruce besiege Carlisle Castle, but the stronghold withstands the assault due to a well-organized defense by Andrew Harclay. The siege is ultimately abandoned, showcasing the resilience of English defenses during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Siege of Carlisle

events.enhanced_description: Otto II, Prince of Anhalt-Aschersleben, dies without heirs, leading to the dissolution of the principality. His death marks a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region as his assets are seized by his cousin.
events.name: Death of Otto II, Prince of Anhalt-Aschersleben

events.enhanced_description: King Louis X issues a charter allowing expelled Jews to return to France under strict conditions, reflecting the complex relationship between the monarchy and the Jewish community. This charter sets a precedent for future interactions and regulations regarding Jewish populations in France.
events.name: Charter for Expelled Jews

events.enhanced_description: King Louis X mobilizes an army along the Flemish border to enforce a grain export ban, aiming to exert control over trade and resources. This military maneuver highlights the tensions between France and Flanders during this period.

image.caption: Medieval miniature depicting Louis X in the Life of Saint Louis.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — Vie de saint Louis , BNF Gallica
image.date_qualification: A later portrait miniature, dated between 1330 and 1340; it does not depict the 1315 mobilization.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Mobilization Along the Flemish Border

events.enhanced_description: After a 10-day siege of Carlisle, King Robert of Scotland withdraws his forces, marking a strategic retreat in the ongoing conflict. This withdrawal underscores the challenges faced by the Scots in their campaign against English strongholds.
events.name: Withdrawal from Carlisle

events.enhanced_description: As the Great Famine of 1315–1317 spreads across Europe, King Edward II visits St Albans and finds food supplies critically low. This moment highlights the severe impact of climate change on agriculture and the ensuing social unrest during this period.
events.name: King Edward II Witnesses Famine

events.enhanced_description: Hōjō Mototoki is appointed as the new shogun and regent of the Kamakura shogunate following the death of Hōjō Hirotoki. This transition marks a significant moment in the governance of Japan during the Kamakura period.
events.name: Hōjō Mototoki Becomes Shogun

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand of Majorca completes the conquest of the Principality of Achaea by capturing its capital, Andravida. This conquest is part of the broader struggle for control over former crusader states in Greece.
events.name: Conquest of Achaea

events.enhanced_description: King Louis X of France marries Clementia of Hungary, strengthening political ties between France and Hungary. Following their marriage, Louis is crowned, marking a new chapter in the Capetian dynasty.
events.name: Marriage of Louis X and Clementia

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Louis X, known as 'Louis the Quarrelsome', takes place in Reims, solidifying his position as King of France. This event is significant as it follows the tumultuous reign of his father, Philip IV.
events.name: Coronation of Louis X

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Montecatini, the Pisan army, led by Uguccione della Faggiuola, defeats the allied forces of Florence and Naples. This battle is a crucial moment in the ongoing conflicts between these Italian city-states.
events.name: Battle of Montecatini

events.enhanced_description: Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy arrives at the court of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in Cairo seeking support against his brother, Humaydah ibn Abi Numayy, who has taken control of Mecca. This event highlights the political intrigue and power struggles within the region.
events.name: Arrival of Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy in Cairo

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Connor, fought on September 10, 1315, was a significant conflict during the Bruce campaign in Ireland. Scottish-Irish forces led by Edward Bruce decisively defeated the army of Richard Óg de Burgh, 2nd Earl of Ulster, leading to a rout that forced the remaining earls to flee to Carrickfergus Castle.
events.name: The Battle of Connor

events.enhanced_description: The Banastre Rebellion, which began on October 9, 1315, was an uprising by a group of English knights in Lancashire seeking revenge against Thomas of Lancaster. Following the rebellion, control of Liverpool Castle was granted to Robert de Holland, marking a shift in local power dynamics.
events.name: Banastre Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Morgarten, fought on November 15, 1315, was a pivotal conflict where the Swiss forces defeated Leopold of Austria. This victory was crucial in ensuring the independence of the Swiss Confederation from external control.
events.name: Battle of Morgarten

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1315, King James II of Aragon married Marie of Lusignan in a ceremony held in Girona, Spain. This marriage was significant for strengthening political alliances in the region.
events.name: Marriage of King James II of Aragon to Marie of Lusignan

events.enhanced_description: The Pact of Brunnen, signed on December 9, 1315, was a mutual defense agreement among the cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden in Switzerland. This pact was a strategic response to the threat of invasion by Austria, solidifying the unity of the Swiss Confederation.
figures: Leaders of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden
events.name: Pact of Brunnen

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1315, Gaston II of Foix-Béarn was appointed as the new French representative to rule the Co-principality of Andorra following the death of his father, Gaston I. This appointment marked a continuation of the Foix family's influence in the region.
events.name: Gaston II of Foix-Béarn becomes representative to Andorra

events.enhanced_description: In 1316, the Pound sterling experienced its greatest inflation in history, reaching a staggering rate of 100.04 percent, which resulted in a loss of over half its value. This economic turmoil had profound effects on the English economy and society.
events.name: The Pound sterling experiences inflation

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Alauddin Khalji of the Delhi Sultanate died on January 4, 1316, after a 19-year reign. He was succeeded by his young son, Shihabuddin Omar, with the support of the general Malik Kafur, amidst a backdrop of power struggles.
events.name: Death of Sultan Alauddin Khalji

events.enhanced_description: Llywelyn Bren led a revolt against English rule in Wales, beginning on January 28, 1316. After laying siege to Caerphilly Castle and facing an expeditionary force from Edward II, he was ultimately forced to surrender on March 18, following a six-week campaign.
events.name: Llywelyn Bren's Revolt

events.enhanced_description: Malik Kafur, who had been ruling as regent of the Delhi Sultanate for just 35 days, was assassinated on February 8, 1316, by former bodyguards of Sultan Alauddin Khalji. His death marked a significant power shift in the Sultanate.
events.name: Assassination of Malik Kafur

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Skaithmuir, fought on February 14, 1316, saw Scottish forces under James Douglas defeat an English raiding party near Coldstream. The skirmish resulted in the death of Edmond de Caillou, a notable figure in the English ranks.
events.name: Battle of Skaithmuir

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Picotin, fought on February 22, 1316, was a significant conflict where Catalan forces led by Prince Ferdinand of Majorca defeated the army of Princess Matilda of Hainaut in the Peloponnese. The battle resulted in substantial casualties for the Burgundian forces.
events.name: Battle of Picotin

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1316, Stefan Vladislav II ascended to the throne as the new King of Syrmia following the death of his father, Stefan Dragutin. This transition marked a continuation of the royal lineage in the region.
events.name: Stefan Vladislav II becomes King of Syrmia

events.enhanced_description: After leading a six-week-long revolt against English rule, Welsh rebel Llywelyn Bren surrendered to King Edward's general, Humphrey de Bohun, at Ystradfellte on March 18, 1316. This marked the end of a significant resistance movement in Wales.
events.name: Llywelyn Bren surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1316, Qutb al-Din Mubarak, the 17-year-old son of Alauddin Khalji, ascended the throne of the Delhi Sultanate. His ascension marked a new chapter in the Sultanate's history, following the tumultuous reign of his father.
events.name: Qutb al-Din Mubarak ascends the throne

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1316, Edward Bruce, brother of King Robert the Bruce of Scotland, was crowned High King of Ireland in a bid to incite rebellion among the Irish nobles against English rule. This event was pivotal in the ongoing conflict between the Irish and English forces.
events.name: Edward Bruce crowned High King of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: King Louis X of France, known as 'Louis the Quarrelsome,' died on June 5, 1316, possibly from poisoning, during a game of tennis at Vincennes. His death left his pregnant wife, Clementia of Hungary, as the widow and initiated a power struggle for regency.
events.name: Death of King Louis X of France

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Manolada, fought on July 5, 1316, saw Latin forces under Louis of Burgundy, supported by Byzantine troops, defeat the Catalan army led by Ferdinand of Majorca. The battle resulted in significant casualties, including the death of Ferdinand and the execution of John II of Nivelet.
events.name: Battle of Manolada

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1316, Hōjō Takatoki was appointed as the 14th regent of the Kamakura shogunate in Japan. His ascension marked a continuation of the Hōjō family's influence over the shogunate during a period of political instability.
events.name: Hōjō Takatoki becomes regent

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1316, Matilda of Hainaut became the sole leader of the Principality of Achaea following the death of her husband, Prince Louis of Burgundy, from poisoning. This event solidified her power in the region after a tumultuous period.
events.name: Matilda of Hainaut becomes sole leader of Achaea

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Gransee, fought on August 5, 1316, was a decisive conflict where a North German-Danish alliance led by Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg, defeated the forces of Waldemar the Great. The battle resulted in significant losses for Waldemar's army and led to subsequent peace negotiations.
events.name: Battle of Gransee

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1316, after a two-year interregnum, Jacques Duèse was elected as Pope John XXII, succeeding Pope Clement V. His election marked a significant moment in the history of the papacy, particularly during the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Election of Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Athenry, fought on August 10, 1316, was a critical engagement during the Bruce campaign in Ireland, where Norman forces managed to retain control at a significant cost, with over 5,000 casualties. This battle underscored the ongoing conflict between the Irish and Norman settlers.
events.name: Second Battle of Athenry

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1316, brothers Albert II and Waldemar I became the joint rulers of the Principality of Anhalt-Zerbst following the death of their father, Prince Albert I. This transition marked a continuation of the ruling lineage in the region.
events.name: Joint rule of Albert II and Waldemar I

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1316, Jacques Deuze was crowned Pope John XXII in Avignon, marking the beginning of his papacy, which would last until 1334. His election came during a tumultuous period for the Catholic Church, as the papacy was situated in Avignon rather than Rome.
events.name: The coronation of Jacques Deuze as Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1316, Birger, King of Sweden, issued a letter of protection for the women of the Karelian people, a significant act that is noted as the oldest document in the National Archives of Sweden. This letter reflects the king's commitment to safeguarding the rights of vulnerable populations within his realm.
events.name: Birger, King of Sweden, issues a letter of protection

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1316, a papal court in Avignon, presided over by Cardinal Berengar Fredol the Elder, confirmed the election of Juan Fernández as Bishop of León, dismissing a challenge from Juan García. This ruling was significant as it underscored the authority of the papacy in ecclesiastical appointments.
events.name: Papal court rules on Bishop of León election

events.enhanced_description: John of the House of Capet was born on November 16, 1316, just four months after the death of his father, King Louis X of France. Although he became King John I of France at birth, he lived only four days before his death on November 20.

image.caption: Effigy of John I the Posthumous at the Basilica of Saint-Denis.
image.credit: Phidelorme — Own work
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the king’s tomb effigy at Saint-Denis, not a depiction of his birth; the photograph is dated 2013-07-05.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Birth of John I of France

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his infant nephew John I on November 20, 1316, Philip the Tall ascended to the throne as King Philip V of France. His coronation marked a significant moment in French history, as it established the precedence of male succession over female heirs.
events.name: Philip the Tall becomes King Philip V of France

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1316, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan succeeded his father Öljaitü as the new ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate, a significant Mongol state in the Middle East. His reign would be marked by continued challenges in maintaining the unity of the Ilkhanate.
events.name: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan becomes ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1317, a Hungarian document first mentioned Basarab I as the leader of Wallachia, marking the recognition of his rule. Historians estimate he had been on the throne since around 1310, establishing the foundation for the House of Basarab.
events.name: First mention of Basarab I as leader of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: The Great Famine of 1315–1317 came to an end in 1317, as crop harvests began to return to normal. However, the effects of the famine lingered, with many communities still suffering from the aftermath of malnutrition and disease.
events.name: End of the Great Famine of 1315–1317

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1317, Philip the Tall was hastily crowned King Philip V of France in Reims, following the death of his nephew John I. His ascension sparked protests among supporters of Joan II of Navarre, highlighting the contentious nature of succession laws in France.
events.name: Philip the Tall crowned King Philip V of France

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1317, Manuel Pessanha of Genoa was appointed as the first Chief Admiral of Portugal by King Denis. He was tasked with organizing a permanent navy for the kingdom, a crucial step in establishing Portugal's maritime power.
events.name: Manuel Pessanha appointed Chief Admiral of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1317, an earthquake estimated at 7.0 magnitude struck Kyoto, Japan, causing significant damage and loss of life. An aftershock of 6.0 magnitude followed on February 22, compounding the devastation.
events.name: Earthquake strikes Kyoto

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1317, Pope John XXII admonished King Frederick III of Sicily to take severe measures against the Fraticelli, a group of Spiritual Franciscans who had broken away from the Roman Catholic Church. This intervention highlighted the ongoing tensions between the papacy and dissident religious movements.
events.name: Pope John XXII admonishes King Frederick III of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1317, Waldemar the Great became the sole ruler of the reunited Margraviate of Brandenburg following the death of his cousin John V. This consolidation of power was significant for the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Waldemar the Great becomes sole ruler of Brandenburg

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1317, Hugues Géraud, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Cahors, was arrested for plotting to assassinate Pope John XXII using poisoned bread. His trial and subsequent execution for witchcraft and sacrilege underscored the intense political and religious strife of the period.
events.name: Hugues Géraud arrested for plotting against Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1317, Pope John XXII asserted the papacy's imperial rights of governance in Italy, a bold move that aimed to strengthen the Church's influence in the region. He also issued the decretal Spondent Pariter, which prohibited alchemy.
events.name: Pope John XXII claims imperial rights in Italy

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1317, Pope John XXII canonized Louis of Toulouse as a saint in the Roman Catholic Church, recognizing his contributions to the faith and his virtuous life. This act was part of the Pope's broader efforts to promote sanctity and piety within the Church.
events.name: Louis of Toulouse canonized by Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1317, the Republic of Massa resumed its coinage, an important economic development facilitated by the Benzi family. This resumption of minting coins was crucial for trade and commerce in the region.
events.name: Coinage resumed in the Republic of Massa

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1317, Pope John XXII ordered the Spiritual Franciscans, including the priest Bernard Délicieux, to come to Avignon to answer for their disobedience. This event marked a significant confrontation between the papacy and the reformist factions within the Church.
events.name: John XXII orders Spiritual Franciscans to Avignon

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1317, King Edward II of England restored the dower lands that had been surrendered by Margaret de Clare, the widow of Piers Gaveston. This act was part of the ongoing political maneuvering following Gaveston's controversial execution.
events.name: King Edward II restores dower lands to Margaret de Clare

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1317, the first of the Spiritual Franciscans appeared before Pope John XXII in Avignon to confront their disobedience. This meeting was a pivotal moment in the tensions between the papacy and the reformist factions within the Church.
events.name: Spiritual Franciscans appear before Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1317, Cardinal Jacques de Via, Bishop of Avignon and nephew of Pope John XXII, was found dead. An investigation later concluded that he had been murdered through witchcraft, reflecting the intense political intrigue of the time.
events.name: Cardinal Jacques de Via found dead

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1317, Thawun Gyi, the monarch of the principality of Toungoo in present-day Myanmar, was assassinated by his younger brother Thawun Nge, who subsequently took his place as ruler. This act of fratricide highlights the violent power struggles common in the region's history.
events.name: Assassination of Thawun Gyi

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1317, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan was proclaimed the ruler of the Ilkhanate, the Mongol-controlled region in the Middle East. His leadership was pivotal in maintaining the Mongol influence in the region during a time of fragmentation.
events.name: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan becomes ruler of the Ilkhanate

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1317, Alexander de Bicknor was consecrated by Pope John XXII as the Archbishop of Dublin, a significant ecclesiastical appointment that would influence the religious landscape of Ireland.
events.name: Alexander de Bicknor consecrated as Archbishop of Dublin

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1317, Hugues Géraud, the Catholic Bishop of Cahors, was personally questioned by Pope John XXII regarding his involvement in a plot against the Pope. Géraud was later convicted of witchcraft and sacrilege, leading to his execution.
events.name: Hugues Géraud questioned by Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1317, English knight Gilbert Middleton initiated a rebellion against King Edward II near Rushyford in County Durham. He captured the newly elected Bishop of Durham and other notable figures, leading to a significant political crisis.
events.name: Gilbert Middleton's rebellion against King Edward II

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1317, Pope John XXII issued the papal bull Quorundam exigit, which allowed for a more lenient treatment of supporters of the Franciscan cause advocating for unconditional poverty. This decision was significant in the context of the ongoing tensions between the Church and various religious orders during the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Pope John XXII issues the bull Quorundam exigit

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1317, Sir Gilbert Middleton released Louis de Beaumont, the Bishop of Durham, and his brother Henry after receiving a ransom of 500 marks. This event highlights the political tensions and power struggles in medieval England, particularly involving the Church and nobility.
events.name: Sir Gilbert Middleton releases the Bishop of Durham

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1317, William II, the son of King Frederick III of Sicily, ascended to the title of Duke of Athens following the death of his elder brother, Manfred. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Duchy of Athens, which was a crucial political entity in medieval Greece.
events.name: William II becomes Duke of Athens

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1317, Yahballaha III, the Patriarch of the Church of the East, passed away after 26 years of leadership. His death marked a significant transition for the Eastern Orthodox Church, leading to the election of Timothy II as his successor.
events.name: Death of Yahballaha III, Patriarch of the Church of the East

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1317, the Treaty of Templin was signed, marking the end of hostilities between the Margraviate of Brandenburg and Denmark. The treaty resulted in Brandenburg ceding several territories, illustrating the shifting power dynamics in Northern Europe during this period.
events.name: Treaty of Templin

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1317, during the infamous Nyköping Banquet, King Birger Magnusson captured his brothers, Dukes Eric and Valdemar, imprisoning them in a dungeon as revenge for their earlier actions against him. This act of betrayal led to a civil war in Sweden, significantly impacting the kingdom's stability.
events.name: Nyköping Banquet

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1317, King Denis of Portugal established the Portuguese Royal Navy, comprising 20 armed galleys. This navy would go on to become one of the oldest continuously serving navies in the world, marking a significant development in maritime military power.
events.name: Creation of the Portuguese Royal Navy

events.enhanced_description: In May 1318, following the capture of Berwick-upon-Tweed, Scottish forces under King Robert the Bruce conducted raids into Yorkshire, burning towns such as Northallerton, Boroughbridge, and Knaresborough. These raids were part of the ongoing conflict between Scotland and England during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Scottish raids in Yorkshire

events.enhanced_description: Following the appointment of Guglielmo di Balaeto as rector by Pope John XXII, the citizens of Benevento revolted, seeking political autonomy. The rebellion was ultimately suppressed by papal forces.
events.name: Rebellion in Benevento

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1318, Pope John XXII issued the papal bull Gloriosam ecclesiam, excommunicating the Fraticelli, a group of Spiritual Franciscans. This action reflected the ongoing conflict between the Church and those advocating for strict adherence to the ideals of poverty and reform.
events.name: Pope John XXII issues the papal bull Gloriosam ecclesiam

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1318, Sir Gilbert Middleton was executed by hanging, drawing, and quartering after being convicted of treason for kidnapping the Bishop of Durham. His execution underscores the brutal nature of medieval justice and the political tensions of the time.
events.name: Execution of Sir Gilbert Middleton

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1318, Cangrande I della Scala, the Lord of Verona, successfully captured Padua after negotiations with the Paduan Greater Council. This event was a significant consolidation of power for Cangrande in northern Italy.

image.caption: Portrait of Cangrande I della Scala.
image.credit: Borde Carlo — http://www.artivisive.sns.it/stampeditraduzione/incisioni.php?indice=Soggetto
image.date_qualification: The image metadata dates the digital image to 2015; no date for the depicted portrait is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Cangrande I della Scala takes Padua

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1318, Henry II ascended to the title of Margrave of Brandenburg-Stendal following the death of his father, Henry Lackland. This transition marked a continuation of the ruling lineage in the region.
events.name: Henry II becomes Margrave of Brandenburg-Stendal

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1318, King Philip of France reached an agreement with the Capetian House of Burgundy regarding his claim to the crown. This agreement was pivotal in stabilizing the royal succession and addressing the claims of Joan of Burgundy.
events.name: Agreement with the Capetian House of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1318, Emperor Hanazono of Japan abdicated the throne after a nine-year reign, paving the way for his cousin Go-Daigo to ascend. This transition was significant in the context of the political struggles of the Japanese imperial family.
events.name: Emperor Hanazono abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII established the Archdiocese of Soltaniyeh, marking the introduction of the Roman Catholic hierarchy into the Ilkhanate of Persia. The Dominican missionary Francesco da Perugia was appointed as the first Archbishop, arriving with six bishops on August 1.

image.caption: Map of Soltaniyeh by Matrakçı Nasuh.
image.credit: Matrakçı Nasuh (1480–1564), circa 1550 — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: circa 1550, more than two centuries after the event dated 1318-04-01
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Creation of the Archdiocese of Soltaniyeh

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1318, Scottish forces led by James the Black successfully retook Berwick-upon-Tweed from the English. This victory was a significant setback for King Edward II and contributed to the ongoing conflicts of the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Berwick-upon-Tweed

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1318, an agreement was reached to release Dukes Valdemar and Eric, who had been imprisoned by their brother King Birger. However, upon discovering their deaths in prison, a rebellion erupted against Birger, leading to further instability in Sweden.
events.name: Release of Dukes Eric and Valdemar

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1318, the coronation ceremony of Go-Daigo as Emperor of Japan was held, marking the beginning of his reign. Go-Daigo's ascension would lead to significant political changes and conflicts in Japan.
events.name: Coronation of Go-Daigo as Emperor of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1318, four members of the Fraticelli were found guilty of heresy and executed by burning at the stake in Marseille. This event highlighted the Church's ongoing struggle against dissenting religious movements during this period.
events.name: Execution of Fraticelli members in Marseille

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1318, the Battle of Dysert O'Dea took place, where an Irish confederation defeated the Hiberno-Normans led by Richard de Clare. The battle resulted in significant casualties and marked a pivotal moment in the ongoing conflicts in Ireland.
events.name: Battle of Dysert O'Dea

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1318, John Hotham was appointed as the Lord Chancellor of England by King Edward II. This position was the highest-ranking office for a member of parliament, reflecting the political dynamics of the time.
events.name: Appointment of John Hotham as Lord Chancellor of England

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1318, Russian forces destroyed areas of Finland, including the burning of Kuusisto Castle. This event was part of the broader conflicts in the region during the early 14th century.
events.name: Destruction of Kuusisto Castle by Russians

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1318, Robert, King of Naples, delivered an ultimatum to Matilda of Hainaut, ruler of the Greek Principality of Achaea, demanding she accept marriage to John of Gravina or lose her right to rule. This ultimatum reflects the complex political landscape of the time.
events.name: Ultimatum delivered by Robert, King of Naples

events.enhanced_description: The arranged marriage of 6-year-old Joan of Burgundy and 12-year-old Philip of Navarre was a strategic alliance aimed at consolidating power in Navarre. This union was part of a larger political maneuver that would see them eventually become co-monarchs in 1328.
events.name: The arranged marriage of Joan of Burgundy and Philip of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: King Birger of Sweden's reign came to an abrupt end when supporters of his deceased brothers, Valdemar and Eric, stormed Nyköping Castle. Birger and his wife fled to Stegeborg Castle, but were forced to escape again when rebels captured it in August.
events.name: End of King Birger's reign

events.enhanced_description: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, the Grand Vizier of the Ilkhanate, was convicted of the murder of Ilkhan Öljaitü and executed alongside his son Ibrahim Izzaddin. This marked a significant political shift within the Mongol administration.
events.name: Execution of Rashid al-Din Hamadani

events.enhanced_description: In a power struggle in northwestern Algeria, Abu Tashufin I assassinated his father, Abu Hammu I, becoming the new Sultan of Tlemcen. This act marked a significant shift in the region's leadership.
events.name: Assassination of Abu Hammu I

events.enhanced_description: Jacopo I da Carrara was appointed as the first Lord of Padua, establishing the Carraresi dynasty that would govern the city-state for nearly 90 years until its annexation by the Republic of Venice in 1405.
events.name: Jacopo I da Carrara becomes Lord of Padua

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Leake was signed by Edward II of England with the 'Middle Party,' led by his cousin Thomas of Lancaster, at East Leake. This agreement aimed to stabilize the political situation in England during a time of internal strife.
events.name: Treaty of Leake

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII initiated the canonization process for Thomas Aquinas, appointing a commission to gather evidence. Testimonies from over 40 witnesses were collected between July and September 1319.
events.name: Canonization process of Thomas Aquinas

events.enhanced_description: Otto the Mild ascended to the rulership of the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg following the death of his father, Albert the Fat. This transition marked a significant moment in the governance of the region.
events.name: Otto the Mild becomes ruler of Brunswick-Lüneburg

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Faughart saw a Hibernian and Norman force defeat a Scotch-Irish army led by Edward Bruce, who had declared himself High King of Ireland. Edward Bruce was killed in the battle, effectively ending his campaign in Ireland.
events.name: Battle of Faughart

events.enhanced_description: Grand Prince Mikhail of Tver was summoned to Sarai by Özbeg Khan, the ruler of the Golden Horde, where he was executed. This event highlighted the tensions between Russian principalities and the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Execution of Grand Prince Mikhail of Tver

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Scotland convened at Scone and voted to designate Robert Stewart, the grandson of King Robert the Bruce, as the heir presumptive. This decision would set the stage for his eventual ascension to the throne as King Robert II.
events.name: Parliament of Scotland designates Robert Stewart as heir presumptive

events.enhanced_description: In August, Magnus Eriksson, already proclaimed King of Sweden, was recognized by the Norwegian assembly as King Magnus VII of Norway. This recognition established a personal union between Sweden and Norway, significantly impacting the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Magnus Eriksson recognized as King of Norway

events.enhanced_description: The Earl of Pembroke and the Earl of Hereford successfully persuaded Walter Reynolds, Archbishop of Canterbury, to consecrate Stephen Gravesend as the Bishop of London. This event was significant in the ecclesiastical hierarchy of England.
events.name: Consecration of Stephen Gravesend as Bishop of London

events.enhanced_description: A convocation was held in York by Archbishop William Melton, following orders sent to the Bishops of Durham and Carlisle. This gathering aimed to bring together abbots, priors, and archdeacons for ecclesiastical matters.
events.name: Convocation at York

events.enhanced_description: Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy and Sayf al-Din Bahadur al-Ibrahimi, both former Emirs of Mecca, were arrested by the current Emir, Shams al-Din Aq Sunqur al-Nasiri, and taken to Cairo for imprisonment. Rumaythah was later pardoned after a month.
events.name: Arrest of Rumaythah ibn Abi Numayy and Sayf al-Din Bahadur al-Ibrahimi

events.enhanced_description: The Military Order of Christ was established in Portugal by King Denis following the issuance of the papal bull Ad ea ex quibus by Pope John XXII. This order was a revival of the Knights Templar, aimed at aiding Portugal's post-war reconstruction.
events.name: Establishment of the Military Order of Christ

events.enhanced_description: Philip I, Prince of Taranto, in his role as King of Albania, conferred the title of Philip, Despot of Romania, upon his second son, Philip II. This title granted him rights over Epirus in Greece, despite the geographical misnomer.
events.name: Philip I gives title to Philip II

events.enhanced_description: King Haakon V Magnusson of Norway died at the age of 49, leaving the throne vacant until the nobles could agree on a successor. Havtore Jonsson managed a guardianship government until Magnus VII Eriksson was chosen.
events.name: Death of King Haakon V of Norway

events.enhanced_description: Özbeg Khan of the Golden Horde engaged in battle against the Ilkhanate in Mianeh, Iran, attempting to expand his territory. The Ilkhanate forces, led by Sultan Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan and General Amir Chupan, emerged victorious, executing numerous rebel leaders afterward.
events.name: Battle between Özbeg Khan and the Ilkhanate

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of the Vega of Granada, Castilian forces led by regents Don Pedro and Don Juan were defeated by a Moorish relief army. Both regents were killed in the fighting, marking a significant setback for Castilian ambitions in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Vega of Granada

events.enhanced_description: Magnus Eriksson was elected King of Sweden, with his mother, Ingeborg of Norway, appointed to the regency. This election marked a significant moment in the Swedish monarchy's history.
events.name: Election of Magnus Eriksson as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: The canonization process for Thomas Aquinas continued with testimony being collected from over 40 witnesses, overseen by Bishop Uberto d'Ormont, Bishop Angelo Tignosi, and notary Pandulpho de Sabbello. This process was crucial for his eventual canonization.
events.name: Canonization process of Thomas Aquinas continues

events.enhanced_description: In 201 BC, the combined fleets of Rhodes and its allies, including Pergamum, Cyzicus, and Byzantium, defeat Philip V of Macedon in the Battle of Chios. This naval battle is a significant victory for the allied forces, showcasing their strength against Macedonian expansion.
events.name: Battle of Chios

events.enhanced_description: The Duchy of Bavaria, which had been divided between two brothers since 1294, was reunited upon the death of Rudolf the Stammerer. Ludwig the Barbarian, Duke of Lower Bavaria, would later be elected as Holy Roman Emperor in 1328.
events.name: Reunion of the Duchy of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 11, Henry the Child ascended to the title of Margrave of Brandenburg following the death of his cousin and guardian, Waldemar the Great. Due to his young age, Wartislaw IV of Pomerania served as regent, controlling the region until Henry's death just 11 months later, marking the end of the House of Ascania's rule over Brandenburg.
events.name: Henry the Child becomes the Margrave of Brandenburg

events.enhanced_description: Following his victory at the Battle of Mianeh, General Chupan of the Ilkhanate was granted permission to marry Sati Beg, the sister of Sultan Abu Sa'id. This marriage was significant as it strengthened political ties within the ruling elite of the Ilkhanate.
events.name: Marriage of General Chupan and Sati Beg

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII issued the papal bull "Imminente Nobis", asserting the Pope's right to appoint all clerical offices within the Roman Catholic Church. This decree effectively ended the autonomy of individual chapters in electing their leaders, centralizing ecclesiastical power.
events.name: Papal Bull "Imminente Nobis" issued by Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Myton, Scottish forces led by James the Black, Lord Douglas, achieved a decisive victory over an English army. The battle, noted for the significant number of clergymen involved, resulted in heavy English casualties and forced King Edward II to lift the siege of Berwick Castle.
events.name: Battle of Myton

events.enhanced_description: Prince Jaime of Aragon married the 12-year-old Princess Leonor of Castile in Gandesa. However, he declared his intention to renounce his royal duties and enter a monastery, leading to a complex situation involving the royal families.
events.name: Marriage of Prince Jaime of Aragon and Princess Leonor of Castile

events.enhanced_description: During an interrogation by the Kamakura shogunate, Nichiin of Japan's Daimoku sect successfully refuted all other Buddhist sects, ensuring the continuation of his sect. This event marked a significant moment in the history of Buddhism in Japan.
events.name: Nichiin refutes other sects of Buddhism

events.enhanced_description: King Eric VI of Denmark passed away after a 33-year reign in Roskilde, leaving a power vacuum that would not be filled until the election of his brother Christopher II in January. His reign was marked by attempts to control trade routes of the Hanseatic League.
events.name: Death of King Eric VI of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: Representatives of King Edward II of England and King Robert the Bruce of Scotland signed a two-year truce, halting hostilities until Christmas Day, 1321. This agreement aimed to stabilize relations, although long-term peace remained elusive due to Edward's refusal to relinquish claims over Scotland.
events.name: Truce between England and Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Sripada Sri Vallabha, regarded as an incarnation of Lord Datta, was born in Pithapur, Andhra Pradesh. His life and teachings have had a profound impact on the spiritual landscape of India, particularly within the Datta tradition.

image.caption: Portrait depicting Sripada Sri Vallabha.
image.credit: Srinivas2498 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image date: 2020-12-02; it does not depict the 1320 birth event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Birth of Sripada Sri Vallabha

events.enhanced_description: Henry III, Count of Gorizia, arrived in Padua as the Imperial Vicar, bringing a large army with him. His presence was intended to provide protection to the Italian city-state amid the turbulent political landscape of the time.
events.name: Henry III arrives in Padua

events.enhanced_description: Duke Władysław I the Short was crowned king of a reunited Poland after receiving approval from Pope John XXII. The coronation took place at the royal cathedral on Wawel Hill in Kraków, amidst a backdrop of surrounding hostile neighbors.
events.name: Władysław I becomes king of Poland

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII granted a mandate to Archbishop William Melton of York to oversee the restitution of confiscated Knights Templar property to the Knights Hospitaller. This decision reflected the ongoing complexities surrounding the fate of the Templars after their dissolution.
events.name: Pope John XXII mandates restitution of Templar property

events.enhanced_description: Walter de Stapledon, the Bishop of Exeter, was appointed as the new Lord High Treasurer of England. His appointment came during a period of significant political and financial challenges for the English crown.
events.name: Walter de Stapledon becomes Lord High Treasurer of England

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Renzong of China, also known as Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan, died after nearly nine years of reign. He was succeeded by his son, Gegeen Khan, marking a transition in leadership during the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Death of Emperor Renzong of China

events.enhanced_description: The Shepherds' Crusade, also known as Le Pastoureaux, began in Normandy when a large group of common people, inspired by a teenage shepherd's vision, banded together to march south. Their journey was marked by violence against various groups, including Jews, and ended when they were halted by Aragonese forces.
events.name: Shepherds' Crusade begins in France

events.enhanced_description: King Robert the Bruce sent the Declaration of Arbroath to Pope John XXII, asserting Scottish sovereignty and his right to rule. This letter was a crucial moment in Scotland's struggle for independence and aimed to lift the excommunication order against him.
events.name: Declaration of Arbroath sent to Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: Gegeen Khan, also known as Prince Shidibala, ascended to the throne as the new Mongol Emperor Yingzong of the Yuan dynasty following the death of his father, Emperor Renzong. His reign marked a continuation of Mongol rule in China.
events.name: Gegeen Khan becomes Mongol Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Pope John VIII of Alexandria, the leader of the Coptic Orthodox Church, died in Egypt after a 20-year reign. His passing led to the election of his successor, Pope John IX, during a critical period for the Coptic Church.
events.name: Death of Pope John VIII of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: King Edward II of England appointed Lord Pembroke as keeper of the realm before embarking on a journey to France. This appointment was crucial for maintaining stability in England during his absence.
events.name: Edward II appoints Lord Pembroke as keeper of the realm

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Ismail I signed an 8-year truce with Castile at Baena, despite King James II's refusal to accept the treaty due to his plans for a crusade against Granada. The treaty aimed to foster cooperation against mutual enemies.
events.name: Treaty of Baena signed

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII, alarmed by the impending arrival of the shepherds in Avignon to commence their crusade, ordered their dispersal. This action reflected the Pope's concern over the potential chaos and violence that could ensue.
events.name: Pope John XXII orders dispersal of Shepherds' Crusade

events.enhanced_description: To strengthen the alliance between Hungary and Poland, Charles I of Hungary married Princess Elizabeth, the 15-year-old daughter of King Wladyslaw I, with the approval of Pope John XXII. This union was intended to solidify political ties between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Marriage of Charles I of Hungary and Princess Elizabeth of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In the Delhi Sultanate, Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah was murdered by his favorite, Khusrau Khan, who subsequently ascended to the throne. This event marked a significant shift in power within the Sultanate.
events.name: Murder of Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah

events.enhanced_description: William II de Soules confessed to treason before the Scottish Parliament during the 'Black Parliament' session held at Scone. He was subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment at Dumbarton Castle for conspiring against King Robert the Bruce.
events.name: William II de Soules confesses to treason

events.enhanced_description: Khusrau Khan, who had betrayed and murdered Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah to seize power, was himself betrayed and killed by his governor, Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq. This event led to the establishment of the Tughlaq dynasty in Delhi.
events.name: Murder of Khusrau Khan

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Saint George saw Byzantine forces led by Andronikos Asen decisively defeat the army of the Principality of Achaea, thus securing control over the strategically important region of Arcadia. The battle resulted in the capture of Latin commander Bartholomew II and several nobles, who were taken prisoner and sent to Constantinople.
events.name: Battle of Saint George

events.enhanced_description: Pope John IX of Alexandria was elected as the new spiritual leader of the Coptic Orthodox Church, succeeding Pope John VIII. His election marked a significant moment in the history of the Coptic Church, which has faced numerous challenges throughout its existence.
events.name: Election of Pope John IX of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his son Michael IX Palaiologos, Andronikos II Palaiologos became the sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire. This transition of power set the stage for internal conflicts, including a rebellion led by his grandson Andronikos.
events.name: Andronikos II Palaiologos becomes sole ruler

events.enhanced_description: Magnus Birgersson, the former crown prince of Sweden, was executed by order of King Magnus Eriksson after defending Stegeborg Castle. His death marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the Swedish monarchy during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Execution of Magnus Birgersson

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 1321, Syrgiannes Palaiologos shifted his allegiance back to Andronikos II Palaiologos, fleeing to Constantinople. His return was rewarded with the title of megas doux, and he played a crucial role in persuading the emperor to resume military actions against Andronikos III.
events.name: Syrgiannes Palaiologos switches support

events.enhanced_description: In 1321, the Anatolian Beylik of Teke was established by the Oghuz Turks, emerging as a frontier principality following the decline of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Anatolia, contributing to the fragmentation of power in the region.
events.name: Establishment of the Beylik of Teke

events.enhanced_description: In 1321, the Republic of Florence established the University of Florence, which would become a significant center of learning and culture during the Renaissance. This institution played a crucial role in the development of humanist thought and the arts in Italy.
events.name: University of Florence established

events.enhanced_description: In 1321, King Stefan Milutin founded the Gračanica Monastery on the ruins of a 6th-century basilica in Kosovo. This monastery became an important cultural and religious site, reflecting the architectural and artistic achievements of the Serbian medieval period.
events.name: Gračanica Monastery founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1321, the Spitakavor Monastery, located near the Armenian town of Yeghegnadzor, was completed. This monastery is notable for its architectural style and its role in the spiritual life of the region.
events.name: Spitakavor Monastery completed

events.enhanced_description: Around 1321, the Kebra Nagast, known as 'The Glory of the Kings', was translated from Arabic to Ge'ez, according to its colophon. This text is significant in Ethiopian history, detailing the lineage of the Solomonic dynasty and the origins of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
events.name: Kebra Nagast translated

events.enhanced_description: King Edward II of England appointed a group of high-ranking officials, including bishops and earls, to negotiate a peace treaty with Scotland. This effort aimed to extend the Pembroke treaty of 1319 before its expiration, reflecting the ongoing tensions between England and Scotland.
events.name: Edward II's Peace Negotiations with Scotland

events.enhanced_description: The English Parliament appointed a commission to investigate illegal confederacies in Wales that posed a threat to the authority of King Edward II. This action highlighted the growing unrest and political challenges faced by the English crown during this period.
events.name: English Parliament's Inquiry into Welsh Confederacies

events.enhanced_description: The English crown issued a ban preventing the Welsh Earls of Hereford, Arundel, and Surrey, along with 26 others, from attending meetings that could influence King Edward II. This decree was part of the broader efforts to maintain control over the Welsh nobility.
events.name: Ban on Welsh Earls from Meetings

events.enhanced_description: A papal verdict announced in the Polish town of Brześć ordered the Teutonic Knights to return the coastal region of Gdańsk Pomerania to Poland, which they had occupied since 1308. This decision led to renewed hostilities and the outbreak of a new Polish–Teutonic War.
events.name: Papal Verdict on Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: The Genkō era marks the beginning of a new period in Japan following the end of the Gen'ō era. This transition reflects the ongoing changes in Japanese society and governance during the Kamakura period.
events.name: Beginning of the Genkō Era in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In spring 1321, Co-Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos fled from Constantinople to Adrianople, where he established his court and initiated an uprising against his grandfather, Andronikos II. This conflict marked the beginning of a civil war that would have lasting implications for the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Byzantine Civil War begins

events.enhanced_description: In the Delhi Sultanate, European Dominican missionaries who had accompanied Jordanus were killed while stranded on Salsette Island. This tragic event highlighted the dangers faced by missionaries in foreign lands during this period.
events.name: Killing of Dominican Missionaries in India

events.enhanced_description: Sweden's governing council voted to bar foreigners from the royal palace and urged the Norwegian council to admonish regent Ingeborg against seeking foreign advice. This decision was a response to growing discontent regarding the regent's governance.
events.name: Sweden's Council Votes Against Foreign Influence

events.enhanced_description: Prince Wenceslaus of Płock allied with the Teutonic Knights by signing an agreement in Golub, pledging to prevent Lithuanian troops from passing through his principality. This alliance was part of the broader geopolitical struggles in the region.
events.name: Alliance of Prince Wenceslaus with Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: On Easter, civil war erupted in Byzantium as Andronikos Palaiologos initiated a rebellion against his grandfather, Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos. Joined by notable figures such as Theodore Synadenos and John Kantakouzenos, this conflict marked a significant power struggle within the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Civil War in Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: The German play 'Ludus de decem virginibus', which dramatizes the New Testament Parable of the Ten Virgins, was first performed. This event reflects the rich tradition of medieval drama and its role in religious and cultural expression.
events.name: First Performance of Ludus de decem virginibus

events.enhanced_description: During the Wars of the Rügen Succession, Dukes Otto I of Pomerania, Vartislav IV of Pomerania-Wolgast, and Barnim III of Pomerania-Stettin reached a mutual inheritance contract with Vitslav III of Rügen. This agreement was crucial in determining the future political landscape of the region.
events.name: Wars of the Rügen Succession

events.enhanced_description: In Egypt's Mamluk Sultanate, a campaign was launched against the Christian settlements of the Coptic Orthodox Church, resulting in the destruction of over 60 churches and monasteries. This violent episode underscored the religious tensions prevalent in the region during this period.
events.name: Campaign Against Coptic Churches in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Johan de Bosco, a French leper, accused a fellow leper named Geraldus of attempting to spread leprosy by contaminating water sources. This incident sparked widespread rumors and paranoia, particularly against the Jewish community, leading to what became known as the 1321 lepers' plot.
events.name: Leprosy Conspiracy Claims in France

events.enhanced_description: Andronikos II Palaiologos concluded a peace agreement that effectively divided the Byzantine Empire, recognizing Andronikos III as co-emperor and granting him control over Thrace and Macedonia. This division was pivotal in shaping the future governance of the empire.
events.name: Peace Agreement in the Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: Guillaume Agasse, head of a leper house in Pamiers, reported to Bishop Jacques Founier that over fifty officials of leper houses had conspired with the Emirate of Granada to spread leprosy throughout France. This claim contributed to the growing hysteria surrounding leprosy during this period.
events.name: Inquiry into Leprosy Conspiracy in France

events.enhanced_description: King Philip V of France ordered the imprisonment and interrogation of all lepers, with those found guilty often facing execution by burning. This drastic measure reflected the intense fear and stigma surrounding leprosy in medieval society.
events.name: King Philip V's Orders Against Lepers

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII approved a second inquiry into the canonization of Thomas Aquinas, appointing four commissioners to gather testimony from witnesses. This inquiry was part of the ongoing efforts to recognize Aquinas' contributions to theology and philosophy.

image.caption: Benozzo Gozzoli’s Triumph of Saint Thomas Aquinas, a religious artwork.
image.credit: Benozzo Gozzoli — Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"g/gozzoli/5various/7aquinas"
image.date_qualification: Retrospective artwork dated 1471, long after the 1321 inquiry; it is contextual imagery, not a depiction of the inquiry itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pope John XXII's Inquiry into Thomas Aquinas' Canonization

events.enhanced_description: María de Molina, the regent for her grandson King Alfonso XI of Castile, passed away at the age of 56. Her death led to a power struggle as two relatives assumed control, further complicating the political landscape of Castile during a time of chaos.

image.caption: Tomb of Queen María de Molina in the church of the convent of Las Huelgas Reales, Valladolid, Spain.
image.credit: Lourdes Cardenal — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image date: 2007-05; this is the depicted tomb’s photograph date, not the date of María de Molina’s death.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of María de Molina

events.enhanced_description: The 'Parliament of Whitebands' convened in England with only 38 barons present, aiming to remove suspected counselors to King Edward II. This gathering reflected the growing discontent among the nobility regarding the king's advisors.
events.name: Parliament of Whitebands in England

events.enhanced_description: A marriage contract was signed for Princess Euphemia, the 4-year-old sister of King Magnus of Sweden and Norway, to marry Albert of Mecklenburg, the 3-year-old son of Henry I, Lord of Mecklenburg. This political alliance would not be realized until many years later.
events.name: Marriage Contract for Princess Euphemia

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1321, King Edward II of England capitulated to the demands of his barons, agreeing to exile both Hugh Despenser the Elder and his son, Hugh Despenser the Younger. This decision was pivotal as the Despensers had been influential in the king's administration, and their removal was seen as a significant victory for the barons opposing Edward's rule.
events.name: King Edward II agrees to the demands from his barons to send Hugh Despenser the Elder and his son Hugh Despenser the Younger into exile

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1321, the renowned Italian poet Dante Alighieri, celebrated for his epic work 'The Divine Comedy', passed away in Ravenna after suffering from malaria. His death marked the end of a significant literary career that profoundly influenced the course of Italian literature and the broader Western literary tradition.
events.name: Dante Alighieri dies

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1321, King Stefan Milutin of Serbia died after a 39-year reign, leaving a legacy of territorial expansion and cultural development. His death led to a power struggle between his son Stefan Konstantin and his half-brother Stefan Uroš III, igniting a civil war that would shape the future of the Serbian monarchy.
events.name: King Stefan Milutin dies

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1321, King Edward II captured Leeds Castle after Lady Margaret de Clare, the wife of Bartholomew Badlesmere, denied Queen Isabella entry. The confrontation escalated when Lady Badlesmere's archers attacked the queen's party, resulting in casualties. Following the castle's capture, Lady Badlesmere became the first woman imprisoned in the Tower of London.
events.name: Edward II captures Leeds Castle

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1321, a second inquiry into the canonization of Thomas Aquinas commenced in Fossanova, Italy. Led by three commissioners, the inquiry gathered testimony from over 100 witnesses, reflecting the significant impact Aquinas had on Christian theology and philosophy.
events.name: Canonization inquiry of Thomas Aquinas

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1321, Rinaldo dei Bonacolsi, Duke of Mantua, initiated the siege of Mirandola against Francesco I Pico. This conflict escalated as Bonacolsi arrested Pico and his sons, leading to a protracted siege that would last for 33 days.
events.name: Siege of Mirandola begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1321, King Edward II arrived in Cirencester to confront the rebellion led by Thomas of Lancaster and his allies. This marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the monarchy and the barons, as Edward sought to reassert his authority in the face of growing opposition.
events.name: Edward II confronts rebellion in Cirencester

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1321, faced with an invasion of London by rebel forces led by Baron Badlesmere, King Edward II offered safe conduct to any rebels willing to join his side. This strategic move aimed to weaken the rebellion while simultaneously ordering the arrest of Badlesmere, showcasing the king's attempts to regain control.
events.name: Edward II offers safe conduct to rebels

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1321, Emperor Go-Daigo of Japan initiated direct governance, marking the end of the cloistered rule of his predecessor, Emperor Go-Uda. This pivotal moment in Japanese history set the stage for significant political changes and the eventual rise of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: Emperor Go-Daigo begins direct government

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1321, Rinaldo dei Bonacolsi, Duke of Mantua, successfully completed the siege of Mirandola, gaining control over the duchy. Following his victory, he ordered the destruction of the castle belonging to Duke Francesco I Pico, solidifying his power in the region.
events.name: Duke of Mantua completes siege of Mirandola

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1322, Charles IV the Fair ascended to the throne of France following the death of his brother, King Philip V, at Longchamp Abbey. His reign would be marked by political challenges, including his refusal to release his imprisoned wife, Blanche of Burgundy.
events.name: Charles IV becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1322, Stephen Uroš III Dečanski was crowned king of Serbia after defeating his half-brother Stefan Konstantin in battle. This event marked a significant shift in the Serbian monarchy, as Uroš appointed his young son, Stefan Dušan, as co-ruler, indicating a dynastic strategy for the future.
events.name: Stephen Uroš III becomes king of Serbia

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1322, Marie of Brabant, the queen consort of France, passed away. Her death marked the end of her influential role in the French court, where she had been a significant figure during the reigns of her husband, King Philip V, and her brother-in-law, King Charles IV.
events.name: Marie of Brabant dies

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1322, the central crossing tower of Ely Cathedral collapsed, likely due to construction work for the Lady Chapel. This incident led to the architectural redesign of the cathedral, resulting in the construction of the Octagon, which remains a prominent feature today.
events.name: Collapse of Ely Cathedral's crossing tower

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1322, the Battle of Burton Bridge took place, where King Edward II ordered an attack on the fortified positions of the rebel army led by Thomas of Lancaster. Despite being heavily outnumbered, Lancaster managed to withdraw and escape to Tutbury Castle, showcasing the ongoing tensions between the monarchy and the barons.
events.name: Battle of Burton Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1322, the Battle of Boroughbridge occurred, where English forces led by Andrew Harclay defeated the rebel barons. Harclay's strategic defense of the bridge forced Thomas of Lancaster to surrender, marking a decisive victory for the royalist forces in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Battle of Boroughbridge

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1322, Thomas of Lancaster was executed after a show trial at Pontefract Castle, where he was convicted of treason against the crown. His public beheading marked a significant moment in the struggle between the monarchy and the rebellious barons, further consolidating Edward II's power.

locations.name: Pontefract Castle, West Yorkshire, United Kingdom

events.name: Execution of Thomas of Lancaster

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1322, Baron Badlesmere was found guilty of treason during a trial in Canterbury, following his failed attempt to overthrow King Edward II. His death sentence was carried out later that day, reflecting the harsh repercussions faced by those who opposed the king.
events.name: Trial and execution of Baron Badlesmere

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1322, Albert IV ascended to the title of Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg following the death of his father, John II. This transition marked a significant moment in the lineage of the House of Ascania, which played a crucial role in the political landscape of medieval Germany.
events.name: Albert IV becomes the new Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1322, Tarabya I ascended to the throne of the Sagaing Kingdom in Burma following the death of King Saw Yun. His reign marked a continuation of the political dynamics in the region, which was characterized by the struggle for power among various Burmese kingdoms.

image.caption: Political map of Myanmar (Burma), showing the regional context of the Sagaing Kingdom.

image.date_qualification: The map depicts c. 1350, as stated in its description, and was created in 2016; it is later than the 1322 event.

events.name: Tarabya I becomes the new ruler of the Sagaing Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1322, at the request of King Charles IV of France, Pope John XXII annulled the marriage between Charles and Blanche of Burgundy. This annulment was significant as it allowed Charles to seek a new marriage alliance, which was crucial for his political ambitions.
events.name: Pope John XXII annuls the marriage of Charles IV and Blanche of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1322, Galeazzo I Visconti succeeded his father, Matteo I Visconti, as the Lord of Milan. His rule would later be marked by significant political maneuvering and the expansion of the Visconti family's influence in northern Italy.
events.name: Galeazzo I Visconti becomes the new Lord of Milan

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1322, Alice de Lacy, Countess of Lincoln, surrendered nearly all her properties to King Edward II to avoid execution. This act highlighted the precarious position of nobles during Edward's reign and the intense political strife of the period.
events.name: Alice de Lacy surrenders properties to King Edward II

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1322, Al-Nasir Muhammad, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, sought military assistance from Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, the Ikhanate Mongol ruler of Iran, in his campaign against the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. The request came amidst rising tensions and military engagements in the region.
events.name: Al-Nasir Muhammad requests aid from Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1322, troops from the semi-independent Patriarchate of Aquileia, led by Bishop Pagano della Torre, faced defeat at the hands of the Duchy of Milan, commanded by Duke Galeazzo I Visconti. This battle underscored the ongoing power struggles in northern Italy.
events.name: Battle of Bassignana

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1322, a significant agreement was reached in the Byzantine civil war between Emperor Andronikos II and his grandson Andronikos III Palaiologos. The two agreed to co-rule the Byzantine Empire, marking a pivotal moment in its governance.
events.name: Agreement in Byzantine civil war

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1322, Pope John XXII issued a decree condemning the Fraticelli, urging King Roberto il Saggio of Naples to suppress their movement. This action reflected the ongoing tensions within the Catholic Church regarding reformist groups.
events.name: Pope John XXII condemns the Fraticelli

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1322, historian Kokan Shiren completed the Genkyo Shakusho, which is recognized as the oldest existing account of the development of Buddhism in Japan. This work is significant for its historical and cultural insights into the spread of Buddhism in the region.
events.name: Kokan Shiren completes Genkyo Shakusho

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1322, Louis Dampierre ascended to the title of Count of Flanders following the death of his grandfather, Robert III, known as 'The Lion of Flanders'. This transition marked a significant moment in the governance of the region.
events.name: Louis Dampierre becomes Count of Flanders

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1322, King Robert the Bruce of Scotland initiated the 'Great Raid' into northern England, starting with an attack on Norham Castle. This military campaign prompted a swift response from King Edward II, who ordered the English army to assemble at Newcastle upon Tyne.

image.caption: Medieval penny of Robert the Bruce, showing his profile on the obverse.
