locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Robert the Bruce begins the Great Raid

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1322, King Charles IV of France married Marie of Luxembourg, the daughter of the late Henry VII, Holy Roman Emperor. This marriage followed the annulment of his previous union with Blanche of Burgundy and was significant for strengthening political alliances.
events.name: Charles IV marries Marie of Luxembourg

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1322, the Battle of Mühldorf took place, where Bavarian forces led by King Louis the Bavarian defeated the Austrians commanded by Frederick the Fair. This battle was pivotal in the struggle for the Bavarian throne, resulting in Frederick's capture.
events.name: Battle of Mühldorf

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1322, the Battle of Old Byland occurred, where Scottish forces led by King Robert the Bruce defeated the English army. This victory was significant as it showcased the effectiveness of Bruce's military tactics against the English forces.
events.name: Battle of Old Byland

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1322, Dmitry of Tver, known as 'Dmitry of the Fearsome Eyes', became the new monarch of the Grand Principality of Vladimir. His ascension was part of the complex political landscape of medieval Russia, characterized by the struggle for power among various principalities.
events.name: Dmitry of Tver becomes monarch of Vladimir

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1322, Margaret de Clare, the widow of Baron Baldesmere, was released from the Tower of London after being the first woman imprisoned there for over a year. Following her release, she chose to retire to a religious life at a convent.
events.name: Margaret de Clare is freed from the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1322, the emirate of Guadix came to an end with the death of Nasr, who had established the emirate after being forced to abdicate as Sultan of Granada in 1314. His death marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Death of Nasr, end of the emirate of Guadix

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1322, Pope John XXII issued the papal bull Ad conditorem canonum, which permanently renounced the doctrine that the Roman Catholic Church owned all properties of the Franciscan Order. This decision was pivotal in the relationship between the Church and the Franciscans.
events.name: Papal bull Ad conditorem canonum issued by Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1322, King James II of Aragon married Elisenda de Montcada in a ceremony held in Tarragona. This marriage was his fourth and was significant for the political alliances it fostered within the region.
events.name: King James II of Aragon marries Elisenda de Montcada

events.enhanced_description: The Flemish Revolt of 1323 was a significant uprising against the oppressive taxation and pro-French policies of Louis I of Nevers. Led by landowning farmers under Nicolaas Zannekin, the revolt saw the local gentry join forces, with Bruges' mayor, William Deken, emerging as a prominent leader.
events.name: Flemish Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1323, Bonagrazia of Bergamo, representing the Fraticelli order of Spiritual Franciscans, protested against Pope John XXII's papal bull 'Ad conditorem canonum'. The Pope revised the bull but punished Bonagrazia by imprisoning him for his insolence.
events.name: Protest by Bonagrazia of Bergamo

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1323, Vilnius was first mentioned as a city in the letters sent by Grand Duke Gediminas of Lithuania to German cities, inviting German Jews and other Germans to settle in the city, marking a significant moment in its history.
events.name: First Mention of Vilnius

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1323, Norway's regency council took action against Ingeborg Haakonsdater, the mother and regent of the young King Magnus VII, removing her from her position due to allegations of power misuse.
events.name: Regency Council's Stand Against Ingeborg Haakonsdater

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1323, the Earl of Carlisle was arrested at Carlisle Castle by warden Anthony de Lucy on charges of treason and subsequently handed over to King Edward II of England.
events.name: Arrest of the Earl of Carlisle

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1323, the Earl of Carlisle was tried and convicted for treason, leading to his execution by hanging, drawing, and quartering, with parts of his body displayed across England.
events.name: Execution of the Earl of Carlisle

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1323, Hugh II, self-styled King of Arborea in Sardinia, became a vassal of King James II of Aragon, initiating a conflict against the Republic of Pisa, achieving a victory at Villanovaforru.
events.name: Hugh II Becomes Vassal of James II of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1323, Elizabeth of Carinthia married Peter, Crown Prince of Sicily, solidifying political alliances within the Kingdom of Sicily.
events.name: Marriage of Elizabeth of Carinthia and Peter of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1323, Nicolò Pistorino was appointed as the new Grand Chancellor of the Republic of Venice, succeeding Jacopo Bertoldi, who had held the position for nearly nine years.
events.name: Nicolò Pistorino Becomes Grand Chancellor of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1323, Marie of Luxembourg was formally crowned as Queen consort of France at Sainte-Chapelle, following her marriage to King Charles IV on September 21.
events.name: Crowning of Marie of Luxembourg

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1323, Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg, signed a peace treaty with King Christopher II of Denmark, confirming his control over the Lordship of Rostock.
events.name: Peace Treaty Between Mecklenburg and Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1323, Grand Duke Gediminas sent his third, fourth, and fifth letters to German cities, encouraging residents to relocate to the Duchy of Lithuania, highlighting the region's growing importance.
events.name: Gediminas' Letters to German Cities

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1323, Zhao Xian, former Emperor of the Song dynasty, committed suicide to avoid execution by the Yuan dynasty's Mongol Emperor Yingzong, marking a tragic end to his reign.
events.name: Death of Zhao Xian

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1323, Bertrand du Pouget, a French papal legate, besieged Milan but retreated when Louis IV of Bavaria sent a relief army to protect the city from the Kingdom of Naples.
events.name: Siege of Milan by Bertrand du Pouget

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Villa di Chiesa concluded on February 7, 1324, when Aragonese forces led by Prince Alfonso captured the city after an eight-month siege. This event marked the beginning of the Aragonese conquest of Sardinia, paving the way for the establishment of the Kingdom of Sardinia.
events.name: Siege of Villa di Chiesa

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1323, Thomas Aquinas, the renowned Italian priest and theologian, was canonized as a saint by Pope John XXII at the Avignon Cathedral, recognizing his significant contributions to Christian theology.
events.name: Canonization of Thomas Aquinas

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1323, Sweden signed the Treaty of Nöteborg with the Novgorod Republic, establishing the border in what is now Finland for the first time, aided by the Hanseatic League to resolve conflicts over the Gulf of Finland.
events.name: Treaty of Nöteborg

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1323, Gegeen Khan, the Mongol Emperor Yingzong of China, was assassinated in a coup orchestrated by Yesün Temür, who subsequently ascended to the throne as the new Emperor.
events.name: Assassination of Gegeen Khan

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1323, Saw Zein ascended to the throne as the new monarch of the Hanthawaddy Kingdom in southern Burma, following the death of his older brother, Saw O.
events.name: Ascension of Saw Zein

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1323, Pope John XXII asserted his right to confirm imperial elections and demanded that Louis IV of Bavaria renounce his claim to be King of the Romans, highlighting the tensions between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Papal Claim by John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1323, hostilities began that would lead to the War of Saint-Sardos when King Charles IV of France claimed the French town of Saint-Sardos, which was under the jurisdiction of King Edward II of England.
events.name: Beginning of Hostilities Leading to the War of Saint-Sardos

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1323, Lord Raymond-Bernard of Montpezat burned the village of Saint-Sardos and executed the French royal sergeant sent by King Charles IV, escalating tensions between England and France.
events.name: Destruction of Saint-Sardos

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1323, Pope John XXII issued the papal bull 'Cum inter nonnullos', declaring the Fraticelli's assertion that Christ and the Apostles possessed no property as heretical, reinforcing the Church's stance against radical poverty movements.
events.name: Papal Bull Cum inter nonnullos

events.enhanced_description: In December 1323, John of Nottingham and Robert of Coventry, believed to be skilled in necromancy, attempted to cast a deadly spell against King Edward II and his associates. Their actions led to a trial for sorcery after one of the intended victims died following the use of a wax figurine.
events.name: Necromancy Attempt Against Edward II

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1323, in retaliation for the Saint-Sardos incident, King Charles IV of France ordered the arrest of Pons Tournemire, Edward II's chief advocate in France's parliament. Tournemire's imprisonment at the Grand Châtelet highlighted the escalating tensions between England and France.
events.name: Arrest of Pons Tournemire

events.enhanced_description: In 1324, Ludwig the Bavarian, King of the Germans, granted the Duchy of Pomerania to his son, Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg. This decision intensified the ongoing Brandenburg-Pomeranian conflict, affecting regional power dynamics.
events.name: Ludwig the Bavarian Grants Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: Osman I, the founder of the Ottoman Empire, died in Bursa after a 25-year reign. His death marked a transition in leadership to his son, Orhan I, who would continue to expand the empire.
events.name: Death of Osman I

events.enhanced_description: Marsilius of Padua authored Defensor pacis, a significant treatise advocating for the separation of church and state, challenging the authority of the clergy. This work contributed to the development of political thought in medieval Europe.
events.name: Marsilius of Padua Writes Defensor pacis

events.enhanced_description: William of Ockham, the renowned Franciscan philosopher, was summoned to the papal court in Avignon by Pope John XXII and subsequently imprisoned. This event reflected the tensions between Ockham's ideas and the papal authority.
events.name: William of Ockham Imprisoned

events.enhanced_description: The Taiding Era commenced on January 3, 1324, shortly after Borjigin Yesün Temür ascended the throne of the Yuan dynasty in China. This era marked a significant period in Mongol rule over China.
events.name: Taiding Era Begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1324, England's envoy Ralph Basset and Raymond-Bernard de Montpezat refused to comply with King Charles IV's order to appear in Paris regarding the burning of Saint-Sardos. This refusal led to the forfeiture of their properties to the French crown.
events.name: Decline to Appear Before Charles IV

events.enhanced_description: On February 29, 1324, the Battle of Lucocisterna saw Aragonese forces led by Prince Alfonso defeat a Pisan army near Capoterra. This battle was significant as it demonstrated the military prowess of the Aragonese during their campaign in Sardinia.
events.name: Battle of Lucocisterna

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1324, Pope John XXII excommunicated Ludwig the Bavarian for failing to seek papal approval during his conflict with Frederick the Fair. This excommunication intensified the political struggle between the papacy and the German monarchy.
events.name: Excommunication of Ludwig the Bavarian

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1324, Marie of Luxembourg, Queen of France, tragically died from injuries sustained in a carriage accident while traveling with her husband, King Charles IV. Her death was compounded by the premature birth of her daughter, who also did not survive.
events.name: Death of Marie of Luxembourg

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1324, Hugh IV ascended to the throne of Cyprus following the death of his father, King Henry II. In addition to ruling Cyprus, Hugh inherited the nominal title of 'King of Jerusalem'.
events.name: Hugh IV Becomes King of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Hugh IV of Cyprus took place on April 15, 1324, at the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Nicosia. This event marked the formal recognition of Hugh's rule following his ascension to the throne.
events.name: Coronation of Hugh IV of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1324, Boleslaw III, Duke of Wrocław, declared his duchy a vassal of the Holy Roman Empire as part of a defense agreement with Ludwig the Bavarian. This declaration underscored the shifting political alliances in Central Europe.
events.name: Boleslaw III Declares Vassalage

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1324, the Consistori del Gay Saber held its inaugural contest in Toulouse to determine the best poet in the Kingdom of France. Arnaut Vidal de Castelnou d'Ari won the first prize, the violeta d'aur, marking the beginning of a tradition that would last for 160 years.
events.name: First Contest of the Consistori del Gay Saber

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1324, King Ludwig the Bavarian publicly defended the Spiritual Franciscans and criticized Pope John XXII, whom he labeled a heretic. This confrontation highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and the papacy during this period.
events.name: Ludwig the Bavarian Defends Franciscans

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1324, a treaty was signed between the Byzantine Empire, represented by Stephen Syropoulos, and the Republic of Venice, led by Doge Giovanni Soranzo. This agreement was significant in the context of Byzantine-Venetian relations.
events.name: Byzantine-Venice Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1324, King Edward II dispatched his envoy, Aymer de Valence, to France to negotiate a peaceful resolution to the Saint-Sardos incident. Unfortunately, Valence suffered a heart attack and died in Saint-Riquier before reaching Paris.
events.name: Envoy Aymer de Valence's Mission

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1324, King Charles IV of France issued an order declaring the Duchy of Aquitaine, ruled by Edward II of England, forfeited to the crown due to Edward's failure to render homage. This act escalated tensions and set the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Forfeiture of the Duchy of Aquitaine

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1324, King Charles IV of France married his cousin Joan of Évreux, the daughter of his uncle Louis, Count of Évreux. This royal union was significant in strengthening political alliances within the French nobility.
events.name: Royal Wedding of Charles IV and Joan of Évreux

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1324, Pope John XXII declared that Ludwig the Bavarian would be deposed as King of the Germans due to his earlier excommunication. Despite this declaration, Ludwig continued to rule and later made his rival Friedrich a co-king.
events.name: Papal Declaration Against Ludwig the Bavarian

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1324, Mansa Musa, the wealthy Emperor of the Mali Empire, arrived in Cairo after camping near the pyramids of Giza. Accompanied by a large entourage and a vast supply of gold, he met with Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad during his pilgrimage to Mecca.
events.name: Mansa Musa Arrives in Cairo

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1324, Basarab I, the ruler of Wallachia, was designated by King Károly Róbert of Hungary as a subject of the Hungarian crown. This designation marked a significant moment in the feudal relationships between the two regions.
events.name: Basarab I Designated as Subject of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1324, the Blitar Regency was established on the island of Java by King Jayanegara of Majapahit. This establishment was part of the broader political landscape of the Majapahit Empire during its height.
events.name: Establishment of Blitar Regency

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1324, the coronation of Christopher II of Denmark took place in Vordingborg, where his son, Prince Erik Christoffersen, was also crowned as a junior co-monarch. This dual coronation symbolized the continuation of royal lineage in Denmark.
events.name: Coronation of Christopher II of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Vaprio d'Agogna, Pagano della Torre, the Patriarch of Aquileia, faced defeat against the Visconti family in his attempt to reclaim Milan. This loss marked a significant setback in his ambitions and led to the abandonment of further military campaigns.
events.name: Battle of Vaprio d'Agogna

events.enhanced_description: During the War of Four Lords, a strategic meeting took place in Remich where King John the Blind of Bohemia and his allies, including Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, plotted the siege of Metz. This collaboration aimed to strengthen their military efforts against the city.
events.name: War of Four Lords Meeting

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his uncle, King Sancho the Peaceful, James the Unfortunate ascended to the throne of Majorca. His reign would be marked by challenges as he navigated the political landscape of the Mediterranean.
events.name: James the Unfortunate Becomes King of Majorca

events.enhanced_description: During the funeral procession of King Sancho of Majorca in Perpignan, a mob attacked, seizing valuables from the procession. This incident highlighted the tensions and unrest in the region during this period.
events.name: Funeral Procession of King Sancho of Majorca

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Metz occurred during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where Allied armies laid siege to the French city and fortress of Metz. This siege was part of the broader campaign to weaken French defenses and ultimately contributed to Napoleon's downfall.
events.name: Siege of Metz

events.enhanced_description: The War of Saint-Sardos concluded with the surrender of Edmund of Woodstock at La Réole, marking a pivotal moment in the conflict between England and France. A six-month truce followed, temporarily easing tensions in the region.
events.name: End of the War of Saint-Sardos

events.enhanced_description: The Shōchū Incident involved the discovery of Emperor Go-Daigo's plot to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate, leading to the arrest of several conspirators. This event underscored the tensions between the imperial authority and the shogunate.
events.name: Shōchū Incident

events.enhanced_description: After a three-month stay in Cairo, Mansa Musa, the emperor of the Mali Empire, continued his pilgrimage to Mecca. His journey is renowned for its display of wealth and the cultural exchanges it fostered.
events.name: Mansa Musa Resumes Pilgrimage

events.enhanced_description: Petronilla de Meath became the first person in the British Isles to be executed by burning at the stake for witchcraft in Kilkenny. This event marked a significant moment in the history of witch hunts in Europe.
events.name: First Witch Burning in the British Isles

events.enhanced_description: Pope John XXII issued the papal bull Quia quorundam, addressing issues of apostolic poverty and reaffirming papal infallibility. This document was significant in the context of the Church's authority and its relationship with secular powers.
events.name: Papal Bull Quia quorundam

events.enhanced_description: Marsilio da Carrara ascended to the position of Lord of Padua following the death of his uncle, Jacopo I da Carrara. His rule would influence the political landscape of northern Italy during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Marsilio da Carrara Becomes Lord of Padua

events.enhanced_description: The Shōchū era commenced during the reign of Emperor Go-Daigo, marking a significant period in Japanese history characterized by political upheaval and the eventual rise of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: Beginning of the Shōchū Era

events.enhanced_description: Afonso IV ascended to the throne of Portugal following the death of his father, King Denis I. His reign would be marked by significant political and military challenges.
events.name: Afonso IV Becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq was murdered after a brief five-year reign in Kara-Manikpur, leading to the ascension of his son, Muhammad bin Tughluq, as the new ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
events.name: Murder of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella of England embarked on a diplomatic mission to Paris to mediate peace between England and France, reflecting the complex political dynamics of the time. Her journey would have lasting implications for both kingdoms.
events.name: Queen Isabella's Mission to Paris

events.enhanced_description: At the young age of 11, Valdemar III ascended to the Duchy of Schleswig following the death of his father, Eric II. His early reign would be characterized by the challenges of youth and the complexities of noble politics.
events.name: Valdemar III Becomes Duke of Schleswig

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Trausnitz was signed, resulting in the release of Frederick the Fair from imprisonment at Trausnitz Castle. This agreement marked a significant moment in the power dynamics between the Duchy of Austria and the Kingdom of Bavaria.
events.name: Treaty of Trausnitz

events.enhanced_description: A truce was established between King Edward II of England and King Charles IV of France, effectively ending the War of Saint-Sardos. This agreement was facilitated by Queen Isabella and had significant implications for the territorial disputes between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Truce Between England and France

events.enhanced_description: The Istrian Demarcation was established, delineating the boundaries of disputed territories in the Adriatic Sea peninsula of Istria. This agreement was significant for the independent Italian states involved and was published in multiple languages.
events.name: Istrian Demarcation

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1325, Pope John XXII issued a papal bull demanding the imprisonment of the Fraticelli, a group of spiritual Franciscans, and their leader, Fra Enrico da Ceva, in Naples. Despite the papal demand and subsequent admonitions, King Robert of Naples and Duke Charles of Calabria ignored the orders, reflecting the tensions between the papacy and local rulers.
events.name: Papal Bull against the Fraticelli

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1325, the Michaelites, a faction of the Spiritual Franciscans led by Michael of Cesena, convened in Lyon, France, to resolve their conflicts with the Roman Catholic Church regarding their vow of poverty. They agreed to make peace with the Church and cease any disrespectful references to Pope John XXII, highlighting the internal struggles within the Franciscan order.
events.name: Assembly of the Michaelites

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1325, Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg, ceded the territories of Prignitz and Uckermark to the Margraviate of Brandenburg through an unfavorable peace treaty signed at Daber, modern-day Dobra Nowogardzka in Poland. This event marked a significant shift in territorial control in the region.
events.name: Cession of Prignitz and Uckermark

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1325, Ulrich III ascended to the title of Count of Württemberg following the death of his father, Eberhard I. This transition marked a new chapter in the governance of the region, as Ulrich III would continue to shape the future of Württemberg.

image.caption: Photograph of a statue of Ulrich III in Stuttgart’s collegiate church choir.

events.name: Ulrich III becomes Count of Württemberg

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1325, the renowned Moroccan scholar and explorer Ibn Battuta embarked on a hajj from his hometown of Tangier to Mecca. His journey would take him across North Africa and beyond, ultimately covering an estimated 73,000 miles over 30 years, making him one of the most traveled individuals of his time.
events.name: Ibn Battuta's Hajj

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1325, Ismail, Sultan of Granada, initiated a siege on the city of Martos in the Kingdom of Castile. However, he lost control of his troops, leading to the city being pillaged after two weeks, showcasing the challenges faced by the Sultan in maintaining order among his forces.
events.name: Siege of Martos

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1325, Sultan Ismail I of Granada was assassinated in his palace, the Alhambra, after a nine-year reign. His death led to the ascension of his ten-year-old son, Muhammad IV, with the vizier Muhammad ibn al-Mahruq acting as regent, setting the stage for political intrigue in the Emirate of Granada.
events.name: Assassination of Sultan Ismail I

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1325, the Battle of Varey took place, where the 16-year-old Guigues VIII, the local ruler of Vienne, successfully defeated the Savoyard forces at Saint-Jean-le-Vieux. The battle was marked by a significant Burgundian cavalry charge that was repulsed, leading to a decisive victory for Guigues and the capture of John I, Count of Auxerre.

image.caption: Château de Varey at Saint-Jean-le-Vieux.
image.credit: BUFO88 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph date: June 28, 2014; this is a later view of the site, not an image of the 1325 battle.

events.name: Battle of Varey

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1325, in Valladolid, Alfonso XI was proclaimed King of Castile at the age of 14 by the Cortes, marking the beginning of his reign. This event signified a transition in power and the responsibilities that lay ahead for the young king.
events.name: Alfonso XI proclaimed King of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1325, Edward II of England was persuaded by his chief adviser, Hugh Despenser the Elder, not to travel to France. Instead, he decided to send his 12-year-old son, Prince Edward of Windsor, to pay homage to King Charles IV of France, a decision that reflected the complex political dynamics of the time.
events.name: Edward II's Decision on France

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1325, Isabella of France conspired with the exiled Roger Mortimer to depose her husband, Edward II of England. To strengthen their position, Isabella arranged for her son, Edward of Windsor, to be engaged to Philippa of Hainault, aiming to build diplomatic and military support for their cause.
events.name: Isabella of France's Conspiracy

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1325, Edward, Prince of Wales, paid homage to King Charles IV of France on behalf of his father, King Edward II of England. This act was part of the ongoing political maneuvers between England and France during a time of tension.
events.name: Edward, Prince of Wales pays homage

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1325, King Edward II of England called for a session of Parliament to convene at Westminster, beginning on November 18, to discuss the concerning absence of his wife, Queen Isabella, who had not returned from France. This meeting was crucial in addressing the political instability surrounding the royal family.
events.name: Edward II calls for Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1325, King Edward II sent a letter to Pope John XXII, who was in Avignon, expressing his deep concern over Queen Isabella's prolonged absence from England. This correspondence highlighted the strained relations between the English crown and the papacy during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Edward II's Letter to Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1325, during the War of the Bucket, the Ghibelline forces, numbering around 7,000 and backed by the Holy Roman Empire, defeated a much larger Guelph army of 32,000 near Bologna. This battle solidified Ghibelline influence in northern Italy and demonstrated the shifting power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Battle of Zappolino

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1325, Yuri III Danilovich, Grand Duke of Moscow, was assassinated by Dmitry of Tver, known as 'the Terrible Eyes.' Following Yuri's death, his younger brother, Ivan I, inherited the throne and began the process of relocating the spiritual capital of the Russian people to Moscow, marking a significant shift in Russian history.
events.name: Assassination of Yuri III Danilovich

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1325, King Edward II made a last-ditch effort to salvage his marriage to Queen Isabella by sending her a letter demanding her immediate return from France. In his letter, he expressed his sorrow over her absence and acknowledged her affair with Roger Mortimer, revealing the deepening crisis within their marriage.
events.name: Edward II's Final Attempt to Save His Marriage

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1325, Charles, Count of Valois, uncle of King Charles IV of France, died at the age of 55 in Nogent-le-Roi. His death left his son Philip as the heir apparent to the French throne, impacting the line of succession in the French monarchy.
events.name: Death of Charles, Count of Valois

events.enhanced_description: Clare College, the second oldest surviving college of the University of Cambridge, was founded in 1326. It has since become an integral part of the university's history and academic life.
events.name: Foundation of Clare College

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1326, the foundation of Oriel College, the fifth oldest college of the University of Oxford, was confirmed by royal charter. This establishment marked an important development in the history of higher education in England.
events.name: Foundation of Oriel College

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1326, the Raid on Brandenburg commenced as Polish-Lithuanian forces led by King Wladyslaw the Elbow-High and Gediminas raided the territories of the Margraviate of Brandenburg. This military action was sanctioned by Pope John XXII and aimed at reclaiming what Wladyslaw considered Polish territory.
events.name: Raid on Brandenburg Begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1326, Queen Ingbeborg, the regent and de facto ruler of Sweden, was stripped of all political authority due to her significant debts, known as the Scania affair. This event marked a pivotal moment in Swedish politics as power dynamics shifted.
events.name: Queen Ingbeborg Stripped of Authority

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1326, Frederick the Fair became the sole Duke of Austria following the death of his younger brother, Leopold I of the House of Habsburg. This consolidation of power would have lasting implications for the Habsburg dynasty.
events.name: Frederick the Fair Becomes Duke of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1326, the Raid on Brandenburg concluded with the Polish-Lithuanian forces looting and destroying the cities of Berlin and Frankfurt an der Oder, capturing 6,000 German prisoners of war. This raid significantly impacted the region's stability and demonstrated the military prowess of the Polish-Lithuanian alliance.

locations.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, Brandenburg, Germany

events.name: Completion of the Raid on Brandenburg

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1326, a peace treaty was signed at Dagnum between Venetian merchants from Ragusa and King Stefan Dečanski of Serbia. This agreement aimed to stabilize trade relations and resolve ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Peace Treaty at Dagnum

events.enhanced_description: In the spring, the Moroccan scholar and explorer Ibn Battuta arrived at the port of Alexandria after an extensive journey of over 3,500 km. His travels would later contribute to a rich narrative of the cultures he encountered.
events.name: Ibn Battuta's arrival in Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1326, Ottoman forces led by Sultan Orhan I successfully captured the Byzantine city of Bursa during a siege. This victory marked Bursa as the first official capital of the Ottoman Empire, establishing a significant foothold in the region.
events.name: Siege of Bursa

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Arques, brokered by King Charles IV of France, aimed to end the Flemish Revolt, a significant uprising in Flanders against the French crown. However, the treaty faced resistance from various rebel districts, leading to ongoing tensions in the region.
events.name: The Peace of Arques

events.enhanced_description: King Christopher II of Denmark, facing an uprising, promised the Danish Principality of Rügen to John III of Werle and Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg. This promise ignited the First War of the Rügen Succession, a conflict over control of the strategically important island.
events.name: First War of the Rügen Succession

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Novgorod established a 10-year armistice, effectively ending decades of border skirmishes between Norway and the Novgorod Republic in the far-northern region of Finnmark. This treaty was crucial for stabilizing relations in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Novgorod

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political shift, the Reichsrat of Denmark voted to remove King Christopher II from power, replacing him with the young Valdemar V, Duke of Schleswig. Gerhard of Holstein was appointed as regent, marking a turbulent period in Danish history.
events.name: Removal of King Christopher II

events.enhanced_description: During the summer, German forces led by Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg, occupied the western territories of the Principality of Rügen. This military action was part of the broader conflicts involving the region's control.
events.name: German occupation of Rügen

events.enhanced_description: Wartislaw IV, Duke of Pomerania, formed an alliance with Gerhard III, Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, amidst the political turmoil following the overthrow of King Christopher II of Denmark. This alliance was pivotal in the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Alliance between Wartislaw IV and Gerhard III

events.enhanced_description: The Scottish Parliament convened at Cambuskenneth, where it voted to restore 10-year-old Robert Stewart, grandson of Robert the Bruce, to the line of succession for the Scottish throne. This decision would shape the future of Scottish monarchy.
events.name: Scottish Parliament meeting at Cambuskenneth

events.enhanced_description: The renowned Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta set out from Cairo on a significant journey through Palestine, eventually making his way to Damascus. His travels would later provide invaluable insights into the cultures and societies of the 14th century.
events.name: Ibn Battuta departs from Cairo

events.enhanced_description: After a three-week journey from Cairo, Ibn Battuta arrived in Damascus, a key cultural and commercial hub of the Islamic world. His experiences in Damascus would contribute to his extensive travel narratives.
events.name: Ibn Battuta arrives in Damascus

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella of France formalized a marriage contract between her 13-year-old son, Prince Edward, and Philippa of Hainault, ensuring their wedding would occur within two years. This alliance would play a significant role in English and European politics.
events.name: Marriage contract between Edward and Philippa

events.enhanced_description: Dmitry, Grand Prince of Tver, was executed on the orders of Özbeg Khan, the ruler of the Golden Horde, for the murder of Grand Duke Yuri of Moscow. This event underscored the political tensions and power struggles in medieval Russia.
events.name: Execution of Dmitry, Grand Prince of Tver

events.enhanced_description: Isabella of France and her supporters, including Roger Mortimer, landed at Orwell in Suffolk, initiating an invasion aimed at dethroning King Edward II. This marked the beginning of a significant power struggle in England.

image.caption: Illuminated psalter initial depicting Queen Isabella praying, flanked by the arms of England and France.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Isabella_Psalter_-_BSB_CodGall16_f94_%28Isabella_praying%29.jpg/401px-Isabella_Psalter_-_BSB_CodGall16_f94_%28Isabella_praying%29.jpg - Psalter of Isabella of England
image.date_qualification: A retrospective image of Isabella in her psalter, dated 1303–1308; it does not depict the 1326 invasion.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Invasion of England by Isabella of France

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn, Gerhard III, Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, allied himself with Danish magnates, prompting a response from the Hanseatic towns of Demmin, Stralsund, Greifswald, and Anklam. This alliance was significant in the context of regional power dynamics.
events.name: Alliance of Gerhard III with Danish magnates

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella of France commenced the Siege of Bristol, which was defended by Hugh Despenser the Elder. This siege was a critical moment in Isabella's campaign against Edward II's rule.
events.name: Siege of Bristol

events.enhanced_description: After eight days of siege, Queen Isabella captured Bristol Castle, taking Hugh Despenser the Elder prisoner. This victory allowed Isabella to consolidate her power and plan further actions against Edward II.
events.name: Capture of Bristol Castle

events.enhanced_description: Following his capture at Bristol, Hugh Despenser the Elder, a key adviser to King Edward II, was publicly executed. His brutal death symbolized the shifting power dynamics in England and the growing influence of Isabella and her supporters.
events.name: Execution of Hugh Despenser the Elder

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella and Crown Prince Edward issued a writ summoning the English Parliament to convene on December 14, claiming to act in the name of King Edward II. This act was pivotal in legitimizing their control over the realm.
events.name: Summoning of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: King Edward II was captured at Neath Abbey in Wales and subsequently imprisoned at Kenilworth Castle. This event marked a significant turning point in the power struggle between Edward II and his estranged wife, Isabella.

locations.name: Kenilworth Castle, Warwickshire, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Capture of King Edward II

events.enhanced_description: Claiming to act on behalf of King Edward II, Queen Isabella and Crown Prince Edward postponed the opening of the English Parliament from December 14 to January 7. This maneuver was part of their strategy to consolidate power.
events.name: Postponement of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In early 1327, Charles I of Hungary and John of Bohemia entered into an alliance at Nagyszombat, now Trnava, Slovakia, to challenge the Austrian Habsburgs. This agreement was crucial in the ongoing territorial disputes in Central Europe.
events.name: Charles I of Hungary and John of Bohemia sign an alliance agreement

events.enhanced_description: In early 1327, a devastating fire broke out in Munich, Bavaria, destroying one-third of the city's buildings over two days. This disaster had significant implications for the city's infrastructure and economy.
events.name: Fire in Munich

events.enhanced_description: In 1327, Richard of Wallingford, an English cleric and abbot, documented the construction of an astronomical clock in his work Tractatus Horologii Astronomici. This clock was notable for its complexity and innovation, reflecting the advancements in medieval science and technology.
events.name: Richard of Wallingford describes astronomical clock

events.enhanced_description: In 1327, the Grand Canal in China, stretching approximately 1,800 kilometers from Beijing to Hangzhou, was completed. This monumental engineering achievement significantly enhanced trade and transportation across the region.
events.name: Completion of the Grand Canal in China

events.enhanced_description: Marinid Prince Uthman ibn Abi al-Ula arrived in Almería to enlist support for his uprising against the Emirate of Granada, aiming to install Muhammad IV's uncle as the new Emir. This event marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the region.
events.name: Uprising against the Emirate of Granada

events.enhanced_description: Imprisoned in Warwickshire, King Edward II was forced to abdicate the throne by his estranged wife, Queen Isabella, and her lover, Roger Mortimer. This event marked a dramatic shift in English monarchy and governance.
events.name: Abdication of King Edward II

events.enhanced_description: The 14-year-old Crown Prince Edward was proclaimed King of England in London, with his mother Isabella serving as regent. This proclamation set the stage for Edward's future reign and the political landscape of England.
events.name: Proclamation of Edward III

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Edward III as King of England took place at Westminster Abbey, with the approval of the English Parliament. Archbishop Walter Reynolds placed the crown upon Edward, marking the beginning of a significant reign.

locations.name: Westminster Abbey, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Coronation of Edward III

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1327, Tarabya I ascended to the throne as the new King of Sagaing in Myanmar, following the death of his brother, King Saw Yun. Despite Saw Yun having an heir, Prince Kyaswa, Tarabya's claim to the throne was recognized, marking a significant moment in the region's dynastic politics.
events.name: Tarabya I becomes King of Sagaing

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1327, Casimir I, Duke of Cieszyn, swore allegiance to John the Blind, King of Bohemia, in Opava. In return for his homage, Casimir was granted the fiefdom of Auschwitz, solidifying political ties between the Polish Silesian nobility and the Bohemian crown.
events.name: Casimir I swears homage to John the Blind

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1327, Charles I of Hungary and John of Bohemia signed an alliance in Nagyszombat, now Trnava, Slovakia, to confront the Austrian Habsburgs occupying Pressburg (modern Bratislava). This agreement marked a pivotal moment in the regional power dynamics of Central Europe.
events.name: Alliance between Charles I of Hungary and John of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1327, several Silesian nobles, following Casimir I's example, pledged their loyalty to John of Bohemia in Opava. This collective homage strengthened John's influence over the Silesian territories and showcased the shifting allegiances among the nobility.
events.name: Silesian nobles swear homage to John of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1327, King Charles IV of France finalized a peace treaty with England, which included the return of Aquitaine and Gascony to English rule. This treaty also resulted in Charles receiving 50,000 livres and the French crown gaining control over several territories.
events.name: Charles IV of France makes peace treaty with England

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1327, during the civil war in Granada, Prince Uthman ibn Abi al-Ula successfully captured the fortress of Laujar de Andarax. This event was a significant development in the power struggles within the Nasrid Kingdom.
events.name: Uthman ibn Abi al-Ula captures Laujar de Andarax

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1327, Edward II was transferred to Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire, under the custody of Thomas Berkeley and John Maltravers. Despite the luxury goods purchased for him, there are indications that he may have been mistreated during his captivity.
events.name: Edward II moved to Berkeley Castle

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1327, on Good Friday, Italian scholar and poet Francesco Petrarca first laid eyes on a woman he would name Laura in the church of Sainte-Claire d'Avignon. This encounter sparked a profound and lasting passion that inspired his renowned collection of poems, Il Canzoniere.
events.name: Petrarch sees Laura

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1327, Ludwig the Bavarian was crowned as King of Italy in Milan, marking the first time since 1313 that the title had been held. His coronation was significant in the context of the Holy Roman Empire and Italian politics.
events.name: Ludwig the Bavarian crowned King of Italy

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1327, Queen Ingeborg of Norway married the Danish nobleman Canute Porse the Elder, a union that led to her deposition from political power in Norway. This event reflects the complex interplay of dynastic politics in Scandinavia during this period.
events.name: Queen Ingeborg marries Canute Porse

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1327, during a banquet hosted by Galeazzo I Visconti in Milan, an assassination attempt was made on Ludwig the Bavarian. The plot failed, resulting in the death of Galeazzo's brother, Stefano, who consumed the poisoned food intended for Ludwig.
events.name: Attempted poisoning of Ludwig the Bavarian

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1327, Demasq Kaja, the Viceroy of Azerbaijan and Iraq in the Ilkhanate, was killed in Soltaniyeh while attempting to evade arrest ordered by the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan. His death underscored the political instability within the Mongol Empire's Middle Eastern territories.
events.name: Demasq Kaja killed in Soltaniyeh

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1327, the former King of England, Edward II, was brutally murdered in Berkeley Castle, Gloucestershire. His death marked a significant turning point in English history, ending a tumultuous reign characterized by conflict and political intrigue.
events.name: Edward II murdered in Berkeley Castle

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1327, Pope John XXII condemned Marsilius of Padua's treatise Defensor pacis, leading to Marsilius's excommunication. This conflict highlighted the tensions between papal authority and emerging political philosophies in medieval Europe.
events.name: Pope John XXII condemns Marsilius of Padua

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1327, Elizabeth de Burgh, Queen consort of Scotland and wife of King Robert the Bruce, suffered fatal injuries after falling from her horse while traveling to Cullen Castle. Her tragic death marked a significant loss for the Scottish royal family.
events.name: Elizabeth de Burgh fatally injured

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1327, Prince Alfonso the Kind was enthroned as King Alfonso IV of Aragon in Barcelona, following the death of his father, King Jaime II. This transition marked a new chapter in the history of the Aragonese crown.
events.name: Alfonso IV becomes King of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1327, Simon Mepeham was elected as the new Archbishop of Canterbury, backed by the Earl of Lancaster. His election was significant as he opposed the candidate favored by Queen Isabella and Roger Mortimer, indicating the ongoing power struggles in England.
events.name: Simon Mepeham elected Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1327, Pope John XXII appointed ten new Roman Catholic cardinals, the largest number during his papacy. Among them was Jacques Fournier, who would later succeed John as Pope Benedict XII in 1334.
events.name: Pope John XXII appoints new cardinals

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1327, the late King Edward II of England was interred in Gloucester Cathedral, three months after his brutal murder. His burial marked the end of a controversial reign and the beginning of a new chapter in English monarchy.
events.name: Edward II buried in Gloucester Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1327, Ala ud-Din Timurtash, the Viceroy for Anatolia within the Ilkhanate, learned of his brother Demasq Kaja's execution. Fearing for his own safety, he fled to Egypt, where he would ultimately meet his own demise in 1328.
events.name: Ala ud-Din Timurtash learns of Demasq's execution

events.enhanced_description: In 1328, the Augustiner-Bräu was first recorded as the brewery of an Augustinian monastery in Munich, Germany. This brewery has since become one of the most famous and oldest breweries in the country.
events.name: First record of Augustiner-Bräu

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1328, Louis the Bavarian was crowned Emperor at St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. The ceremony was conducted by three Italian bishops due to Louis's excommunication by the Pope, highlighting the tensions between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Louis the Bavarian crowned Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1328, Philippa of Hainault married Edward III of England at Westminster Abbey. This union not only solidified political alliances but also produced ten children, including the renowned Edward the Black Prince.
events.name: Philippa of Hainault marries King Edward III of England

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1328, the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton was signed, marking England's recognition of Scotland as an independent nation following the Wars of Scottish Independence. This treaty was a significant milestone in Scottish history, affirming its sovereignty.
events.name: Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1328, Antipope Nicholas V was consecrated at St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City by the Bishop of Venice. His election was part of the ongoing conflict within the Catholic Church during the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Consecration of Antipope Nicholas V

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1328, William of Ockham secretly departed from Avignon, France, due to threats from Pope John XXII. Ockham's departure marked a significant moment in the philosophical and theological debates of the time.
events.name: William of Ockham leaves Avignon

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1328, Philip VI was crowned King of France at Reims Cathedral, establishing the House of Valois after the death of Charles IV, who left no male heirs. This event marked a pivotal shift in the French monarchy.

image.caption: Detail of a miniature depicting Philip VI in *Le procès de Robert d'Artois*.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Jean-Marie Perouse de Montclos : Paris - Kunstmetropole und Kulturstadt, Ullmann/Tandem 2008.
image.date_qualification: Portrait detail in a miniature dated circa 1336, later than the 1328 coronation; it is contextual imagery, not a depiction of the coronation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Coronation of King Philip VI of France

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1328, the Battle of Cassel took place, where French troops successfully quelled an uprising of Flemish farmers. This battle was significant in maintaining French control over the region.
events.name: Battle of Cassel

events.enhanced_description: In April 1329, Antipope Nicholas V was excommunicated by Pope John XXII. This event underscored the ongoing schism and power struggles within the Catholic Church during the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Excommunication of Antipope Nicholas V

events.enhanced_description: In 1329, Aimone of Savoy was appointed Count of Savoy, a title that would play a significant role in the politics of the region. His leadership would influence the dynamics of power in the area.
events.name: Aimone of Savoy becomes Count of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: In 1329, construction began on the Archcathedral Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Andrew in Frombork, Poland. This basilica would become a significant religious site in the region.
events.name: Construction of Archcathedral Basilica in Frombork

events.enhanced_description: In 1329, Michael of Cesena was deposed as General of the Franciscans. His removal was part of the ongoing tensions within the Franciscan order and the Church.
events.name: Deposition of Michael of Cesena

events.enhanced_description: In 1329, Stefan Uroš IV Dušan of Serbia defeated Stephen II, Ban of Bosnia. This victory was part of the broader conflicts in the Balkans during this period.
events.name: Stefan Uroš IV Dušan defeats Stephen II of Bosnia

events.enhanced_description: In 1329, Wiesbaden was granted the right of coinage by Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor. This privilege was significant for the economic development of the city.
events.name: Wiesbaden granted right of coinage

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1329, King John of Bohemia captured the fortress of Medvėgalis, an important stronghold of the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and baptized 6,000 of its defenders. This event was part of the broader Christianization efforts in the region.
events.name: Capture of Medvėgalis by King John of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1329, Amda Seyon I, Emperor of Ethiopia, commenced military campaigns in the southern Muslim provinces. His reign was marked by significant territorial expansion and consolidation of power.
events.name: Amda Seyon I begins campaigns in Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1329, Pope John XXII condemned certain teachings of Meister Eckhart as heretical. This condemnation reflected the tensions within the Church regarding mysticism and theological interpretations.
events.name: Pope John XXII condemns Meister Eckhart

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1329, Edward III of England paid homage to Philip VI of France for the duchy of Aquitaine. This act was part of the feudal obligations that underscored the complex relationship between the two monarchs.
events.name: Edward III pays homage to Philip VI

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1329, David II was crowned King of Scots at the age of five. His reign would span nearly 42 years, during which Scotland would face numerous challenges and conflicts.
events.name: David II becomes King of Scots

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1329, the Braganstown massacre occurred in County Louth, Ireland, where over 160 individuals were killed. This tragic event highlighted the violent conflicts of the period.
events.name: Braganstown massacre

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1329, the Battle of Maltepe (Pelekanon) took place, where the Ottoman Turks defeated the Byzantine Empire. This battle marked a significant step in the Ottoman expansion into Byzantine territories.
events.name: Battle of Maltepe

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1329, the Treaty of Pavia was signed, dividing the Wittelsbach possessions into those of the Bavarian line and those of the Palatinate line. This division would not be reconciled until 1777.
events.name: Treaty of Pavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1330, Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, was granted its coat-of-arms, symbolizing its status and identity as a city. This event marked a significant milestone in the city's early history, reflecting its growing importance in the region.
events.name: Vilnius receives its coat-of-arms

events.enhanced_description: Ivan Alexander ascended to power as the despot of Lovech in the early 1330s, a significant figure in Bulgarian history. His rule would later lead to his elevation as Tsar of Bulgaria, marking a period of cultural and political revival.
events.name: Ivan Alexander becomes the despot of Lovech

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1330, the Battle of Velbazhd occurred, where the Bulgarians under Tsar Michael Shishman faced defeat against the Serbs. Although Bulgaria did not lose territory, the battle marked a significant moment in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Battle of Velbazhd

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1330, Edward III of England began his personal reign by arresting his regent, Roger Mortimer, and subsequently executing him. This marked a decisive turn in Edward's rule and the assertion of his authority.
events.name: Edward III starts personal reign

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1330, the Battle of Posada took place, where the Wallachians, led by Basarab I, defeated the Hungarians despite being heavily outnumbered. This victory was a significant assertion of Wallachian independence.
events.name: Battle of Posada

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1330, a great storm struck the British Isles, resulting in the formation of large areas of sand dunes on Anglesey. This natural disaster had lasting effects on the landscape and local communities.
events.name: Great storm hits the British Isles

events.enhanced_description: The Gümmenenkrieg, fought between the city-states of Bern and Fribourg from 1331 to 1333, was a conflict that highlighted the territorial and political rivalries in medieval Switzerland. This war is notable for its role in shaping local alliances and governance.
events.name: Gümmenenkrieg

events.enhanced_description: In 1331, the sieges of Cividale del Friuli and Alicante marked significant military campaigns in Italy and Spain, respectively. These sieges were part of broader conflicts involving local powers and reflected the ongoing struggles for territorial control during this period.
events.name: Sieges of Cividale del Friuli and Alicante begin

events.enhanced_description: The Genkō War, which began in 1331, was a pivotal conflict in Japan that saw the rise of the Ashikaga clan against the Kamakura shogunate. This war ultimately led to significant changes in Japanese governance and the eventual establishment of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: Genkō War begins in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1331, the famed Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa, an important trading city on the Swahili Coast. His accounts provide valuable insights into the culture, trade, and political dynamics of East Africa during this period.
events.name: Ibn Battuta visits Kilwa

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded outbreak of the Black Death occurred in Hubei, China, in 1331, marking the beginning of one of the deadliest pandemics in human history. This outbreak would eventually spread across Asia and Europe, leading to profound social and economic changes.
events.name: First recorded outbreak of the Black Death

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1331, Stefan Dušan proclaimed himself king of Serbia, marking the beginning of a significant expansion of Serbian territory and influence. His reign is noted for the establishment of the Serbian Empire and the promotion of Orthodox Christianity.
events.name: Stefan Dušan declares himself king of Serbia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Płowce on September 27, 1331, was a significant confrontation between the Teutonic Knights and Polish forces, resulting in a stalemate. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between Poland and the Teutonic Order, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Battle of Płowce

events.enhanced_description: In September 1332, Edward Balliol crowned himself King of Scotland, a controversial act that challenged the legitimacy of David II's rule. His claim to the throne was supported by English forces, further complicating the ongoing conflict for Scottish independence.
events.name: Edward Balliol crowns himself King of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In 1332, the city of Marosvásárhely, now known as Târgu Mureș in Romania, was first documented in the papal registry under the name Novum Forum Siculorum. This documentation marks an important point in the city's history and its recognition in medieval records.
events.name: First documentation of Marosvásárhely

events.enhanced_description: In February 1332, Amda Seyon I, the Emperor of Ethiopia, initiated military campaigns in the southern Muslim provinces, aiming to expand his empire and consolidate power. His reign is noted for significant military successes and the promotion of Christianity.
events.name: Amda Seyon I begins campaigns in southern Muslim provinces

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1332, the Battle of Dupplin Moor took place, where Edward Balliol's forces defeated the loyalists of David II of Scotland. This battle was a significant event in the Wars of Scottish Independence, impacting the power dynamics in Scotland.
events.name: Battle of Dupplin Moor

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1332, Lucerne joined the Swiss Confederation, strengthening the alliance among the cantons. This event was crucial in the formation of a united Switzerland, which would later play a significant role in European politics.
events.name: Lucerne joins the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Annan on December 16, 1332, saw the loyalists of David II defeat the forces of Edward Balliol. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the Wars of Scottish Independence, showcasing the ongoing struggle for control of the Scottish crown.
events.name: Battle of Annan

events.enhanced_description: In 1333, a devastating famine broke out in China, lasting until 1337 and resulting in the deaths of approximately six million people. This famine was part of a series of agricultural crises that affected the region during the 14th century.
events.name: Famine in China

events.enhanced_description: In 1333, a great famine struck Southern Europe, known to historians in Catalonia as Lo mal any primer, or 'the First Bad Year.' This famine was part of a series of agricultural failures that would lead to widespread suffering across the continent.

image.caption: Erfurt Biblia Pauperum Apocalypse illustration showing Death riding a lion and Famine pointing to her mouth.
image.credit: Scanned (by me) from the cover of The Great Famine (1996) by William Chester Jordan. Original cover art from a photograph courtesy of Stiftung Weimarer Klassik, Herzogin Anna Amalia Bibliothek. — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image date is supplied as 1315—1317; description identifies the image as from an illuminated manuscript made around the famine. The event record’s 1333 date is not supported by the cited article excerpt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Great famine in Southern Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1333, Jan IV of Dražic, Bishop of Prague, founded a friary and constructed a stone bridge in Roudnice, contributing to the architectural and religious landscape of the region. This initiative reflected the growing influence of the church in medieval society.
events.name: Jan IV of Dražic founds friary and bridge

events.enhanced_description: The Kapellbrücke, a wooden bridge over the Reuss River in Lucerne, was built in 1333. By the 20th century, it became known as the world's oldest truss bridge and Europe's oldest covered bridge, symbolizing the architectural ingenuity of the time.
events.name: Kapellbrücke bridge built

events.enhanced_description: In 1333, the Venetian historian Marino Sanudo Torsello published his seminal work, 'History of the realm of Romania', which provides invaluable insights into the history of Latin Greece during the period of the Latin Empire. This work remains a critical source for understanding the socio-political landscape of the region in the 13th and 14th centuries.
events.name: The Venetian historian Marino Sanudo Torsello publishes his History of the realm of Romania

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1333, the Siege of Kamakura marked a decisive moment in Japanese history as forces loyal to Emperor Go-Daigo, led by Nitta Yoshisada, captured and destroyed the city. This event effectively ended the Kamakura shogunate and initiated the Kenmu Restoration.
events.name: Siege of Kamakura

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1333, William Donn de Burgh, the 3rd Earl of Ulster, was murdered during the Burke Civil War in Ireland. His death marked a significant turning point in the power struggles among the Irish nobility during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Murder of William Donn de Burgh

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1333, King Edward III of England seized the Isle of Man from Scottish control, further asserting English dominance in the region. This event was part of the broader context of the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Edward III seizes the Isle of Man

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1333, Ashikaga Takauji led his army into Kyoto as part of the Kenmu Restoration, marking a pivotal moment in Japanese history. This action contributed to the downfall of the Kamakura shogunate and the establishment of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: Ashikaga Takauji leads army into Kyoto

events.enhanced_description: The reign of Emperor Kōgon of Japan, the first of the Northern Court (Ashikaga) Pretenders, ended on July 7, 1333. His reign was marked by the political turmoil of the time, as rival factions vied for control of the imperial throne.
events.name: End of Emperor Kōgon's reign

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1333, during the Wars of Scottish Independence, Edward III of England decisively defeated Sir Archibald Douglas at the Battle of Halidon Hill. This victory allowed the English to regain control over Berwick-upon-Tweed, significantly impacting the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Halidon Hill

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1333, the River Arno flooded, causing extensive damage in Florence, as recorded by the chronicler Giovanni Villani. This event highlighted the vulnerability of urban centers to natural disasters during the medieval period.

image.caption: Carabinieri officer cadets in work clothes collect their meal after relief work in Florence.
image.credit: Francesco Memoli — Private correspondence
image.date_qualification: Described as November 1966; image metadata gives 2018-01-23, which is an upload/original metadata date and not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Flood of the River Arno

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1334, the Battle of Adramyttion took place, where a Christian league achieved a significant victory over the fleet of the Turkish Beylik of Karasi. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between Christian states and Muslim principalities in the region.
events.name: Battle of Adramyttion

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1334, the bishop of Florence blessed the first stone laid for the new campanile of the Florence Cathedral, designed by the renowned artist Giotto di Bondone. This event marked the beginning of a significant architectural project that would become a defining feature of Florence's skyline.

image.caption: Giotto’s Campanile in Florence, Italy.
image.credit: Thermos — Own work
