events.name: The bishop of Florence blesses the first foundational stone for the new campanile of the Florence Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1334, Pope Benedict XII was elected as the 197th pope, succeeding Pope John XXII. His papacy would be marked by efforts to reform the church and address the challenges posed by the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Pope Benedict XII succeeds Pope John XXII

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, the Georgians, under the leadership of King George V (the Brilliant), achieved a decisive victory over the Mongolian forces. This victory was pivotal in restoring Georgian sovereignty and allowed King George V to reclaim significant territories.
events.name: Georgians defeat the Mongolians

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, Sweden took a significant step towards social reform by abolishing slavery. This decision reflected the changing attitudes towards human rights and the treatment of individuals within society.
events.name: Slavery is abolished in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, the Congress of Visegrád convened, bringing together the monarchs of Bohemia, Hungary, and Poland to form an anti-Habsburg alliance. This coalition aimed to counter the growing influence of the Habsburgs in Central Europe.
events.name: Congress of Visegrád forms an anti-Habsburg alliance

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, following the death of Duke Henry, Carinthia and Carniola came under Habsburg rule as they were bestowed by Louis the Bavarian on the Dukes of Austria. This marked the beginning of a long period of Habsburg influence in the region.
events.name: Carinthia and Carniola come under Habsburg rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, Pope Benedict XII initiated reforms within the Cistercian order, aiming to address issues of discipline and adherence to the monastic rule. His efforts were part of a broader movement to strengthen the church's moral authority.
events.name: Pope Benedict XII begins to reform the Cistercians

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, the excommunication of Frederick III of Sicily was lifted, along with the interdict placed on Sicily. This event marked a significant reconciliation between the papacy and the Sicilian crown.
events.name: The excommunication of Frederick III of Sicily ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, construction began on the papal palace in Avignon, which would become a symbol of the papacy's power and influence during the Avignon Papacy. This architectural project reflected the need for a fortified residence for the popes.
events.name: Construction begins on the papal palace in Avignon

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, Aabenraa was officially chartered as a city, marking its development as an important urban center in Denmark. This charter facilitated trade and governance in the region.
events.name: Aabenraa is chartered as a city

events.enhanced_description: In 1335, the School of Arts was founded in Zaragoza, Spain, which would later evolve into the University of Zaragoza in the 16th century. This institution played a crucial role in the education and intellectual development of the region.
events.name: The School of Arts in Zaragoza is founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1335, Otto the Merry was appointed as Duke of Carinthia, a title that would enhance his influence in the region. His reign was characterized by efforts to consolidate power and navigate the complex political landscape of the time.
events.name: Otto the Merry becomes Duke of Carinthia

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1335, the Battle of Boroughmuir occurred, where John Randolph, 3rd Earl of Moray, led his forces to victory against Guy, Count of Namur. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Second War of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Boroughmuir

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1335, ex-emperor Hanazono, the 95th emperor of Japan, took the vows to become a Zen priest. This transition marked a significant personal and spiritual transformation for the former emperor.
events.name: Ex-emperor Hanazono becomes a Zen priest

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1335, the Battle of Culblean took place, where David Bruce achieved a decisive victory over Edward Balliol. This battle was significant in the context of the ongoing struggle for the Scottish throne during the Second War of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Culblean

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1335, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan died, succumbing to the plague that ravaged the Ilkhanate. His death marked a pivotal moment, leading to the disintegration of the Ilkhanate due to the lack of a clear heir.
events.name: Death of Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan

events.enhanced_description: In 1336, as the Teutonic Knights besieged Pilėnai, approximately 4,000 defenders chose to commit mass suicide rather than surrender. This act of defiance is remembered as a significant moment of resistance against foreign invaders in Lithuanian history.
events.name: Mass Suicide at Pilėnai

events.enhanced_description: The Kenmu Restoration, a brief period of imperial rule in Japan, ended in 1336, leading to the establishment of the Muromachi period. This transition marked the beginning of a new era characterized by the rise of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: End of the Kenmu Restoration

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1336, in a desperate act of defiance against the advancing Teutonic Knights, approximately 4,000 defenders of Pilėnai committed mass suicide rather than face capture. This tragic event highlighted the fierce resistance of the Lithuanian people during the Teutonic invasions.
events.name: Mass suicide of defenders of Pilėnai

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1336, brothers Harihara and Bukka Raya are believed to have founded the Vijayanagara Empire in the southern part of the Deccan Plateau in India. This empire would go on to become a significant power in South India, known for its cultural and architectural achievements.
events.name: Founding of the Vijayanagara Empire

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1336, the Italian poet Petrarch ascended Mount Ventoux, claiming to be the first since classical antiquity to climb a mountain for the view. This event is often regarded as a significant moment in the history of nature appreciation and the human experience of landscape.
events.name: Petrarch's ascent of Mount Ventoux

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1336, Oirat 'Ali Padsah, the governor of Baghdad, defeated Arpa Ke'un near Maraga. This battle contributed to the ongoing disintegration of the Ilkhanate, showcasing the fragmentation of power in the region.
events.name: Oirat 'Ali Padsah defeats Arpa Ke'un

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1336, the Battle of Minatogawa took place, where Ashikaga Takauji defeated the Japanese Imperial forces led by Kusunoki Masashige and Nitta Yoshisada. This battle was a crucial moment in the struggle for power during the Kamakura period.
events.name: Battle of Minatogawa

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1336, during the Second War of Scottish Independence, English forces burned the city of Aberdeen. This act of destruction was part of the broader conflict between Scotland and England, highlighting the devastation of war on Scottish towns.
events.name: Burning of Aberdeen during the Second War of Scottish Independence

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1336, the reign of Emperor Kōmyō began, marking the start of his rule as the second of the Ashikaga Pretenders to the Northern Court of Japan. His reign would be characterized by the ongoing conflicts between the Northern and Southern courts.
events.name: Reign of Emperor Kōmyō begins

events.enhanced_description: In August 1337, English forces successfully relieved Stirling Castle during the Second War of Scottish Independence, marking the end of Edward III's last campaign in Scotland. This event underscored the ongoing struggle for Scottish independence.
events.name: Relief of Stirling Castle

events.enhanced_description: In October 1337, Edward III of England formally rejected Philip VI's claim to the French throne, an act that initiated hostilities and marked the beginning of the Hundred Years' War. This rejection set the stage for a prolonged conflict between the two nations.
events.name: Rejection of Philip VI's Claim

events.enhanced_description: In November 1337, English troops raided the Flemish island of Cadzand, marking a significant military engagement during the early stages of the Hundred Years' War. This raid demonstrated the English naval capabilities and intentions in the region.
events.name: Battle of Cadzand

events.enhanced_description: In 1337, Bisham Priory was founded in England, serving as a religious institution that contributed to the spiritual and cultural landscape of the region. The priory played a role in the local community and the broader ecclesiastical structure.
events.name: Foundation of Bisham Priory

events.enhanced_description: In 1337, the Scaligeri Family lost control of Padua, leading to Alberto della Scala relocating to Verona. This shift in power dynamics was significant in the political landscape of northern Italy during the late medieval period.
events.name: Loss of Control of Padua

events.enhanced_description: In 1337, Petrarch, often regarded as the 'father' of Renaissance humanism, visited Rome to explore its ancient ruins. His observations and writings during this visit sparked a renewed interest in classical civilization and aesthetics.
events.name: Petrarch's Visit to Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Sofia Psalter was produced in Bulgaria in 1337, representing a significant contribution to the cultural and religious literature of the region. This manuscript is an important artifact of medieval Bulgarian history.
events.name: Production of the Sofia Psalter

events.enhanced_description: In 1337, the Byzantine Empire conquered the Despotate of Epirus, consolidating its power in the region. This conquest was part of the broader efforts of the Byzantine Empire to reclaim territories lost to various invaders.
events.name: Conquest of the Despotate of Epirus

events.enhanced_description: The devastating famine in China, which began in 1332 and resulted in the deaths of approximately 6 million people, came to an end in 1337. This famine had significant social and economic impacts on the region.
events.name: End of the Famine in China

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Nicomedia in 1337 marked the expansion of the Ottoman Empire into Bithynia, as they captured territory from the Byzantine Empire. This event was a key moment in the rise of Ottoman power in Anatolia.
events.name: Siege of Nicomedia

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1337, Edward, the Black Prince, was granted the title of Duke of Cornwall, becoming the first English Duke. This establishment was significant in the development of the English peerage system and royal titles.
events.name: Establishment of the Duchy of Cornwall

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1337, Philip VI of France confiscated Gascony from English control, escalating tensions that would lead to the Hundred Years' War. This act was a pivotal moment in the conflict between England and France.
events.name: Confiscation of Gascony

events.enhanced_description: In 1338, Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor, appointed Edward III of England as a vicar-general of the Holy Roman Empire. This appointment was part of the political maneuvering during the Hundred Years' War, as Louis supported Edward's claim to the French throne.
events.name: Appointment of Edward III as Vicar-General

events.enhanced_description: In 1338, Philip VI of France besieged Guienne in Southwest France, intensifying the conflict with England. This siege was part of the broader military campaigns during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Guienne

events.enhanced_description: In 1338, Ashikaga Takauji was granted the title of shōgun by the emperor of Japan, marking the beginning of the Ashikaga Shogunate. This event initiated a new political era in Japan characterized by the rise of the samurai class.
events.name: Ashikaga Takauji Becomes Shōgun

events.enhanced_description: In 1338, Nicomedia was captured by the Ottoman Empire, furthering their expansion into Byzantine territories. This event was significant in the establishment of Ottoman dominance in the region.
events.name: Capture of Nicomedia

events.enhanced_description: In 1338, a strain of the Black Death plague was identified to have originated near Lake Issyk-Kul in modern Kyrgyzstan. This discovery is crucial for understanding the historical spread of the plague that devastated populations across Europe and Asia.
events.name: Origin of Black Death Strain

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1338, during the Hundred Years' War, Southampton was destroyed in a naval campaign. This event highlighted the ongoing conflict between England and France and the vulnerability of coastal towns.
events.name: Destruction of Southampton

events.enhanced_description: In June 1339, the Canton of Bern defeated the forces of Fribourg in the Battle of Laupen. This victory was significant in the context of the Swiss Wars, showcasing the military prowess of the Swiss cantons.
events.name: Battle of Laupen

events.enhanced_description: In 1339, after defeating Kota Rani, the Hindu queen regnant of Kashmir, in battle at Jayapur (modern Sumbal), Shams-ud-Din Shah Mir proposed marriage to her. Upon her refusal, she committed suicide, leading to his sole rule and the establishment of the Muslim Shah Mir Dynasty.
events.name: Shams-ud-Din Shah Mir's Ascendancy

events.enhanced_description: In 1339, Florence became the first European city in post-Roman times to have all its streets paved. This development marked a significant advancement in urban infrastructure and public works during the medieval period.
events.name: Paving of Florence Streets

events.enhanced_description: The Moscow Kremlin, a fortified complex in the heart of Moscow, is first documented as a 'kremlin' in 1339. This term refers to a major fortified structure that served as a political and religious center, symbolizing the power of the Russian state.
events.name: The Moscow Kremlin is first referred to as a kremlin

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1339, Emperor Go-Murakami acceded to the throne of Japan. His reign was marked by political instability and the ongoing power struggles between the imperial court and the shogunate.
events.name: Accession of Emperor Go-Murakami

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1339, Simone Boccanegra was elected as the first Doge of Genoa. His election marked a significant moment in the political history of the city, as he sought to strengthen Genoa's influence in Mediterranean trade.
events.name: Election of Simone Boccanegra

events.enhanced_description: In 1340, Valdemar IV of Denmark was elected king following an eight-year interregnum after the death of his father, Christopher II. His ascension marked the beginning of a new era in Danish history as he sought to consolidate power and stabilize the kingdom.
events.name: Valdemar IV of Denmark is elected to the throne

events.enhanced_description: In 1340, Europe was estimated to have a population of approximately 74 million inhabitants. This demographic figure reflects the social and economic conditions of the time, prior to the devastating effects of the Black Death later in the century.
events.name: Europe has about 74 million inhabitants

events.enhanced_description: In 1340, an epidemic in northern Italy was documented by Augustine of Trent in his work 'Epistola astrologica.' This early record highlights the health crises that were common in medieval Europe, often exacerbated by poor living conditions and lack of medical knowledge.
events.name: An epidemic in northern Italy recorded by Augustine of Trent

events.enhanced_description: In 1340, Japan celebrated the traditional 2,000-year anniversary of its monarchy, a significant cultural milestone that reflects the deep historical roots and continuity of the imperial lineage in Japanese society.
events.name: The Monarchy of Japan reaches its 2,000 year anniversary

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1340, Edward III of England publicly declared himself King of France in Ghent, marking a significant escalation in the tensions that would lead to the Hundred Years' War. This declaration was rooted in his claim to the French throne through his mother, Isabella of France.
events.name: King Edward III of England declares himself King of France at Ghent, Flanders

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1340, the Church sanctioned a military expedition known as the Bohemian Crusade aimed at suppressing heretical movements in Bohemia. This event reflects the Church's ongoing struggle against perceived threats to its authority during the medieval period.
events.name: Bohemian Crusade: The Church authorizes a military expedition against heretics

events.enhanced_description: Between April and July 1340, the Trapezuntine Civil War saw an abortive uprising against Irene Palaiologina, the Empress of Trebizond. This conflict marked the beginning of a series of political struggles and succession disputes within the Byzantine successor state.
events.name: Trapezuntine Civil War: An abortive uprising against Irene Palaiologina

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1340, the Marinid fleet, commanded by Muhammad ibn Ali al-Azafi, achieved a decisive victory over the Castellan fleet near Algeciras. This battle was part of the broader conflict between the Marinid dynasty and the Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Marinid galleys rout the Castellan fleet off the coast of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1340, Rotterdam was officially granted city rights, marking a significant step in its development as an urban center in the Netherlands. This status allowed for greater autonomy and the establishment of local governance.
events.name: Rotterdam is officially declared a city

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1340, the Battle of Sluys was fought between the English fleet, commanded by Edward III, and the French fleet, led by Admiral Hugues Quiéret. The English victory effectively destroyed the French naval power and marked a pivotal moment in the early stages of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Battle of Sluys

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1340, the Battle of Saint-Omer took place during the Hundred Years' War, resulting in a French victory over the English forces. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between England and France for control of territories in France.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Battle of Saint-Omer

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1340, the Truce of Espléchin was signed, temporarily halting hostilities between England and France during the Hundred Years' War. This truce provided a brief respite in the ongoing conflict, allowing both sides to regroup.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Truce of Espléchin

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1340, the Battle of Río Salado occurred, where the kings of Castile and Portugal defeated the Nasrid ruler of Granada and his Moroccan allies. This battle was significant in the context of the Reconquista, as it marked a decisive victory for the Christian kingdoms.

image.caption: 17th-century painting depicting the Battle of Salado (Battle of Río Salado).
image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist — National Geographic.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated to the 17th century; it depicts the 1340 battle retrospectively.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Río Salado

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, an earthquake with a magnitude of 6.0 struck Crimea, causing significant damage and disruption. This event is noted for its severity, with a maximum Mercalli intensity of VIII, indicating severe effects on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: An earthquake with a magnitude of 6 affects Crimea

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, the Breton War of Succession commenced, a conflict over the control of the Duchy of Brittany. This war involved various factions and was part of the larger context of feudal disputes in medieval France.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Breton War of Succession from Jean Froissart’s *Chroniques*.

events.name: The Breton War of Succession begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Margarete Maultasch, Countess of Tyrol, expelled her husband John Henry of Bohemia, whom she had married as a child. This act led to her subsequent marriage to Louis of Bavaria, resulting in their excommunication due to the lack of a formal divorce.
events.name: Margarete Maultasch expels her husband John Henry of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Tbilisi was established as a capital of the European Christian Cathedra, following the city of Smirna. Under the leadership of George V, Tbilisi became a significant center for Christianity in the region.
events.name: Tbilisi becomes a capital of European Christian Cathedra

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Saluzzo was sacked by Manfred V of Saluzzo, an event that underscored the ongoing conflicts and power struggles within the region during the medieval period.
events.name: Saluzzo is sacked by Manfred V of Saluzzo

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Casimir III of Poland commissioned the construction of a masonry castle in Lublin, encircling the city with defensive walls. This project was part of his broader efforts to strengthen and modernize the Polish state.
events.name: Casimir III of Poland builds a masonry castle in Lublin

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, the Sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, appointed the famous traveler Ibn Battuta to lead a diplomatic mission to the Yuan Dynasty in China. This journey would further enhance the cultural exchanges between the Islamic world and East Asia.
events.name: Ibn Battuta leads a diplomatic mission to Yuan Dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, a catastrophic flood in the Periyar River dramatically altered its course, leading to the closure of the ancient port of Muziris and the emergence of the new harbor at Cochin (Kochi). This event not only submerged several islands but also resulted in the formation of new landmasses, significantly impacting trade routes and local settlements.
events.name: Great Flood of the Periyar River

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, the Chinese poet Zhang Xian penned the 'Iron Cannon Affair,' a significant literary work that critiques the destructive potential of gunpowder and cannons in warfare. This poem reflects the growing awareness of the impact of military technology on society and the moral implications of its use.
events.name: Iron Cannon Affair

events.enhanced_description: Around 1341, Magnus IV of Sweden promulgated the Landslag, a comprehensive legal code that aimed to unify and standardize laws across his kingdom. This legal framework played a crucial role in the governance of Sweden and laid the groundwork for future legal developments.
events.name: Promulgation of Magnus Eriksson's Landslag

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Danish King Valdemar IV Atterdag sold southern Halland to King Magnus IV of Sweden for 8,000 marks. This transaction was part of Valdemar's strategy to finance the reunification of Denmark, reflecting the complex political dynamics of the time.
events.name: Sale of Southern Halland

events.enhanced_description: In 1341, Saint Bridget of Sweden and her husband Ulf Gudmarsson embarked on a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, a significant religious journey that reflects the medieval Christian practice of pilgrimage. This journey would later influence Bridget's spiritual writings and her establishment of the Bridgettine Order.
events.name: Pilgrimage of Saint Bridget of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1341, The Queen's College was founded as a constituent college of the University of Oxford. This institution has since played a significant role in the academic and cultural life of England.
events.name: The Queen's College, University of Oxford is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1341, the Italian poet Petrarch was crowned poet laureate in Rome, marking a significant cultural event as he became the first individual since antiquity to receive this honor. This event symbolized the revival of classical literature and the humanist movement in Renaissance Italy.
events.name: Petrarch is crowned poet laureate in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In September 1341, the Byzantine civil war erupted between John VI Kantakouzenos and the regency for the infant John V Palaiologos. This conflict would last until 1347, significantly impacting the political landscape of the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347 breaks out

events.enhanced_description: In 1342, Guy de Lusignan was crowned as Constantine II, King of Armenia. His reign was characterized by efforts to strengthen the Armenian Kingdom during a period of external threats and internal challenges.
events.name: Guy de Lusignan becomes King of Armenia

events.enhanced_description: In 1342, the Greek Orthodox patriarch of Antioch was transferred to Damascus under the leadership of Ignatius II. This move was significant for the Orthodox Church in the region, reflecting the shifting religious and political landscape.
events.name: Transfer of Greek Orthodox Patriarch to Damascus

events.enhanced_description: In 1342, Kitzbühel was incorporated into the Tyrol region, marking a significant administrative change in the governance of the area. This integration played a role in the development of Tyrol as a political entity in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Kitzbühel becomes part of Tyrol

events.enhanced_description: During the Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347, the Zealots seized power in Thessaloniki, expelling the aristocrats and establishing a regency. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the Byzantine Empire, highlighting the tensions between different social classes.
events.name: Byzantine Civil War of 1341–1347: Zealots seize power in Thessalonica

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1342, Pope Clement VI succeeded Pope Benedict XII as the 198th Pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy would be marked by significant events, including the Black Death and the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Papal Succession of Pope Clement VI

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1342, An-Nasir Ahmad, the Sultan of Egypt, was deposed by his half-brother As-Salih Ismail. This power struggle marked a significant moment in the Mamluk Sultanate's turbulent political landscape during the 14th century.
events.name: Deposition of An-Nasir Ahmad

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1342, Louis I of Anjou ascended to the throne as King of Hungary. His reign would be characterized by military campaigns and efforts to strengthen the kingdom's position in Central Europe.
events.name: Louis I becomes King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1342, the Battle of Zava took place, where Mu'izz al-Din Husayn achieved a decisive victory over the Sarbadars. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Persia during the 14th century.
events.name: Battle of Zava

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1342, St. Mary Magdalene's flood occurred, marking one of the worst flooding events on record for Central Europe. This disaster had significant impacts on local communities and economies.
events.name: St. Mary Magdalene's Flood

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1342, John III Comnenus was proclaimed Emperor of Trebizond. His reign would be marked by efforts to maintain the independence of the empire amidst the pressures from neighboring powers.
events.name: John III of Trebizond becomes Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1342, Louis 'the Child', at just four years old, was crowned King of Sicily in Palermo Cathedral. His ascension to the throne occurred during a tumultuous period in Sicilian history, marked by political instability.
events.name: Louis 'the Child' crowned King of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: In 1343, Tsar Dušan of Serbia successfully conquered Albania, expanding his empire and asserting dominance in the Balkans. This conquest was part of his broader campaign to establish a Serbian Empire.
events.name: Tsar Dušan conquers Albania

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1343, Arnošt of Pardubice was appointed as the last bishop of Prague and subsequently became the first Archbishop of Prague. His elevation marked a significant moment in the ecclesiastical history of Bohemia.
events.name: Arnošt of Pardubice becomes Archbishop of Prague

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1343, Pope Clement VI issued the papal bull Unigenitus, which defined the doctrine of 'The Treasury of Merits' as the basis for issuing indulgences by the Catholic Church. This doctrine had lasting implications for the Church's practices and its relationship with the faithful.
events.name: Pope Clement VI issues Unigenitus

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1343, the St. George's Night Uprising began in Estonia, a significant revolt against the German nobility. This uprising was a pivotal moment in Estonian history, reflecting the struggle for independence and local governance.
events.name: St. George's Night Uprising begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1343, during the St. George's Night Uprising, the 'Four Estonian Kings' were murdered during negotiations with the Livonian Order. This event intensified the conflict and galvanized the Estonian resistance against foreign rule.
events.name: Murder of the Four Estonian Kings

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1343, Magnus IV of Sweden abdicated from the throne of Norway in favor of his son Haakon VI. Although Haakon was still a minor, this transition marked a significant moment in the dynastic politics of Scandinavia.
events.name: Magnus IV of Sweden abdicates throne of Norway

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1343, a naval league was formed between the Pope, the Republic of Venice, the Knights Hospitaller, and the Kingdom of Cyprus to prepare for the Smyrniote Crusades. This coalition aimed to reclaim territories and strengthen Christian influence in the Eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: Formation of Naval League for Smyrniote Crusades

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1343, a devastating tsunami, triggered by an earthquake, struck the Maritime Republic of Amalfi, causing widespread destruction. This natural disaster had significant repercussions for the coastal communities and their economies.
events.name: Tsunami devastates Maritime Republic of Amalfi

events.enhanced_description: King Edward III of England introduced three new gold coins: the florin, leopard, and helm. However, discrepancies in the gold content led to their withdrawal and melting down by August of the same year.
events.name: Introduction of new gold coins by Edward III

events.enhanced_description: Bablake School was founded in Coventry, England, by the dowager Queen Isabella. This institution would go on to play a significant role in the education of future generations.
events.name: Foundation of Bablake School

events.enhanced_description: The Compagnia dei Bardi, one of the prominent banks in Florence, went bankrupt, along with the Peruzzi Bank and the Acciaiuoli Bank. This event marked a significant financial crisis in the region.
events.name: Bankruptcy of Compagnia dei Bardi

events.enhanced_description: A large public dial clock was installed in the tower of the Palazzo Capitaniato in Padua, commissioned by Prince Ubertino I da Carrara and supervised by the renowned clockmaker Jacopo Dondi dell'Orologio. This installation represented a significant advancement in timekeeping technology.
events.name: Installation of public dial clock in Padua

events.enhanced_description: King Peter IV of Aragon successfully defeated and deposed his cousin, James III of Majorca, thereby incorporating the Balearic Kingdom of Majorca into the Crown of Aragon. This event solidified Aragon's power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Conquest of Majorca by Peter IV of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: Newaya Krestos succeeded his father, Amda Seyon I, as Emperor of Ethiopia. This transition marked a continuation of the Solomonic dynasty's influence in the region.
events.name: Succession of Newaya Krestos as Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1344, the Siege of Algeciras concluded with the surrender of the Muslim city to the forces of the Kingdom of Castile. This siege was notable for being one of the first military engagements in Europe where gunpowder was used, marking a significant evolution in warfare.
events.name: Siege of Algeciras ends

events.enhanced_description: Constantine II, the King of Armenia, was killed during an uprising, leading to the ascension of his distant cousin, Constantine III. This event marked a significant shift in the Armenian monarchy amidst ongoing political instability.
events.name: Death of Constantine II of Armenia

events.enhanced_description: During the St. George's Night Uprising, the Livonian Order executed Vesse, the rebel Estonian Elder of Saaremaa Island. This uprising was part of a larger resistance against foreign rule in the region.
events.name: St. George's Night Uprising

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Pallene, a Christian fleet achieved victory over a Turkish fleet, marking a significant naval engagement in the ongoing conflicts between Christian and Muslim powers in the region.
events.name: Battle of Pallene

events.enhanced_description: The Smyrniote Crusade culminated in a successful assault by a Christian fleet on the port city of Smyrna, which was under the control of the Aydinid Turks. This victory was part of the broader Crusading efforts in the region.
events.name: Smyrniote Crusade

events.enhanced_description: In a notable political move, five-year-old Erik Magnusson, the eldest son of King Magnus IV of Sweden, was appointed as the heir to the Swedish throne, despite the elective nature of the monarchy at the time.
events.name: Appointment of Erik Magnusson as heir

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political maneuver, Edward III of England publicly offered his 'defiance' to Philip VI of France, escalating tensions that would lead to the outbreak of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Edward III's defiance of Philip VI

events.enhanced_description: Led by Umur Beg, the Turks sailed from Asia Minor to the Balkan Peninsula, conducting raids into Bulgarian territory. This incursion was part of the broader Ottoman expansion into Europe.
events.name: Turks raid Bulgarian territory

events.enhanced_description: In a politically significant union, Louis IV's son, Louis VI the Roman, married Cunigunde, a Lithuanian princess. This marriage aimed to strengthen ties between the Holy Roman Empire and the Baltic region.
events.name: Marriage of Louis VI the Roman and Cunigunde

events.enhanced_description: During the Gascon campaign of 1345, the Battle of Bergerac saw English troops achieve victory over the French forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict known as the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Bergerac

events.enhanced_description: The Turks launched an attack on Smyrna, intensifying the ongoing conflicts in the region. This assault was part of the broader struggle for control over key territories in Asia Minor.
events.name: Turks attack Smyrna

events.enhanced_description: The Miracle of the Host occurred, an event commemorated in Amsterdam, which had significant implications for the religious landscape of the time. This miracle was seen as a divine endorsement of the Eucharist.
events.name: Miracle of the Host

events.enhanced_description: Guy de Chauliac observed the planets Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars conjoined in the sky, along with a solar eclipse on the same day. This celestial event was interpreted as a foreboding sign, which Chauliac later associated with the onset of the Black Plague.
events.name: Guy de Chauliac's astronomical observations

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Gamenario, the Lombards achieved a decisive victory over the Angevins in the northwest region of present-day Italy, just southeast of Turin. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Gamenario

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Peritheorion, the forces of Momchil, an autonomous ruler of the Rhodope, were defeated by the Turkish allies of John VI Kantakouzenos. This battle underscored the shifting allegiances and conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Peritheorion

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1345, during the Hundred Years' War, English forces captured La Réole, a strategic town in Gascony, from the French. This victory was part of a broader campaign to assert English control over the region.
events.name: The English take La Réole in Gascony

events.enhanced_description: In December 1345, English forces successfully captured Aiguillon, a fortified town in Gascony, further consolidating their territorial gains during the early stages of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The English take Aiguillon in Gascony

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1346, a severe outbreak of Bubonic Plague began in the Crimea, marking the onset of the first major epidemic of the Black Death. This devastating plague would eventually spread across Europe, leading to significant population decline.
events.name: A severe Bubonic Plague epidemic begins in the Crimea

events.enhanced_description: In 1346, significant repairs were undertaken in the Hagia Sophia, a monumental structure originally built as a cathedral in the 6th century. This architectural marvel has served various religious purposes and remains a symbol of Byzantine and Ottoman heritage.
events.name: Repairs are made in the Hagia Sophia

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1346, the French military began preparations to defend their channel coasts against potential English incursions, anticipating the escalation of hostilities in the ongoing conflict known as the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The French prepare to defend the channel coasts

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1346, Dušan Silni proclaimed the Serbian Empire in Skopje, marking a significant expansion of Serbian territory and influence in Southeast Europe. This event established Dušan as a powerful ruler in the region.

image.caption: Medieval fresco depicting Serbian ruler Stefan Dušan with his wife Jelena at Lesnovo Monastery.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — From this page , this image . image .
image.date_qualification: The image is a fresco dated to the 14th century, not a contemporary photograph of the 1346 proclamation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Serbian Empire is proclaimed in Skopje by Dusan Silni

events.enhanced_description: In May and June of 1346, an English invasion fleet gathered at Portsmouth in preparation for an assault on France. This mobilization was part of Edward III's strategy to reclaim territories lost to the French.
events.name: An English invasion fleet assembles at Portsmouth

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1346, the English army achieved a decisive victory over the forces of Charles of Blois at the Battle of St Pol de Léon in Brittany. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of St Pol de Léon: The English army defeats Charles of Blois in Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1346, Genoese forces led by Simone Vignoso successfully landed on the island of Chios, capturing it from local Greek control. The operation marked a significant expansion of Genoese influence in the Aegean Sea.
events.name: Genoese forces land on the Mediterranean island of Chios

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1346, the English forces secured a minor victory at La Roche-Derrien in Brittany, reinforcing their presence in the region during the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years' War.

image.caption: 15th-century miniature depicting Charles de Blois being captured after the Battle of La Roche-Derrien.
image.credit: Loyset Liédet — Paris. Bibliothèque nationale de France, Département des manuscrits, Français 2643 f.180
image.date_qualification: The image is dated to the 15th century; it depicts the aftermath of the battle in 1347, not a contemporary photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The English win a small victory at La Roche-Derrien in Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1346, the leaders of the cities of Ghent, Bruges, and Ypres pledged their support to Edward III of England. This alliance was crucial in bolstering English efforts during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The leaders of Ghent, Bruges and Ypres agree to support Edward III

events.enhanced_description: In July 1346, Edward III ordered the closure of English ports to prevent information from reaching France about his military plans. This strategic move was part of his preparations for the invasion of France.
events.name: Edward III orders the closing of English ports

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1346, the English fleet attempted to sail from Portsmouth to Normandy but was thwarted by adverse winds. This setback delayed their plans for invasion during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The English fleet attempts to sail from Portsmouth to Normandy

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1346, Charles IV, Count of Luxembourg, was elected King of the Romans, a significant step in his rise to power within the Holy Roman Empire. His election would later lead to his coronation as Holy Roman Emperor.
events.name: Charles IV, Count of Luxembourg is elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1346, Edward III and his army successfully crossed the English Channel, marking the beginning of their invasion of France. This event set the stage for a series of significant battles in the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Edward III and the English army cross the English Channel

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1346, the English forces conducted raids on the Cotentin Peninsula, burning neighboring towns and villages. This aggressive tactic aimed to weaken French morale and disrupt supply lines.
events.name: The English raid and burn towns in the Cotentin Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1346, during the Hundred Years' War, the English army captured and sacked the French city of Caen. This victory was a significant blow to French defenses in Normandy.
events.name: Battle of Caen (1346)

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1346, Jaume Ferrer embarked from Majorca on an expedition to the Senegal River, known as the 'River of Gold.' This journey was part of the broader exploration and trade efforts of the time.
events.name: Jaume Ferrer sets out for the Senegal River

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1346, the French forces attempted to besiege Aiguillon but were unsuccessful in dislodging the English defenders. This failure highlighted the ongoing struggle for control in Gascony during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Aiguillon: The French fail to take Aiguillon from its English defenders

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1346, the English forces achieved a victory over the French at the Battle of Blanchetaque. This battle was part of the larger military engagements during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Blanchetaque: The English defeat the French

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1346, the English army, utilizing longbowmen and gunpowder for the first time in European warfare, defeated the French at the Battle of Crécy. This pivotal battle marked a turning point in the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Crécy: The English defeat the French

events.enhanced_description: From September to October 1346, Anglo-Gascon forces launched offensives that overran significant portions of southwest France, further establishing English dominance in the region during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Anglo-Gascon offensives overrun large parts of southwest France

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1346, the English forces initiated the siege of Calais, a strategic port city. This siege would become one of the most significant military operations of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The English begin the siege of Calais

events.enhanced_description: In October and November 1346, the Black Death led to the depopulation of several Mongol towns in the Crimea, marking the early stages of a pandemic that would sweep across Europe.
events.name: Several Mongol towns in the Crimea are cleared of inhabitants by the Black Death

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1346, the English army captured and sacked the French city of Poitiers, further demonstrating their military prowess during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: The English capture and sack the French city of Poitiers

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1346, the English army achieved a significant victory over the Scots at the Battle of Neville's Cross, reinforcing English dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Neville's Cross: The English army defeats the Scots

events.enhanced_description: In 1347, an agreement was reached in Constantinople to reorganize the Byzantine Empire's affairs, culminating in the marriage of John V Palaiologos to Helena, the daughter of John VI Kantakouzenos. This alliance aimed to stabilize the empire amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Agreement reorganizing Byzantine Empire's affairs

events.enhanced_description: In 1347, Genoese ships fleeing the Black Death in Theodosia stopped in Constantinople, inadvertently contaminating the city with the plague. This event significantly contributed to the spread of the disease throughout the region.

image.caption: Map showing the spread of the Black Death in Europe between 1346 and 1353.

" The origin and early spread of the Black Death in Italy: first evidence of plague victims from 14th-century Liguria (northern Italy) ". Anthropological Science 125 (1): 15–24. DOI : 10.1537/ase.161011 . ISSN 0918-7960 . (page 17)
image.date_qualification: Map depicts the period 1346–1353; the image itself is dated 2018-02-15.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Genoese ships contaminate Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In late 1347, Pope Clement VI successfully united the upper-class nobility of Rome to expel Cola di Rienzo from the city. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within Rome, showcasing the influence of the papacy.
events.name: Pope Clement VI unites nobility against Cola di Rienzo

events.enhanced_description: In late 1347, King Philip VI of France convened the Estates General to seek funding for military efforts against the English during the ongoing Hundred Years' War. This meeting highlighted the financial strains faced by the French monarchy.
events.name: King Phillip of France meets with Estates General

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1347, Charles University was founded in Prague by a papal bull issued by Pope Clement VI at the request of Charles IV, King of Bohemia. It became the first university in Central Europe and played a crucial role in the development of higher education in the region.

image.caption: Building of the Faculty of Arts of Charles University in Prague, at Palach Square.
image.credit: VitVit — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2016 photograph of a university building, serving as a site image; it does not depict the university’s 1347 founding.
