events.name: Charles University in Prague is founded

events.enhanced_description: The Byzantine civil war of 1341-1347 concluded on February 2, 1347, with John VI Kantakouzenos entering Constantinople, marking a significant shift in power within the Byzantine Empire. This conflict was characterized by a struggle between Kantakouzenos and the regency for the young Emperor John V Palaiologos.

image.caption: Map of the Byzantine, Ottoman and Serbian empires and neighboring states.
image.credit: William Robert Shepherd — William R. Shepherd 's Historical Atlas , p. 89, published by Henry Holt and Company, New York 1911
image.date_qualification: The map depicts 1355, after the 1347 event; 1911 is the map's publication date, not its depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Byzantine civil war ends with Kantakouzenos entering Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1347, the Maona of Chios and Phocaea was established to manage the overseas possessions of the Republic of Genoa. This organization played a crucial role in the administration and economic exploitation of Genoese territories in the Aegean Sea.
events.name: Formation of the Maona of Chios and Phocaea

events.enhanced_description: In April 1347, the Knights Hospitaller achieved a significant victory against a Turkish fleet off the coast of Imbros, sinking approximately 100 ships. This battle underscored the military prowess of the Knights during a period of increasing conflict in the region.
events.name: Knights Hospitaller defeat Turkish fleet

events.enhanced_description: In May 1347, a significant political agreement was finalized in Constantinople, as John V Palaiologos married Helena, the daughter of John VI Kantakouzenos. This union was intended to stabilize the Byzantine Empire amidst ongoing internal strife.
events.name: Marriage agreement in Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1347, Cola di Rienzo, a Roman commoner, proclaimed himself Emperor of Rome in a bold response to the ongoing power struggles among the city's barons. His declaration aimed to restore the glory of the Roman Republic but ultimately led to his downfall.
events.name: Cola di Rienzo declares himself Emperor of Rome

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1347, the Islamic Bahmani Kingdom was established on the Indian subcontinent, marking a significant development in the region's political landscape. This kingdom would become one of the major powers in South India, influencing culture and trade.
events.name: Establishment of the Bahmani Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In September 1347, during the Hundred Years' War, the English forces successfully captured the strategic port city of Calais. This victory was pivotal for England, providing a crucial foothold in France and facilitating further military campaigns.
events.name: English win Calais during Hundred Years' War

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1347, the Black Death reached the French port city of Marseille, marking the beginning of a devastating pandemic that would sweep across Europe. The arrival of the plague had catastrophic effects on the population and economy.
events.name: Black Death reaches Marseille

events.enhanced_description: In October 1347, ships arrived in the Sicilian city of Messina carrying individuals afflicted with the Black Death. This event marked a critical point in the spread of the plague throughout Europe, leading to widespread mortality.
events.name: Black Death arrives in Messina

events.enhanced_description: In November 1347, Pope Clement VI united the upper-class nobility of Rome to expel Cola di Rienzo from the city. This event highlighted the ongoing power struggles in Rome and the influence of the papacy in political affairs.
events.name: Pope Clement VI drives Cola di Rienzo out of Rome

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1347, the Black Death spread to Aix-en-Provence, contributing to the widespread devastation caused by the plague across Europe. The disease's rapid transmission led to significant social and economic upheaval.
events.name: Black Death spreads to Aix-en-Provence

events.enhanced_description: In December 1347, the plague struck the island of Mallorca, further spreading the devastation of the Black Death throughout the Mediterranean. The impact of the plague would have lasting effects on the island's population and economy.
events.name: Plague hits Mallorca

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1347, Pembroke College was founded in the University of Cambridge by Marie de St Pol, Countess of Pembroke. This institution has since become one of the leading colleges in the university, contributing to the academic landscape of England.
events.name: Pembroke College founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1347, the first cases of the plague were recorded in the city of Split, Croatia. This marked the beginning of the city's struggle against the Black Death, which would lead to significant loss of life.
events.name: First cases of plague in Split

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1347, the Republic of Genoa borrowed at a high interest rate from an association of creditors known as the Compera nuova acquisitionis Corsicæ to fund military operations in Corsica. This financial maneuver reflects the economic pressures faced by the Republic during this period.
events.name: Genoa borrows for military operations in Corsica

events.enhanced_description: In January 1348, Gonville Hall, the precursor to Gonville and Caius College, was founded in Cambridge, England. This institution has played a significant role in the history of higher education in the UK.
events.name: Gonville Hall founded

events.enhanced_description: The Black Death pandemic, which began in Asia, spread to central and western Europe and reached Cairo by 1348. This catastrophic event would lead to unprecedented mortality rates and social upheaval across the continent.
events.name: The Black Death pandemic spreads to central and western Europe and to Cairo

events.enhanced_description: In 1348, Stefan the Mighty, the Emperor of Serbia, successfully conquered the regions of Thessaly and Epirus, expanding Serbian influence in the Balkans during a period of regional instability. This conquest played a crucial role in the territorial dynamics of the region.
events.name: Stefan the Mighty, Emperor of Serbia, conquers Thessaly and Epirus

events.enhanced_description: The Pskov Republic gained independence from the Novgorod Republic through the treaty of Bolotovo in 1348. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region, allowing Pskov to establish itself as a separate entity.
events.name: The Pskov Republic gains independence from the Novgorod Republic with the treaty of Bolotovo

events.enhanced_description: The ongoing Hundred Years' War between England and France saw a de facto truce emerge by 1348 due to the devastating effects of the Black Death. This temporary cessation of hostilities lasted until 1355, as both nations grappled with the pandemic's impact.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: The effects of the Black Death cause a de facto truce between England and France

events.enhanced_description: By 1348, Hangzhou in Mongolian China was estimated to have become the largest city in the world, surpassing Cairo. This shift highlighted the economic and cultural prominence of Hangzhou during the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Estimation: Hangzhou in Mongolian China becomes the largest city of the world

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1348, a 6.9-magnitude earthquake struck Friuli, Northern Italy, and was felt across Europe. This seismic event was contemporaneously linked to the fears surrounding the Black Death, as many believed it signified the onset of the Apocalypse.
events.name: Friuli earthquake felt across Europe

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1348, the Battle of Strėva took place, where the Teutonic Order secured a victory over the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. This battle was significant in the ongoing conflicts between the two powers, although the impact was somewhat muted due to the Black Death.
events.name: Battle of Strėva

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1348, Charles IV granted privileges to Charles University in Prague, which had been founded the previous year. This act solidified the university's status and importance in the academic landscape of Central Europe.
events.name: Privileges granted to Charles University

events.enhanced_description: In 1348, Edward III established the Most Noble Order of the Garter, the first English order of chivalry, at Windsor Castle. This prestigious order was created to promote the ideals of knighthood and loyalty among the English nobility.
events.name: Edward III of England creates the first English order of chivalry, the Most Noble Order of the Garter

events.enhanced_description: By June 24, 1348, the Black Death pandemic reached England, likely brought by fleas on rats from a ship arriving at the port of Melcombe (modern-day Weymouth). The disease would spread rapidly, leading to devastating mortality rates across the country.
events.name: The Black Death pandemic reaches England

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1348, Pope Clement VI issued a papal bull aimed at protecting Jewish communities from violence and persecution during the Black Death. This was a significant act in a time when Jews were unjustly blamed for the plague.
events.name: A papal bull is issued by Pope Clement VI, protecting Jews against popular aggression during the Black Death pandemic

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1348, the anti-royalist Union of Valencia launched an attack against the Jewish community of Murviedro (modern Sagunto), viewing them as royalists due to their status as serfs of the King of Valencia. This event exemplified the rising tensions and violence against Jews during the Black Death.
events.name: The anti-royalist Union of Valencia attacks the Jews of Murviedro

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1348, Emperor Kōmyō of Japan abdicated the throne in favor of his son, Emperor Sukō, marking a significant transition in the Northern Court during the Ashikaga period. This event was part of the ongoing power struggles within the imperial lineage.
events.name: Emperor Kōmyō of Japan abdicates the throne in favour of his son Emperor Sukō

events.enhanced_description: In 1349, the Black Death spread from England to the north, reaching Askøy and Bjørgvin (modern-day Bergen) in Norway. This marked the further expansion of the pandemic, which would have dire consequences for the population of Scandinavia.
events.name: The Black Death in England spreads to the north

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1349, a devastating earthquake struck L'Aquila in southern Italy, registering a maximum Mercalli intensity of X (Extreme). The disaster caused severe damage to the city and resulted in approximately 2,000 fatalities.
events.name: An earthquake affects L'Aquila in southern Italy

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1349, during the height of the Black Death, approximately 2,000 Jews were burned to death in Strasbourg, as they were scapegoated for the plague. This tragic event marked one of the darkest moments of persecution against Jewish communities in Europe.
events.name: Strasbourg massacre during the Black Death

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1349, the entire Jewish community in the remote village of Saulgau, Germany, was wiped out during the Black Death persecutions. This event reflects the widespread violence and scapegoating faced by Jews across Europe during this period.
events.name: The entire Jewish community in Saulgau is wiped out

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1349, the Jewish community of Erfurt, Germany, was subjected to a brutal pogrom, resulting in murder and expulsion. This massacre was part of the widespread anti-Jewish sentiment that escalated during the Black Death.
events.name: Erfurt massacre during the Black Death

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1349, an earthquake struck Meaux Abbey in England, causing significant damage to the structure. This event was part of a series of seismic activities that affected various regions in Europe during this period.
events.name: An earthquake strikes Meaux Abbey in England

events.enhanced_description: By May 1349, the Black Death pandemic had ceased in Ireland, marking a significant turning point for the population that had endured the ravages of the plague. The cessation allowed for recovery and rebuilding in the affected communities.
events.name: The Black Death ceases in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1349, in Breslau (modern Wrocław), Silesia, 60 Jews were murdered following a disastrous fire that destroyed part of the city. This incident exemplified the scapegoating of Jewish communities during the Black Death.
events.name: In Breslau, Silesia, 60 Jews are murdered following a disastrous fire

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1349, the Black Death pandemic broke out in Elbing (modern Elbląg), Poland. This marked the spread of the plague further into Eastern Europe, contributing to the widespread devastation already felt across the continent.
events.name: The Black Death breaks out in Elbing (Poland)

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1349, a series of earthquakes struck the Apennine region of Italy, causing extensive damage in Rome, including the collapse of part of the Colosseum. This natural disaster added to the turmoil of the era marked by the Black Death.
events.name: 1349 Apennine earthquakes

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1349, Pope Clement VI issued a papal bull condemning the Flagellants, a movement that arose during the Black Death, advocating for public penance through self-flagellation. The bull aimed to curb the excesses and violence associated with this movement.
events.name: Pope Clement VI publishes a papal bull that condemns the Flagellants

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1349, the renowned Moroccan explorer Ibn Battuta arrived in Fez, Morocco. His travels would later be documented in 'The Rihla', providing invaluable insights into the cultures and societies of the 14th century.
events.name: Ibn Battuta arrives in Fez, Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1349, Pope Clement VI annulled the marriage between William Montacute, 2nd Earl of Salisbury, and Joan of Kent due to her prior marriage to Thomas Holland. This decision reflected the complexities of noble marriages and papal authority during the period.
events.name: Pope Clement VI annuls the marriage of William Montacute, 2nd Earl of Salisbury, and Joan of Kent

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1349, Alexios III ascended to the throne of Trebizond, effectively ending the Trapezuntine Civil Wars. His reign marked a period of relative stability for the region amidst the broader geopolitical challenges of the time.
events.name: The rise of Alexios III of Trebizond to the throne ends the Trapezuntine Civil Wars

events.enhanced_description: In 1350, Hayam Wuruk ascended to the throne of the Majapahit Empire, a significant power in Southeast Asia. His reign is noted for the expansion of the empire and the promotion of Hindu-Buddhist culture across the region.
events.name: Hayam Wuruk becomes ruler of the Majapahit Empire

events.enhanced_description: The Punta Lobos massacre, occurring in 1350, was a tragic event where members of the Chimu Empire perpetrated a violent attack resulting in the deaths of approximately 200 individuals. This incident highlighted the internal conflicts and power struggles within pre-Columbian Peru.
events.name: Punta Lobos massacre

events.enhanced_description: In 1350, the Black Death made its first appearances in Scotland and Sweden, marking the beginning of a devastating pandemic that would sweep across Europe. This outbreak had profound social, economic, and demographic impacts on both regions.
events.name: The Black Death first appears in Scotland and Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1350, Rudolf Brun, the mayor of Zürich, ordered the destruction of Rapperswil Castle, a significant stronghold in the region. This act was part of the broader conflicts between the growing power of urban centers and the feudal nobility in Switzerland.
events.name: Destruction of Rapperswil Castle

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1350, Giovanni II Valente was elected as the Doge of Genoa. His leadership would play a significant role in the maritime and commercial activities of the city-state during a tumultuous period in Italian history.
events.name: Giovanni II Valente becomes Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The Hook and Cod wars were a series of conflicts in the County of Holland during the 14th century, primarily between the progressive cities supporting William V and the conservative nobility led by his mother, Margaret I. The formation of the Cod League and the signing of the Cod Alliance Treaty marked significant political maneuvering in this power struggle.
events.name: Hook and Cod wars in the County of Holland

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Winchelsea, fought on August 29, 1350, was a naval engagement where an English fleet commanded by King Edward III decisively defeated a Castilian fleet. This victory solidified England's naval dominance during the early stages of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Winchelsea

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1350, the Republic of Genoa secured a loan at a steep interest rate of 10% from a group of creditors known as the Compera imposita per gerra Venetorum. This financial maneuver was crucial for funding their military efforts against the Republic of Venice.
events.name: Genoa's loan for war expenses

events.enhanced_description: The Red Turban Rebellions erupted in China around 1351, leading to significant unrest and the eventual weakening of the Mongolian-run Yuan dynasty. This series of uprisings was fueled by widespread discontent among the populace and marked a turning point in Chinese history.
events.name: Red Turban Rebellions

events.enhanced_description: In 1351, King Gongmin ascended to the throne of Goryeo, a period marked by efforts to strengthen royal authority and reduce the influence of powerful families. His reign would see significant changes in the political landscape of Korea.
events.name: King Gongmin ascends the throne in Goryeo

events.enhanced_description: In 1351, the region of Vantaa in Finland was first mentioned in historical records as Helsinge. This mention marks an important point in the documentation of Finnish history and the development of local governance.
events.name: First mention of Vantaa

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1351, King Edward III of England instituted the Treason Act, which defined treason in English law for the first time. This act has had a lasting impact on the legal framework of the United Kingdom, remaining in effect into the 21st century.
events.name: Treason Act 1351

events.enhanced_description: In February 1351, the Parliament of England enacted the Statute of Labourers to address the severe labor shortages caused by the Black Death. This legislation aimed to regulate wages and working conditions, reflecting the social upheaval of the time.
events.name: Statute of Labourers

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1351, King Uthong, also known as Ramathibodi I, established the Ayutthaya Kingdom in modern-day Thailand. His reign marked the beginning of a prosperous era characterized by the promotion of Theravada Buddhism as the state religion.
events.name: Establishment of the Ayutthaya Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1351, Firuz Shah Tughlaq succeeded Mohammad Tughlaq as the ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. His reign is noted for significant administrative reforms and the establishment of a more stable government.
events.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq succeeds Mohammad Tughlaq

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1351, during the War of the Breton Succession, the Combat of the Thirty took place, where thirty knights from both France and England fought to determine the rightful ruler of Brittany. The battle ended in a Franco-Breton victory, significantly impacting the succession dispute.
events.name: Combat of the Thirty

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1351, the Battle of Saintes occurred during the Hundred Years' War, where the French forces faced defeat against the English. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict for control over French territories.
events.name: Battle of Saintes

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Taillebourg, fought on April 8, 1351, was another significant engagement in the Hundred Years' War, resulting in a French defeat at the hands of the English forces. This battle further illustrated the challenges faced by the French monarchy during the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Taillebourg

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1351, the city of Zürich officially joined the Old Swiss Confederacy, marking a significant expansion of this alliance of cantons. This union would play a crucial role in the political landscape of Switzerland.
events.name: Zürich joins the Old Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1351, Emperor Sukō abdicated as the third Emperor of the Northern Court of Japan, a significant event during the Nanboku-chō period. His abdication marked a pivotal moment in the ongoing power struggles between the Northern and Southern courts.
events.name: Emperor Sukō abdicates

events.enhanced_description: In October 1352, during the Byzantine civil war, the Battle of Demotika saw the Ottoman beylik achieve its first victory on European soil, fighting alongside John VI Kantakouzenos against Serbian forces. This battle marked a significant moment in the expansion of Ottoman influence in the Balkans.
events.name: Battle of Demotika

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, Süleyman Pasha, the son of Orhan, was granted control of Çimpe Castle by Byzantine Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos. This event marked the first territorial acquisition of the Ottoman Empire west of the Bosporus, setting the stage for further expansion into Europe.
events.name: Süleyman Pasha is granted control of Çimpe Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, the Bengal Sultanate was established when the realms of Satgaon, Lakhnauti, and Sonargaon united under the leadership of Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah. This unification marked a significant development in the political landscape of Bengal, leading to a period of prosperity and cultural flourishing.
events.name: The Bengal Sultanate is formed

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, the noble Vlach Dragoș, arriving from Hungary, was recognized as the first voivode of Moldova, establishing the foundations of this principality. His leadership is often regarded as the beginning of Moldovan statehood, although some sources suggest this event may have occurred as early as 1345.
events.name: Dragoș becomes the first voivode of Moldova

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father Basarab, Nicholas Alexander ascended to the position of voivode of Wallachia in 1352, having served as co-ruler for approximately eight years. His reign would be characterized by efforts to consolidate power and navigate the complex political landscape of the region.
events.name: Nicholas Alexander becomes voivode of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, the town of Biel/Bienne in Switzerland finalized its alliance with the city of Bern, strengthening their political and military ties. This alliance was part of the broader context of the Old Swiss Confederacy's formation and expansion during the late medieval period.
events.name: Biel/Bienne finalizes alliance with Bern

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, Lionel of Antwerp, a prominent English noble, married Elizabeth, the daughter of William de Burgh, 3rd Earl of Ulster. This marriage was significant in strengthening ties between English and Irish nobility during a time of political turbulence.
events.name: Lionel of Antwerp marries Elizabeth de Burgh

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, Reginald de Cobham, 1st Baron Cobham, was appointed as a Companion of the Most Noble Order of the Garter, one of the highest honors in England. This recognition highlighted his loyalty and service to the English crown during a period marked by political strife.
events.name: Reginald de Cobham becomes a Companion of the Order of the Garter

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, the Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church began relocating back to Kyiv after having moved to Halych in 1299. This move was significant as it restored the ecclesiastical authority in Kyiv, which had been a center of Christianity in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Metropolitan of Halych relocates back to Kyiv

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, Zhu Yuanzhang, a penniless peasant and former Buddhist monk, joined the Red Turban Rebellions against the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty in China. His involvement in this uprising would eventually lead him to become the first emperor of the Ming dynasty, marking a significant shift in Chinese history.
events.name: Zhu Yuanzhang joins the Red Turban Rebellions

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, Tommaso da Modena created a fresco in the chapter house of the Dominican convent of San Nicolò in Treviso, depicting Hugh of Saint-Cher wearing spectacles. This artwork is considered the earliest surviving illustration of spectacles, highlighting advancements in vision correction during the medieval period.
events.name: Earliest surviving illustration of spectacles

events.enhanced_description: In 1352, the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta documented the existence of the ngoni and balafon musical instruments at the court of Mansa Musa, the famed ruler of the Mali Empire. This account provides valuable insight into the cultural richness and musical traditions of West Africa during this period.
events.name: Ibn Battuta reports musical instruments at Mansa Musa's court

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1352, the canton of Glarus joined the Old Swiss Confederacy, further strengthening the alliance among the Swiss cantons. This expansion was significant for the political dynamics of the region.
events.name: Glarus joins the Old Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1352, Zug became a member of the Old Swiss Confederacy, marking another step in the formation of a powerful alliance among the Swiss cantons. This union would play a crucial role in the region's political landscape.
events.name: Zug joins the Old Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1352, Emperor Go-Kōgon ascended as the fourth Emperor of the Northern Court of Japan during the Nanboku-chō period. His reign was characterized by continued conflict between the Northern and Southern courts.

image.caption: Signature of Emperor Go-Kōgon, reproduced from a document.
image.credit: 後光嚴天皇 — 《後光厳院御文類》（局部）
image.date_qualification: A signature associated with Emperor Go-Kōgon, dated 1362-01-01; it is not a depiction of his 1352 accession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Emperor Go-Kōgon becomes 4th Emperor of the Northern Court of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1352, Corpus Christi College was founded as part of the University of Cambridge by the Guilds of Corpus Christi and the Blessed Virgin Mary. This institution has since become one of the prominent colleges within the university, contributing to its rich academic heritage.

image.caption: New Court at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, England.
image.credit: Diliff — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2014 photograph of the college site, not a depiction of its 1352 foundation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Corpus Christi College

events.enhanced_description: Pope Innocent VI, born Étienne Aubert, was elected as the 199th pope on December 18, 1352, succeeding Pope Clement VI. His papacy would be marked by efforts to restore the authority of the papacy and address the challenges posed by the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Pope Innocent VI succeeds Pope Clement VI as the 199th pope

events.enhanced_description: The Earldom of Kent, created for William de Montacute, became extinct on December 26, 1352, following the death of the last earl. This marked a significant moment in the shifting power dynamics of English nobility during the 14th century.
figures: William de Montacute, 2nd Earl of Salisbury
events.name: The Earldom of Kent of the 5th creation in England becomes extinct

events.enhanced_description: In 1353, the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta made his first recorded visit to Timbuktu and Kabara while returning from a stay in the capital of the Mali Empire. His accounts of these cities contributed significantly to the understanding of West African culture and trade during the medieval period.
events.name: Ibn Battuta visits Timbuktu and Kabara

events.enhanced_description: In 1353, Giovanni Boccaccio completed his renowned work, 'The Decameron,' a collection of novellas that provides a vivid portrayal of life during the Black Death. This literary masterpiece is celebrated for its rich storytelling and insight into human nature.
events.name: The Decameron is finished by Giovanni Boccaccio

events.enhanced_description: By 1353, the Black Death, which had ravaged Europe since 1331, began to subside. This pandemic had profound effects on the social, economic, and cultural landscape of Europe, leading to significant changes in population and labor dynamics.
events.name: The Black Death subsides

events.enhanced_description: In 1353, Fa Ngum founded the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang, which would become a significant power in Southeast Asia. This kingdom is notable for its cultural and political achievements, including the promotion of Theravada Buddhism.
events.name: The Lao kingdom of Lan Xang is founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1353, Bern signed an alliance with the Old Swiss Confederacy, solidifying its position within the growing network of Swiss alliances. This agreement was crucial for the defense and autonomy of the Swiss regions during the tumultuous medieval period.

image.caption: Map showing the territorial development of the Old Swiss Confederacy from 1291 to 1797.
image.credit: Marco Zanoli ( Sidonius ) — Eigenes Werk (own work); according to Adolf Gasser: Die territoriale Entwicklung der Eidgenossenschaft 1291–1797 . Sauerländer, Aarau 1932.
image.date_qualification: The map’s stated original date is 2009-04-09; it depicts territorial development across 1291–1797, not the event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Bern signs an alliance with the Old Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: In early 1354, Ibn Battuta returned from his extensive travels at the command of Abu Inan Faris, the Sultan of Morocco. His journeys would later be documented, providing invaluable insights into the cultures and societies he encountered.
events.name: Ibn Battuta returns from travels

events.enhanced_description: In March 1354, following a devastating earthquake, the Ottomans besieged and captured Gallipoli, marking it as their first stronghold in Europe. This conquest was pivotal for the Ottoman expansion into the Balkans.
events.name: Ottomans capture Gallipoli

events.enhanced_description: In 1354, after years of struggle for independence since the Battle of Posada, Nicholas Alexander of Wallachia became a vassal to King Louis I of Hungary. This relationship would influence the political landscape of Eastern Europe for years to come.
events.name: Nicholas Alexander becomes a vassal to Louis I of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In 1354, Sahab-ud-Din ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Kashmir, marking a significant moment in the region's history. His reign is noted for its cultural and political developments within the Kashmir Valley.
events.name: Sahab-ud-Din becomes Sultan of Kashmir

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1354, the Treaty of Stralsund was signed, resolving long-standing border disputes between the duchies of Mecklenburg and Pomerania. This treaty was significant in stabilizing the region and establishing clearer territorial boundaries.
events.name: The Treaty of Stralsund settles border disputes

events.enhanced_description: During the night between March 1 and 2, 1354, a strong earthquake struck Gallipoli, causing widespread destruction to the city and its defenses. This disaster weakened the town's fortifications, making it vulnerable to subsequent military actions.
events.name: Earthquake destroys Gallipoli

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1354, Cola di Rienzo, the self-proclaimed 'tribune' of Rome, was killed by an angry mob. His death marked the end of his tumultuous attempts to restore the glory of ancient Rome and highlighted the volatile political climate of the city.
events.name: Cola di Rienzo is killed by an angry mob

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1354, John VI Kantakouzenos was deposed as Byzantine Emperor after John V Palaiologos retook Constantinople. This event marked a significant shift in Byzantine politics and the ongoing power struggles within the empire.
events.name: John VI Kantakouzenos is deposed

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ihtiman occurred in 1355, where the Ottoman Turks defeated the Bulgarian Empire. This battle was part of the Ottoman expansion into the Balkans, which would have lasting implications for the region.
events.name: Battle of Ihtiman

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1355, Charles IV of Bohemia was crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy in Milan, solidifying his claim to the Italian throne. This event was part of his broader efforts to strengthen the Holy Roman Empire and his own authority.
events.name: Charles IV of Bohemia crowned King of Italy

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1355, Inês de Castro, the beloved of Prince Peter of Portugal, was assassinated on the orders of King Alphonso IV. This act incited a civil war led by Peter, who sought vengeance for her death, profoundly impacting the Portuguese monarchy.
events.name: Inês de Castro assassination

events.enhanced_description: The St Scholastica Day riot erupted on February 10, 1355, in Oxford, resulting in the deaths of 63 scholars and around 30 locals over two days. This violent conflict highlighted the tensions between the townspeople and the university students.
events.name: St Scholastica Day riot

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1355, during the Red Turban Rebellions, Han Lin'er, claiming descent from Emperor Huizong of Song, was proclaimed emperor in Bozhou. This event marked a significant moment in the struggle against the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Han Lin'er proclaimed emperor

events.enhanced_description: In April 1355, Philip II, Prince of Taranto, married Maria of Calabria, the daughter of Charles, Duke of Calabria. This marriage was significant in strengthening political alliances in the region.
events.name: Philip II marries Maria of Calabria

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1355, Charles IV was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome, a pivotal moment that reinforced his authority and the significance of the Holy Roman Empire in European politics.
events.name: Charles IV crowned Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1355, Doge Marin Falier was executed by beheading by the Council of Ten in Venice for conspiring against them. This event underscored the political tensions and power struggles within the Venetian government.
events.name: Marin Falier beheaded

events.enhanced_description: In May 1355, Guo Zixing, a leader in the Red Turban Rebellion, passed away, leaving his forces to his son-in-law, Zhu Yuanzhang. His death marked a turning point in the rebellion, as Zhu would later rise to prominence.
events.name: Guo Zixing dies

events.enhanced_description: In August 1355, the Scottish army achieved a decisive victory over the English at the Battle of Nesbit Moor. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between Scotland and England during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Nesbit Moor

events.enhanced_description: In September 1355, the old town of Visoki was first mentioned in a charter by Tvrtko I of Bosnia, marking its historical significance in the region. This charter indicated the town's importance in the medieval Bosnian state.

locations.name: Visoki, Zenica-Doboj Canton, Bosnia and Herzegovina

events.name: First mention of Visoki

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1355, during the Hundred Years' War, Edward the Black Prince led a large mounted Anglo-Gascon force on a chevauchée from Bordeaux to Narbonne, devastating French territory along the way. This military campaign exemplified the tactics used by the English during the war.
events.name: Black Prince's chevauchée

events.enhanced_description: In 1356, the Hanseatic League, a powerful trading alliance among various cities in northern Europe, held its first meeting. This coalition significantly influenced trade and commerce in the region for centuries.
events.name: Hanseatic League first meeting

events.enhanced_description: In 1356, Stockholm issued its first guild privileges for tailors, marking a significant development in the organization of trades and crafts in Sweden. This initiative laid the groundwork for future guild systems in the country.
events.name: First guild privileges in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1356, Ghazan II succeeded Anushirwan as the ruler of the Ilkhanate in Persia. His reign was marked by efforts to stabilize the region and manage the complex political landscape of the time.
events.name: Ghazan II replaces Anushirwan

events.enhanced_description: In 1356, Zhu Yuanzhang captured Nanjing from the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty during the Red Turban Rebellion. This victory established Nanjing as his base of power, leading to the founding of the Ming dynasty in 1368.
events.name: Zhu Yuanzhang captures Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: In 1356, Bahri Sultan An-Nasir Hasan ordered the removal of the majority of the Great Pyramid of Giza's limestone casing stones to construct fortresses and mosques in Cairo. This act left the ancient wonder in its current step-stone condition.
events.name: Removal of casing stones from the Great Pyramid

events.enhanced_description: The Castelvecchio Bridge, designed by architect Alberto Cavalli, is completed in Verona, Italy. At the time, its main span of 48.7 meters (160 feet) is the longest arch in the world, showcasing advanced medieval engineering and serving as a vital connection across the Adige River.
events.name: Completion of the Castelvecchio Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1356, Edward Balliol surrendered his claim to the Scottish throne to Edward III of England, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between Scotland and England.
events.name: Edward Balliol surrenders title

events.enhanced_description: In February 1356, Edward III of England ordered the burning of every town and village in Lothian, Scotland, in a brutal campaign during the ongoing conflicts with Scotland. This act of destruction was part of the larger context of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Burnt Candlemas

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1356, the city of Lwów was granted Magdeburg rights by Casimir III of Poland, enhancing its political and economic status. This legal framework allowed for greater autonomy and self-governance.
events.name: Lwów granted Magdeburg rights

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, the English forces led by Edward the Black Prince achieved a stunning victory at the Battle of Poitiers, capturing the French King John II. This battle significantly shifted the balance of power in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Poitiers

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1356, Erik XII proclaimed himself king of Sweden in opposition to his father, King Magnus IV. This declaration initiated a civil war that would last until Erik's death in 1359.
events.name: Erik XII proclaims himself king

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1356, the Basel earthquake struck northern Switzerland, causing widespread destruction and resulting in approximately 1,000 deaths. It is recorded as one of the most devastating earthquakes in central Europe.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Basel earthquake, envisioned by painter Karl Jauslin.
image.credit: Karl Jauslin — upload by Parpan
image.date_qualification: The event is dated 18 October 1356 in the article excerpt. No depicted date is supplied; the 2008 metadata date is an upload date, not the date of the scene or artwork.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Basel earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1356, Charles IV promulgated the Golden Bull, a fundamental constitutional document for the Holy Roman Empire. This decree established important regulations regarding the election of the emperor and the rights of the princes.
events.name: Golden Bull promulgated

events.enhanced_description: The Blue Horde successfully unseats Ghazan II as the ruler of the Il-Khanate, appointing their own governor in his place. This event signifies the declining influence of the Il-Khanate and the rise of regional powers in the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Unseating of Ghazan II by the Blue Horde

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Bubat, the Sundanese royal family is massacred by the Majapahit Army under the orders of Gajah Mada. The battle results in the deaths of King Lingga Buana and Princess Dyah Pitaloka Citraresmi, who tragically commits suicide, marking a significant event in the history of Indonesian kingdoms.
events.name: Battle of Bubat

events.enhanced_description: Rao Kanhadev ascends as the Rathore ruler of Marwar, a region in present-day Rajasthan, India. His rule marks a significant period in the history of the Rathore dynasty, which played a crucial role in the region's politics and culture.
events.name: Rao Kanhadev becomes Rathore ruler of Marwar

events.enhanced_description: Influenza is first identified as a distinct disease, marking a significant advancement in medical understanding. This identification lays the groundwork for future studies and public health responses to influenza outbreaks.
events.name: First identification of Influenza as a disease

events.enhanced_description: The first public exhibition of the Shroud of Turin is recorded, showcasing this significant religious artifact. The shroud is believed by many to be the burial cloth of Jesus Christ, and its exhibition attracts considerable attention and devotion.
events.name: First public exhibition of the Shroud of Turin

events.enhanced_description: The Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat, also known as the Famous Wat Yai, is constructed in Phitsanulok, Thailand. This temple becomes an important center of worship and a significant cultural site in the region.
events.name: Construction of Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat Temple

events.enhanced_description: The Estates General convenes in Paris, where Étienne Marcel presents the Great Ordinance aimed at limiting the powers of the monarchy, particularly in fiscal and monetary matters. This meeting marks a significant moment in the struggle for political reform in France during the 14th century.
events.name: Meeting of the Estates General in France

events.enhanced_description: Erik Magnusson is recognized as the king of most of Sweden, opposing his father, King Magnus IV Eriksson. This recognition reflects the ongoing power struggles within the Swedish monarchy during a tumultuous period in the nation's history.
events.name: Erik Magnusson recognized as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Peter I ascends to the throne of Portugal following the death of his father, Alfonso IV. His reign is marked by significant political and social changes, including conflicts with the nobility and efforts to strengthen royal authority.
events.name: Peter I becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: Construction formally begins on the Charles Bridge in Prague, a key architectural project that will connect the Old Town and Lesser Town across the Vltava River. This bridge will later become an iconic symbol of the city and a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.
events.name: Construction begins on Charles Bridge

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Jani Beg, his son Berdi Beg is recognized as Khan of the Blue Horde. To secure his position, Berdi Beg orders the execution of at least twelve close relatives, illustrating the brutal power struggles within the Mongol khanates.
events.name: Succession of Berdi Beg as Khan of the Blue Horde

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Berwick concludes the Second War of Scottish Independence, resulting in the release of King David II of Scotland by the English in exchange for a substantial ransom. This treaty marks a pivotal moment in the ongoing conflict between Scotland and England.
events.name: Treaty of Berwick

events.enhanced_description: Mubariz al-Din Muhammad, leader of the Arab Muzaffarid tribe, expels the Blue Horde from Ilkhanate territory in Persia. This event leads to the disbanding of the Ilkhanate and the rise of the Jalayirid dynasty, marking a significant shift in regional power.
events.name: Expulsion of the Blue Horde from Persia

events.enhanced_description: Shah Shuja successfully overthrows his father, Mubarazuddin Muhammad, to become the leader of the Muzaffarid tribe. This power shift reflects the internal dynamics and struggles within the Muzaffarid dynasty.
events.name: Shah Shuja overthrows Mubarazuddin Muhammad

events.enhanced_description: Nanjing in Yuan China is estimated to become the largest city in the world, surpassing Hangzhou. This shift reflects the significant urbanization and economic development occurring in China during the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Nanjing becomes the largest city in the world

events.enhanced_description: Muhammad II as Said ascends to the throne of the Marinid dynasty in Morocco following the assassination of his predecessor, Abu Inan Faris. His reign will be marked by efforts to consolidate power and navigate the complexities of Moroccan politics.
events.name: Muhammad II as Said becomes ruler of the Marinid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Mohammed Shah I ascends as the Bahmani Sultan of Deccan, succeeding Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah. His rule will influence the political landscape of southern India during a period of significant cultural and economic development.
events.name: Mohammed Shah I becomes Bahmani Sultan

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Zadar is signed between Louis I of Hungary/Croatia and the Republic of Venice, resulting in the Venetians losing influence over their former Dalmatian holdings. This treaty reshapes the political landscape of the Adriatic region.
events.name: Treaty of Zadar

events.enhanced_description: King Haakon VI of Norway designates Skien as a city with trading privileges, elevating its status and contributing to its development as a commercial center. This decision reflects the growing importance of urban centers in medieval Norway.
events.name: King Haakon VI designates Skien as a city

events.enhanced_description: The Jacquerie, a peasant rebellion, erupts in France, fueled by social unrest and economic hardship. The rebellion consumes the region of Beauvais and aligns with Étienne Marcel's earlier seizure of Paris, highlighting the growing discontent among the lower classes.
events.name: Jacquerie peasant rebellion begins in France

events.enhanced_description: The Republic of Ragusa is founded after gaining independence from the Republic of Venice. This marks the beginning of a new political entity that will play a significant role in the Adriatic trade and diplomacy.
events.name: Foundation of the Republic of Ragusa

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Mello sees the Jacquerie rebellion decisively defeated by a coalition of nobles led by Charles II of Navarre. This battle effectively quashes the peasant uprising and restores noble power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Mello

events.enhanced_description: In August 1359, Qulpa ascended to the position of Khan of the Blue Horde following the death of Berdi Beg, a transition that reflected the ongoing power dynamics within the Mongol successor states.
events.name: Qulpa becomes Khan of the Blue Horde after the death of Berdi Beg

events.enhanced_description: In September 1359, Margaret, Countess of Tyrol, and her husband Louis V, Duke of Bavaria, were absolved from excommunication, a significant event that restored their standing within the Church and political landscape of the time.
events.name: Margaret, Countess of Tyrol, and Louis V, Duke of Bavaria, are absolved from excommunication

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, Abu Salim Ali II seized power from Muhammad II as-Said, marking a significant shift in the leadership of the Marinid dynasty in Morocco, which had profound implications for the region's political landscape.
events.name: Abu Salim Ali II overthrows Muhammad II as-Said as ruler of the Marinid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, the Zayanids, led by Abu Hamuw II, successfully recaptured the Kingdom of Tlemcen in Algeria, reinforcing their control over this strategically important region.
events.name: The Zayanids under Abu Hamuw II recapture Kingdom of Tlemcen

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, Shah Mahmud overthrew his brother Shah Shuja to become the leader of the Muzaffarid tribe in Persia, a move that would alter the power dynamics within the region.
events.name: Shah Mahmud overthrows his brother, Shah Shuja, as leader of the Muzaffarid tribe

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, Ananda Patel, considered a common ancestor for most of the modern-day population of Bhadran, migrated from Anklav, establishing a lineage that would shape the community's identity.
events.name: Ananda Patel moves to Bhadran from Anklav

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, Berlin became a member of the Hanseatic League, a powerful economic alliance of trading cities in Northern Europe, enhancing its commercial influence and connectivity.
events.name: Berlin joins the Hanseatic League

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, a Christian coalition achieved a significant victory against a Turkish raider fleet in the Battle of Megara, showcasing the ongoing conflicts between Christian and Muslim forces in the region.
events.name: Battle of Megara: A Christian coalition defeats a Turkish raider fleet

events.enhanced_description: In 1359, Bogdan I emerged as the Prince of Moldavia after liberating the region from Hungarian control, laying the foundation for a principality that would endure for centuries.

image.caption: Mural at Bogdana Monastery depicting Bogdan I at the far left.
image.credit: https://www.crestinortodox.ro/biserici-manastiri/manastirea-bogdana-67925.html
image.date_qualification: Retrospective mural, not a contemporary depiction of the 14th-century accession; image date: 2012-06-15.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Bogdan I becomes Prince of Moldavia after freeing it from Hungarian control

events.enhanced_description: The French States-General repudiates the terms of the Second Treaty of London, which had been signed earlier in the year between England and France. This rejection signifies the ongoing tensions and conflicts between the two nations during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: French States-General repudiates Second Treaty of London

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of Erik Magnusson, his claims to the Swedish throne die with him, restoring power to his father, King Magnus IV Eriksson. This event alters the political landscape of Sweden and sets the stage for future conflicts with Denmark.
events.name: Death of Erik Magnusson

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1359, Francesco II Ordelaffi, the lord of Forlì, surrendered to the Papal commander Gil de Albornoz, marking a significant moment in the power struggles of the Italian city-states during the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Francesco II Ordelaffi surrenders to the Papal commander, Gil de Albornoz

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1359, Ismail II successfully overthrew his uncle Muhammed V to become Sultan of Granada, a pivotal moment in the history of the Nasrid dynasty and the Islamic presence in Spain.
events.name: Ismail II overthrows his uncle, Muhammed V, as Sultan of Granada

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1359, the Catalan Courts convened in Cervera, leading to the establishment of the Deputation of the General of Catalonia, known as the Generalitat, which played a crucial role in the governance of Catalonia.
events.name: The Catalan Courts are held in Cervera

events.enhanced_description: In June 1360, King Valdemar IV Atterdag of Denmark launched an attack on Skåne, successfully conquering Lindholmen Castle, which was a strategic victory in his campaign to reclaim territories lost to Sweden.
events.name: Valdemar IV Atterdag attacks Skåne and conquers Lindholmen Castle

events.enhanced_description: In August 1360, peace was concluded between Sweden and Denmark through arbitration in Helsingborg, where Magnus IV Eriksson ceded significant territories to Denmark in exchange for military support against domestic threats.
events.name: Peace is concluded between Sweden and Denmark with the arbitration in Helsingborg

events.enhanced_description: During the Red Turban Rebellions in 1360, Chen Youliang assassinated Xu Shouhui in Wuchang, subsequently declaring himself the emperor of Han, which intensified the conflict against Zhu Yuanzhang's forces.

image.caption: Map depicting rebels and warlords at the end of the Yuan dynasty.
image.credit: SY — Own work
