events.name: Red Turban Rebellions: Chen Youliang murders Xu Shouhui

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, King Valdemar IV Atterdag of Denmark successfully reconquered Scania, a region that had been under Swedish control since 1332, marking a significant territorial gain for Denmark.
events.name: King Valdemar IV Atterdag of Denmark reconquers Scania

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, following the death of his brother Shah Mahmud, Shah Shuja regained control over the Muzaffarid tribe in Persia, re-establishing his authority in a tumultuous period.
events.name: Shah Shuja regains rule of the Muzaffarid tribe in Persia

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, Nawruz Beg overthrew his brother Qulpa to become the Khan of the Blue Horde, a significant shift in leadership within the Mongol successor states.
events.name: Nawruz Beg overthrows Qulpa as Khan of the Blue Horde

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, Muhammed VI successfully overthrew his brother-in-law Ismail II to become the King of Granada, continuing the turbulent history of the Nasrid dynasty.
events.name: Muhammed VI overthrows Ismail II as King of Granada

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, Dmitri Konstantinovich was installed as the ruler of Vladimir by the Khan of the White Horde, reflecting the complex political dynamics of the region during the Mongol influence.
events.name: Dmitri Konstantinovich is installed as ruler of Vladimir

events.enhanced_description: In 1360, the earliest known Kırkpınar oil wrestling tournament took place in the Ottoman Empire, a tradition that continues to be celebrated in Turkey to this day.
events.name: Earliest known Kırkpınar oil wrestling tournament in the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1360, the Treaty of Brétigny was ratified in Calais, effectively ending the first phase of the Hundred Years' War, with Edward III renouncing his claim to the French throne in exchange for territorial gains.
events.name: The Treaty of Brétigny is ratified at Calais

events.enhanced_description: In early 1361, a power struggle unfolded in the Marinid Empire, located in modern-day Morocco, leading to the overthrow of Abu Salim Ibrahim by Abu Umar. This was followed by another coup, resulting in Abu Zayyan taking control, highlighting the instability within the empire.
events.name: Overthrow of Abu Salim Ibrahim

events.enhanced_description: The Great Troubles of the Blue Horde began around 1361, characterized by a period of anarchy and instability where over 20 khans succeeded each other in various parts of the Blue Horde's territory. This turmoil significantly weakened the power of the Blue Horde in Central Asia.
events.name: Great Troubles of the Blue Horde

events.enhanced_description: In 1361, Chinese rebels captured the capital of the Goryeo dynasty, Kaesong, marking a significant moment in the conflict between the Goryeo and the Red Turban rebels. This event contributed to the eventual decline of the Goryeo dynasty.
events.name: Capture of Goryeo capital by Chinese rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 1361, the earliest known musical keyboard instrument was built, featuring the layout of black and white keys that would later become standard in keyboard instruments. This innovation laid the groundwork for the development of future musical instruments.
events.name: Invention of the earliest known musical keyboard instrument

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1361, An-Nasir Hasan, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, was assassinated by Yalbugha al-Umari, leading to the installation of al-Mansur Muhammad as the new sultan, a pivotal moment in Mamluk history.
events.name: An-Nasir Hasan is killed by Yalbugha al-Umari

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1361, the University of Pavia was founded in Italy, becoming one of the oldest universities in the world and a center of learning during the Renaissance.
events.name: The University of Pavia is founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1361, King Magnus IV Eriksson of Sweden issued a warning to the inhabitants of Visby regarding an impending Danish invasion, highlighting the tensions between the two kingdoms.
events.name: King Magnus IV Eriksson warns the inhabitants of Visby of an upcoming Danish invasion

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Visby on July 27, 1361, marked a significant conflict in which King Valdemar IV of Denmark successfully conquered the city of Visby, defeating the local Gutnish yeomen. This victory allowed Denmark to take control of Gotland, a strategic island in the Baltic Sea.
events.name: Battle of Visby

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1361, Edward, the Black Prince, married Joan of Kent at Windsor Castle, solidifying a powerful alliance between two noble families. This marriage was significant in the context of English royal politics and lineage.
events.name: Marriage of Edward, the Black Prince and Joan of Kent

events.enhanced_description: In 1362, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania became the first country to officially switch the New Year celebration to January 1, a significant cultural shift that influenced calendar practices in Europe.
events.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania switches New Year to January 1

events.enhanced_description: In March 1362, Murad I succeeded his father, Orhan, as the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. His reign marked the expansion and consolidation of Ottoman power in the region.
events.name: Murad I succeeds Orhan as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In April 1362, Muhammed V returned to the throne of Granada following the assassination of the usurper Muhammed VI. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing power struggles within the Nasrid dynasty.
events.name: Muhammed V returns to the throne of Granada

events.enhanced_description: In June 1362, under the terms of Sir John de Wingfield's will, the church of St. Andrew and a college of priests were founded in Wingfield, Suffolk, England. This establishment contributed to the religious and educational landscape of the region.
events.name: Foundation of St. Andrew's Church and College

events.enhanced_description: In November 1362, Lionel of Antwerp, the son of King Edward III of England, was created Duke of Clarence. This title was significant in the context of English nobility and royal lineage.
events.name: Lionel of Antwerp created Duke of Clarence

events.enhanced_description: During the Red Turban Rebellions in 1362, Hu Dahai, an aide to Zhu Yuanzhang, was killed by Miao chieftains in Yanzhou, which is part of modern-day Jinhua and Hangzhou. This event underscored the violent power struggles during the rebellion.
events.name: Red Turban Rebellions: Death of Hu Dahai

events.enhanced_description: In 1362, the Ottomans captured Philippopolis and Adrianople from the Byzantine Empire, significantly reducing Byzantine territory to just Constantinople and a few islands. This marked a crucial step in the Ottoman expansion into Europe.
events.name: Ottomans capture Philippopolis and Adrianople

events.enhanced_description: The eruption of the Öræfajökull volcano in Iceland in 1362 led to catastrophic flooding and tephra fall that devastated the district of Litlahérað. This event is significant in Icelandic history as it marked one of the most destructive volcanic eruptions in the region.
events.name: The Öræfajökull volcano erupts in Iceland

events.enhanced_description: In 1362, the English Hospice of the Most Holy Trinity and St Thomas was established in Rome, serving as a refuge for English pilgrims and expatriates. This institution later evolved into the English College, which became a significant center for the education and training of English priests.
events.name: The English Hospice of the Most Holy Trinity and St Thomas is founded in Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Kensington Runestone, purportedly inscribed in 1362, was discovered in Solem, Minnesota, and is believed by some to be evidence of pre-Columbian Norse exploration in North America. The authenticity of the stone has been a subject of debate among historians and archaeologists.
events.name: Purported date of the inscription of the Kensington Runestone

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1362, the Grote Mandrenke storm tide struck the North Sea region, devastating coastal areas in the Netherlands, England, Germany, and Denmark. This catastrophic event destroyed the Danish settlement of Rungholt and significantly altered the geography of the affected regions.
events.name: Grote Mandrenke storm tide

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1362, King Haakon VI of Norway proclaimed himself king of Sweden in opposition to his father, Magnus IV of Sweden. This declaration led to a temporary rift between father and son, although they later reconciled and ruled together.
events.name: King Haakon VI of Norway proclaims himself king of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1362, the Free Companies achieved a decisive victory against a French army at the Battle of Brignais. This battle exemplified the ongoing conflicts during the Hundred Years' War and the rise of mercenary forces in France.
events.name: Battle of Brignais

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1362, Kaunas Castle in Lithuania fell to the Teutonic Order after a month-long siege. This event was part of the broader conflict between the Teutonic Knights and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
events.name: Fall of Kaunas Castle to the Teutonic Order

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1362, an alliance was formed between England and Castile, strengthening political ties between the two kingdoms. This alliance was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts in Europe.
events.name: Alliance between England and Castile

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1710, the Battle of Helsingborg took place, where a Swedish army led by Magnus Stenbock decisively defeated a Danish force commanded by Jørgen Rantzau. This battle was a significant event in the Great Northern War, showcasing the military capabilities of Sweden during this period.
events.name: Battle of Helsingborg

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1362, Pope Urban V succeeded Pope Innocent VI as the 200th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy was marked by efforts to reform the church and address the challenges of the time.
events.name: Pope Urban V succeeds Pope Innocent VI

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1362, the Chancellor of England made history by opening Parliament with a speech in English for the first time. This change was part of the Pleading in English Act, which established English as the official language in law courts.
events.name: Chancellor of England opens Parliament in English

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1362, Constantine IV succeeded his cousin Constantine III as King of Armenia. His reign was marked by the challenges of maintaining Armenian sovereignty amid regional pressures.
events.name: Constantine IV succeeds Constantine III as King of Armenia

events.enhanced_description: In 1363, Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania achieved a significant victory over the Tatars at the Battle of Blue Waters, capturing Kyiv. This battle was pivotal in expanding Lithuanian influence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Blue Waters

events.enhanced_description: In August 1363, the Revolt of Saint Titus erupted in the Kingdom of Candia (modern-day Crete) against the Republic of Venice's rule. This uprising was part of a broader resistance against foreign domination and highlighted the tensions between local populations and Venetian authorities.
events.name: The Revolt of Saint Titus begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1363, the Ottoman Turks captured Filibe (modern-day Plovdiv, Bulgaria) during the Byzantine–Ottoman wars, marking a significant expansion of Ottoman influence in the Balkans. This event was part of the larger conflict between the declining Byzantine Empire and the rising Ottoman power.
events.name: Ottoman Turks seize Filibe (Philippopolis)

events.enhanced_description: In 1363, Dmitry Donskoy, a prominent figure in Russian history, dethroned Dmitry of Suzdal to become the Grand Prince of Vladimir. His reign marked a significant period in the consolidation of power in the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
events.name: Dmitry Donskoy becomes Grand Prince of Vladimir

events.enhanced_description: In 1363, Philip the Bold was appointed as the Duke of Burgundy, a title that would significantly enhance his family's power and influence in France and Europe. His reign marked the beginning of the Valois dynasty's prominence in the region.
events.name: Philip the Bold becomes duke of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: In 1363, Al-Afdal al-Abbas succeeded Al-Mujahid Ali as the Rasulid Sultan of Yemen, continuing the lineage of the Rasulid dynasty that ruled over parts of the Arabian Peninsula. His reign was marked by efforts to maintain stability and prosperity in the region.
events.name: Al-Afdal al-Abbas succeeds Al-Mujahid Ali as Rasulid Sultan of Yemen

events.enhanced_description: The Mosque-Madrassa of Sultan Hassan was completed in 1363 in Cairo, Egypt, and is considered one of the finest examples of Mamluk architecture. This monumental structure served both as a mosque and a school, reflecting the cultural and religious significance of the period.

image.caption: Floor plan of the Mosque of Sultan Hasan in Cairo.
image.credit: unknown draftsman — Encyclopædia Britannica (9th ed.), v. 16, 1883, p. 865. See also 11th ed., v. 18, 1911, p. 900.
image.date_qualification: A floor plan illustrating the mosque, not a photograph of its completion. The source identifies it as published in 1883; no supported display date is provided.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Mosque-Madrassa of Sultan Hassan is completed

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1363, Haakon VI of Norway married Margaret I of Denmark, a union that would later lead to the formation of the Kalmar Union, uniting the crowns of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch. This marriage was significant in shaping the political landscape of Scandinavia.
events.name: Haakon VI of Norway marries Margaret I of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1363, the Battle of Lake Poyang took place, marking a pivotal moment in the Red Turban Rebellion against the Yuan Dynasty. The battle saw Zhu Yuanzhang's forces defeat the Dahan rebel forces led by Chen Youliang, making it one of the largest naval battles in history.
events.name: Battle of Lake Poyang

events.enhanced_description: In 1364, Vladislav I, also known as Vlaicu-Vodă, ascended to the position of voivode of Wallachia. His rule was characterized by efforts to strengthen the principality against external threats.
events.name: Vladislav I becomes voivode of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: The Bogdana Monastery was constructed in Moldavia in 1364, serving as an important religious and cultural center in the region. It played a significant role in the development of Orthodox Christianity in Moldavia.
events.name: Bogdana Monastery is built in Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1364, Rana Kshetra Singh succeeded Rana Hamir Singh as the ruler of Mewar, a region in modern-day Rajasthan, India. His reign was marked by efforts to consolidate power and defend against external threats.
events.name: Rana Kshetra Singh succeeds Rana Hamir Singh as ruler of Mewar

events.enhanced_description: In 1364, Anavema Reddy succeeded Anavota Reddy as the ruler of the Reddy Dynasty in Andhra Pradesh, India. His leadership continued the legacy of the dynasty in the region.
events.name: Anavema Reddy succeeds Anavota Reddy as ruler of the Reddy Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The Kingdom of Ava was established by Thado Minbya in 1364 in modern-day northern Myanmar. This kingdom played a crucial role in the history of Burma, with its influence extending over several centuries.
events.name: The Kingdom of Ava is established

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1364, the joint kings Magnus Eriksson and Haakon Magnusson of Sweden were deposed by noblemen, who elected Magnus's nephew Albrekt of Mecklenburg as the new king. This political shift marked a significant change in the governance of Sweden.
events.name: Joint kings Magnus Eriksson and Haakon Magnusson of Sweden are deposed

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1364, David II of Scotland married Margaret Drummond, strengthening political alliances within Scotland. This marriage was significant for the royal lineage and the stability of David's reign.
events.name: David II of Scotland marries Margaret Drummond

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1364, Charles V ascended to the throne as King of France, a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the monarchy and reclaim lost territories from the English.
events.name: Charles V becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: The Jagiellonian University was founded in Kraków on May 12, 1364, and is one of the oldest universities in the world. It became a significant center for education and scholarship in Central Europe.
events.name: The Jagiellonian University is founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1364, the Battle of Cascina occurred, where the forces of the Republic of Florence, led by Galeotto Malatesta, defeated the troops of Pisa. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between these city-states in Tuscany.
events.name: Battle of Cascina

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1364, Ignatius Saba I was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Tur Abdin. His leadership played a crucial role in the preservation of the Syriac Orthodox Church during a time of significant challenges.
events.name: Ignatius Saba I becomes Patriarch of Tur Abdin

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1364, Philip of Anjou was recognized as the Titular Emperor of Constantinople and Prince of Taranto. This title reflected the ongoing claims and aspirations of various European nobles over the remnants of the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Philip of Anjou becomes Titular Emperor of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1364, the Battle of Auray concluded the Breton War of Succession, resulting in a decisive victory for the House of Montfort over Charles of Blois. This battle solidified the Montfort family's claim to the Duchy of Brittany.

image.caption: 15th-century manuscript illustration by Loyset Liédet depicting the Battle of Auray.
image.credit: Loyset Liédet — Loyset Liédet ; Illustration from the Chroniques de Froissart (manuscript of Gruuthuse) - Français 2643 (Manuscript)
image.date_qualification: Created in the 15th century; the supplied image date gives circa 1450. The battle occurred on 29 September 1364.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Auray

events.enhanced_description: In 1365, Adrianopole, known today as Edirne, was established as the capital of the Ottoman Sultanate under Sultan Murad I. This strategic move marked a significant expansion of Ottoman influence in the Balkans.
events.name: Adrianopole becomes the capital city of the Ottoman Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1365, Bahmani Sultan Mohammed Shah I launched an invasion against the Vijayanagara Empire, marking a significant conflict between the two powers in southern India. This invasion was part of ongoing territorial disputes in the region.
events.name: Bahmani Sultan Mohammed Shah I invades the Vijayanagara Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1365, the Sukhothai Kingdom in northern Thailand became a tributary state of the more powerful Ayutthaya Kingdom. This shift in allegiance marked a significant change in the political dynamics of the region.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Sukhothai Kingdom becomes a tributary state of the Ayutthaya Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 1365, Sultan Muhammed V of Granada initiated the construction of the Maristan of Granada, a hospital that exemplified the advanced medical practices of the time. This institution would serve as a model for healthcare in the region.
events.name: Muhammed V begins building the Maristan of Granada

events.enhanced_description: In 1365, the Chagatai Khanate achieved a significant victory over Timur in the Battle of Tashkent. This battle was pivotal in the power struggles of Central Asia during this period.
events.name: The Chagatai Khanate defeats Timur in the Battle of Tashkent

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1365, the Battle of Gataskogen took place, where Albert of Mecklenburg defeated and captured Magnus Eriksson, leading to Albert's ascension to the throne of Sweden. This battle was pivotal in the power struggles of the Swedish monarchy.
events.name: Battle of Gataskogen

events.enhanced_description: The University of Vienna was founded on March 12, 1365, by Rudolf IV of Austria, making it one of the oldest universities in the German-speaking world. It has played a significant role in the development of higher education in Europe.
events.name: The University of Vienna is founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1365, Louis I of Hungary captured the city of Vidin, marking the beginning of Hungarian occupation in the region. This event also led to the imprisonment of the Bulgarian ruler Ivan Sratsimir, significantly impacting the political landscape of the Balkans.
events.name: The Hungarian occupation of Vidin begins

events.enhanced_description: In October 1365, during the Alexandrian Crusade, the city of Alexandria was sacked by an allied force led by Peter I of Cyprus and the Knights of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem. This event was part of a larger conflict involving Christian and Muslim powers in the region.
events.name: Alexandrian Crusade: The city of Alexandria is sacked

events.enhanced_description: The Nagarakretagama, a significant Javanese literary work chronicling the reign of King Hayam Wuruk of the Majapahit Empire, was completed by the poet Mpu Prapanca on November 30, 1365. This text is crucial for understanding the history and culture of the Majapahit period.
events.name: Completion of the Nagarakretagama

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, hostilities continued between the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire and the Muslim Bahmani Sultanate in southern India. This ongoing conflict was marked by territorial disputes and cultural clashes.
events.name: War continues between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bahmani Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, Dmitri Donskoi, the ruler of Moscow, successfully negotiated peace with Dmitri Konstantinovich, the former ruler of Vladimir. This peace agreement was crucial for stabilizing the region.
events.name: Dmitri Donskoi makes peace with Dmitri Konstantinovich

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz I ascended to the throne of the Marinid Empire in Morocco following the assassination of his predecessor, Abu Zayyan. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize the empire.
events.name: Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz I succeeds as Sultan of the Marinid Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, the Statutes of Kilkenny were enacted in Ireland, aimed at curbing the decline of the Hiberno-Norman Lordship. These laws sought to reinforce English control and reduce the influence of the Gaelic Irish.
events.name: The Statutes of Kilkenny are passed

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, the Den Hoorn brewery was established in Leuven, which would later be renamed Brouwerij Artois in 1717. This brewery became famous for producing Stella Artois beer, a well-known brand worldwide.
events.name: The Den Hoorn brewery is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, Zhu Yuanzhang, the leader of the Red Turban Rebellion, began constructing walls for a new capital city at Nanjing. This city would later become the capital of the Ming dynasty, which he established after overthrowing the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Zhu Yuanzhang begins building walls for a new capital city at Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: In 1366, Thomas Fraser obtained lands in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, where he began constructing a towerhouse that would later be known as Muchalls Castle. This structure represents the feudal architecture of the period.
events.name: Thomas Fraser begins building Muchalls Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1366, Henry II of Castile successfully deposed his half-brother, Pedro of Castile, to become the King of Castile. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Spain.
events.name: Henry II deposes Pedro of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1366, Frederick III of Sicily issued a decree forbidding decorations on synagogues, reflecting the tensions between different religious communities in medieval Sicily.
events.name: Frederick III of Sicily forbids decorations on synagogues

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1366, Comet 55P/Tempel–Tuttle made a close approach to Earth, coming within 0.0229 AU (approximately 3,430,000 km) of the planet. This event was notable for astronomers of the time.
events.name: Comet 55P/Tempel–Tuttle passes near Earth

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the stone Moscow Kremlin Wall began in the winter of 1367 as a defensive measure against the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. This fortification would become a symbol of Moscow's power and resilience.
events.name: Construction of the Moscow Kremlin Wall

events.enhanced_description: Petru I ascended to the position of voivode of Moldavia, succeeding his grandfather Bogdan I. His rule marked a significant period in the history of Moldavia, characterized by attempts to strengthen the principality's autonomy.
events.name: Petru I succeeds Bogdan I as voivode of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: King Louis I of Anjou founded the first university in Pécs, Hungary, in 1367, establishing a center for higher education that would contribute to the cultural and intellectual life of the region.
events.name: Founding of the University in Pécs

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1367, Ferdinand I ascended to the throne of Portugal following the death of his father, Peter I. His reign would be marked by political challenges and conflicts with neighboring kingdoms.
events.name: Ferdinand I becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1367, the Battle of Nájera took place, where Pedro of Castile was restored to the throne after defeating his half-brother Henry II with the aid of English forces led by Edward, the Black Prince. This battle was a significant moment in the struggle for the Castilian crown.
events.name: Battle of Nájera

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1367, Otto I, known as 'the Evil', became Duke of the independent city of Göttingen following the death of his father, Ernst I. His rule would be characterized by local conflicts and political maneuvering.
events.name: Otto I becomes Duke of Göttingen

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1367, during the Red Turban Rebellions, Zhu Yuanzhang captured Suzhou from Zhang Shicheng, who attempted suicide before being captured. This victory was crucial for Zhu's rise to power and the eventual establishment of the Ming dynasty.
events.name: Zhu Yuanzhang takes Suzhou from Zhang Shicheng

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1367, Pope Urban V made the first attempt to return the Papacy to Rome from Avignon. This move, however, was reversed in 1370 due to political pressures, and Urban V would die shortly thereafter.
events.name: Pope Urban V attempts to move the Papacy back to Rome

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1367, during the Red Turban Rebellions, Hu Mei captured Shaowu, while Xu Da and Chang Yuchun took Jinan, consolidating Zhu Yuanzhang's control over these regions. These victories were pivotal in the rebellion against the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Red Turban Rebellions: Hu Mei captures Shaowu

events.enhanced_description: The Revolt of Saint Titus against the Republic of Venice in the Kingdom of Candia ended in failure in 1368. This uprising was part of the broader resistance against Venetian rule on the island of Crete.

image.caption: Map of Crete with the winged lion of St. Mark above the island.
image.credit: Marco Boschini — Il regno tutto di Candia delineato a parte a parte, et intagliato da Marco Boschini venetiano. Al serenissimo prencipe e regal collegio di Venetia , Venezia, 1651
image.date_qualification: Published in 1651, nearly three centuries after the revolt; not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Revolt of Saint Titus

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, Karl Thopia, a powerful feudal prince, captured the city of Durrës from the Angevins. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Capture of Durrës by Karl Thopia

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, Lațcu, son of Bogdan I, deposed his nephew Petru I to become the voivode of Moldavia. This power struggle was indicative of the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Lațcu becomes voivode of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: Timur ascended to the throne of Samarkand in 1368, marking the beginning of his rise to power. He would go on to establish a vast empire and become one of history's most formidable conquerors.
events.name: Timur ascends the throne of Samarkand

events.enhanced_description: Maha Thammaracha II ascended to the throne of the Sukhothai Kingdom in 1368 following the death of his predecessor, Maha Thammaracha I. His reign continued the legacy of the Sukhothai period.
events.name: Maha Thammaracha II becomes ruler of Sukhothai

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, work began on the surviving sections of the Great Wall of China, which would serve as a crucial defense against invasions. This construction marked a significant effort to fortify the northern borders of the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: Work begins on the Great Wall of China

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, Mikhail Aleksandrovich became the sole ruler of Tver after the death of his co-ruler and rival, Vasiliy Mikhailovich of Kashin. This consolidation of power was significant in the political landscape of medieval Russia.
events.name: Mikhail Aleksandrovich becomes sole ruler of Tver

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, Moscow launched an attack on Tver, which retaliated with the support of Lithuania and the Blue Horde. This conflict was part of the ongoing power struggles in the region.
events.name: Moscow attacks Tver

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, the King of Norway dispatched the last Royal Ship to the Greenland Eastern Settlement, marking a significant moment in the Norse colonization efforts in the Americas and the history of Greenland.
events.name: Last Royal Ship sent to Greenland

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, a peace treaty was signed between Norway and the Hanseatic League, aimed at stabilizing trade relations and reducing hostilities between the two entities.
events.name: Peace treaty between Norway and the Hanseatic League

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, Charles V of France established the Bibliothèque nationale de France as the Royal Library at the Louvre Palace in Paris. This institution would become a cornerstone of French cultural heritage.
events.name: Founding of the Bibliothèque nationale de France

events.enhanced_description: In 1368, the Italian poet Petrarch completed his sequence of sonnets and poems known as Il Canzoniere. This work is considered a cornerstone of Renaissance literature and has had a lasting impact on poetry.
events.name: Petrarch concludes Il Canzoniere

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1368, the Hongwu Emperor, Zhu Yuanzhang, established the Ming Dynasty in China, marking the end of the Mongol Yuan Dynasty. His reign initiated significant reforms, including the establishment of granaries and the cessation of taxation on books.
events.name: Establishment of the Ming Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Chōkei ascended to the throne of Japan on March 29, 1368. His reign was part of a tumultuous period marked by political strife and the influence of the Ashikaga shogunate.
events.name: Accession of Emperor Chōkei

events.enhanced_description: In May 1369, King Charles V of France renounced the Treaty of Brétigny, which had previously established peace with England. This act marked the resumption of hostilities in the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Charles V renounces Treaty of Brétigny

events.enhanced_description: In September 1369, during the Hundred Years' War, French forces burned Portsmouth, England, while English raiders targeted Picardy and Normandy. This event exemplified the ongoing conflict between the two nations.
events.name: Burning of Portsmouth during the Hundred Years' War

events.enhanced_description: In December 1369, financed by Charles V of France, Welshman Owain Lawgoch launched an invasion fleet against the English in an attempt to claim the throne of Wales. However, a storm forced him to abandon the invasion.
events.name: Owain Lawgoch's invasion attempt

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, the Ottoman Empire launched an invasion of Bulgaria, marking the beginning of a series of conflicts that would lead to the eventual Ottoman domination of the region.
events.name: Ottoman invasion of Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, Venice successfully repelled a Hungarian invasion, demonstrating its military strength and strategic importance in the region during this turbulent period.
events.name: Venice repels Hungarian invasion

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, the Thai Ayutthaya Kingdom launched a military campaign to conquer Cambodia for the second time, asserting its dominance over the region and expanding its territory. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between the Ayutthaya Kingdom and the Khmer Empire.
events.name: The Thai Ayutthaya Kingdom conquers Cambodia for a second time

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, Charles V of France commissioned Hugues Aubriot to construct the fortress of the Bastille in Paris, initially intended as a fortress to defend the eastern approach to the city. Over time, the Bastille would become a symbol of royal tyranny and a focal point of the French Revolution.
events.name: Charles V of France orders Hugues Aubriot to construct the fortress of the Bastille in Paris

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, Timur, the Central Asian conqueror, declared Samarkand as the capital of his burgeoning empire. This decision marked the beginning of a significant cultural and architectural revival in the city, which would become a center of trade and learning.
events.name: Timur names the city of Samarkand as the capital of his empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, Košice was officially granted its own coat of arms, becoming the first town in Europe to receive such an honor. This event symbolized the town's growing importance and autonomy within the region.
events.name: Košice becomes the first town in Europe to be granted its own coat of arms

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty mandated that every magistrate in the empire establish a Confucian school, promoting education and Confucian values throughout China. This decree was part of his broader efforts to consolidate power and restore traditional Chinese culture.
events.name: The Hongwu Emperor of the Chinese Ming dynasty issues a decree ordering every country magistrate in the empire to open a Confucian school of learning

events.enhanced_description: In 1369, Jingdezhen, known as the 'Porcelain Capital' of China, officially recorded the production of its renowned porcelain. This marked the beginning of a significant industry that would flourish and influence global trade for centuries.
events.name: The official production of Jingdezhen porcelain in Ming dynasty China is on record

events.enhanced_description: In February 1369, Vladislav I of Wallachia liberated Vidin from Hungarian control, leading to the restoration of Ivan Sratsimir on the throne of Bulgaria in the autumn. This event was pivotal in the regional power dynamics.
events.name: Liberation of Vidin by Vladislav I

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1369, the Battle of Montiel took place, where Pedro of Castile faced defeat against an alliance of French forces and his half-brother, Henry II. This battle was a significant event in the Castilian civil war.
events.name: Battle of Montiel

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1369, during the Hundred Years' War, Charles V of France successfully recaptured most of Aquitaine from English control. This victory was a significant turning point in the conflict.
events.name: Recapture of Aquitaine by Charles V

events.enhanced_description: In 1370, the Grand Duchy of Moscow launched another attack on Tver, which counter-attacked with the support of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Blue Horde. This conflict highlighted the ongoing power struggles in the region.
events.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow attacks Tver

events.enhanced_description: In 1370, Khun Luang Pa-Ngua, the ruler of Suphanburi, marched into the Ayutthaya Kingdom and usurped the throne, marking a significant shift in power within the kingdom. This event was part of the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Khun Luang Pa-Ngua usurps the throne of the Ayutthaya Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 1370, the city of Xi'an, known historically as Chang'an, received a new defensive city wall as part of the Ming dynasty's efforts to fortify its cities against potential invasions. This construction reflected the era's military and architectural advancements.
events.name: The city of Xi'an is given a new defensive city wall

events.enhanced_description: In 1370, Hugues Aubriot commenced the construction of the Bastille fortress in Paris, which would later become a symbol of royal authority and oppression. The fortress was initially built for defense but gained notoriety during the French Revolution.
events.name: Hugues Aubriot begins construction of the fortress of the Bastille in Paris

events.enhanced_description: In 1370, the steel crossbow was first utilized as a weapon of war, marking a significant advancement in military technology. This innovation allowed for greater power and accuracy in ranged combat, influencing warfare strategies.
events.name: The steel crossbow is first used as a weapon of war

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1370, the Battle of Rudau was fought between the Teutonic Knights and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania near the village of Rudau. The Lithuanians suffered a significant defeat, which had lasting implications for the power dynamics in the region.

image.caption: Historical map of the Teutonic Order’s state, 1308–1455, locating Rudau.
image.credit: self made by en:User:Space Cadet / modified de:User:Magister. Original uploader was Magister at de.wikipedia — File:Teutonic state 1455.png modified ( diese Version )
image.date_qualification: Map covers 1308–1455; image date: 2007-02-12. The date is not the date of the battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Battle of Rudau

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1370, Timur was declared the first Amir of the Timurid Empire after successfully besieging Balkh, solidifying his control over the Chagatai Khanate. This event marked the culmination of his conquests in Central Asia and the establishment of a powerful empire.
events.name: Timur becomes first Amir of the Timurid Empire

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1370, the Treaty of Stralsund was signed, effectively ending the conflict between Denmark and the Hanseatic League. This treaty restored peace and established trade relations, marking a significant moment in Northern European politics.
events.name: The Treaty of Stralsund ends the war between Denmark and the Hanseatic League

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1370, during the Hundred Years' War, the English forces led by Edward the Black Prince stormed the city of Limoges, resulting in widespread destruction and effectively ending the local enamel industry. This brutal siege exemplified the harsh realities of medieval warfare.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Siege of Limoges

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1370, Philip of Anjou, the Titular Emperor of Constantinople, married Elizabeth of Slavonia, strengthening political ties through this union. This marriage was part of the broader dynastic strategies of the time.
events.name: Philip of Anjou marries Elizabeth of Slavonia

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1370, Casimir III the Great, the king of Poland, died due to a hunting accident. His death marked the end of an era and led to a succession crisis, with his sister and her son taking over the rule.
events.name: Casimir III the Great dies

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1370, Trần Nghệ Tông deposed Dương Nhật Lễ as emperor of Đại Việt, asserting his authority and continuing the Trần dynasty's rule. This event was part of the ongoing power struggles within the Vietnamese court.
events.name: Trần Nghệ Tông deposes Dương Nhật Lễ

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1370, during the Hundred Years' War, a French army led by Bertrand du Guesclin achieved a decisive victory over an English force at the Battle of Pontvallain. This battle was significant in shifting the momentum of the war in favor of the French.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Battle of Pontvallain

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1370, Pope Gregory XI succeeded Pope Urban V, becoming the 201st pope. His papacy would later be marked by efforts to return the papacy to Rome from Avignon, ending the Avignon Papacy.
events.name: Pope Gregory XI succeeds Pope Urban V

events.enhanced_description: In January 1371, Edward, the Black Prince, relinquished his administration of Aquitaine and returned to England due to poor health and mounting debts. This decision had significant implications for English control over the region during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Edward, the Black Prince, gives up the administration of Aquitaine

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, the first widely accepted historical reference to playing cards was made in Spain, marking the introduction of this popular pastime to European culture. This event signifies the growing influence of leisure activities in medieval society.
events.name: First reference to playing cards

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, Polish priest Andrzej Jastrzębiec was appointed as the first bishop of Siret, establishing Catholicism in Moldavia. His appointment marked a significant step in the spread of Christianity in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Andrzej Jastrzębiec becomes bishop of Siret

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, Zhao Bing Fa ascended to the throne as King of Mong Mao following the death of his father, Si Kefa. This transition marked a continuation of the local leadership in the region of modern-day Yunnan, China.
events.name: Zhao Bing Fa becomes King of Mong Mao

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, Kalamegha claimed the vacant title of King of Cambodia as the power of the Thai invaders from Ayutthaya began to wane. His claim was a pivotal moment in the struggle for control over the region, leading to the eventual expulsion of the Ayutthayans in 1375.
events.name: Kalamegha claims the title of King of Cambodia

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, Byzantine co-emperor John V Palaiologos pledged loyalty to the Ottoman Empire in a desperate attempt to prevent the Turks from invading Constantinople. This act of submission highlighted the precarious position of the Byzantine Empire during this period.
events.name: John V Palaiologos pledges loyalty to the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1371, the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty implemented the lijia census registration system throughout the Yangzi Valley. This system was designed to organize households for taxation and labor, significantly impacting governance and administration in China.
events.name: Hongwu Emperor introduces census registration system

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1371, rival brothers Ivan Sratsimir and Ivan Shishman ascended as co-Emperors of Bulgaria following the death of their father, Ivan Alexander. This division weakened the Bulgarian state and led to internal strife.
events.name: Ivan Sratsimir and Ivan Shishman become co-Emperors of Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1371, Robert II was crowned as the first Stuart king of Scotland following the death of his uncle, David II. His reign marked the beginning of the Stewart dynasty, which would play a significant role in Scottish history.
events.name: Robert II becomes the first Stuart king of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1371, the London Charterhouse, a Carthusian monastery, was founded in Aldersgate, London. This establishment became a significant religious site and contributed to the spread of monasticism in England.
events.name: The London Charterhouse is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1371, Emperor Go-En'yu succeeded Emperor Go-Kōgon, becoming the 5th and last Emperor of the Northern Court in Japan. His reign was marked by the ongoing struggles between the Northern and Southern courts during the Nanboku-chō period.
events.name: Emperor Go-En'yu succeeds Emperor Go-Kōgon of Japan

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Baesweiler on August 22, 1371, marked a significant defeat for the Duchy of Brabant against the forces of the Duchy of Jülich. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region, reflecting the power struggles among the noble houses of the Low Countries.
events.name: Battle of Baesweiler

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1371, John of Gaunt, the son of King Edward III of England, married Constance of Castile, the daughter of King Pedro of Castile. This marriage not only strengthened ties between England and Castile but also provided John with a claim to the Castilian throne, influencing the political landscape of the time.
events.name: Marriage of John of Gaunt and Constance of Castile

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Maritsa, fought on September 26, 1371, resulted in a devastating defeat for the Serbian nobility at the hands of the Ottoman forces led by Sultan Murad I. This battle significantly weakened Serbian resistance against the Ottomans and marked a pivotal moment in the expansion of Ottoman power in the Balkans.

locations.name: Near the Maritsa River, Thrace, Bulgaria

events.name: Battle of Maritsa

events.enhanced_description: In December 1371, Lazar Hrebeljanović succeeded his distant cousin, Stefan Uroš V, as the ruler of Serbia. Despite his ascension to power, Lazar declined the title of Tsar, focusing instead on consolidating his authority in a time of political instability.
events.name: Lazar Hrebeljanović becomes ruler of Serbia

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, during the Encounter of Sintra, a small force of twenty Portuguese knights successfully routed a much larger contingent of four hundred Castilian infantrymen. This event underscored the tactical prowess of the Portuguese forces in their ongoing conflicts with Castile.
events.name: Encounter of Sintra

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, peace was declared between the Kingdom of Sicily and the Kingdom of Naples, ending a period of conflict between the two regions. This agreement was significant for stabilizing the political landscape of Southern Italy.
events.name: Peace declared between Sicily and Naples

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, the Kingdom of Chūzan, located in modern-day Okinawa, Japan, established tributary relations with the Ming dynasty of China. This relationship facilitated trade and cultural exchange between the two regions.
events.name: Chūzan enters tributary relations with Ming China

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, four-year-old Muhammad as-Said succeeded his father, Abu l-Fariz Abdul Aziz I, as the Marinid Sultan of Morocco. His ascension represented a continuation of the Marinid dynasty during a time of political instability.
events.name: Muhammad as-Said becomes Sultan of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, Newaya Maryam succeeded his father, Newaya Krestos, as ruler of Ethiopia. His reign marked a continuation of the Solomonic dynasty during a period of significant political and religious change.
events.name: Newaya Maryam becomes ruler of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: In 1372, the city of Aachen became the first in the world to add a Roman numeral Anno Domini date to its coins. This innovation reflected the growing importance of standardized dating in commerce and governance.
events.name: Aachen begins adding Anno Domini dates to coins

events.enhanced_description: In March 1372, Saint Bridget embarked on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, where she experienced significant visions, including one of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem. Her journey reflects the spiritual fervor and devotion of the period.
events.name: Saint Bridget's pilgrimage to the Holy Land

events.enhanced_description: In May 1372, Owain Lawgoch made a second attempt to seize the throne of Wales, launching from Harfleur with French support. However, his campaign was interrupted as he chose to assist the French in their conflict at La Rochelle.
events.name: Owain Lawgoch's second attempt to take the throne of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1372, the Battle of La Rochelle saw the French and Castilian forces defeat the English, marking a significant shift in control over the English Channel. This victory was crucial for the French in the ongoing Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of La Rochelle

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1372, the Treaty of Tagilde was signed between Ferdinand I of Portugal and representatives of John of Gaunt of England, establishing the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance. This treaty laid the foundation for a long-lasting diplomatic relationship between the two nations.
events.name: Treaty of Tagilde

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1372, Trần Duệ Tông succeeded his brother Trần Nghệ Tông as King of Vietnam. His ascension marked a continuation of the Trần dynasty's rule during a period of internal and external challenges.
events.name: Trần Duệ Tông succeeds as King of Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, Louis I of Hungary successfully captured Severin, a strategic location in present-day Romania. However, this victory was short-lived as the Vlachs managed to reclaim it between 1376 and 1377.
events.name: Louis I of Hungary takes Severin

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, Andronikos IV Palaiologos revolted against his father, John V Palaiologos, due to his father's agreement to make Constantinople a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. The rebellion failed, leading to a brutal command from Ottoman Emperor Murad I for John V to blind his son.
events.name: Andronikos IV Palaiologos rebels against John V Palaiologos

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, Constantine IV, the ruler of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, was assassinated, leading to the ascension of his distant cousin Leo V. This event marked a significant shift in the leadership of the kingdom amidst ongoing regional conflicts.
events.name: Assassination of Constantine IV of Cilicia

events.enhanced_description: The death of Sultan Muhammad III ibn Abd al-Aziz in 1373 initiated a period of political instability in Morocco, affecting the governance and power dynamics within the region.
events.name: Death of Sultan Muhammad III ibn Abd al-Aziz

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, the city of Phnom Penh was founded, which would later become the capital of Cambodia. Its establishment marked an important development in the region's urban and cultural landscape.

image.caption: Cityscape of Phnom Penh viewed from Toul Kork.
image.credit: Looppty — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2024 cityscape of Phnom Penh, not a depiction of the city's founding; the article states it was founded in 1372.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Phnom Penh

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, Bristol was granted the status of a county corporate, becoming the first town in England outside London to receive this designation. This status allowed Bristol greater autonomy and self-governance.
events.name: Bristol made a county corporate

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, a city wall was constructed around Lisbon to fortify the city against potential invasions from Castile. This defensive measure was part of the broader military strategies employed during the period.
events.name: Construction of city wall around Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, Merton College Library was built in Oxford, England, marking an important development in the history of education and scholarship in the region. It became one of the earliest college libraries in the English-speaking world.
events.name: Construction of Merton College Library

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, the Adina Mosque was constructed in Bengal, which became one of the largest mosques in the Indian subcontinent. This architectural achievement reflects the cultural and religious influences of the time.
events.name: Construction of the Adina Mosque

events.enhanced_description: In 1373, the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty suspended the traditional civil service examination system, citing concerns over the incompetence of newly appointed officials. This decision shifted the focus to a recommendation-based system until the exams were reinstated in 1384.
events.name: Suspension of civil service examination by Hongwu Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1373, the Treaty of Santarém was signed between Ferdinand I of Portugal and Henry II of Castile, effectively ending the second war between the two kingdoms. This treaty was crucial for restoring peace and stability in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Treaty of Santarém

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1373, during the ongoing Hundred Years' War, French forces successfully recaptured most of Brittany from the English, although they failed to take the strategic port of Brest. This victory was a significant step in the French efforts to regain control over their territories.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: French recapture of Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1373, Julian of Norwich, an English anchoress, received the sixteen Revelations of Divine Love, which would later become a foundational text of Christian mysticism. Her writings reflect profound theological insights and personal spirituality.
events.name: Julian of Norwich receives Revelations of Divine Love

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1373, the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty was signed in London, establishing one of the oldest active treaties in the world. This agreement solidified the alliance between England and Portugal, influencing diplomatic relations for centuries.
events.name: Anglo-Portuguese Treaty signed in London

events.enhanced_description: In August 1373, John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster, initiated a new military campaign against France during the ongoing Hundred Years' War. This invasion was part of England's efforts to reclaim territories lost to the French and assert its influence in the region.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: John of Gaunt launches a new invasion of France

events.enhanced_description: In November 1373, Philip II, Prince of Taranto, transferred control of Achaea to his cousin, Joanna I of Naples. This political maneuver was significant in the context of feudal allegiances and territorial governance in the region.
events.name: Philip II hands over the rule of Achaea to Joanna I of Naples

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, Rao Biram Dev succeeded his father Rao Kanhadev as the ruler of Marwar, a significant region in present-day Rajasthan, India. This transition of power was part of the ongoing feudal structure in medieval India.
events.name: Rao Biram Dev succeeds Rao Kanhadev as ruler of Marwar

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, Shaikh Hasan Jalayir succeeded his father, Shaykh Uways Jalayir, as the ruler of the Jalayirid Sultanate. His rule was marked by unpopularity, leading to his execution shortly thereafter.
events.name: Shaikh Hasan Jalayir succeeds his father

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, Musa II succeeded his father, Mari Djata II, as Mansa of the Mali Empire, which was a significant power in West Africa. His reign continued the legacy of wealth and cultural development in the region.
events.name: Musa II succeeds as Mansa of the Mali Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, Robert de Juilly succeeded Raymond Berenger as the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, an important military and religious order during the medieval period.
events.name: Robert de Juilly succeeds as Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, princes from the Kingdom of Granada selected Abu al-Abbas Ahmad to succeed Muhammad as-Said as Sultan of the Marinid Empire. This decision reflected the political complexities and alliances within North Africa.
events.name: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad chosen as Sultan of the Marinid Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, a form of the Great Plague re-emerged in Europe, contributing to ongoing health crises and societal upheaval. This resurgence highlighted the vulnerabilities of medieval populations to pandemics.
events.name: Return of the Great Plague to Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1374, the Château de Compiègne, a royal residence, was constructed in France. This architectural project was part of the broader efforts to enhance royal power and influence in the region.
events.name: Construction of Château de Compiègne

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1374, King Edward III of England granted the writer Geoffrey Chaucer a daily allowance of a gallon of wine for life, recognizing his contributions to English literature. This gesture reflects the growing importance of literary figures in the royal court.
events.name: Edward III grants Chaucer a gallon of wine

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1374, a phenomenon known as dancing mania began in Aix-la-Chapelle, possibly linked to ergotism. This unusual event saw groups of people dancing uncontrollably, reflecting the social and psychological tensions of the time.
events.name: Dancing mania begins in Aix-la-Chapelle

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1374, King Gongmin of Goryeo was assassinated, leading to the ascension of U of Goryeo to the throne. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the Goryeo dynasty.
events.name: Assassination of King Gongmin of Goryeo

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1374, James of Baux succeeded his uncle Philip II as the Prince of Taranto, a title that also conferred him as the titular ruler of the Latin Empire. This succession was part of the complex feudal dynamics in southern Italy and the Balkans.
events.name: James of Baux succeeds as Prince of Taranto

events.enhanced_description: In 1375, the Grand Duchy of Moscow and Tver signed a truce, marking a temporary cessation of hostilities. This agreement was crucial as Tver agreed to assist Moscow in its conflicts against the Blue Horde, reflecting the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Truce between Grand Duchy of Moscow and Tver

events.enhanced_description: The presumed death of Tenoch, the ruler of the Mexica, occurred around 1375, leading to the succession of Acamapichtli as the first tlatoani of Tenochtitlan. This transition marked the beginning of the Aztec imperial dynasty, which would dominate central Mexico for centuries.
events.name: Death of Tenoch and succession of Acamapichtli

events.enhanced_description: In 1375, Petru succeeded as Voivode of Moldavia, becoming the first ruler from the House of Bogdan. His reign marked the establishment of a significant principality in Eastern Europe, which would play a crucial role in the region's history.
events.name: Petru becomes Voivode of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: Coluccio Salutati was appointed Chancellor of Florence in 1375, a position that allowed him to influence the political landscape of the city during a time of significant cultural and social change. His tenure is noted for promoting humanism and the revival of classical learning.
events.name: Coluccio Salutati appointed Chancellor of Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1375, the Russian town of Kostroma was destroyed by ushkuynik pirates from Novgorod. This event highlighted the ongoing conflicts and instability in the region during the late medieval period, as piracy and raiding were common threats to settlements.
events.name: Destruction of Kostroma by ushkuynik pirates

events.enhanced_description: Heirin-ji Temple was founded near modern-day Tokyo in 1375, serving as a significant site for the practice of Buddhism in Japan. The temple's establishment reflects the spread of Buddhist teachings and the cultural developments of the period.
events.name: Foundation of Heirin-ji Temple

events.enhanced_description: In 1375, Ru Taisu, a bureau secretary of the Ministry of Justice, presented a lengthy memorial to the Hongwu Emperor in Nanjing. The incident, which resulted in Ru being punished for perceived insults, illustrates the complexities of court politics and the emperor's sensitivity to criticism.
events.name: Ru Taisu's memorial to the Hongwu Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Around 1375, the Battle of Gardiki took place, where the Principality of Achaea achieved victory over the Despotate of the Morea. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region, reflecting the power struggles among the Greek states during the late medieval period.
events.name: Battle of Gardiki

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1375, the Mamluks completed their conquest of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, imprisoning Levon V Lusignan for several years. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Mamluks complete conquest of Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1375, Mujahid Shah succeeded his father, Mohammed Shah I, as the ruler of the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan Plateau of southern India. His ascension marked a continuation of the dynasty's influence in the region.

image.caption: Gateway to Bidar Fort, a historic fort site associated with the Bahmani Sultanate.
image.credit: Vamsi Rimmalapudi — originally posted to Flickr as Gateway to Bidar fort
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-08-22; not contemporary with the 1375 succession.

events.name: Mujahid Shah succeeds Mohammed Shah I

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1375, John I of Castile married Eleanor of Aragon, strengthening the political alliance between the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of Aragon. This union was significant in the context of the dynastic struggles and territorial disputes in the Iberian Peninsula during the late Middle Ages.
events.name: Marriage of King John I of Castile and Eleanor of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1375, the Treaty of Bruges was signed, marking a significant concession by the English during the Hundred Years' War. The treaty resulted from the English being weakened by the Black Death, leading them to relinquish much of their territorial gains in France, retaining only key coastal towns.
events.name: Treaty of Bruges

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1375, Margaret I of Denmark ascended to the regency following the death of her father, Valdemar IV. Her rule marked the beginning of a significant period in Scandinavian history, as she would later unite the crowns of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under her leadership.

events.enhanced_description: In March 1376, the peace treaty between England and France was extended until April 1377, reflecting the ongoing negotiations during the Hundred Years' War. This extension aimed to maintain a temporary cessation of hostilities amidst the backdrop of political and military strife.
events.name: Extension of peace treaty between England and France

events.enhanced_description: In June 1376, Catherine of Siena visited Pope Gregory XI in Avignon, advocating for peace with Florence and the relocation of the Papacy back to Rome. Her efforts were part of her broader mission to reform the Church and restore its authority.
events.name: Catherine of Siena visits Pope Gregory XI

events.enhanced_description: In September 1376, John of Gaunt summoned the religious reformer John Wyclif to appear before the Royal Council. This event underscored the tensions between emerging reformist ideas and established religious authority in England.
events.name: Summons of John Wyclif by John of Gaunt

events.enhanced_description: In 1376, Acamapichtli was appointed as the first tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, marking the beginning of the Aztec imperial dynasty. His leadership laid the foundation for the expansion and consolidation of power that characterized the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Acamapichtli becomes tlatoani of Tenochtitlan

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1376, Pope Gregory XI excommunicated all members of the government of Florence and placed the city under an interdict. This action was part of the broader conflict between the Papacy and the city, reflecting the tensions of the time.
events.name: Excommunication of Florence by Pope Gregory XI

events.enhanced_description: The Good Parliament convened on April 28, 1376, in England, notable for its attempts to reform the corrupt Royal Council. This Parliament is remembered for its efforts to address grievances and improve governance during a tumultuous period in English history.
events.name: The Good Parliament begins in England

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1376, Olav IV Haakonsson was elected King Oluf II of Denmark following the death of his grandfather, Valdemar IV. His election marked a continuation of the royal lineage and the ongoing political dynamics in Scandinavia.
events.name: Election of Olav IV Haakonsson as King Oluf II of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1376, the dying Prince Edward summoned his father, Edward III, and brother, John of Gaunt, making them swear to uphold the claim to the throne of his son, Richard. This moment marked a significant point in the succession crisis of the English monarchy.
events.name: Prince Edward's dying summons

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1376, the Good Parliament was dissolved, having been the longest Parliament to sit in England at that time. Its dissolution marked the end of a significant attempt at reforming the English government amidst ongoing political strife.
events.name: Dissolution of the Good Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1376, Andronicus IV Palaeologus, with the support of the Genoese, invaded Constantinople and dethroned his father, John V Palaeologus. This coup was part of the internal power struggles within the Byzantine Empire during a period of decline.
events.name: Andronicus IV Palaeologus invades Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1376, Richard of Bordeaux, the son of the Black Prince, was created Prince of Wales. This title was significant as it established him as the heir apparent to the English throne amidst the ongoing political turmoil.
events.name: Creation of Richard of Bordeaux as Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1376, John of Gaunt presented his nephew, Richard of Bordeaux, to the feudatories of the realm, swearing to uphold Richard's right to succeed Edward III. This act was crucial in solidifying Richard's claim to the throne during a time of uncertainty.
events.name: John of Gaunt presents Richard of Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: In January 1377, during the Battle of Đồ Bàn, Trần Duệ Tông, the Emperor of the Trần dynasty in Đại Việt (Vietnam), was killed. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Trần dynasty's struggle against foreign invasions.
events.name: Battle of Đồ Bàn

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1377, Pope Gregory XI moved the Papacy back from Avignon to Rome, a pivotal moment in the history of the Catholic Church. This decision was influenced by various factors, including the desire to restore the Church's authority and connection to its historical roots.
events.name: Pope Gregory XI moves Papacy back to Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Bad Parliament, influenced by John of Gaunt, 1st Duke of Lancaster, convened to reverse the reforms made by the previous Good Parliament aimed at reducing corruption within the Royal Council. This parliament also introduced a controversial poll tax, which would later lead to widespread discontent among the populace.
events.name: The Bad Parliament begins sitting in England

events.enhanced_description: In February, Robert of Geneva, acting on behalf of the Pope, led a brutal campaign against antipapal rebels in Cesena, resulting in the massacre of approximately 4,000 individuals. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the papacy and its opponents during the Western Schism.
events.name: Massacre of Cesena

events.enhanced_description: The Bad Parliament was dissolved, leading to the appointment of the first Speaker of the House of Commons, a pivotal moment in the development of parliamentary democracy in England. This event marked the beginning of a more structured legislative process within the English government.
events.name: The Bad Parliament dissolves; the first Speaker of the House of Commons of England is appointed

events.enhanced_description: Trần Phế Đế ascended to the throne of Vietnam following the death of his father, continuing the Trần dynasty's rule during a period marked by internal strife and external threats. His reign would be characterized by efforts to stabilize the kingdom amidst ongoing challenges.
events.name: Trần Phế Đế succeeds his late father as ruler of Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In response to continuous riots in Rome, Pope Gregory XI made the decision to temporarily relocate back to Avignon, where the papacy had resided for much of the 14th century. This move highlighted the ongoing tensions between the papacy and the Roman populace during a tumultuous period in church history.
events.name: Pope Gregory XI moves temporarily back to Avignon

events.enhanced_description: Pope Gregory XI issued five papal Bulls condemning the views of John Wycliffe, particularly his belief that priests should live in poverty akin to the apostles. This action was part of the broader conflict between the church and emerging reformist ideas that would later contribute to the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Pope Gregory XI issues Bulls condemning John Wycliffe

events.enhanced_description: Richard II, at just 10 years old, was crowned king of England in a ceremony at Westminster Abbey, marking the beginning of his tumultuous reign. Due to his youth, a minority government was established to rule on his behalf, leading to significant political maneuvering and unrest in the years to come.
events.name: Richard II is crowned king of England

events.enhanced_description: At the age of fourteen, Maria of Sicily ascended to the throne following the death of her father, Frederick the Simple. Her reign would be marked by the challenges of ruling as a young queen in a politically complex environment.
events.name: Maria of Sicily succeeds her father

events.enhanced_description: The Battle on the Pyana River resulted in a significant defeat for the Russian forces, with their commander tragically drowning in the river during the conflict. This battle was part of the ongoing struggles between the Russian principalities and external threats.
events.name: Battle on Pyana River

events.enhanced_description: Richard II convened his first parliament, marking an important step in his governance as a young king. This meeting would set the stage for the political dynamics of his reign and the challenges he would face from both nobles and commoners.
events.name: Richard II of England's first parliament meets

events.enhanced_description: Tvrtko I was crowned as the king of Bosnia, marking the establishment of a significant medieval state in the region. His reign would see the expansion of Bosnian territory and influence during a time of political fragmentation in the Balkans.

locations.name: Kraljeva Sutjeska, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina

events.name: Tvrtko I of Bosnia is crowned

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, Raseborg Castle was mentioned for the first time in historical documents, marking its significance in the region's medieval history, although its exact date of foundation remains unknown.

image.caption: Ruins of Raseborg Castle near Snappertuna in southern Finland.
image.credit: Cecil — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2008-06-22; the image does not depict the 1378 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: First Mention of Raseborg Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, Tokhtamysh dethroned Temur-Malik to become the Khan of the White Horde, a significant power shift in the region that influenced the political landscape of Central Asia.
events.name: Tokhtamysh Becomes Khan of the White Horde

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, Uthman Beg founded the Aq Qoyunlu dynasty in Diyarbakır, modern-day Turkey, establishing a significant Turkoman state that would play a crucial role in regional politics.
events.name: Uthman Beg Establishes Aq Qoyunlu Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, the Ottoman Turks captured the town of Ihtiman in western Bulgaria, further expanding their influence in the Balkans during their campaign against the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Ottoman Turks Capture Ihtiman

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, Tai Bian succeeded Zhao Bing Fa as the King of Mong Mao, a region in modern-day northern Myanmar, continuing the lineage of local leadership amidst regional power struggles.
events.name: Tai Bian Becomes King of Mong Mao

events.enhanced_description: In 1378, Sa'im al-Dahr was hanged for the act of defacing the Great Sphinx of Giza, an event that highlights the cultural tensions and attitudes towards historical monuments in medieval Egypt.
events.name: Sa'im al-Dahr Hanged for Defacing the Sphinx

events.enhanced_description: In March 1378, John Wycliffe presented his theses advocating for reform within the Catholic Church to the English Parliament. His actions led to his summons before Archbishop Simon of Sudbury at Lambeth Palace, marking a significant moment in the early calls for church reform.
events.name: John Wycliffe's Theses Presented to Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1378, following the death of Pope Gregory XI, the cardinals elected Bartolomeo Prignano as Pope Urban VI amidst riots in Rome demanding a Roman pope. This election marked the beginning of a contentious papacy that would lead to the Western Schism.
events.name: Election of Pope Urban VI

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1378, Da'ud Shah succeeded his assassinated nephew Aladdin Mujahid Shah as the ruler of the Bahmani Sultanate in southern India. His reign was short-lived as he was assassinated shortly thereafter.
events.name: Da'ud Shah Becomes Ruler of the Bahmani Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In May 1378, Uskhal Khan Tögüs Temür succeeded his father, Biligtü Khan Ayushiridara, as the ruler of the Northern Yuan dynasty in Mongolia, continuing the lineage of Mongolian leadership during a time of fragmentation.
events.name: Uskhal Khan Tögüs Temür Succeeds as Ruler

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1378, the Ciompi Revolt erupted in Florence as discontented wool carders temporarily seized control of the government, reflecting the social and economic tensions of the time.
events.name: Ciompi Revolt in Florence

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1378, Gian Galeazzo Visconti succeeded his father, Galeazzo II Visconti, as the ruler of Milan, solidifying the Visconti family's power in northern Italy during a period of political strife.
events.name: Gian Galeazzo Visconti Becomes Ruler of Milan

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1378, Prince Dmitri Ivanovich of Moscow led a successful defense against an invasion by the Mongol Blue Horde under Mamai at the Vozha River, marking a significant victory for the Russian principalities.
events.name: Battle of the Vozha River

events.enhanced_description: In September 1378, a contract was established between Richard le Scrope, 1st Baron Scrope of Bolton, and mason Johan Lewyn for the construction of Bolton Castle, a significant architectural project in northern England.
events.name: Contract for Bolton Castle Construction

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1378, a majority of cardinals dissatisfied with Pope Urban VI convened in Fondi and elected Clement VII as antipope, establishing a rival papal court in Avignon. This event initiated the Western Schism, dividing Christendom.
events.name: Election of Antipope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1378, Halley's Comet made its estimated appearance, a celestial event that has been recorded throughout history and continues to be a subject of astronomical study.
events.name: Appearance of Halley's Comet

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1378, Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor, died in Prague. His death led to his son Wenceslaus becoming King of Bohemia, while the title of Holy Roman Emperor remained unfilled until 1433.
events.name: Death of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 1379, Bairam Khawaja established the independent principality of the Kara Koyunlu in modern-day Armenia, contributing to the complex political dynamics of the region.
events.name: Bairam Khawaja Establishes Kara Koyunlu Principality

events.enhanced_description: In 1379, Dmitry Donskoy of Moscow conducted raids into Estonia, reflecting the ongoing conflicts and territorial ambitions of the Russian principalities during this period.
events.name: Dmitry Donskoy Raids Estonia

events.enhanced_description: In 1379, during the Hundred Years' War, the French lost control of most of Brittany to the English, a significant territorial shift that impacted the balance of power in the region.
events.name: French Loss of Brittany to the English

events.enhanced_description: In 1379, Wisbech Grammar School was founded in Wisbech, England, contributing to the educational development of the region during the late medieval period.

image.caption: Wisbech Grammar School viewed across the River Nene.
image.credit: Rob enwiki — Own work
