image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu retires as shōgun of Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Jongmyo royal ancestral shrine were constructed in Hanseong, modern-day Seoul. These structures became central to the cultural and political life of the Joseon dynasty.
events.name: Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Jongmyo royal ancestral shrine are built in Hanseong

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Sultan Mahmud II in 1394, a civil war erupted in the Delhi Sultanate, leading to a division of the state between eastern and western factions. This conflict significantly weakened the Sultanate and set the stage for future power struggles.
events.name: Civil war breaks out in the Delhi Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ros-Mhic-Thriain occurred in 1394, where the Kingdom of Leinster, led by King Art mac Art MacMurrough-Kavanagh, successfully defeated an invading English army commanded by King Richard II and Roger Mortimer, 4th Earl of March. This battle was a significant event in the ongoing conflict between the Irish and English forces.
events.name: Battle of Ros-Mhic-Thriain

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, Ștefan I succeeded Roman I as the Prince of Moldavia, marking a pivotal moment in the region's leadership. His reign would later be characterized by efforts to strengthen Moldavia against external threats.
events.name: Ștefan I succeeds Roman I, as Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, Abu Zayyan II succeeded his brother Abul Hadjdjadj I as the ruler of the Abdalwadid dynasty in eastern Algeria. This transition of power was significant in the context of North African politics during the late medieval period.
events.name: Abu Zayyan II succeeds Abul Hadjdjadj I, as ruler of the Abdalwadid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, Abd al-Aziz II succeeded Abu al-Abbas Ahmad II as the ruler of the Hafsid dynasty in present-day Tunisia. This succession was part of the ongoing dynastic struggles within the Hafsid leadership.
events.name: Abd al-Aziz II succeeds Abu al-Abbas Ahmad II, as ruler of the Hafsid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, the Allgäuer Brauhaus brewery was founded in present-day Germany, marking the beginning of a significant brewing tradition in the Allgäu region. This establishment contributed to the local economy and culture surrounding beer production.
events.name: The Allgäuer Brauhaus brewery is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1394, the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming dynasty ordered the Ministry of Public Works to allocate land for planting mulberry and jujube trees, emphasizing agricultural development in the empire. This initiative aimed to improve silk production and food resources.
events.name: The Hongwu Emperor orders land for planting mulberry and jujube trees

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1394, King Richard II of England granted poet Geoffrey Chaucer a pension of 20 pounds a year for life, recognizing his contributions as a diplomat and Clerk of The King's Works. This grant underscored Chaucer's importance in English literature and royal service.
events.name: Richard II of England grants Geoffrey Chaucer 20 pounds a year for life

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1394, the Venetians seized control of Argos from Despot Theodore I Palaiologos, furthering their influence in the region. This takeover was part of the larger Venetian efforts to expand their territories in the Aegean and Peloponnesian regions.
events.name: The Venetians take over possession of Argos

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1394, King Charles VI of France issued an edict expelling all Jews from France, a significant act of religious intolerance during the medieval period. This decree led to the forced migration of Jewish communities and marked a dark chapter in French history.
events.name: King Charles VI of France orders the expulsion of all Jews from France

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1394, Antipope Benedict XIII was elected to succeed Antipope Clement VII, continuing the Western Schism within the Catholic Church. This election reflected the ongoing conflict over papal legitimacy and authority during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Antipope Benedict XIII is elected to succeed Antipope Clement VII

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1394, the Battle of Karanovasa took place, where Wallachia, led by Mircea I, successfully resisted an invasion by the Ottomans and their Serb and Bulgarian vassals. This battle was pivotal in maintaining Wallachian independence during the Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Battle of Karanovasa

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1394, the capital of the Joseon dynasty was relocated from Gaegyeong to Hanseong, modern-day Seoul. This strategic move was aimed at enhancing the dynasty's governance and defense capabilities.
events.name: The capital city of the Joseon dynasty is moved from Gaegyeong to Hanseong

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1394, the astronomical clock of St. Nicholas Church in Stralsund was completed and signed by Nikolaus Lilienfeld. This clock was a significant advancement in horological technology and a notable cultural artifact of the period.
events.name: The astronomical clock of St. Nicholas Church in Stralsund is finished

events.enhanced_description: The death of Mary of Hungary in 1395 marked the end of the Capet-Anjou family's reign over Hungary. Following her passing, her estranged husband, Sigismund, became the sole ruler, consolidating power in the kingdom.
events.name: Death of Mary of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In 1395, Ramaracha succeeded Ramesuan as the ruler of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, a significant Thai kingdom that played a crucial role in the region's history.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Ramaracha succeeds Ramesuan

events.enhanced_description: In 1395, the Gwanghwamun Gate and Jogyesa Temple were constructed in present-day Seoul, marking significant architectural achievements during the early Joseon Dynasty.
events.name: Construction of Gwanghwamun Gate and Jogyesa Temple

events.enhanced_description: In 1395, the revered Theotokos of Vladimir icon was relocated to Moscow, a significant event in the religious and cultural history of Russia.
events.name: The Theotokos of Vladimir icon is moved to Moscow

events.enhanced_description: In 1395, John Rykener, a transvestite prostitute, was arrested in London for cross-dressing. This case is notable for being one of the few surviving legal records from this period that mention same-sex intercourse.
events.name: Arrest of John Rykener

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1395, during the Tokhtamysh–Timur war, the Battle of the Terek River took place, where Timur decisively defeated Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde. This battle resulted in the destruction of the Golden Horde's capital, Sarai, and solidified Timur's dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Terek River

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1395, the Duchy of Milan was established when Lord Gian Galeazzo Visconti purchased the title of Duke from Wenceslaus, King of the Romans. This act marked a significant shift in the political landscape of northern Italy.
events.name: The Duchy of Milan is created

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1395, the Battle of Rovine occurred, where Wallachia, aided by Hungarian forces, successfully resisted an Ottoman invasion. Despite the victory, Mircea I temporarily fled to Transylvania, highlighting the ongoing struggles against Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Battle of Rovine

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1395, Sultan Bayezid I of the Ottoman Empire executed Emperor Ivan Shishman of eastern Bulgaria, accusing him of collusion with Wallachian forces during the previous year's Battle of Karanovasa. This act exemplified the brutal tactics employed by the Ottomans to consolidate power in the Balkans.
events.name: Sultan Bayezid I beheads Emperor Ivan Shishman

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1395, Albert IV ascended to the position of Duke of Austria following the death of his father, Albert III. His reign marked a significant period in the consolidation of the Habsburg power in the region.
events.name: Albert IV succeeds his father, Albert III, as Duke of Austria

events.enhanced_description: The death of King Stjepan Dabiš on September 8, 1395, led to the election of his wife, Jelena Gruba, as Queen of Bosnia. However, her reign was challenged as King Sigismund of Hungary soon appropriated much of the Bosnian territory.
events.name: The death of King Stjepan Dabiš

events.enhanced_description: In September 1396, the Battle of the North Inch, also known as the Battle of the Thirty, took place in Perth, Scotland, where the Clan Cameron emerged victorious over the Clan Mackintosh in a trial by combat.
events.name: Battle of the North Inch

events.enhanced_description: In October 1396, a Transylvanian expedition successfully captured Vlad I Uzurpatorul, allowing for the restoration of Mircea I to the throne of Wallachia, thus re-establishing his rule over the principality.
events.name: Restoration of Mircea I of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, the Ottomans captured the Bulgarian fortress of Vidin along with Tsar Ivan Sratsimir, effectively ending the Second Bulgarian Empire and marking a significant expansion of Ottoman territory.
events.name: Ottomans capture Vidin and Tsar Ivan Sratsimir

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, France successfully conquered the Republic of Genoa, a significant maritime power, thereby enhancing its influence in the Mediterranean region.
events.name: France conquers the Republic of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: After a 14-year interregnum, Pedro de San Superano was declared ruler of the Principality of Achaea in 1396, marking a return to governance in this region of southern Greece.
events.name: Pedro de San Superano declared ruler of the Principality of Achaea

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, Abu Amir succeeded Abdul Aziz II as the ruler of the Marinid dynasty in Morocco, continuing the legacy of this influential North African dynasty.
events.name: Abu Amir succeeds Abdul Aziz II as ruler of the Marinid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, Timur appointed his son Miran Shah as the Timurid viceroy of present-day Azerbaijan, solidifying his family's control over the region.
events.name: Timur appoints Miran Shah as viceroy

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, the Kart dynasty in east Persia came to an end when its remaining rulers were murdered at a banquet by Miran Shah, marking a significant shift in regional power dynamics.
events.name: End of the Kart dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1396, Philibert de Naillac succeeded Juan Fernández de Heredia as Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, leading the order during a time of significant challenges and changes.

image.caption: The Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes.
image.credit: User:Piotrus — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2009 photograph of the palace, a site associated with the Knights Hospitaller; it is not a depiction of the 1396 succession itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Philibert de Naillac succeeds Juan Fernández de Heredia

events.enhanced_description: Huitzilihuitl ascended to the throne as the second ruler of the Aztec Empire, following his father Acamapichtli. His reign marked a significant period of consolidation and expansion for the Aztecs, laying the groundwork for future territorial growth.
events.name: Huitzilihuitl succeeds his father, Acamapichtli, as ruler of the Aztecs

events.enhanced_description: The Ulu Camii, or Grand Mosque, was constructed in Bursa, serving as a significant religious and architectural landmark of the early Ottoman Empire. Its design reflects the transition from Byzantine to Ottoman architectural styles, influencing future mosque constructions.
events.name: The Ulu Camii Mosque is built in Bursa by the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In an effort to mediate a dispute between the Ava Kingdom and the Tai polity of Mong Mao, the Ming dynasty dispatched envoys Qian Guxun and Li Sicong. Their mission highlighted the Ming dynasty's diplomatic engagement in Southeast Asia during this period.
events.name: Ming dynasty court sends envoys to the Ava Kingdom and Mong Mao

events.enhanced_description: Timur, the Turco-Mongol conqueror, commissioned the creation of a stunning garden known as the House of Flowers in Samarkand. This garden exemplified the Persian influence on Timurid architecture and landscape design, reflecting the empire's wealth and cultural sophistication.
events.name: Timur orders the construction of a garden in a meadow, House of Flowers

events.enhanced_description: In a remarkable agricultural initiative, peasants in the provinces of Hunan and Hubei planted an astounding 84 million fruit trees. This effort not only aimed to enhance food security but also to improve the local economy and environment.
events.name: Peasants plant 84 million fruit trees in China

events.enhanced_description: The University of Zadar was established as the first university in Croatia, marking a significant milestone in the region's educational history. It became a center for learning and scholarship, influencing the cultural and intellectual landscape of the area.

image.caption: University of Zadar building.
image.credit: Maestralno — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2005-04-17; this is not a contemporary image of the 1396 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The University of Zadar is founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1396, Martin I succeeded his brother John I as King of Aragon, continuing the lineage of the Crown of Aragon during a time of significant political and territorial challenges.
events.name: Martin I succeeds John I as King of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1396, Queen Margaret I of Denmark published the Treaty of Kalmar, which proposed a personal union between the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, significantly shaping the political landscape of Scandinavia.
events.name: Publication of the Treaty of Kalmar

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1396, Queen Margaret I appointed her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania as joint ruler of Sweden, further solidifying her influence over the Scandinavian kingdoms.
events.name: Eric of Pomerania made joint ruler of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1396, John V, Duke of Brittany, married Joan of France, a union that strengthened political ties between Brittany and the French crown.
events.name: Marriage of John V of Brittany and Joan of France

events.enhanced_description: In December 48 BC, King Pharnaces II of Pontus defeated the Roman forces led by Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus at the Battle of Nicopolis. This defeat underscored the challenges faced by Caesar's supporters and the shifting dynamics of power in the region during the civil war.
events.name: Battle of Nicopolis

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1396, Richard II of England married six-year-old Isabella of Valois in Calais, a union that temporarily eased tensions between England and France amidst the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Marriage of Richard II of England and Isabella of Valois

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1396, the Transit of Venus, the last of its kind not part of a pair, was possibly observed by Aztec astronomers, showcasing their advanced understanding of astronomy.
events.name: Transit of Venus observed by Aztec astronomers

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1396, Ralph Neville, 1st Earl of Westmorland, married Joan Beaufort, strengthening the ties between the Neville family and the royal lineage.
events.name: Marriage of Ralph Neville and Joan Beaufort

events.enhanced_description: In January, Mircea I successfully reclaimed the throne of Wallachia, restoring his rule after a period of instability. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the principality against external threats and internal dissent.
events.name: Mircea I takes back the throne of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: Temür Qutlugh was crowned as the Khan of the Golden Horde, with the influential general Edigu playing a crucial role in his ascension. Despite his title, Edigu continued to wield significant power behind the scenes, shaping the direction of the khanate.
events.name: Temür Qutlugh is crowned as Khan of the Golden Horde

events.enhanced_description: The Università, a form of local government, was established in Malta, marking a significant step in the development of self-governance on the island. This institution played a crucial role in the administration and political organization of Malta.
events.name: The Università is established in Malta

events.enhanced_description: The Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery was founded in northwestern Russia, becoming a significant center for Orthodox Christianity. Its establishment contributed to the spread of monasticism and religious education in the region.
events.name: The Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery is founded

events.enhanced_description: The Sretensky Monastery was established in Moscow, serving as a vital religious institution in the heart of Russia. It became known for its role in the spiritual life of the city and its contributions to Orthodox Christianity.
events.name: The Sretensky Monastery is founded in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: The first hospital in al-Andalus was established in Granada, marking a significant advancement in medical care in the region. This institution reflected the sophisticated healthcare practices of the time and the cultural achievements of Islamic Spain.
events.name: The first hospital in al-Andalus is created at Granada

events.enhanced_description: The brewery located at Neuhausergasse 4 in Munich, known for producing Spaten beer, was officially listed in the register of Munich breweries. This event highlights the importance of brewing culture in Bavaria and the city's economic development.
events.name: Neuhausergasse 4, the brewer of Spaten, is listed on the register of Munich breweries

events.enhanced_description: Gregory of Tatev composed the Book of Questions, an extensive ten-volume encyclopedic work, at the Tatev Monastery in Armenia. This significant literary contribution reflects the intellectual pursuits of the time and the monastery's role as a center of learning.
events.name: Gregory of Tatev writes the Book of Questions

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, John Beaufort was elevated to the title of Earl of Somerset, a significant noble title in England. This appointment solidified his family's influence and power within the English nobility during a tumultuous period.
events.name: John Beaufort becomes Earl of Somerset

events.enhanced_description: Richard Whittington was nominated as the Lord Mayor of London for the first time on June 6. His tenure would later become legendary, associated with tales of his wealth and philanthropy, contributing significantly to the city's governance.
events.name: Richard Whittington is nominated as Lord Mayor of London for the first time

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, Eric of Pomerania was crowned in Kalmar as the ruler of the Kalmar Union, a significant political entity uniting Denmark, Norway, and Sweden. His ascension was orchestrated by Queen Margaret I, who retained considerable influence over the union.

image.caption: Reconstruction of Eric of Pomerania’s coat of arms, based on his seal.
image.credit: A.T — Own work
image.date_qualification: Modern reconstruction, dated 2014-05-14; depicts heraldry reconstructed from a 1398 seal.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Eric of Pomerania is crowned in Kalmar as ruler of the Kalmar Union

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, King Richard II of England took decisive action to reassert his authority by arresting members of the Lords Appellant, a powerful faction of barons. This move was part of his broader strategy to regain control over his fractious kingdom.
events.name: Richard II attempts to reassert authority over his kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Kalmar, signed on September 25, established a formal agreement between the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under the Kalmar Union. This treaty aimed to promote unity and cooperation among the three realms during a period of political strife.
events.name: The Treaty of Kalmar is signed

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, John Holland, previously the Earl of Huntingdon, was elevated to the title of Duke of Exeter by his half-brother, King Richard II. This promotion reflected the ongoing consolidation of power among the English nobility.
events.name: John Holland is created Duke of Exeter

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, Thomas Arundel was replaced by Roger Walden as Archbishop of Canterbury after being accused of high treason by King Richard II. This event underscored the political tensions within the church and the monarchy during Richard's reign.
events.name: Thomas Arundel is replaced as Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, as France withdrew its support for Antipope Benedict XIII, an army led by Geoffrey Boucicaut occupied Avignon and initiated a five-year siege of the papal palace. This military action was part of the larger conflict surrounding the Western Schism.
events.name: Siege of Avignon begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Teutonic Knights resumed their military raids into Lithuania, continuing their long-standing conflict with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. This resurgence of hostilities contributed to the ongoing tensions in the region.
events.name: The Teutonic Knights recommence their raids of Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Teutonic Knights successfully conquered the island of Gotland, which had previously been under the control of the Victual Brothers, a group of pirates. This conquest solidified the Knights' influence in the Baltic Sea region.
events.name: The Teutonic Knights conquer Gotland

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, Martin of Aragon initiated a crusade against the Moors in North Africa, reflecting the ongoing Christian-Muslim conflicts of the period. This military campaign aimed to reclaim territories lost to Muslim forces.
events.name: Martin of Aragon launches a crusade against the Moors

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Kingdom of Singapura fell to the invading forces of the Majapahit Empire, marking a significant shift in power in Southeast Asia. This event contributed to the decline of local kingdoms and the rise of larger empires in the region.
events.name: The Kingdom of Singapura falls

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, Abdullah succeeded his father, Abu Amir, as the ruler of the Marinid dynasty in Morocco. His ascension marked a continuation of the Marinid rule during a period characterized by internal strife and external pressures.
events.name: Abdullah succeeds Abu Amir as ruler of the Marinid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, Bunei succeeded his father, Satto, as the King of Chūzan, a kingdom located in modern-day Okinawa, Japan. His reign continued the legacy of Chūzan during a time of regional consolidation and cultural development.
events.name: Bunei succeeds his father as King of Chūzan

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Glendalough monastery in County Wicklow, Ireland, was destroyed by English troops. This event was part of the broader conflicts between the English crown and Irish chieftains during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Glendalough monastery is destroyed

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Ferapontov Monastery was founded in modern-day northwest Russia by Therapont of Belozersk. This monastery became an important center of Orthodox Christianity and culture in the region.
events.name: Ferapontov Monastery is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, the Munmyo Confucian shrine and Sungkyunkwan University were established in modern-day Seoul, Korea. These institutions played a crucial role in the promotion of Confucian ideals and education during the Joseon dynasty.
events.name: The Munmyo Confucian shrine and Sungkyunkwan University are founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1398, Mount Grace Priory was established in North Yorkshire, England. This Carthusian monastery became known for its unique architectural style and its role in the religious life of the region.
events.name: Mount Grace Priory is established

events.enhanced_description: According to fringe theorists, in 1398, the Scottish explorer Henry I Sinclair, Earl of Orkney, is believed to have reached North America. This claim, while controversial, suggests early European exploration of the continent.
events.name: Henry I Sinclair reaches North America (theory)

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, Trần Thuận Tông was forced to abdicate as the ruler of the Trần dynasty in favor of his three-year-old son, Trần Thiếu Đế. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the Vietnamese monarchy during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Trần Thuận Tông abdicates as ruler of the Trần dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In April and May of 1398, the Bosnian nobility orchestrated a coup that led to the dethronement of Queen Helen, replacing her with Stephen Ostoja, who became the new ruler of Bosnia. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region, reflecting the power struggles among the nobility.
events.name: The Bosnian nobility dethrone Queen Helen and replace her with Stephen Ostoja

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1398, Jianwen ascended to the throne as the second emperor of the Ming dynasty, following the death of his grandfather, the Hongwu Emperor. His reign was marked by attempts to consolidate power and reduce the influence of the nobility, which ultimately led to his downfall.
events.name: Jianwen succeeds his grandfather, Hongwu, as Emperor of Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: In July 1398, the Stecknitz Canal was completed, connecting the rivers Elbe and Trave near Lübeck, Germany. This canal is recognized as one of the earliest navigable summit level canals in the world, significantly enhancing trade and transportation in the region.

image.caption: Map of southern Schleswig-Holstein and western Mecklenburg-Vorpommern showing the Elbe–Lübeck Canal and the Elbe and Trave rivers.
image.credit: Bryan Rutherford — Own work , based on File:Schleswig-Holstein_2010.png
image.date_qualification: A 2016 map of the later Elbe–Lübeck Canal and connected rivers, not a contemporary depiction of the Stecknitz Canal’s completion in 1398.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Stecknitz Canal is completed

events.enhanced_description: In September 1398, King Richard II of England exiled his cousin Henry Bolingbroke for ten years to resolve a feud with Thomas de Mowbray, the Duke of Norfolk. This political maneuver set the stage for future conflicts that would ultimately lead to Bolingbroke's rise as Henry IV.
events.name: King Richard II of England exiles Henry Bolingbroke

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1398, the Treaty of Salynas was signed between Vytautas, the Grand Duke of Lithuania, and Konrad von Jungingen, the Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights. This treaty aimed to cede the region of Samogitia to the Knights, reflecting the ongoing territorial disputes in Eastern Europe.

image.caption: Historical map of the Teutonic state and surrounding territories.
image.credit: Original raster by Space Cadet , vector created by Offnfopt — Own work modeled after File:Teutonic state 1455.png
image.date_qualification: The source gives an image date of 2017-10-16; this is not the date of the depicted historical geography.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Treaty of Salynas is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1398, King Taejo of the Joseon dynasty abdicated the throne following the murder of his heir, Yi Bangsuk, during a coup led by his half-brother, Yi Bang-won. This event marked a significant turning point in the Joseon dynasty's history, leading to the rise of a new ruler.
events.name: King Taejo of Joseon abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1398, Janus ascended to the throne as King of Cyprus, succeeding his father, James I. His reign was characterized by efforts to maintain the kingdom's independence amidst external pressures from neighboring powers.
events.name: Janus succeeds his father as King of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1398, Timur defeated the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, Nasir al-Din Mahmud Shah, after a prolonged civil war. Following his victory, Timur's forces sacked Delhi, resulting in widespread devastation and loss of life among the city's Hindu population.

image.caption: Zafarnama manuscript illustration depicting Timur pursuing Sultan Mahmud-Khan Tughluq’s forces back into Delhi.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective manuscript illustration created in 1436, about the 1398 campaign; it is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Timur defeats the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In January 1399, Timur the Lame captured and sacked Haridwar, a significant city in northern India. This event was part of Timur's campaign to expand his empire and assert dominance over the region.
events.name: Timur the Lame captures and sacks Haridwar

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Faraj succeeded his father, Barquq, as the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt. His reign would be marked by internal strife and external threats, particularly from the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Faraj succeeds his father, Barquq, as Mamluk Sultan of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Sultan Bayezid I of the Ottoman Empire launched an invasion of Mamluk-occupied Syria, intensifying the conflict between the Ottomans and the Mamluks. This invasion highlighted the growing ambitions of the Ottoman Empire in the region.
events.name: Sultan Bayezid I of the Ottoman Empire invades Mamluk-occupied Syria

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Ladislaus regained the throne of Naples after successfully overthrowing King Louis II. His return to power was significant in the ongoing conflicts for control of southern Italy.
events.name: Ladislaus regains the throne of Naples

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, King Jogaila became the sole ruler of Poland following the death of his co-ruling wife, Queen Jadwiga. His reign would be marked by significant political and military developments in the region.
events.name: King Jogaila becomes sole ruler of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Abu Said Uthman III succeeded his father Abdullah as the ruler of the Marinid dynasty in Morocco. His reign would face challenges from both internal factions and external threats.
events.name: Abu Said Uthman III succeeds Abdullah as ruler of the Marinid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, the Principality of Achaea, located in southern Greece, successfully resisted an invasion by the Ottoman Empire. This resistance was part of the broader struggle against Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: The Principality of Achaea resists an invasion by the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: The year 1399 is traditionally recognized as the foundation date of the Kingdom of Mysore in India, which would endure until 1950. This kingdom played a significant role in the history of southern India.
events.name: Traditional foundation date of the Kingdom of Mysore in India

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Iuga ascended to the position of prince of Moldavia, a region that would experience significant political changes during his reign. His leadership was crucial in navigating the challenges posed by neighboring powers.
events.name: Iuga becomes prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1399, John of Gaunt, the uncle of King Richard II of England and father of Henry Bolingbroke, died in Leicester. His death created a power vacuum that would have significant implications for the English monarchy.
events.name: John of Gaunt dies

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1399, Richard II of England canceled the legal documents that allowed the exiled Henry Bolingbroke to inherit his father's lands. This act further escalated tensions between Richard and Bolingbroke, setting the stage for future conflict.
events.name: Richard II cancels Henry Bolingbroke's inheritance

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1399, while Richard II was away on a military campaign in Ireland, Henry Bolingbroke returned to England with the support of exiled former Archbishop Thomas Arundel. This marked the beginning of Bolingbroke's military campaign to reclaim his confiscated lands, ultimately leading to Richard's downfall.
events.name: Henry Bolingbroke returns to England

events.enhanced_description: In 1399, Zhu Di, the Prince of Yan, initiated a rebellion against the ruling Ming dynasty from his base in Beijing, seeking to claim the throne for himself. This conflict marked the beginning of a power struggle that would ultimately lead to his ascension as the Yongle Emperor.

image.caption: Seated portrait of Emperor Ming Chengzu, also known as the Yongle Emperor.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Digitized by NPM; image is directly from Shuge
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated broadly to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644); not a contemporary event image with a specific date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Prince of Yan (Zhu Di) of China starts a rebellion in Beijing

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1399, the Battle of the Vorskla River took place, where the Mongol Golden Horde, led by Khan Temür Qutlugh and Emir Edigu, decisively defeated a coalition army comprising former Khan Tokhtamysh and Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania. This battle significantly weakened the influence of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Vorskla River

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1399, King Richard II of England was captured upon his return from Ireland, marking a pivotal moment in the political turmoil of England. His imprisonment set the stage for the rise of Henry Bolingbroke, who would later become Henry IV.
events.name: Richard II of England is taken prisoner upon his return from Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1399, following the capture of Richard II, Henry Bolingbroke was urged by Parliament to seize the crown, citing Richard's misrule and crimes against his subjects. This event led to the eventual deposition of Richard II and the rise of Bolingbroke as Henry IV.
events.name: Henry Bolingbroke is urged to take the crown from Richard II

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1399, Parliament formally accepted Henry Bolingbroke as the new king of England, marking the end of Richard II's reign. This transition was pivotal in establishing the Lancastrian dynasty.
events.name: Parliament accepts Henry Bolingbroke as the new king of England

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1399, Henry IV was crowned king of England at Westminster Abbey, solidifying his claim to the throne after the deposition of Richard II. His coronation marked the beginning of a new era in English history.
events.name: Henry IV of England is crowned

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1399, Thomas Arundel was restored as Archbishop of Canterbury, replacing Roger Walden. His reinstatement was significant in the context of the Church's influence during a time of political upheaval.
events.name: Thomas Arundel is restored as Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1399, John V ascended to the ducal throne of Brittany, marking the beginning of his reign. His leadership would play a crucial role in the political landscape of France during the early 15th century.
events.name: John V, Duke of Brittany begins his reign

events.enhanced_description: In February 1400, Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, led incursions into Scotland, marking a period of conflict between England and Scotland. These military actions were part of the ongoing tensions that characterized the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Henry Percy (Hotspur) incursions into Scotland

events.enhanced_description: King Swa Saw Ke of Ava died after a lengthy reign of 33 years, leading to the ascension of his son, King Tarabya. However, Tarabya's reign was short-lived, lasting less than seven months before he was assassinated.
events.name: Death of King Swa Saw Ke

events.enhanced_description: The Epiphany Rising was a failed rebellion in England aimed at restoring the deposed King Richard II. The uprising was quickly suppressed, resulting in the execution of several nobles involved, including the Earl of Salisbury and the Earl of Kent.
events.name: The Epiphany Rising

events.enhanced_description: Richard II, the deposed King of England, died under mysterious circumstances in Pontefract Castle, likely ordered by King Henry IV to prevent any potential uprisings. His death marked the end of a tumultuous period in English history.
events.name: Death of Richard II

events.enhanced_description: Five-year-old Trần Thiếu Đế was forced to abdicate the throne of Đại Việt in favor of his maternal grandfather, Hồ Quý Ly, marking the end of the Trần dynasty after 175 years and the beginning of the Hồ dynasty.
events.name: Abdication of Trần Thiếu Đế

events.enhanced_description: Sir Thomas Percy, 1st Earl of Worcester, resigned from his position as Admiral of the North and West to join the resistance against King Henry IV. His resignation signified a growing discontent among the nobility during this turbulent period.
events.name: Sir Thomas Percy resigns as Admiral

events.enhanced_description: Alexandru cel Bun was installed as the new Prince of Moldavia by Mircea the Elder after the removal of the reigning monarch, Prince Iuga. This event marked a significant shift in the leadership of Moldavia during a time of regional instability.
events.name: Installation of Alexandru cel Bun

events.enhanced_description: During the Jingnan campaign, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, achieved a decisive victory against the Imperial forces led by General Li Jinglong at the Battle of Baigou River. The battle was notable for the chaos caused by a sudden gust of wind that disrupted the Imperial flag.
events.name: Battle of Baigou River

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political maneuver, three prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire convened in Frankfurt to discuss the deposition of Emperor Wenceslaus due to his ineffective leadership. They ultimately selected Frederick I, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, as a potential replacement.
events.name: Meeting of Prince-electors in Frankfurt

events.enhanced_description: Frederick I of Brunswick-Lüneburg was assassinated shortly after being identified as a rival to Emperor Wenceslaus. His assassination occurred while he was returning from a meeting of the prince-electors, highlighting the intense political rivalries of the time.
events.name: Assassination of Frederick I of Brunswick-Lüneburg

events.enhanced_description: Sir John Swinton, an envoy of King Robert III of Scotland, crossed into England with a group of knights under a writ of safe conduct from King Henry IV. This diplomatic mission aimed to negotiate peace during a tense period between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Envoy of King Robert III crosses into England

events.enhanced_description: Jagiellonian University was re-established in Kraków by order of King Władysław II, marking a significant moment in the history of education in Poland. The creation of the Faculty of Theology was partly funded by the sale of jewelry from the late Queen Jadwiga.
events.name: Re-establishment of Jagiellonian University

events.enhanced_description: King Henry IV of England sent a formal demand to King Robert III of Scotland, insisting on a meeting to discuss the obligations of Scotland to England. This demand was made against the backdrop of ongoing tensions between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Demand from King Henry IV to King Robert III

events.enhanced_description: After receiving no response from King Robert III, King Henry IV led the English army into Scotland, reaching Haddington and then Leith. This military campaign was part of the ongoing conflict between England and Scotland.
events.name: Henry IV leads army into Scotland

events.enhanced_description: At Lahneck Castle, the princes of the German states convened to vote on the deposition of Holy Roman Emperor Wenceslaus due to his ineffective leadership. This meeting reflected the growing discontent among the nobility regarding the Emperor's rule.
events.name: Meeting at Lahneck Castle

events.enhanced_description: Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine, was elected as King of the Romans, a significant event in the political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire. His election was part of the broader efforts to stabilize the Empire amidst internal conflicts.
figures: Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine
events.name: Election of Rupert as King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: After failing to secure a pledge of fealty from King Robert III of Scotland, King Henry IV returned to England. This retreat marked a setback in his attempts to assert English dominance over Scotland.
events.name: Henry IV returns to England

events.enhanced_description: Owain Glyndŵr was proclaimed Prince of Wales by his followers, initiating a series of attacks on English strongholds in northeast Wales. This marked the beginning of a significant Welsh uprising against English rule.
events.name: Proclamation of Owain Glyndŵr

events.enhanced_description: Tamerlane, the Mongol conqueror, halted at the Turkish garrison in Behesna during his campaign. After an initial provocation, he launched a successful attack that led to the surrender of the garrison.
events.name: Tamerlane's stop at Behesna

events.enhanced_description: During the Jingnan campaign, Prince Zhu Di of Yan captured Cangzhou in Hebei province, further expanding his conquests. This victory was part of his broader efforts to assert control over the Ming dynasty.
events.name: Capture of Cangzhou

events.enhanced_description: Tamerlane initiated the destruction of Aleppo, overwhelming the defenders from the Mamluk Sultanate. This brutal campaign resulted in significant loss of life and marked a pivotal moment in the region's history.
events.name: Destruction of Aleppo

events.enhanced_description: The Mamluk Sultanate surrendered the city of Aleppo to Tamerlane's forces, leading to a massacre of many inhabitants. This event underscored Tamerlane's ruthless military strategy and the fragility of Mamluk power.

image.caption: The entrance to Aleppo Citadel, with a bridge crossing the surrounding ditch.
image.credit: Dosseman — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the citadel entrance, not a depiction of the 1400 surrender; original image date is 2010-09-27 10:42:19.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Surrender of Aleppo

events.enhanced_description: Minkhaung I ascended to the throne of Ava following a power struggle that ensued after the assassination of King Tarabya. His rise marked a new chapter in the history of the largest kingdom in northern Myanmar.
events.name: Ascension of Minkhaung I

events.enhanced_description: Manuel II Palaiologos became the only Byzantine Emperor to visit England, where he was warmly received by King Henry IV at Blackheath. This visit occurred during the Christmas holiday and highlighted the diplomatic relations between the Byzantine Empire and England.
events.name: Visit of Manuel II Palaiologos to England

events.enhanced_description: In a significant setback during the Jingnan campaign, Prince Zhu Di's forces faced a serious defeat at the Battle of Dongchang, where they were encircled by Imperial General Sheng Yong. Despite the loss, Zhu Di managed to escape and regroup for future engagements.
events.name: Battle of Dongchang

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Timur launched a campaign against the Black Sheep Turkomans and the Jalayirid dynasty, successfully conquering their territories in present-day Azerbaijan and Iraq. The rulers Qara Yusuf and Sultan Ahmad fled to seek refuge with the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I, marking a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Timur conquers the Empire of The Black Sheep Turkomans, in present-day Azerbaijan, and the Jalayirid dynasty in present-day Iraq

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, King Jeongjong of the Joseon Dynasty abdicated the throne due to fears of an impending attack from his younger brother, Taejong, who was known for his ambition. This event marked a significant power shift within the royal family and set the stage for Taejong's eventual ascension to the throne.
events.name: In modern-day Korea, King Jeongjong of Joseon abdicates in fear of an attack by his ambitious younger brother, Taejong

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Prince Parameswara founded the Malacca Sultanate, which would become a significant trading empire in Southeast Asia. This establishment marked the beginning of a powerful maritime kingdom that played a crucial role in regional trade and cultural exchange.
events.name: Prince Parameswara establishes the Malacca Sultanate, in present-day western Malaysia and northern Sumatra

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Hananchi ascended to the throne as the King of Hokuzan, succeeding Min. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Ryukyu Kingdom, which would later play a vital role in regional politics and trade.
events.name: Hananchi succeeds Min as King of Hokuzan, in modern-day north Okinawa, Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the principality of Wallachia successfully resisted an invasion by the Ottoman Empire, showcasing the military prowess of its ruler, Mircea the Elder. This resistance was a significant event in the ongoing struggle between the Ottomans and the Balkan states.
events.name: Wallachia (modern-day southern Romania) resists an invasion by the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, a Wallachian army captured the strategic location of Iuga, leading to the appointment of Alexandru cel Bun as the Prince of Moldavia. This event was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of the region during this period.
events.name: A Wallachian army captures Iuga, and makes Alexandru cel Bun the Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the Kingdom of Kongo was established in Central Africa, marking the rise of one of the most powerful and influential kingdoms in the region. This kingdom would play a significant role in trade and cultural exchanges between Africa and Europe.
events.name: The Kingdom of Kongo begins

events.enhanced_description: Around 1401, the Haast's eagle and Moa, two iconic species of New Zealand, were driven to extinction largely due to hunting by the Māori people. This event highlights the impact of human activity on biodiversity in isolated ecosystems.
events.name: The Haast's eagle and Moa are both driven to extinction by Māori hunters

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the Mississippian culture, known for its complex societies and mound-building, began to experience a decline. This decline was attributed to various factors, including environmental changes and social upheaval.
events.name: The Mississippian culture starts to decline

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, it was estimated that Europe had a population of approximately 52 million inhabitants. This demographic data provides insight into the social and economic conditions of the continent during the late medieval period.
events.name: Europe is reported to have around 52 million inhabitants

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the House of Medici began to rise in power within Florence, establishing themselves as a dominant political and cultural force. Their influence would shape the Renaissance and the development of art and politics in Italy.
events.name: The House of Medici becomes powerful in Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Newcastle upon Tyne was granted the status of a county corporate by King Henry IV of England. This designation allowed the city to govern itself and marked an important step in its development as a significant urban center.

locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, Tyne and Wear

events.name: Newcastle upon Tyne is created a county corporate, by Henry IV of England

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the chronicler Jean Froissart completed his seminal work, 'Chronicles,' which provided a detailed account of the events of the 14th century in France. His writings are considered a crucial source for understanding medieval history.
events.name: Jean Froissart completes his Chronicles, detailing the events of the 14th Century in France

events.enhanced_description: The Jingnan campaign was a pivotal military conflict during the Ming dynasty, where Prince Zhu Di mobilized his forces from Beijing to challenge the Jianwen Emperor. This campaign marked the beginning of Zhu Di's efforts to claim the throne, leading to significant political upheaval within the dynasty.
events.name: Jingnan campaign

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, John Barry was appointed as the new Attorney-General for Ireland, a significant role in the governance of the country during a time of political strife and conflict. His appointment reflected the ongoing struggles for power and legal authority in Ireland.
events.name: Appointment of John Barry

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Dilawar Khan established the Malwa Sultanate in present-day northern India, marking the rise of a new political entity in the region. This development was significant in the context of the fragmented political landscape of India during this period.

image.caption: Map depicting the Malwa Sultanate under the Ghurids.
image.credit: Beylarbey — Own work
image.date_qualification: A map of the sultanate’s territorial extent during 1401–1436, not a depiction of the 1401 founding event. Original image date: 2026-07-29.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of the Malwa Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, the Joseon dynasty in present-day Korea officially entered into a tributary relationship with Ming dynasty China, solidifying diplomatic and trade ties between the two nations. This relationship was pivotal for Korea's political and cultural development.
events.name: Tributary relationship of Joseon with Ming

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Japan re-entered into a tributary relationship with Ming dynasty China, marking a significant diplomatic shift. This relationship facilitated trade and cultural exchanges, influencing both nations' interactions.
events.name: Japan re-enters tributary relationship with China

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1401, Rupert of Germany was crowned King of the Romans in Cologne, solidifying his claim to the imperial title within the Holy Roman Empire. This event was significant in the context of the political struggles of the time.
events.name: Rupert, King of Germany, is crowned King of the Romans at Cologne

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1401, Emperor Hồ Quý Ly of Dai Ngu abdicated the throne in favor of his son, Hồ Hán Thương. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of Vietnam, as it reflected the dynastic changes of the period.
events.name: Emperor Hồ Quý Ly of Dai Ngu (now Vietnam) passes the throne to his son, Hồ Hán Thương

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1401, following a significant defeat in the Battle of Dongchang during the Jingnan campaign, the forces of the Principality of Yan retreated to Beiping, present-day Beijing. This event was part of a larger power struggle within the Ming dynasty.
events.name: After their disastrous defeat on December 25 in the Battle of Dongchang in the Jingnan campaign, the forces of the Principality of Yan within China return to Beiping (located at the site of present-day Beijing)

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1401, King Henry IV opened a session of the Parliament of England at Westminster. This event was significant in the context of the political landscape of England during the early 15th century.
events.name: The Parliament of England is opened at Westminster by King Henry IV

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1401, Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos, after spending time in England, accepted a payment of 3,000 English gold marks from King Henry IV. This financial support was aimed at strengthening the alliance between England and the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: The Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos accepts a payment of 3,000 English gold marks in support of an alliance between England and Byzantium

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1401, William Sawtrey, a Roman Catholic priest and Lollard, was burned at the stake in Smithfield, London, becoming the first victim of the De heretico comburendo law. This event marked a significant moment in the history of religious persecution in England.
events.name: William Sawtrey becomes the first person in England to be burned at the stake under the new De heretico comburendo law

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1401, King Henry IV of England granted royal assent to the Suppression of Heresy Act, which allowed secular authorities to punish religious crimes. This act was influenced by the Archbishop of Canterbury and targeted the Lollards, followers of John Wycliffe.
events.name: King Henry IV gives royal assent to the Suppression of Heresy Act

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1401, the Samogitians, supported by Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania, rebelled against the Teutonic Knights, successfully burning two of their castles. This rebellion was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Teutonic Order and the local populations.
events.name: The Samogitians rebel against the Teutonic knights and burn two castles

events.enhanced_description: In 1401, Timur, the Turko-Mongol conqueror, successfully captured Damascus after defeating both the Ottoman Empire and the Mamluk Sultanate. Following the conquest, his troops committed widespread massacres against the city's inhabitants, marking a brutal chapter in the region's history.
events.name: Timur defeats both the Ottoman Empire and the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, to capture the city of Damascus in present-day Syria

events.enhanced_description: On Good Friday in 1401, Conwy Castle was captured through cunning tactics by Welsh brothers Rhys and Gwilym ap Tudur, supporting the rebellion led by Owain Glyndŵr against English rule. This event was a significant moment in the Welsh struggle for independence.
events.name: Capture of Conwy Castle

events.enhanced_description: King Zsigmond of Hungary was taken prisoner on April 28, 1401, after refusing to comply with demands from Archbishop John Kanizsai and Palatine Derek Bebek. His imprisonment highlighted the political tensions and struggles for power within the kingdom.
events.name: Imprisonment of King Zsigmond

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1401, the council of the Republic of Venice enacted a law to prevent the Doge from using the state-owned ship, the Bucentaur, for private purposes. This legislation was part of broader efforts to maintain the integrity of state resources.
events.name: Law prohibiting private use of the Bucentaur

events.enhanced_description: Maria, Queen of Sicily, passed away on May 25, 1401, after a reign of nearly 34 years. Her death marked a significant transition in the political landscape of Sicily, impacting the region's governance and alliances.
events.name: Death of Maria, Queen of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1401, Laurence Allerthorp was appointed as the new Lord High Treasurer of England, succeeding Sir John Norbury. This position was crucial for managing the kingdom's finances during a period of political instability.
events.name: Laurence Allerthorp becomes Lord High Treasurer

events.enhanced_description: In June 1401, the English Pale in Ireland was significantly reduced to include only Dublin, County Kildare, County Louth, and County Meath. This contraction reflected the declining influence of English rule in Ireland amidst growing local resistance.
events.name: Reduction of the English Pale

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1401, during the Jingnan campaign, rebel Yan forces destroyed food supplies belonging to the Ming Chinese government at Dezhou. This act was part of a broader strategy to weaken the imperial forces and assert control over the region.

image.caption: English-language map of the Jingnan Campaign (1399–1402).

events.name: Destruction of food supplies at Dezhou

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1401, Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu dispatched a mission to Ming Dynasty China, marking a significant step towards establishing trade relations between the two nations. This diplomatic effort was crucial for fostering economic and cultural exchanges.
events.name: Mission dispatched to Ming China

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1401, the Schaffhausen massacre resulted in the brutal killing of 30 Jewish residents, following the murder of a young boy named Konrad Lori. This tragic event highlighted the rampant anti-Semitism and violence against Jewish communities in medieval Europe.
events.name: Schaffhausen massacre

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1401, Timur launched a brutal raid on Baghdad, resulting in a massacre of its inhabitants as punishment for their resistance. This event was marked by horrific violence, with reports of tens of thousands killed and the city left in ruins.
events.name: Timur's raid on Baghdad

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1401, Chinese imperial troops led by Fang Zhao launched a raid on the Yan principality's capital at Beiping, forcing Prince Zhu Di to retreat north. This confrontation was part of the larger Jingnan campaign, which sought to consolidate imperial power.
events.name: Raid on Beiping

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1401, the County of Geneva was sold to Amadeus VIII, Count of Savoy, marking the end of its independence after over 300 years. This transaction significantly altered the political landscape of the region.
events.name: End of the County of Geneva

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1401, the Yan principality achieved a significant victory over Chinese imperial forces at Beiping after a prolonged siege. This battle was a crucial moment in the Jingnan campaign, showcasing the resilience of Zhu Di's forces.
events.name: Yan principality defeats Chinese forces

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1401, the late cleric John Twenge was canonized as Saint John of Bridlington by Pope Boniface IX. This canonization reflected the growing veneration of saints in medieval Christianity and the influence of the papacy.
events.name: Canonization of John Twenge

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1401, Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq was restored to power in Delhi, marking a significant moment in the tumultuous history of the Delhi Sultanate. His return to the throne was pivotal in stabilizing the region after a period of unrest.
events.name: Restoration of Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1401, King Zsigmond of Hungary was released from imprisonment by order of the Royal Council, allowing him to resume his rule. His release was a critical turning point in the political dynamics of Hungary during this period.
events.name: Release of King Zsigmond

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1401, the Battle of Tuthill occurred at Caernarfon, where Owain Glyndŵr's forces faced a significant defeat, losing 300 soldiers to the English Army. This battle marked the first display of Glyndŵr's banner, The Golden Dragon, symbolizing his resistance against English rule.
events.name: Battle of Tuthill

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1401, during the Jingnan campaign, Zhu Di adopted a new military strategy, moving southward from Beiping to the Yangtze River and capturing several key locations including Dong'e, Dongping, Wenshang, and Pei. This shift in tactics was crucial for his campaign against the Ming dynasty.

locations.name: Yangtze River, near Nanjing, Jiangsu, China

events.name: Zhu Di's military campaign

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the Battle of Bryn Glas saw Welsh rebels under Owain Glyndŵr defeat the English on the England/Wales border. The Welsh captured Edmund Mortimer, a significant figure who later married Glyndŵr's daughter.

locations.name: Bryn Glas, Powys, Wales, United Kingdom

events.name: Battle of Bryn Glas

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the Malacca Sultanate was established in Melaka, Malaysia, marking a significant point in the region's history as a center of trade and Islamic culture. This sultanate would play a crucial role in the maritime trade routes of Southeast Asia.
events.name: Establishment of the Malacca Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, King Henry III of Castile commissioned French explorer Jean de Béthencourt to colonize the Canary Islands. Béthencourt was granted the title of King of the Canary Islands, although he recognized Henry as his overlord, marking the beginning of Spanish influence in the archipelago.
events.name: Conquest of the Canary Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the Republic of Genoa successfully regained control of Monaco, reinforcing its influence in the Mediterranean region. This event was part of the broader power struggles among Italian city-states during this period.
events.name: Genoa regains control of Monaco

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the Aq Qoyunlu tribal confederation moved its capital from Amida to Diyarbakır, reflecting the shifting political landscape in the region. This move was significant for the consolidation of power within the confederation.
events.name: Aq Qoyunlu moves capital

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, Moldavia became a vassal of the Kingdom of Poland to protect itself from potential invasions by Hungary. This alliance was crucial for Moldavia's survival during a turbulent period in Eastern European history.
events.name: Moldavia becomes a vassal of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, Maria II Zaccaria succeeded her husband, Pedro de San Superano, as regent of the Principality of Achaea in southern Greece. Her leadership marked a significant moment in the governance of the region during a time of political instability.
events.name: Maria II Zaccaria becomes regent

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, Conchobar an Abaidh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh succeeded Maelsechlainn mac William Buidhe O Cellaigh as King of Uí Maine, a Gaelic kingdom in modern-day County Galway and County Roscommon, Ireland. His reign was part of the complex tapestry of Gaelic leadership during this period.
figures: Conchobar an Abaidh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh
events.name: Conchobar an Abaidh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh becomes King of Uí Maine

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the University of Würzburg was founded, contributing to the spread of education and scholarship in Germany. This institution would become a significant center for learning in the region.
events.name: Founding of the University of Würzburg

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, the Gangnido map of the world was completed during the Joseon dynasty in Korea. This map is significant for its representation of the world as understood in East Asia at the time, showcasing the geographical knowledge of the period.
events.name: Completion of the Gangnido map

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, a great comet was sighted, capturing the attention of astronomers and the public alike. Such celestial events were often interpreted as omens or significant occurrences in medieval society.
events.name: Great comet sighting

events.enhanced_description: In 1402, a significant fire broke out in the city of Utrecht, starting near the Jacobikerk. This event caused considerable damage and highlighted the vulnerabilities of medieval urban centers to such disasters.
events.name: Fire in Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1402, King Jogaila of the Poland–Lithuania Union married Anna of Celje, a strategic alliance aimed at consolidating his rule and addressing dissent against his authority in Poland. This marriage was significant for the political landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Marriage of King Jogaila

events.enhanced_description: In early February 1402, the Great Comet was first observed in the Northern Hemisphere, captivating the attention of people across various regions. Visible for eight days, it became a significant astronomical event, influencing cultural interpretations and scientific inquiries.
events.name: Observation of the Great Comet of 1402

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1402, Sigismund of Křižanov, Prokop of Luxemburg, and King Wenceslas IV of Bohemia led an unsuccessful raid against the military garrison of Jihlava, targeting the Kingdom of Croatia. The raid ended in defeat, resulting in the capture of Wenceslas IV.
events.name: Unsuccessful raid on Jihlava

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1402, David Stewart, Duke of Rothesay and heir to the Scottish throne, died while imprisoned by his uncle, Robert Stewart, 1st Duke of Albany. His death raised suspicions of foul play and intensified the power struggle within the Scottish nobility.
events.name: Death of David Stewart, Duke of Rothesay

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1402, during the Jingnan campaign, the Yan Army, led by Prince Zhu Di, reached Suishui, located west of Huaibei in present-day Anhui province. This marked a significant advance in their military campaign against the Imperial forces of Southern China.
events.name: Yan Army reaches Suishui

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1402, King Henry IV of England was married by proxy to Joan of Navarre in a ceremony held at Eltham Palace near London. This marriage was politically significant, strengthening ties between England and Navarre.
events.name: Marriage by proxy of Henry IV and Joan of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1402, during the Jingnan campaign, the Yan Army led by Zhu Di decisively defeated the Imperial Army of Southern China at Linghi, capturing General Ping An. This victory further solidified Zhu Di's position in the conflict.
events.name: Yan Army overwhelms Imperial Army at Linghi

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1402, the Yan Army continued its advance during the Jingnan campaign, capturing Sixian and reaching the north bank of the Huai River. This strategic movement brought them closer to the Imperial capital.
events.name: Yan Army captures Sixian

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1402, following the death of Queen Maria of Sicily, her husband Martin I married Blanche of Navarre by proxy. This union was significant for the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Marriage of Martin I of Sicily and Blanche of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1402, the Yan Army, after crossing the Huai River and capturing Yangzhou and Luhe, crossed the Yangtze River at Guazhou. This maneuver brought them within striking distance of the Imperial capital, Nanjing.

locations.name: Yangtze River, near Nanjing, Jiangsu, China

events.name: Yan Army crosses Yangtze River

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1402, the Yan Army arrived at the walls of Nanjing, the capital of Imperial China, and surrounded the city. The defenders opened the gates, leading to a tragic end for Emperor Zhu Yun Wen and his court.
events.name: Yan Army surrounds Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1402, Zhu Di, the King of the Yan State, was proclaimed the new Ming Dynasty Emperor Yongle in Nanjing, marking a significant unification of northern and southern China under his rule.
events.name: Zhu Di becomes Emperor Yongle

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1402, the Battle of Casalecchio occurred, where Gian Galeazzo Visconti, the Duke of Milan, crushed the forces of Bologna and Florence. This victory solidified Visconti's power in Northern Italy.
events.name: Battle of Casalecchio

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1402, Zhu Di was formally crowned as the new Ming Dynasty Emperor Yongle in Nanjing, marking the conclusion of the Jingnan campaign and the beginning of a new era in Chinese history.
events.name: Crowning of Zhu Di as Emperor Yongle

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1402, the Battle of Ankara resulted in a decisive victory for the invading Timurid Empire against the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I, who was captured. This battle led to a significant power vacuum in the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Ankara

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1402, Edward of Norwich became the second Duke of York following the death of his father, Edmund of Langley. He would play a significant role in the Wars of the Roses before his death in 1415.
events.name: Edward of Norwich becomes Duke of York

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1402, King Enrique III of Castile signed a peace treaty with his brother-in-law, King João I of Portugal, effectively ending hostilities that had begun in 1396. This treaty was significant for the political landscape of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Peace treaty between Castile and Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1402, Gian Maria Visconti ascended to the position of Duke of Milan following the death of his father, Gian Galeazzo Visconti. His rule would be marked by political intrigue and conflict.
events.name: Gian Maria Visconti becomes Duke of Milan

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1402, the Battle of Homildon Hill saw Northern English nobles, led by Sir Henry Percy (Hotspur), decisively defeat a Scottish raiding army and capture their leader, the Earl of Douglas. This battle was a significant victory for the English during the ongoing conflicts with Scotland.
events.name: Battle of Homildon Hill

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1402, King Henry IV opened a new session of the English Parliament in Coventry, which lasted for nearly two months. This session was crucial for addressing ongoing conflicts and governance issues.
events.name: Opening of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1402, a rare conference between the House of Commons and the House of Lords took place in Coventry, resulting in a tax agreement to support military efforts against Scotland and other regions.
events.name: House of Commons conference

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1402, the 'False Olaf', a Bohemian immigrant who impersonated the late King Olaf of Denmark, was burned at the stake as punishment for his deception. This event highlighted the tensions and political intrigue of the time.
events.name: Execution of the False Olaf

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1402, the Republic of Genoa resumed control of Monaco, deposing Louis Grimaldi. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, with Genoese control lasting for over 16 years.
events.name: Genoa resumes control of Monaco

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1402, Stefan Lazarević led the Serbian Despotate to a decisive victory over the Ottoman Governor Durad Branković at the Battle of Tripolje. This battle was significant in the ongoing struggle between the Serbian forces and the expanding Ottoman Empire.

image.caption: Fresco depicting Stefan Lazarević and Đurađ Branković.
image.credit: Bratislav — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image dated 2009-11-16; the date of the depicted fresco is not specified.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Tripolje

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1402, Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos departed from France after nearly two years of diplomatic engagement. His visit was part of efforts to seek support against the encroaching Ottoman threat to the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Departure of Manuel II Palaiologos from France

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1402, the fourth parliament of King Henry IV of England concluded at Westminster after two months of deliberation. This session resulted in the passage of new laws, including penal laws against the Welsh, restricting their rights and freedoms.
events.name: Fourth Parliament of King Henry IV of England

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1402, Tamerlane began the Siege of Smyrna, capturing the city after two days of intense fighting. The siege ended with the massacre of the Christian population after the Knights of Saint John refused to convert to Islam or pay tribute.

image.caption: Persian miniature depicting the Siege of Smyrna, from a manuscript of the Zafarnama.
image.credit: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād — http://warfare.ga/Persia/Timurid/Timurid-Garrett_Zafarnama-Johns_Hopkins.htm
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the 1402 siege, dating to circa 1480s.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Smyrna

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1402, during the Ava–Hanthawaddy War, King Minkhaung I of the Ava Kingdom defeated King Razadarit of Hanthawaddy at the Battle of Nawin, forcing Razadarit to abandon the siege of Prome. This victory solidified Ava's dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Nawin

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Jan Hus began preaching Wycliffite ideas in Bohemia, advocating for reforms within the Church and challenging established doctrines. His teachings would later contribute to the Hussite movement and significant religious upheaval in the region.
events.name: Jan Hus begins preaching Wycliffite ideas

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, a decision that would have lasting implications for the political and cultural landscape of China. This move was part of a broader strategy to consolidate power and enhance the emperor's authority.
events.name: Yongle Emperor moves capital to Beijing

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Temple of a City God was constructed in Shanghai, serving as a significant cultural and religious site for the local community. This temple reflects the rich spiritual traditions and architectural styles of the time.
events.name: Construction of the Temple of a City God

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Timur commissioned the construction of the Gur-e Amir Mausoleum in Samarkand after the death of his grandson Muhammad Sultan. This mausoleum would later become the final resting place for Timur and his descendants, symbolizing the grandeur of the Timurid dynasty.
events.name: Construction of the Gur-e Amir Mausoleum

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Georgia made peace with Timur, recognizing him as a suzerain and agreeing to pay tribute. This agreement was part of Timur's broader strategy to consolidate power in the region and exert influence over neighboring territories.
events.name: Georgia makes peace with Timur

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Lazzaretto Vecchio was constructed in Venice as the world's first quarantine station, established to protect the city from the Black Death. This facility marked a significant development in public health measures during a time of widespread disease.
events.name: Construction of the Lazzaretto Vecchio

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania ended his alliance with Muscovy and captured the cities of Vyazma and Smolensk. This shift in alliances and territorial control was significant in the ongoing power struggles in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Vytautas ends alliance with Muscovy

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Stefan Lazarević established Belgrade as the capital of the Serbian Despotate. This decision was pivotal in the consolidation of power and the administrative organization of the region during a time of political fragmentation.
events.name: Stefan Lazarević establishes Belgrade as capital

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, a guild of stationers was founded in the City of London, known as the Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers. This organization played a crucial role in the regulation of the printing industry and the dissemination of literature in England.
events.name: Foundation of the Worshipful Company of Stationers

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Tadhg Ruadh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh succeeded Conchobar an Abaidh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh as King of Hy-Many, a territory encompassing parts of present-day counties Galway and Roscommon. This succession was part of the complex lineage and power dynamics within Gaelic Ireland.
figures: Tadhg Ruadh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh
Conchobar an Abaidh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh
events.name: Tadhg Ruadh mac Maelsechlainn O Cellaigh succeeds as King of Hy-Many

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Ououso ascended to the throne as the King of Nanzan, a significant kingdom in the Ryukyu Islands, which is present-day Okinawa, Japan. His reign marked an important period in the history of the Ryukyu Kingdom, characterized by trade and cultural exchanges with neighboring regions.
events.name: Ououso becomes King of Nanzan

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Yongle Emperor moved the capital of the Ming Dynasty from Nanjing to Beijing, establishing the latter as the political center of China. This decision was pivotal in shaping the future of the Chinese imperial system and the development of Beijing as a major city.
events.name: Capital moved from Nanjing to Beijing

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Yongle Emperor commissioned the creation of the Yongle Encyclopedia, which became one of the largest and most comprehensive encyclopedias in history. This monumental work aimed to consolidate knowledge and preserve Chinese culture during the Ming Dynasty.
