events.name: Commissioning of the Yongle Encyclopedia

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, the Yongle Emperor ordered the construction of a vast fleet of ships to enhance maritime power, with shipbuilding concentrated at Longjiang near Nanjing. This initiative was part of a broader strategy to expand China's influence and engage in maritime exploration.
events.name: Construction of a vast fleet ordered

events.enhanced_description: In 1403, Maolmhordha mac Con Connacht succeeded Giolla Iosa mac Pilib as the King of East Breifne, a territory in medieval Ireland. His ascension reflects the ongoing shifts in power among Gaelic lords during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Maolmhordha mac Con Connacht succeeds as King of East Breifne

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1403, peace negotiations began in Pegu between King Razadarit of Hanthawaddy and emissaries of Minkhaung I of the Kingdom of Ava, following the recent defeat of Razadarit's forces at the Battle of Nawin. These talks aimed to establish a ceasefire and restore stability in the region.
events.name: Peace negotiations between Hanthawaddy and Ava

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1403, the Yongle Era in China commenced with the first day of the Chinese New Year, marking the beginning of a new imperial reign under Emperor Yongle, who had deposed the previous emperor. This era is noted for its cultural and political achievements.

image.caption: Seated portrait of the Yongle Emperor, also known as Ming Chengzu.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Digitized by NPM; image is directly from Shuge
image.date_qualification: Portrait from the Ming dynasty; the saved date range does not establish a more specific portrait date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Beginning of the Yongle Era

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1403, King Henry IV of England married Joan of Navarre at Winchester Cathedral. This marriage was politically motivated, strengthening ties between England and Navarre.
events.name: Marriage of Henry IV of England and Joan of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1403, the Treaty of Gallipoli was signed, with Süleyman Çelebi making significant concessions to the Byzantine Empire and other Christian powers. This treaty was part of the complex diplomatic relations in the southern Balkans during this period.

image.caption: Portrait of Emperor John VII Palaiologos in a manuscript illustration.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.fhw.gr/ , ultimately History of John Zonaras , Mutinensis gr.122, f.294r, Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena ( details ).
image.date_qualification: 15th-century portrait; contextual image of a Byzantine ruler, not a depiction of the treaty signing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Gallipoli

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1403, King Martin I of Aragon intervened to help end the siege of the papal palace in Avignon by the French, leading to the flight of Antipope Benedict XIII to Aragon. This event was significant in the context of the Western Schism.
events.name: Siege of the Papal Palace in Avignon

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1403, Muhammad Sultan Mirza, the favored grandson and heir of Tamerlane, died from injuries sustained in the Battle of Ankara. His death marked a significant loss for the Timurid Empire and impacted its future leadership.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of Timur at Muhammad Sultan Mirza’s funeral, from the Zafarnama.
image.credit: 1436 artist — Islamic Art: Vol. IV (1990-1991)
image.date_qualification: Depicts the funeral of Muhammad Sultan Mirza in 1403; this is a 1436 manuscript illustration, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Muhammad Sultan Mirza

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1403, Stříbrná Skalice in Central Bohemia was razed by Sigismund of Luxembourg. This act was part of the broader conflicts during the Hussite Wars, reflecting the turbulent political climate of the time.
events.name: Razing of Stříbrná Skalice

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1403, Prince Henry of England was appointed by his father, King Henry IV, to serve as the Royal Lieutenant of Wales. This role included command over English troops to combat Welsh rebels, highlighting the ongoing tensions in the region.
events.name: Appointment of Prince Henry as Royal Lieutenant of Wales

events.enhanced_description: In April 1403, Balša III ascended to the throne of the Principality of Zeta, succeeding his father Đurađ II. This transition marked a significant moment in the region's political landscape as it continued to navigate the complexities of feudal allegiances and external pressures.
events.name: Balša III succeeds Đurađ II as ruler of the Principality of Zeta

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1403, Jean II Le Maingre, known as Boucicaut, led a fleet to defend Cyprus against Muslim attacks, besieging the city of Candelore. His actions were crucial in maintaining Christian control over the island during a period of conflict.
events.name: Boucicaut's defense of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1403, Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo departed from Cádiz as an ambassador of the King of Castile, embarking on a journey to meet Timur in Samarkand. His travels not only aimed to strengthen diplomatic ties but also provided valuable insights into the cultures and politics of Central Asia.
events.name: Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo's journey to Timur

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1403, Eleanor of Castile was crowned Queen of Navarre in Pamplona, solidifying her role in the political landscape of the region. This event underscored the importance of dynastic marriages and alliances in medieval European politics.
events.name: Coronation of Eleanor of Castile as Queen of Navarre

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1403, Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos returned to Constantinople after a two-year absence in Western Europe. His return was pivotal as it marked the resumption of his efforts to secure alliances and support against the encroaching Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Manuel II Palaiologos returns to Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1403, Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos restored Matthew I as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. This restoration was significant for the Eastern Orthodox Church, as it aimed to stabilize the church's leadership during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Restoration of Matthew I as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1403, John III of Soltaniyeh, a Dominican friar, arrived in Paris as an emissary from Timur. His mission aimed to establish trade relations between the Timurid Empire and France, highlighting the interconnectedness of European and Asian powers.
events.name: John III of Soltaniyeh arrives in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1403, King Henry IV of England achieved a decisive victory against a rebel army led by Henry Percy, known as 'Hotspur', at the Battle of Shrewsbury. This battle was significant in quelling the rebellion and solidifying Henry IV's claim to the throne.
events.name: Battle of Shrewsbury

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1403, Ladislaus of Naples was crowned King of Hungary and Croatia in Zadar. His reign was short-lived, lasting less than four months before he was deposed, reflecting the turbulent political climate of the time.
events.name: Coronation of Ladislaus of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1403, the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty ordered the construction of the first 200 treasure ships from the Capital Guards in Nanjing. This initiative marked the beginning of China's maritime exploration and trade expansion.
events.name: First Chinese treasure ships ordered

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1403, the Genoese fleet led by Jean Le Maingre was defeated by the Republic of Venice at the Battle of Modon. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between the Genoese and Venetian maritime powers in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Modon

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1403, an English fleet organized by John Hawley and Thomas Norton seized seven French merchant vessels in the English Channel. This act of piracy was part of the ongoing hostilities between England and France during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Seizure of French merchant vessels

events.enhanced_description: In November 1403, Sir William Wilford led an English revenge raid on Brittany, capturing 40 ships and causing significant damage ashore. This raid was part of the broader conflict between England and France during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: English revenge raid on Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1403, Waleran III, Count of Ligny, informed King Henry IV of England about plans for a French attack. This communication highlighted the ongoing tensions and political maneuvering between England and France during this period.
events.name: Waleran III informs Henry IV of French attack plans

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1403, local English forces successfully repelled a French raid on the Isle of Wight led by Waleran III, Count of Ligny. This victory was significant in maintaining English control over the strategically important island.
events.name: Local English forces defeat French raid on Isle of Wight

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1403, Pope Boniface IX annulled numerous indulgences previously granted by the Roman Catholic Church, which had been paid for a reduction of time in purgatory. This decision reflected the ongoing debates within the Church regarding the sale of indulgences.
events.name: Pope Boniface IX annuls indulgences

events.enhanced_description: In April or May 1404, the Battle of Blackpool Sands occurred when local English forces successfully repelled a raid from Saint-Malo on the port of Dartmouth, resulting in the death of the French commander, William du Chastel. This battle underscored the ongoing conflicts between England and France during this period.
events.name: Battle of Blackpool Sands

events.enhanced_description: Jean de Béthencourt is appointed as the first ruler of the Kingdom of the Canary Islands, establishing a new governance structure in the archipelago that would influence its future.
events.name: Jean de Béthencourt becomes the first ruler of the Kingdom of the Canary Islands

events.enhanced_description: Stephan Tvrtko II ascends to the throne as King of Bosnia following the reign of Stefan Ostoja, continuing the lineage of Bosnian rulers during a time of regional instability.
events.name: Stephan Tvrtko II succeeds Stefan Ostoja as King of Bosnia

events.enhanced_description: A peace agreement is reached between Lithuania and the Teutonic Knights, involving land exchanges and a strategic alliance against Muscovy, reflecting the complex political landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Peace is declared between Lithuania and the Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: A civil war erupts within the Majapahit Empire, a significant power in Southeast Asia, leading to internal strife that would affect its stability and influence in the region.
events.name: Civil war in the Majapahit Empire

events.enhanced_description: Under the leadership of Mircea cel Bătrân, Wallachia expands to its greatest territorial extent, consolidating power and influence in the region during a period of political fragmentation.
events.name: Wallachia reaches its maximum extent under Mircea cel Bătrân

events.enhanced_description: The University of Turin is established, contributing to the intellectual and cultural development of Italy during the Renaissance and serving as a center for higher education.
events.name: The University of Turin is founded

events.enhanced_description: Timur, the Mongol conqueror, falls ill with a fever while preparing for an ambitious invasion of China, a pivotal moment that could alter the course of his military campaigns.
events.name: Timur is hit by a fever

events.enhanced_description: Virupaksha Raya ascends to the throne of the Vijayanagara Empire, continuing the legacy of his predecessor and overseeing a period of cultural and economic prosperity in southern India.
events.name: Virupaksha Raya succeeds Harihara Raya II

events.enhanced_description: Narayana Ramadhipati takes over the kingship of Cambodia from Ponthea Yat, marking a transition in leadership during a time of significant cultural and political change.
events.name: Narayana Ramadhipati succeeds Ponthea Yat

events.enhanced_description: Ruaidri Caech MacDermot ascends as the new king of Magh Luirg, succeeding Conchobair Óg MacDermot, amidst the ongoing power struggles in medieval Ireland.
events.name: Ruaidri Caech MacDermot succeeds Conchobair Óg MacDermot

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1404, the fourth Parliament of King Henry IV of England convened for a session lasting two months. This parliament was crucial for addressing various political issues and consolidating the king's power during a period of unrest.
events.name: Fourth Parliament of King Henry IV of England opens

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1404, Thomas of Lancaster, the second son of King Henry IV of England, was appointed as the Admiral of the North and South, succeeding Admiral Thomas Beaufort. This position was significant for naval command during a time of conflict.
events.name: Thomas of Lancaster becomes Admiral of the North and South

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1404, King Guadarfia of the Canary Islands surrendered to the French explorer Jean de Béthencourt, who declared himself the new king, albeit under the authority of King Enrique III of Castile. This event marked a significant moment in the European colonization of the Canary Islands.
events.name: King Guadarfia of the Canary Islands surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1404, under the Yongle Emperor, China ordered the construction of 50 new seagoing ships from the Capital Guards in Nanjing. This initiative was part of a larger effort to strengthen China's naval capabilities and expand its maritime influence.
events.name: Construction of 50 new seagoing ships ordered

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1404, as the English Parliament adjourned, King Henry IV gave royal assent to the Multipliers Act, which prohibited the practice of alchemy aimed at transmuting base metals into gold or silver. This law remained in effect for 284 years, reflecting the king's efforts to regulate economic practices.
events.name: King Henry IV gives royal assent to the Multipliers Act

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1404, Centurione II Zaccaria purchased the Principality of Achaea from King Ladislaus of Naples. This acquisition was significant in the context of the fragmented political landscape of the late medieval Mediterranean.
events.name: Centurione II Zaccaria buys the Principality of Achaea

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1404, the War of Padua commenced as the Republic of Venice, led by General Malatesta dei Sonetti, launched an attack on Padua, ruled by Francesco Novello da Carrara. This conflict marked the beginning of a 19-month struggle for control over the region.
events.name: War of Padua begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1404, Jean sans Peur was appointed as the new Duke of Burgundy in Dijon following the death of his father, Philippe II le Hardi. His ascension marked a pivotal moment in Burgundian history, influencing the political dynamics of France.
events.name: Jean sans Peur becomes Duke of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1404, the Peace of Raciazek treaty was signed by representatives of King Władysław II Jagiełło of Poland, Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania, and the Teutonic Knights. This treaty aimed to stabilize relations and resolve ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Peace of Raciazek treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1404, Welsh rebel leader Owain Glyndŵr forged an alliance with the French against the English, marking a significant moment in the Welsh struggle for independence. This alliance facilitated parliamentary assemblies and strengthened Glyndŵr's position.
events.name: Owain Glyndŵr enters alliance with the French

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1404, the formal coronation of Owain Glyndŵr as Prince of Wales took place at Harlech. This event symbolized the height of Glyndŵr's rebellion and his claim to Welsh sovereignty against English rule.
events.name: Coronation of Owain Glyndŵr as Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1404, Bukka Raya II ascended as the new ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire, which encompassed parts of modern-day Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala. His reign was marked by significant cultural and economic developments in South India.
events.name: Bukka Raya II becomes ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1404, King Henry IV of England summoned a new parliament, scheduled to open on October 16. This move was part of his ongoing efforts to consolidate power and address various political challenges.
events.name: King Henry IV summons a new parliament

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1404, Albert IV, Duke of Austria, died at the age of 26 from an illness contracted during military campaigns in Bohemia and Moravia. His death marked a significant transition in the leadership of the Austrian duchy, as he was succeeded by his young son.
events.name: Albert IV, Duke of Austria, dies

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1404, the 5th Parliament of King Henry IV, known as the 'Unlearned Parliament', opened for a four-week session. This parliament was characterized by its lack of legal expertise among its members, reflecting the political turmoil of the time.
events.name: The Unlearned Parliament opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1404, Cosimo de' Migliorati was elected unanimously by eight cardinals to succeed Pope Boniface IX, taking the papal name Innocent VII. His election came during a tumultuous period in the Catholic Church, marked by political and religious challenges.
events.name: Election of Pope Innocent VII

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1404, the 'Unlearned Parliament' of England closed its session, marking the sixth parliamentary meeting during the reign of King Henry IV. This session was notable for its lack of legal knowledge among its members, which influenced legislative outcomes.
events.name: The Unlearned Parliament closes

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1421, St. Elizabeth's flood devastated the coastal area near Dordrecht, resulting in the drowning of 72 villages and approximately 10,000 fatalities. This catastrophic event significantly altered the course of the Meuse River and had lasting impacts on the region's geography.
events.name: St. Elizabeth's flood

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of Albrecht I, Duke of Lower Bavaria, Willem VI ascends to the title of Count of Holland, marking a significant transition in the governance of the region.
events.name: Willem VI becomes the new Count of Holland

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded instance of whiskey consumption in Ireland dates back to this year, where it was distilled by Catholic monks. This event marks the beginning of Ireland's long-standing whiskey tradition.
events.name: First record of whiskey consumption in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: Bellifortis, a significant work on military technology, was published by Konrad Kyeser. This book provided insights into the advancements in warfare and engineering during the medieval period.
events.name: Publication of Bellifortis

events.enhanced_description: Christine de Pizan authored The Book of the City of Ladies, a pioneering work in feminist literature that defended women's roles in society and celebrated their contributions. This text is considered one of the first to advocate for women's rights.
events.name: Christine de Pizan writes The Book of the City of Ladies

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Prince Sigismund of Anhalt-Dessau, his four sons become joint rulers of the principality, setting the stage for future conflicts and power dynamics within the region.
events.name: Joint rule of Anhalt-Dessau

events.enhanced_description: Khalil Sultan ascends to rule the western part of the Timurid Empire following the death of his grandfather, Tamerlane, while his father, Shah Rukh, takes control of the eastern territories.
events.name: Khalil Sultan becomes ruler of the western Timurid Empire

events.enhanced_description: The death of Tamerlane is announced, leading to a period of mourning across the Timurid Empire as he is interred at the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum in Samarkand, a significant cultural and historical site.
events.name: Tamerlane's death and mourning period

events.enhanced_description: John the Fearless inherits the title of Count of Flanders upon the death of his mother, Margaret III, uniting the French-speaking Burgundians and Flemish citizens under a single rule.
events.name: John the Fearless becomes Count of Flanders

events.enhanced_description: Antonio I Acciaioli, Duke of Athens, negotiates with the Venetian Senate and Doge Michele Steno to pay reparations, ensuring his continued rule over Athens amidst Venetian interests.
events.name: Antonio I Acciaioli's agreement with Venice

events.enhanced_description: The sons of Philip the Bold convene in Arras to divide their father's Burgundian territories, establishing a new political landscape in the region with John retaining Flanders.
events.name: Partition of Burgundian lands

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Pwll Melyn, Baron Grey of Codnor leads English forces to victory against Welsh rebels, capturing Owain Glyndwr's son and killing his brother, intensifying the conflict in Wales.
events.name: Battle of Pwll Melyn

events.enhanced_description: Ralph Neville, 1st Earl of Westmorland, deceives Richard le Scrope and Thomas Mowbray into disbanding their rebellious forces, subsequently imprisoning them, showcasing the political maneuvering of the time.

image.caption: Retrospective portrait of Ralph de Neville, 1st Earl of Westmorland.
image.credit: Richard Gough — Sepulchral Monuments of Great Britain by Richard Gough, London, 1796
image.date_qualification: 1796; a retrospective depiction, not a contemporary image of the 1405 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ralph Neville tricks rebellious leaders

events.enhanced_description: On the orders of King Henry IV, Richard le Scrope and Thomas Mowbray are executed in York, a significant event that underscores the harsh measures taken against dissent during this turbulent period.
events.name: Execution of Richard le Scrope and Thomas Mowbray

events.enhanced_description: Ming Dynasty fleet commander Zheng He embarks on his first voyage from Suzhou, initiating a series of maritime explorations that would expand China's influence across the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Zheng He's first voyage

events.enhanced_description: Cardinal Angelo Acciaioli is appointed by Pope Innocent VII as the Grand Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, filling a crucial administrative role within the Church's hierarchy.
events.name: Cardinal Angelo Acciaioli appointed Grand Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: An-Nasir Faraj, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, flees Cairo amidst political turmoil, appointing his brother Izz al-Din Abd al-Aziz as regent, before returning to reclaim his throne.
events.name: An-Nasir Faraj flees Cairo

events.enhanced_description: Christine de Pizan writes a compelling letter to Queen Isabeau, urging her to intervene in the escalating political conflict between the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans, highlighting the role of women in political discourse.
events.name: Christine de Pizan writes to Queen Isabeau

events.enhanced_description: The Sultanate of Sulu is established in the Sulu Archipelago, marking the beginning of a significant political entity that would play a crucial role in the history of the Philippines.
events.name: Establishment of the Sultanate of Sulu

events.enhanced_description: The War of Padua concluded with the surrender of Padua and Ferrara to the Venetian Republic, led by General Malatesta IV. Following the victory, Venice annexed the territories of the defeated lordships, solidifying its power in northern Italy.
events.name: The War of Padua ends

events.enhanced_description: King Zsigmond of Hungary married Barbara of Cilli in a politically motivated union that aimed to strengthen alliances within Central Europe. This marriage played a significant role in the dynastic politics of the region.
events.name: Marriage of King Zsigmond of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: King Henry IV of England summoned the members of the Long Parliament, marking the sixth session of the English House of Commons and the House of Lords. This assembly was crucial for addressing the political turmoil of the time.
events.name: Summoning of the Long Parliament

events.enhanced_description: The Imperial Chinese Army launched an invasion of the Lan Na kingdom, an area that now spans parts of Myanmar and Thailand. This military action was part of China's broader efforts to exert control over its southern territories.

locations.name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, Chiang Mai, Thailand

events.name: Invasion of the Lan Na kingdom

events.enhanced_description: James I ascended to the throne of Scotland following the death of his father, King Robert III. However, he remained a hostage in England for 18 years, significantly affecting the governance of Scotland during his absence.
events.name: James I becomes King of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Tran Thien Binh, a pretender to the throne of Đại Ngu, arrived in Vietnam with a Chinese emissary. Their arrival triggered a violent confrontation with local forces, leading to their deaths and escalating tensions with China.
events.name: Tran Thien Binh's arrival in Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In 1406, construction began on the Forbidden City in Beijing during the Ming dynasty, which would later serve as the imperial palace for 24 emperors and become a symbol of China's historical and cultural heritage.
events.name: Construction of the Forbidden City begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1406, Pisa was subjugated by Florence, marking a significant shift in power dynamics within Tuscany and contributing to Florence's rise as a dominant city-state in Italy.
events.name: Pisa is subjugated by Florence

events.enhanced_description: Pope Innocent VII declared that Ladislaus was deposed as King of Naples, although he refused to acknowledge the order. This political maneuvering reflected the complexities of papal influence in Italian politics during this period.
events.name: Pope Innocent VII declares Ladislaus deposed

events.enhanced_description: Following the Venetian Republic's victory in the War of Padua, Francesco Novello da Carrara was executed on the orders of the Venetian Consejo de i Diexe. This act was seen as a necessary measure to eliminate threats to Venetian power.
events.name: Execution of Francesco Novello da Carrara

events.enhanced_description: Abū al-Faḍl Al-Musta'in was appointed as the new Abbasid caliph of Cairo, succeeding his father Al-Mutawakkil I. This transition marked a continuation of the Abbasid lineage in the Mamluk Sultanate.
events.name: Abū al-Faḍl Al-Musta'in becomes Abbasid caliph

events.enhanced_description: Scottish nobles Henry II Sinclair and David Fleming were tasked by King Robert III to transport Crown Prince James to Bass Rock for evacuation to France. However, they were ambushed by Robert Stewart, resulting in Fleming's death and Sinclair's escape with the prince.
events.name: Transport of Crown Prince James

events.enhanced_description: Pir Muhammad bin Jahangir was forced to retreat from Khalil Sultan's forces after an unsuccessful invasion of Transoxiana, a region marked by political instability following Tamerlane's death. This retreat highlighted the ongoing power struggles in the region.
events.name: Pir Muhammad bin Jahangir's retreat

events.enhanced_description: The Scottish Parliament issued a proclamation mandating that a lighted lantern be hung outside each house during meetings. This measure was intended to enhance visibility and security during parliamentary sessions.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration titled “The Downsitting of the Scottish Parliament,” from Châtelain and Gueudeville’s Atlas Historique.
image.credit: Châtelain and Gueudeville — Atlas Historique
image.date_qualification: Created in 1720, centuries after the reported 1406 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Scottish Parliament's lantern proclamation

events.enhanced_description: Prince James, the 10-year-old son of King Robert III of Scotland, was captured by privateers while being transported across the English Channel to France. He was subsequently held hostage by King Henry IV of England for 18 years, significantly impacting Scottish politics.
events.name: Capture of Prince James

events.enhanced_description: An unspecified event occurred in Lang Son, Vietnam, marking a significant moment during the turbulent period of Chinese invasions and local resistance.
events.name: Lang Son event

events.enhanced_description: China's Emperor Chengzu ordered an invasion of the Kingdom of Đại Ngu, now part of modern Vietnam, sending two battalions under the command of Duke Zhu Neng. This marked the beginning of a significant military campaign in the region.
events.name: Ming conquest of Đại Ngu

events.enhanced_description: Pope Innocent VII issued the bull Piae Postulatio to protect the charity and hospice of Santa Maria dell'Anima in Rome, which served the German-speaking community. This act demonstrated the papacy's role in supporting charitable institutions.
events.name: Pope Innocent VII's bull Piae Postulatio

events.enhanced_description: Troops under the command of Johann von Paderborn, Bishop of Hildesheim, utilized cannons to destroy the walls of Gebhardshagen Castle in Salzgitter. This event marked a significant use of artillery in medieval warfare.
events.name: Destruction of Gebhardshagen Castle

events.enhanced_description: Chinese merchant Chen Yanxiang and his crew of 121 departed from Java to Korea, claiming to be ambassadors. Their ship carried various Southeast Asian products, highlighting the trade networks of the time.
events.name: Chen Yanxiang's voyage to Korea

events.enhanced_description: Ernst der Eiserne of the Habsburg line was appointed as the new Duke of Inner Austria, which included the duchies of Styria, Carinthia, and Carniola. His ascension marked a significant moment in Habsburg territorial consolidation.
events.name: Ernst der Eiserne becomes Duke of Austria

events.enhanced_description: The Chinese imperial court issued the 'Edict to Invade Annam', outlining 20 formal reasons for the impending conquest of the Kingdoms of Annam and Đại Ngu. This edict set the stage for military action in the region.
events.name: Edict to Invade Annam

events.enhanced_description: Chen Yanxiang and his crew were attacked by Japanese pirates off the coast of Gunsan while en route to Korea for trade. The encounter resulted in significant casualties among his crew, but they managed to reach the shore.
events.name: Attack on Chen Yanxiang's crew

events.enhanced_description: China's Imperial Court sent a delegation to Inwa, the capital of the Kingdom of Ava, to persuade King Minkhaung I to cease hostilities against the Shan States. This diplomatic effort reflected the complexities of regional politics.
events.name: Chinese delegation to Inwa

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1406, a group of nobles convened in Appenzell, Switzerland, to create a political alliance known as the "" at Hegau, aiming to strengthen their collective power against external threats.
events.name: Creation of the "" at Hegau

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1406, Chinese merchant Chen Yanxiang and his surviving crew were hosted by King Taejong of Korea in Seoul, following a maritime incident that prompted diplomatic communication between the two nations.
events.name: Visit of Chen Yanxiang to King Taejong of Korea

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1406, Richard Whittington was elected for a second full term as Lord Mayor of London, a position he held concurrently with his role as Mayor of the Calais Staple, reflecting his significant influence in both trade and governance.
events.name: Election of Richard Whittington as Lord Mayor of London

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1406, Eric of Pomerania, the ruler of the Kalmar Union, married Philippa, the daughter of Henry IV of England, in Lund Cathedral, strengthening political ties between the two realms.
events.name: Marriage of Eric of Pomerania and Philippa

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1406, after trading his ship for a smaller vessel in gratitude to the King of Korea, Chen Yanxiang departed Korea but encountered a storm while approaching Japan's Seto Inland Sea, highlighting the perils of maritime trade during this era.
events.name: Chen Yanxiang's departure from Korea

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1406, Chinese troops commanded by General Zhang Fu crossed into Vietnam from Guanxi, while another contingent led by Mu Sheng advanced from Yunnan, marking the beginning of a significant military campaign during the Ming–Vietnamese War.
events.name: Chinese troops cross into Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1406, Cardinal Angelo Correr was elected as Pope Gregory XII after a 12-day conclave in Rome, succeeding Pope Innocent VII, who had died earlier that month, thus continuing the papal lineage during a tumultuous period in the Church.
events.name: Election of Pope Gregory XII

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1406, John II ascended to the throne as King of Castile at the tender age of 21 months following the death of his father, marking the beginning of a reign that would see significant political developments in the region.
events.name: John II becomes King of Castile

events.enhanced_description: In 1407, the Yongle Emperor of China issued an order to Marquis Zhang Fu, who had recently conquered Vietnam, instructing him to avoid harming innocent Vietnamese civilians. This directive highlighted the emperor's concern for the welfare of the local population amidst military campaigns.
events.name: Yongle Emperor's order to Marquis Zhang Fu

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1414, the English Parliament closed its session after 29 days, during which King Henry V granted royal assent to numerous laws. This session was notable for its legislative activity and the consolidation of royal authority.
events.name: Closure of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In 1407, Rudolfo Belenzani led a revolt against Bishop Georg von Liechtenstein in Trento, Italy. This uprising was part of the broader struggles between local leaders and ecclesiastical authorities during the late medieval period.
events.name: Rudolfo Belenzani's revolt in Trento

events.enhanced_description: In 1407, David Holbache founded Oswestry School in Oswestry, England. This institution has since become one of the oldest schools in the region, contributing to the educational landscape of the area.
events.name: Founding of Oswestry School

events.enhanced_description: In 1407, Mateu Texidor completed the Puente de la Trinidad bridge in Valencia, Spain. This architectural achievement contributed to the city's infrastructure and remains a significant landmark.
events.name: Completion of the Puente de la Trinidad bridge

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1407, during the Ming–Vietnamese War, Chinese forces conquered Dong Do, the eastern capital of Dai Ngu, now known as Hanoi, followed by the capture of Tay Do six days later, solidifying Chinese control over the region.
events.name: Conquest of Dong Do by China

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1407, Hô Nguyên Trúng, commander of the Vietnamese armada, launched a counterattack against invading Chinese ships on the Thai Binh River, but the Chinese forces utilized cannons to decimate the Viet fleet, resulting in heavy casualties.
events.name: Counterattack by Hô Nguyên Trúng

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1407, Pir Muhammad Mirza, co-ruler of the Timurid Empire, was murdered by his vizier, Pir Ali Taz, leading to a power shift as his cousin Khalil Sultan became the sole ruler until his overthrow in 1409.
events.name: Murder of Pir Muhammad Mirza

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1407, Persian astronomer and mathematician Jamshid al-Kashi completed his influential treatise titled Sullam al-sama', or "The Ladder of the Sky," contributing significantly to the fields of astronomy and mathematics.
events.name: Completion of Sullam al-sama'

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1407, at the age of 12, Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga ascended to the title of Marquis of Mantua following the death of his father, Francesco I Gonzaga, marking the beginning of his rule over the Lombardy region.
events.name: Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga becomes Marquis of Mantua

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1407, during the Ming–Vietnamese War, Chinese troops utilized the da jiangjun chong cannon to destroy more Vietnamese ships in Phung Hoa, demonstrating the technological superiority of the Chinese forces.
events.name: Chinese troops destroy Viet ships

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1407, the lama Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa of Tibetan Buddhism, visited the Yongle Emperor in Nanjing, impressing the court with his alleged miracles and securing his position within the Ming dynasty's religious landscape.
events.name: Visit of Deshin Shekpa to Yongle Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1407, the Banco di San Giorgio was founded by the government of the Republic of Genoa, marking a significant development in the financial history of Italy and Europe.
events.name: Foundation of Banco di San Giorgio

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1407, a Vietnamese force of 70,000 troops attempted to halt the advance of Chinese forces at the Hong River in Hưng Yên province, but suffered heavy losses due to superior Chinese firepower.
events.name: Vietnamese attempt to stop Chinese advance

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1407, the Earl of Somerset resigned from his position as Admiral of the North and West of the English Navy, leaving the office vacant until Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter, assumed it in September 1408.
events.name: Resignation of the Earl of Somerset

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1407, during the Ming–Vietnamese War, Vietnamese forces engaged in a final battle at Thanh Hóa, where they suffered significant casualties and the royal family fled, marking a pivotal moment in the conflict.
events.name: Final battle at Thanh Hóa

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1407, during the Ming–Hồ War, Ho Han Thuong, the Emperor of Vietnam, was captured by the Imperial Chinese Army, along with his father, marking the completion of the Chinese conquest of Vietnam.
events.name: Capture of Ho Han Thuong

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1407, a group of high officials from the former Vietnamese government were put on trial before the Yongle Emperor in Nanjing, charged with treason for the assassination of the previous ruler, resulting in the execution of most of the prisoners.
events.name: Trial of Vietnamese officials

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1407, the English Parliament was opened at Gloucester after being summoned by King Henry IV, marked by significant debates between the House of Lords and the House of Commons regarding legislative powers.
events.name: Opening of the English Parliament at Gloucester

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1407, a solemn truce was agreed upon in Paris between John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, and Louis I, Duke of Orléans, facilitated by John, Duke of Berry. This agreement aimed to halt the ongoing conflict between their factions, which had been exacerbated by political rivalries in France.
events.name: Truce between John the Fearless and Louis I of Orléans

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1407, Louis I of Orléans was assassinated in Paris, an event that reignited the violent conflict between the Burgundians and the Orléanists. This assassination marked a significant escalation in the power struggle that characterized the late medieval period in France.
events.name: Assassination of Louis I of Orléans

events.enhanced_description: In December 1407, the Yongle Encyclopedia was completed in Nanjing, China, after four years of collaborative work by 2,169 scholars at the Hanlin Academy and the Imperial University. This monumental work became the largest encyclopedia in history until the 21st century, reflecting the vast knowledge and culture of the Ming dynasty.
events.name: Completion of the Yongle Encyclopedia

events.enhanced_description: In March 1408, during the Ava–Hanthawaddy War, King Razdarit of Burma led an invasion into the Kingdom of North Arakan, overthrowing its ruler, Anawrahta of Launggyet, and executing him. This event marked a significant expansion of Burmese influence in the region.
events.name: Ava–Hanthawaddy War: Invasion of North Arakan

events.enhanced_description: The town of Iași, located in modern-day Romania, was first mentioned in historical records in 1408. This event marks the beginning of Iași's significance as a cultural and political center in the region.
events.name: The Moldavian town of Iași is first mentioned

events.enhanced_description: The Yongle Encyclopedia, a monumental work of Chinese literature and knowledge, was completed in 1408 under the reign of the Yongle Emperor, Zhu Di. This encyclopedia is considered one of the largest and most comprehensive works of its kind in history, reflecting the cultural and intellectual ambitions of the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: The Yongle Encyclopedia is completed

events.enhanced_description: In 1408, the island of Gotland came under Danish rule, a significant shift in the political landscape of the Baltic region. This event was part of the broader conflicts involving the Kalmar Union and the power struggles among Scandinavian kingdoms.
events.name: Gotland passes under Danish rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1408, the Chinese admiral Zheng He delivered 300 virgins from Korea to the Chinese emperor, a notable event that highlights the diplomatic and cultural exchanges during the Ming Dynasty. This act was part of Zheng He's larger voyages that aimed to establish Chinese influence across Asia.
events.name: Zheng He delivers 300 virgins from Korea to the Chinese emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 1408, Mihail I became co-ruler of Wallachia alongside his father, Mircea cel Bătrân. This partnership was significant in maintaining the stability and continuity of leadership in Wallachia during a tumultuous period marked by external threats.
events.name: Mihail I becomes co-ruler of Wallachia, with his father Mircea cel Bătrân

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1408, King Charles VI of France sent a letter to Antipope Benedict XIII in Avignon, demanding an end to the Western Schism in the Roman Catholic Church. This ultimatum threatened to withdraw French support for the Avignon Papacy, escalating tensions within the church.
events.name: Western Schism: Charles VI's ultimatum

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1408, during the Appenzell Wars, an alliance in the Appenzell region of Switzerland attempted to liberate the city of Bregenz from Austrian rule but ultimately failed. This conflict highlighted the ongoing struggles for autonomy and power in the region.
events.name: Appenzell Wars: Failed liberation attempt

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1408, the Battle of Bramham Moor took place, where a royalist army defeated the last remnants of the Percy Rebellion. This battle marked a significant moment in the power struggles of early 15th-century England.

locations.name: Bramham Moor, Wetherby, West Yorkshire, England

events.name: Battle of Bramham Moor

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1408, John of Bourbon was appointed as the Grand Chamberlain of France by King Charles VI. This appointment was part of the ongoing political maneuvering during a tumultuous period in French history.
events.name: Appointment of John of Bourbon

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1408, the Bund ob dem See, an alliance in the Appenzell region of Switzerland, was dissolved following its failed attempt to liberate Bregenz from Austrian control. This dissolution was ordered by King Rupert of Germany, reflecting the complex political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Appenzell Wars: Dissolution of the Bund ob dem See

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1408, in response to King Charles VI's ultimatum, Antipope Benedict XIII published a bull excommunicating anyone who withdrew obedience to the Avignon Papacy. This act intensified the conflict within the church and led to further political ramifications in France.
events.name: Western Schism: Benedict XIII's excommunication bull

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1408, a representative of Burma's Kingdom of Ava apologized to the Ming dynasty Emperor of China for the occupation of the Shan States, particularly the Mongyang State. This diplomatic gesture aimed to mend relations following the violent events of the previous years.
events.name: Burma's apology to the Ming dynasty

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1408, Antipope Benedict XIII convened the Council of Perpignan in response to the declining support from France. This council was part of his efforts to maintain authority amidst the growing challenges to his papacy.
events.name: Benedict XIII's Council of Perpignan

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1408, a group of 13 Roman Catholic Cardinals allied with Pope Gregory began sending encyclical letters summoning Christian leaders to the Council of Pisa, scheduled for March 25, 1409. This council aimed to address the ongoing Western Schism.
events.name: Council of Pisa summons

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1408, Abdul Majid Hassan, the Sultan of Brunei, set off on a voyage to China at the invitation of the Yongle Emperor. He arrived in Nanjing, becoming the first foreign monarch to visit the Chinese Empire peacefully, although he fell ill and died shortly thereafter.
events.name: Sultan of Brunei's voyage to China

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1408, Thorstein Olafsson married Sigrid Björnsdatter in Hvalsey Church, marking the last recorded event of Norse history in Greenland. This marriage symbolizes the cultural and social practices of the Norse settlers in the region.
events.name: Marriage of Thorstein Olafsson

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1408, Andronikos Palaiologos ascended to the position of Byzantine Emperor of Thessalonica following the death of his brother, John VIII Palaiologos. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Byzantine Empire during its decline.
events.name: Andronikos Palaiologos becomes Byzantine Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1408, Henry, Prince of Wales, later known as Henry V of England, successfully retook Aberystwyth from the Welsh leader Owain Glyndŵr. This event was part of the ongoing conflict during the Welsh Revolt against English rule.
events.name: Henry, Prince of Wales retakes Aberystwyth

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1408, Awang Pateh Berbai became the new Sultan of Brunei following the death of his nephew, Abdul Majid Hassan, in Nanjing, China. This transition marked a significant moment in the leadership of Brunei during a period of expanding influence.
events.name: Awang Pateh Berbai becomes Sultan of Brunei

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1408, Antipope Benedict XIII convened the Council of Perpignan in an attempt to address the challenges posed by the declining support from France. This council was part of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Western Schism.
events.name: Council of Perpignan convened by Benedict XIII

events.enhanced_description: In December 1408, Emir Edigu of the Golden Horde reached Moscow, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between the Mongol Empire and the Russian principalities. This event underscored the power struggles in Eastern Europe during the late medieval period.
events.name: Emir Edigu of the Golden Horde reaches Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1408, King Sigismund of Hungary founded the Order of the Dragon, a chivalric order aimed at defending Christianity and combating the Ottoman Empire. This order played a pivotal role in the politics and military strategies of Central Europe during the late Middle Ages.

image.caption: Ceremonial sword of the Order of the Dragon, with a gilded crosspiece and ivory hilt.
image.credit: Unknown, North Italy, c. 1433. — Photograph by Sandstein
image.date_qualification: A ceremonial object associated with the Order, not a photograph of its 1408 founding. The sword was presumably made for Sigismund’s 1433 imperial coronation; the original image date is not supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Order of the Dragon is founded under King Sigismund of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1409, the Welsh surrendered Harlech Castle to the English forces, marking a significant event in the context of the ongoing conflicts during the Welsh Wars of Independence. This surrender represented a pivotal moment in the struggle for Welsh autonomy.
events.name: The Welsh surrender Harlech Castle to the English

events.enhanced_description: In early 1409, representatives of the Venetian Republic and the Principality of Zeta signed a peace treaty to halt the First Scutari War for one year. This agreement aimed to stabilize relations and reduce hostilities in the region, reflecting the complex political landscape of the time.
events.name: Peace treaty signed between the Venetian Republic and the Principality of Zeta

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1409, King Henry IV of England summoned the English Parliament to assemble, starting on January 27. This parliamentary session was crucial for addressing various political issues and consolidating the king's power during a tumultuous period.
events.name: King Henry IV of England summons Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In 1409, Ulugh Beg was appointed governor of Samarkand, a significant cultural and scientific center of the Timurid Empire. His leadership contributed to the flourishing of astronomy and mathematics during this period.
events.name: Ulugh Beg becomes governor of Samarkand

events.enhanced_description: In 1409, the Republic of Venice finalized the purchase of the port of Zadar from Hungary, enhancing its strategic position in the Adriatic Sea. This acquisition was part of Venice's broader efforts to expand its influence and control over trade routes.
events.name: The Republic of Venice purchases the port of Zadar from Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In 1409, Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen of the Teutonic Knights sold the Baltic Sea island of Gotland to Queen Margaret of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, thereby securing peace with the Kalmar Union. This transaction was pivotal in maintaining stability in the region during a time of conflict.
events.name: Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen guarantees peace with the Kalmar Union

events.enhanced_description: In 1409, Cheng Ho, the admiral of the Ming dynasty fleet, led an expedition that resulted in the deposition of the king of Sri Lanka. This event underscored the Ming dynasty's naval power and its influence over maritime Southeast Asia.
events.name: Cheng Ho deposes the king of Sri Lanka

events.enhanced_description: In 1409, Mircea cel Bătrân successfully defended the fortress of Silistra against Ottoman forces, showcasing his military prowess and the resilience of Wallachia during a period of Ottoman expansion in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Mircea cel Bătrân defends Silistra against the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1409, the Decree of Kutná Hora was issued, strengthening the Bohemian Nation at the expense of foreign students, particularly German-speaking ones, at the University of Prague. This decree led to significant changes in the academic landscape and prompted many students to seek education elsewhere.
events.name: The Decree of Kutná Hora strengthens the Bohemian Nation

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1409, the Galle Trilingual Inscription was installed by the Chinese admiral Zheng He in Galle, Sri Lanka. This inscription, featuring texts in Chinese, Tamil, and Persian, symbolizes the cultural exchanges and maritime trade routes established during Zheng He's voyages.
events.name: The Galle Trilingual Inscription is installed

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1409, Father Joan Gilabert Jofré, known as 'Padre Jofré', witnessed an assault on a mentally ill man in Valencia. This incident inspired him to establish the Hospital dels Ignoscents, recognized as the world's first psychiatric hospital, marking a significant advancement in the care of the mentally ill.

image.caption: Sculpture of Joan Gilabert Jofré in Valencia.
image.credit: José Aixa Iñigo — www.jdiezarnal.com
image.date_qualification: Sculpture by José Aixa, dated 1886; it is a later depiction of Jofré, not a contemporary image of the 1409 assault.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Father Joan Gilabert Jofré witnesses an assault

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1409, the Council of Pisa convened at the Cathedral of Pisa with the aim of resolving the Western Schism by addressing the conflict between Pope Gregory XII and Antipope Benedict XIII. This council was a pivotal moment in the history of the Catholic Church, seeking to restore unity.
events.name: The Council of Pisa opens

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1409, during the Hussite Wars, King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia decided to halt military actions against the rebel leader Jan Žižka in Budějovice. This decision reflected the complexities of the internal conflicts within Bohemia during this turbulent period.
events.name: Hussite Wars: King Wenceslaus IV decides to stop fighting

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1409, the Council of Pisa voted overwhelmingly to depose the warring popes Gregory XII and Benedict XIII, a significant step in the efforts to resolve the Western Schism. This vote highlighted the council's determination to restore unity within the Catholic Church.
events.name: The Council of Pisa votes on the removal of the popes

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1409, the Timurid War of Succession concluded when Khalil Sultan surrendered Samarkand to Shah Rukh, the ruler of the Timurid Empire. This event solidified Shah Rukh's power and marked a significant moment in the history of Central Asia.
events.name: The Timurid War of Succession ends

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1409, Pir Muhammad, the son of Timurid Emperor Umar Shaikh, was assassinated near Shiraz by his own soldiers. This assassination reflected the internal strife and power struggles within the Timurid dynasty during this period.
events.name: Pir Muhammad is assassinated

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1409, the second Samogitian Uprising commenced in what is now Lithuania against the Teutonic Knights, who had been granted rights to the Duchy of Samogita. This uprising was part of the broader resistance against foreign domination in the region.
events.name: The second Samogitian Uprising begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1409, the Council of Pisa issued an order to depose both Pope Gregory XII and Antipope Benedict XIII, holding them responsible for the ongoing Western Schism. This decision was a crucial step in the council's efforts to restore unity within the Catholic Church.
events.name: The Council of Pisa issues the order deposing both Gregory XII and Benedict XIII

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1409, Pietro Filargo was crowned as Pope Alexander V by the Council of Pisa, creating a unique situation in which three different popes claimed authority within the Catholic Church. This event further complicated the Western Schism and the politics of the church.

image.caption: Nuremberg Chronicle illustration depicting Alexander V.
image.credit: Michel Wolgemut, Wilhelm Pleydenwurff ( Hartmann Schedel , editor) — http://www.obrasraras.usp.br/obras/000192/ → File:Liber Chronicarum f 235v.jpg
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration from 1493, not a contemporary depiction of the 1409 coronation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pope Alexander V is crowned

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1409, King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia pardoned the rebel leader Jan Žižka and ordered the city of Budejovice to do the same. This act was significant in the context of the Hussite Wars, reflecting a shift in the king's approach to the rebellion.

image.caption: Portrait of Jan Žižka by Jan Vilímek.
image.credit: Jan Vilímek (1860–1938) — National Library of the Czech Republic
image.date_qualification: Portrait date: 1890/1891. It does not depict the event in 1409.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: King Wenceslaus pardons Jan Zizka

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1409, the Battle of Sanluri was fought in Sardinia between the Kingdom of Sicily and the Judicate of Arborea. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts over control of the island and its resources.
events.name: The Battle of Sanluri is fought

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1409, the Republic of Venice, under Doge Michele Steno, purchased the Dalmatian coast from King Ladislaus the Magnanimous of the Kingdom of Naples for 100,000 ducats. This acquisition allowed Venice to strengthen its control over trade routes in the Adriatic Sea.
events.name: The Republic of Venice gains control of the Dalmatian coast

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1409, Martin I of Aragon ascended to the throne as Martin II of Sicily following the death of his son. This transition marked a continuation of the Aragonese influence in Sicily during a period of political instability.
events.name: Martin I becomes King of Martin II of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1409, the Council of Pisa concluded its sessions, having addressed significant issues regarding the Western Schism and the legitimacy of the papal authority. The council's decisions had lasting implications for the Catholic Church.
events.name: The Council of Pisa closes

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1409, Pope Alexander V issued a papal bull that granted a charter to the University of Leipzig, establishing it as a significant center of learning in Europe. This event marked a pivotal moment in the history of higher education, contributing to the intellectual landscape of the time.
events.name: Pope Alexander V issues a papal bull granting a charter to the University of Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1409, Jean de Montagu, a prominent advisor to King Charles VI of France, was arrested on the orders of John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy. Montagu's subsequent execution ten days later at the Gibbet of Montfaucon highlighted the intense political rivalries and instability during the period leading up to the French Civil Wars.
events.name: Jean de Montagu is arrested on orders of John the Fearless

events.enhanced_description: The University of Leipzig officially opened its doors on December 2, 1409, becoming one of the oldest universities in Germany. It played a crucial role in the development of education and scholarship in Europe, attracting students and scholars from various regions.
events.name: The University of Leipzig opens

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1409, Louis II of Anjou established the University of Aix-en-Provence, furthering the spread of education in France. This institution contributed to the cultural and intellectual development of the region during the late medieval period.
events.name: Louis II of Anjou founds the University of Aix-en-Provence

events.enhanced_description: In 1410, at the Onon River, the Chinese army, commanded by the Yongle Emperor, decisively defeated the Mongol forces led by Khagan Öljei Temür Khan. This battle marked a significant moment in the Ming dynasty's efforts to assert dominance over the Mongol tribes.
events.name: Battle of Onon River

events.enhanced_description: During the Ottoman Interregnum in 1410, Sultan Süleyman Çelebi defeated his brother Musa Çelebi at the Battle of Kosmidion, located near the Byzantine capital of Constantinople. This battle was pivotal in the struggle for control over the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Kosmidion

events.enhanced_description: In 1410, Jan Hus was excommunicated by the Archbishop of Prague, marking a significant moment in the early stages of the Bohemian Reformation. Hus's teachings would later lead to widespread religious and social upheaval.
events.name: Excommunication of Jan Hus

events.enhanced_description: In 1410, construction began on Castle Woerden in the Netherlands, a significant fortification that would play a role in the region's defense. The castle's architecture reflects the military needs of the time.
events.name: Construction of Castle Woerden

events.enhanced_description: In 1410, the construction of the Prague Astronomical Clock, also known as the Prague Orloj, was completed by Mikuláš of Kadaň and Jan Šindel. This remarkable timepiece became a symbol of the city and an important advancement in medieval astronomy.
events.name: Construction of Prague Astronomical Clock

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1410, King Henry IV of England opened the 8th Parliament, with Thomas Chaucer serving as Speaker of the House of Commons. This session was significant for addressing pressing issues of governance and royal authority.
events.name: The 8th Parliament of King Henry IV of England is opened

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1410, Thomas Beaufort, Duke of Exeter, was appointed as the new Lord Chancellor of England. His role was crucial in the administration of the kingdom during a time of political instability.
events.name: Thomas Beaufort becomes Lord Chancellor of England

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1410, a papal bull was issued from Avignon by Antipope Benedict XIII, authorizing Joan Gilabert Jofré to establish the Hospital dels Ignoscents, the world's first hospital dedicated to the treatment of mental illness. This marked a significant advancement in the understanding and treatment of mental health.
events.name: Papal bull issued for the creation of the Hospital dels Ignoscents

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1410, the Yongle Emperor launched the first of his military campaigns against the Mongols, mobilizing at least 100,000 soldiers from Beijing. This campaign aimed to consolidate Ming control over northern territories and assert dominance over the Mongol tribes.
events.name: Yongle Emperor's campaign against the Mongols begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1410, Aragonese forces captured Oristano, the capital of the Giudicato di Arborea in Sardinia. This event marked a significant step in the Aragonese expansion in the Mediterranean, leading to greater control over the island.
events.name: The Aragonese capture Oristano

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1410, during the wedding of Charles, Duke of Orléans, to Bonne of Armagnac in Gien, powerful French nobles formed the League of Gien to oppose John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy. This alliance marked the beginning of a civil war that would last for three decades.
events.name: Formation of the League of Gien

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1410, the English Parliament concluded its session for the year, during which King Henry IV granted royal assent to various acts, including the Sealing of Cloths Act 1409 and the Unlawful Games Act. This session was significant for legislative developments in England.
events.name: The English Parliament closes its session

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1410, Cardinal Baldasare Cossa was elected as the successor to the antipope Alexander V during the Council of Pisa. He would later take the name John XXIII, a name that would be reused centuries later by Pope John XXIII.
events.name: Cardinal Baldasare Cossa elected as antipope John XXIII

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1410, the death of Rupert, King of the Romans and Elector of Palatine, created a succession crisis in Germany. His son, Louis III, would take over as Elector Palatine, but the power struggle that ensued highlighted the fragility of the German monarchy.

image.caption: A painted portrait of Rupert III of the Palatinate, King of the Romans, in the choir of Neustadt Collegiate Church.
image.credit: Diözese Speyer — Festschrift Stiftskirche
image.date_qualification: Portrait painted in 1420, after Rupert's death in 1410; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Rupert, King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1410, during his campaign against the Eastern Mongols, the Yongle Emperor ordered the carving of an inscription on rocks at the Kerulen River, marking the passage of his troops. This campaign was part of a broader effort to secure Ming dominance in the region.
events.name: Yongle Emperor's campaign against the Eastern Mongols

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1410, King Martin I of Aragon died at the age of 53, leading to a succession crisis as five contenders vied for the thrones of Aragon and Sicily. The eventual resolution of this conflict would shape the political landscape of the region for years to come.
events.name: Death of King Martin I of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1410, an unspecified event occurred at the Onon River in Mongolia. Details surrounding this event are limited, but the location is historically significant as part of the Mongolian landscape.
events.name: Event on the Onon River

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1410, during the Ottoman Interregnum, Süleyman Çelebi emerged victorious against his brother Musa Çelebi just outside the Ottoman capital of Edirne. This conflict was part of a larger power struggle within the Ottoman dynasty.
events.name: Battle of Edirne

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Grunwald, fought on July 24, 1410, was a decisive conflict between the Teutonic Knights and the allied forces of Poland and Lithuania. This battle is considered one of the largest in medieval Europe and marked a turning point in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Battle of Grunwald

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Marienburg began on July 26, 1410, when Polish and Lithuanian forces attacked the Teutonic Knights' stronghold at Malbork. Despite an initial advantage, the siege was ultimately lifted on September 19 due to lack of progress and dissatisfaction among the besieging forces.
events.name: Siege of Marienburg

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1410, Bogislaw VIII, Duke of Pomerania, submitted his duchy to become a fiefdom within the Kingdom of Poland, led by King Władysław II. This act marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Duchy of Pomerania-Stargard submission

events.enhanced_description: After a four-month siege, the Muslim city of Antequera surrendered to the Crown of Castile on September 16, 1410. The siege was led by Prince Ferdinand of Aragon, marking a significant victory in the Reconquista.
events.name: Surrender of Antequera

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1410, after nearly two months of stagnation, the siege of Marienburg was lifted due to dissatisfaction among the Polish and Lithuanian forces. The Teutonic Knights successfully defended their stronghold against the siege.
events.name: Lifting of the Siege of Marienburg

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1410, following the death of Rupert, King of the Romans, a council of electors elected Sigismund of Hungary as the new King of the Romans. This election was contentious, as many electors refused to accept Sigismund's claim to the throne.
events.name: Election of Sigismund of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1410, a different set of electors elected Jobst of Moravia as King of the Romans, creating a conflict with Sigismund of Hungary's election. This division among the electors would lead to a prolonged power struggle.

image.caption: Miniature depicting Wenceslaus IV, Charles IV, and Jobst of Moravia.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — Aus der tschechischen Wikipedia; http://www.ngprague.cz/html/slezsko/img/016.gif
image.date_qualification: The miniature is dated 1430, later than Jobst’s 1410 election; it is a contextual depiction, not an image of the election.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Election of Jobst of Moravia

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1410, the Polish-Lithuanian alliance achieved a significant victory over the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Koronowo. This battle further weakened the Teutonic Order's influence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Koronowo

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1410, Euthymius II was elected as the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Matthew I, who had died in August. Euthymius's leadership would play a crucial role in the Eastern Orthodox Church during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Euthymius II becomes Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1410, a temporary truce was signed at Bicetre, near Paris, to halt the ongoing Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War in France. This agreement aimed to bring a momentary peace to a region ravaged by conflict.
events.name: Truce at Bicetre

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1410, a 32-day truce was established between the Teutonic Council, led by Grand Master Heinrich von Plauen, and King Jogaila of Poland. This truce aimed to pause hostilities following the recent battles.
events.name: Truce between Teutonic Council and Poland

events.enhanced_description: During the Friso-Hollandic Wars, Friesland soldiers captured the city of Staveren, the last stronghold in Friesland, after a harsh winter prevented both sides from crossing the Zuiderzee. This event marked a significant shift in control during the conflict.
events.name: Friso-Hollandic Wars: Capture of Staveren

events.enhanced_description: In 1411, Sultan Ahmen Shah I declared Ahmedabad as the new capital of Gujarat, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of the region. This decision not only established Ahmedabad as a center of power but also initiated its development into a major urban hub.
events.name: Gujarat Sultan Ahmen Shah I declares the new city of Ahmedabad to be the new Gujarat capital

events.enhanced_description: In 1411, under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty, extensive work began to restore the ancient Grand Canal of China, which had fallen into disrepair during the Yuan dynasty. This monumental project involved thousands of laborers and aimed to enhance trade and transportation.
events.name: Work begins on Grand Canal restoration

events.enhanced_description: In 1411, Constantinople was briefly besieged by the Ottoman pretender Musa Çelebi, who sought to reclaim power during the Ottoman Interregnum. The siege was a reflection of the internal strife within the Ottoman Empire and the city's strategic importance.
events.name: Constantinople besieged by Musa Çelebi

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1411, Ahmad Shah I ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Gujarat following the death of his grandfather, Muzaffar Shah I. His reign marked the establishment of the Gujarat Sultanate as a significant power in western India.
events.name: Ahmad Shah I becomes Sultan of Gujarat

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1411, Jobst of Moravia, King of the Romans, died under suspicious circumstances at the age of 35. His death led to a power vacuum that allowed Sigismund of Hungary to strengthen his claim to the throne.
events.name: Death of Jobst of Moravia

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1411, the First Peace of Thorn was signed, concluding the Polish–Lithuanian–Teutonic War. The treaty resulted in the Teutonic Knights ceding Dobrzyń Land to the Kingdom of Poland, reshaping the balance of power in the region.

image.caption: A depiction of the Peace of Thorn of 1411.
image.credit: King of Poland Jogaila (original uploader was Appleseed at en.wikipedia ) — Original image: http://dziedzictwo.polska.pl
image.date_qualification: Retrospective depiction of the treaty, not a contemporary photograph; the image date is unsupported, so no display date is assigned.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Peace of Thorn

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1411, a parliament convened in Calatayud, Spain, to elect a successor to the recently deceased King Martin of Aragon. Despite nominations, the parliament failed to reach a consensus on a new king, leading to a political impasse.
events.name: Parliament in Calatayud

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1411, Sultan Süleyman Çelebi was strangled to death after being forced to flee Edirne by his brother Musa Çelebi. This event marked a significant turning point in the Ottoman Interregnum, leading to Musa's ascension.
events.name: Death of Süleyman Çelebi

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1411, Ahmad Shah I laid the foundation of Ahmedabad at the site of Asawal, marking the establishment of a city that would become a major center of trade and culture in India.
events.name: Foundation of Ahmedabad

events.enhanced_description: In April 1411, Carlo I Tocco arrived in Ioannina to assume control over the Despotate of Epirus, a former Byzantine territory. His rule marked a continuation of the complex political dynamics in the region following the decline of Byzantine authority.

image.caption: Map illustrating Carlo I Tocco’s conquests.
image.credit: Constantine Plakidas — Own work
image.date_qualification: The map covers 1376–1429; the supplied image date is 2018-03-25, not the date of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Carlo I Tocco arrives at Ioannina in Greece to become the new ruler of the former Byzantine state, the Despotate of Epirus

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1411, Sandalj Hranić, Duke of Bosnia, sold the coastal town of Ostrovica to the Republic of Venice. This transaction significantly enhanced Venetian control over the Dalmatian coast and solidified their maritime dominance in the Adriatic Sea.
events.name: Sandalj Hranić sells Ostrovica to the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1411, General Muzio Attendolo, under the command of Louis II of Anjou, achieved a decisive victory against King Ladislaus of Naples at the Battle of Roccasecca. This battle was a crucial moment in the ongoing power struggles in Italy during the early 15th century.
events.name: Battle of Roccasecca

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1411, Friedrich IV, known as 'Friedrich of the Empty Pockets', ascended to the title of Duke of Further Austria following the death of his brother, Leopold the Fat. His reign would be marked by the challenges of managing the diverse territories of the Habsburgs.
events.name: Friedrich IV becomes Duke of Further Austria

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1411, King Charles VI of France granted exclusive rights to the city of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon for the ripening and marketing of Roquefort cheese. This decree helped establish the region's reputation for producing this renowned cheese.
events.name: Roquefort cheese rights granted

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1411, Admiral Zheng He returned to Nanjing after his second voyage, bringing with him the Sinhalese king, who had been captured during the Ming–Kotte War. This event underscored the Ming Dynasty's naval prowess and its expanding influence in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Zheng He returns to Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1411, Sigismund was unanimously elected as King of the Romans by the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire. His election was a pivotal moment in the governance of the empire, which faced numerous challenges during his reign.
events.name: Sigismund elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1411, the Battle of Harlaw took place in Scotland, where Domhnall of Islay, Lord of the Isles, faced off against an army commanded by Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar. The battle ended in a bloody draw, highlighting the ongoing conflicts over control in the Scottish Highlands.
events.name: Battle of Harlaw

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1411, Parameswara of Malacca, also known as Iskandar Shah, was hosted by the Ming Court in Nanjing for a series of banquets. This visit marked a significant diplomatic engagement between the Malay Sultanate and the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: Parameswara of Malacca hosted by Ming Court

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1411, the Treaty of Selymbria was concluded between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice, marking a significant diplomatic agreement that shaped the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Selymbria concluded

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1411, King Henry IV of England summoned his ninth parliament, a crucial assembly that would address various political issues of the time, including governance and taxation.
events.name: King Henry IV calls ninth parliament

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1411, John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, hosted negotiations at the Abbey of St Vaast in Arras with English Bishop Henry Chichele and envoys regarding English support in the French civil war. The discussions ultimately failed to secure significant backing.
