events.name: Negotiations at Abbey of St Vaast

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1411, the Duke of Burgundy, with the assistance of English mercenaries, successfully captured Paris. This event marked a significant turning point in the ongoing conflicts during the French civil war.
events.name: Duke of Burgundy captures Paris

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1411, the English Parliament was convened by King Henry IV, during which Thomas Chaucer was elected as Speaker of the House of Commons. This assembly was significant for addressing the governance of the kingdom.
events.name: English Parliament assembles

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1411, the Swiss canton of Appenzell entered into an alliance with most of the cantons of the Swiss Confederacy. This alliance strengthened the political unity and military cooperation among the Swiss regions.
events.name: Appenzell enters alliance with Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1411, King Henry IV dismissed Prince Henry and his supporters from the government, a move that reflected the ongoing tensions within the English court and the struggle for power.
events.name: Henry IV dismisses Prince Henry

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1411, King Henry IV granted royal assent to numerous acts passed by the English Parliament, including the Riot Act 1411, which aimed to address civil disorder and maintain peace.
events.name: Royal assent to acts passed by Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1411, King Henry IV of England issued pardons to nearly all Welsh rebels involved in the Glyndŵr rebellion, sparing only the leaders Owain Glyndŵr and Thomas of Trumpington. This act was part of the ongoing efforts to stabilize relations with Wales.
events.name: Henry IV issues pardons to Welsh rebels

events.enhanced_description: Possibly in early 1412, the Battle of İnceğiz occurred between the rival brothers Mehmed Çelebi and Musa Çelebi during the Ottoman Interregnum. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for control of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of İnceğiz

events.enhanced_description: The first mention of Wallachian knights competing in a jousting tournament took place in Buda, highlighting the cultural exchange and the popularity of chivalric tournaments in medieval Europe.
events.name: Jousting tournament in Buda

events.enhanced_description: John II of Castile declared the Valladolid laws, which restricted the social rights of Jews, including forcing them to wear distinctive clothing and barring them from administrative positions. This legislation reflected the growing anti-Semitic sentiments in medieval Spain.
events.name: Valladolid laws declared by John II of Castile

events.enhanced_description: In 1412, Jiao Yu, a prominent artillery officer of the Ming Dynasty, added a preface to his seminal work, the Huolongjing, which detailed advancements in gunpowder warfare and artillery technology. This work significantly influenced military tactics and technology in China and beyond.
events.name: Jiao Yu adds preface to Huolongjing

events.enhanced_description: The Black Death, which ravaged Europe in the 14th century, returned to England for a final wave around 1412, exacerbating the already dire social and economic conditions. This pandemic led to significant population loss and social upheaval across the country.
events.name: The Black Death sweeps England for a final time

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1412, the Medici Family was officially appointed as the bankers of the Papacy, solidifying their financial influence and power in Renaissance Italy. This role would enable them to play a crucial part in the politics and culture of the time.
events.name: Medici Family made bankers of the Papacy

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1412, Ernest, Duke of Austria, married Cymburgis of Masovia. This marriage was significant for strengthening political alliances in Central Europe during a period of territorial disputes.

image.caption: Glass painting depicting Ernest the Iron-Willed with his sons Friedrich, Albrecht, and Ernst.
image.credit: The original uploader was Caro1409 at German Wikipedia . — Transferred from de.wikipedia to Commons by Ireas using CommonsHelper .
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the glass painting to between 1418 and 1424. “8 July 2006” is the original upload date, not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ernest marries Cymburgis of Masovia

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1412, the 'Mining Code' (Zakon o Rudnishma) was enacted in Serbia by Despot Stefan Lazarević to regulate mineral extraction. This legislation aimed to promote responsible mining practices and economic development in the region.
events.name: Mining Code enacted in Serbia

events.enhanced_description: The Alcañiz Concord was a pivotal agreement reached in the city of Alcañiz, where nine delegates were selected to choose a new, undisputed King of Aragon. This event was crucial in resolving the succession crisis following the death of King Martin of Aragon.
events.name: The Alcañiz Concord

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Morvedre was fought in the Kingdom of Valencia, where supporters of Ferdinand of Antequera clashed with those loyal to James II, Count of Urgell. This battle was a significant moment in the power struggle for the throne of Aragon.
events.name: Battle of Morvedre

events.enhanced_description: The University of St Andrews, one of the oldest universities in the English-speaking world, was granted a charter of privilege by the local bishop in 1412. This charter marked a significant step in the establishment of higher education in Scotland.

locations.name: St Andrews, Fife, Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: Charter of the University of St Andrews

events.enhanced_description: The Compromise of Caspe was a crucial agreement reached in the town of Caspe, where nine delegates were chosen to resolve the succession crisis following the death of King Martin of Aragon. This led to the election of Ferdinand of Antequera as the new King of Aragon.
events.name: Compromise of Caspe

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his father, Duke Albert IV, Albert V ascended to the title of Duke of Mecklenburg. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the region as it continued the lineage of the House of Mecklenburg.
events.name: Duke Albert V becomes Duke of Mecklenburg

events.enhanced_description: In Cairo, Abu’l-Fa’dl Abbas Al-Musta'in was installed as the Sultan of Egypt by rebels, serving as a temporary replacement for his father, Sultan An-Nasir Faraj. His rule lasted only six months before he returned to his role as Caliph.
events.name: Installation of Abu’l-Fa’dl Abbas Al-Musta'in

events.enhanced_description: Gian Maria Visconti, the Duke of Milan, was assassinated in front of the church of San Gottardo by Milanese Ghibellines on the orders of his rival, Facino Cane. This event marked a significant shift in power within the city.
events.name: Assassination of Gian Maria Visconti

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Bourges was signed between King Henry IV of England and Charles, Duke of Orléans, granting England full sovereignty over Aquitaine and Gascony in exchange for military support against the Burgundians. This treaty was a significant diplomatic maneuver during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Treaty of Bourges

events.enhanced_description: An-Nasir Faraj, the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt and Syria, was assassinated in Damascus after surrendering to the Emirs of Syria. His death led to a power vacuum in the region, with his son being confirmed as the ruler of Egypt.
events.name: Assassination of An-Nasir Faraj

events.enhanced_description: Antipope John XXIII signed an agreement with King Ladislaus of Naples, investing him with the Neapolitan crown in exchange for military support against Pope Benedict XII. This agreement highlighted the complex interplay between religion and politics during this period.
events.name: Agreement between Antipope John XXIII and King Ladislaus of Naples

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand of Antequera was officially proclaimed King of Aragon by delegates in Caspe, following a two-year succession crisis that began with the death of King Martin. This event solidified his claim to the throne and marked a new chapter in Aragonese history.
events.name: Ferdinand of Antequera proclaimed King of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: As the Compromise of Caspe was read aloud by Friar Vicent Ferrer, Ferdinand I was proclaimed King of Aragon by the delegates. This proclamation marked the end of a contentious succession crisis and established Ferdinand's rule.
events.name: Proclamation of Ferdinand I as King of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: Behnam Hadloyo was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Mardin, a significant religious leadership position within the Syriac Orthodox Church. His leadership would influence the Christian community in the region.
events.name: Behnam Hadloyo becomes Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Auxerre was signed between the Duchy of Burgundy and the Armagnacs, arranging a marriage between Philip, Count of Vertus, and Catherine of Burgundy. Although the marriage never took place, this agreement aimed to solidify political alliances.
events.name: Peace of Auxerre

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Motta was fought when the Republic of Venice faced an invasion by a coalition of Hungarians, Germans, and Croats. The Venetian forces achieved a decisive victory, inflicting heavy casualties on the invading army.
events.name: Battle of Motta

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand I of Aragon was declared Count of Barcelona, a title that further solidified his political power in the region. This declaration was part of his broader efforts to unify the crowns of Aragon and Castile.
events.name: Ferdinand I declared Count of Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Go-Komatsu abdicated the throne, leading to the accession of Emperor Shoko in Japan. This transition was part of the complex political landscape of the Nanboku-chō period, characterized by rival imperial lines.
events.name: Accession of Emperor Shoko

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Queen Margaret, Eric of Pomerania became the sole ruler of the Kalmar Union, which united Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. His reign would be marked by challenges in maintaining the union's stability.
events.name: Eric of Pomerania becomes sole ruler of the Kalmar Union

events.enhanced_description: Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh forced Sultan Al-Musta'in to abdicate, becoming the new Mamluk Sultan of Egypt. This power shift was indicative of the turbulent political climate in the region during this period.
events.name: Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh becomes Mamluk Sultan

events.enhanced_description: During the Ava–Hanthawaddy War, King Razadarit of Hanthawaddy led an invasion of Prome with a force of 4,000 troops. This conflict was part of the ongoing struggle for dominance in the region of modern-day Myanmar.
events.name: Ava–Hanthawaddy War

events.enhanced_description: King Henry IV of England issued a summons for the English Parliament for the last time, directing the members of Commons and the House of Lords to assemble. This event marked the end of his active involvement in parliamentary affairs.
events.name: Final summons of the English Parliament by Henry IV

events.enhanced_description: In December, the Battle of Chalagan saw the Kara Koyunlu Turkomans defeat the Georgians led by Constantine I and their ally Ibrahim I of Shirvan. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region during the early 15th century.
events.name: Battle of Chalagan

events.enhanced_description: The Yongle Emperor of China ordered the fourth of the Ming treasure voyages, to be led by Admiral Zheng He. These voyages were significant for establishing Chinese maritime power and expanding trade networks across the Indian Ocean.

image.caption: Seated portrait of Emperor Ming Chengzu.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Digitized by NPM; image is directly from Shuge
image.date_qualification: The image is described as a Ming-dynasty portrait; the supplied date does not identify a specific year. The article says the Yongle Emperor ordered the fleet's construction in 1403.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ming treasure voyages ordered by Yongle Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 1413, Samogitia became the last region in Europe to be Christianized, marking a significant milestone in the spread of Christianity across the continent. This event reflected the broader religious transformations occurring during this period.
events.name: Christianization of Samogitia

events.enhanced_description: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, a crucial historical record of Korea, began in 1413. These annals provide a detailed account of the political, social, and cultural history of the Joseon period, which lasted for several centuries.
events.name: Beginning of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The First Scutari War, fought between the Kingdom of Zeta and the Venetian Republic, concluded on January 30, 1413. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for control over the Adriatic region and highlighted the tensions between local powers and Venetian interests.

image.caption: Rozafa Fortress (Burg Rozafa) in Shkodër, Albania.
image.credit: Sigismund von Dobschütz — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2011-06-06; not a contemporary image of the 1405–1412 war.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: End of the First Scutari War

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1413, the 10th and final Parliament of King Henry IV convened in Westminster. However, it was short-lived, closing after six weeks due to the king's declining health and eventual death.
events.name: Opening of the 10th Parliament of King Henry IV

events.enhanced_description: King Henry IV of England passed away on March 20, 1413, at Westminster Abbey, where Parliament was in session. His death marked the end of a tumultuous reign and set the stage for the ascension of his son, Henry V.
events.name: Death of King Henry IV of England

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1413, Henry, Prince of Wales, was proclaimed King Henry V of England, following the death of his father, Henry IV. His ascension marked the beginning of a new era in English history, characterized by military campaigns in France.
events.name: Henry V ascends to the throne

events.enhanced_description: King Henry V summoned the English Parliament to convene at Westminster on March 22, 1413, as part of his efforts to consolidate power and address pressing national issues following his recent ascension to the throne.
events.name: Henry V summons Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1413, the Republic of Genoa regained its independence from French control, electing Giorgio Adorno as Doge for life. This marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region and the restoration of local governance.
events.name: Genoa regains independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1413, Trung Quang De, the Emperor of Dai Viet (modern-day Vietnam), surrendered his kingdom to Chinese control. This event marked the beginning of a period of Chinese domination over Vietnam.
events.name: Surrender of Dai Viet to China

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Henry V as King of England took place on April 9, 1413, at Westminster Abbey. This ceremony solidified his claim to the throne and marked the beginning of his reign, which would be characterized by military campaigns in France.
events.name: Coronation of Henry V

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1413, the Cabochien revolt erupted in Paris, led by Simon Caboche, as rebels seized the Bastille prison and took the Provost of Paris, Pierre des Essarts, hostage. This uprising reflected the growing discontent among the populace against the ruling elite.
events.name: Cabochien revolt begins

events.enhanced_description: The first Parliament of King Henry V convened at Westminster on May 14, 1413, shortly after his coronation. This assembly was crucial for addressing the pressing issues of the kingdom and establishing Henry's authority.
events.name: First Parliament of Henry V assembles

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1413, amidst the turmoil of the Cabochien revolt, King Charles VI of France enacted the 'Ordonnance cabochienne,' which limited his royal powers. This law was a response to the growing unrest and highlighted the challenges faced by the monarchy.
events.name: Ordonnance cabochienne signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1413, Ali Shah Miri ascended to the throne as the new Sultan of Kashmir, following the death of his father, Sultan Sikandar Shah Miri. His reign would be marked by the challenges of governance in a region with a rich cultural heritage.
events.name: Ali Shah Miri becomes Sultan of Kashmir

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1413, King Ladislaus of Naples led his troops to conquer and sack the city of Rome, driving out Antipope John XXIII. This event underscored the political instability in Italy during this period and the ongoing power struggles among various factions.
events.name: Ladislaus of Naples sacks Rome

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1413, the English Parliament concluded its session, with King Henry V granting royal assent to several acts, including the Corn Measure Act and the Parliamentary Elections Act. These laws were significant for regulating elections and agricultural practices.
events.name: Parliament closes in England

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1413, Ludwig ascended to the throne as the new Landgrave of Hesse following the death of his father, Hermann II. His reign would play a crucial role in the political landscape of the German principalities.
events.name: Ludwig becomes Landgrave of Hesse

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1413, the Battle of Çamurlu took place, where Mehmed I defeated his brother Musa, effectively ending the Ottoman Interregnum. This victory solidified Mehmed's position as the Sultan and marked a significant moment in Ottoman history.
events.name: Battle of Çamurlu

events.enhanced_description: The Cabochien revolt in Paris came to an end on August 3, 1413, as the citizenry and nobles rose against the rebel control. The aftermath saw the execution of many Cabochiens, while key leaders managed to escape, highlighting the volatility of the period.
events.name: End of the Cabochien revolt

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1413, the University of St Andrews in Scotland was chartered by papal bull, establishing it as one of the oldest universities in the English-speaking world. This event marked a significant development in higher education in Scotland.
events.name: University of St Andrews chartered

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1413, the French government repealed the 'Ordonnance cabochienne,' restoring the powers of King Charles VI. This repeal was a response to the political turmoil and the need to stabilize royal authority.
events.name: Repeal of the Ordonnance cabochienne

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1413, the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania signed the Union of Horodło, strengthening their political alliance. This agreement was pivotal in shaping the future of both nations and their regional influence.
events.name: Union of Horodło signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1413, Tewodros I ascended to the throne as Emperor of Ethiopia following the death of his father, Dawit I. His reign would be marked by efforts to modernize the empire and strengthen its central authority.
events.name: Tewodros I ascends the throne of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1413, the Margraviate of Brandenburg renewed its alliance with the Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast against the Duchy of Pomerania-Stettin. This alliance was significant in the context of regional power struggles in Northern Europe.
events.name: Renewal of alliance between Brandenburg and Pomerania-Wolgast

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1413, King Henry V of England summoned Parliament to assemble on April 30 at Westminster. This call to Parliament was part of his strategy to address governance and military matters following his recent coronation.
events.name: Henry V summons Parliament to assemble

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1413, King Henry V of England ordered the remains of his predecessor, King Richard II, to be moved from King's Langley Priory to Westminster Abbey, a significant act of reconciliation and respect for the former monarch whom Henry's father had overthrown. This reinterment underscored the importance of Westminster Abbey as the traditional burial site for English monarchs.
events.name: Reinterment of King Richard II

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1413, the betrothal ceremony of Prince Charles of France to Marie of Anjou took place at the Palais du Louvre in Paris. This union was politically significant as it aimed to strengthen alliances between the French royal family and the powerful Anjou dynasty.
events.name: Betrothal of Prince Charles of France

events.enhanced_description: Michele Steno's rule as the Doge of Venice came to an end with his death on December 26, 1413, after 26 years in office. He was succeeded by Tommaso Mocenigo, marking a significant transition in the leadership of the Venetian Republic.
events.name: Death of Michele Steno

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1414, Ernest, Duke of Austria, becomes the last duke to be enthroned in Carinthia through the ancient Carantanian ritual at the Prince's Stone, subsequently adopting the title of Archduke.
events.name: Ernest, Duke of Austria adopts the title of Archduke

events.enhanced_description: In 1414, the Alien Priory Cells, which were foreign monastic establishments in England, are suppressed, reflecting the growing tensions and nationalistic sentiments during this period.
events.name: Suppression of Alien Priory Cells in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1414, the prominent Tibetan lama Je Tsongkhapa declines an invitation from the Yongle Emperor to appear in Nanjing, sending instead his disciple Chosrje Shākya Yeshe, who is honored with the title 'State Teacher'.
events.name: Je Tsongkhapa declines Yongle Emperor's invitation

events.enhanced_description: In 1414, Durham School is established as a grammar school by Thomas Langley, Prince-Bishop of Durham, and continues to thrive as an independent institution over 600 years later.
events.name: Durham School founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1414, Michael Küchmeister von Sternberg was appointed as the 28th Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, succeeding Heinrich von Plauen. His leadership would influence the Order's military and political strategies in the region.
events.name: Michael Küchmeister von Sternberg becomes Grand Master

events.enhanced_description: The Oldcastle Revolt began on January 9, 1414, led by John Oldcastle, as an uprising by the Lollards against King Henry V. The rebellion was quickly suppressed by Henry's forces, resulting in the capture and execution of many rebels.
events.name: Oldcastle Revolt

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand I was crowned King of Aragon on February 11, 1414, in Zaragoza. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the Crown of Aragon, as Ferdinand's reign would influence the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Coronation of Ferdinand I as King of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1414, the speech of French theologian Jean Petit was publicly burned in Paris by order of the inquisitor Gerard de Montaigu. This act highlighted the tensions between emerging reformist ideas and established religious authorities during this period.
events.name: Burning of Jean Petit's Speech

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1414, Abu’l-Faḍl Abbas Al-Musta'in was ousted from his position as Caliph of Cairo, following his earlier abdication as Sultan of Egypt. This power shift was orchestrated by Sultan Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh, who appointed his brother as the new Caliph.
events.name: Abu’l-Faḍl Abbas Al-Musta'in forced out as Caliph

events.enhanced_description: The rebellion led by Vietnamese Emperor Tran Quy Khoang against the Ming dynasty came to an end on March 30, 1414, when he was captured by General Zhang Fu. This marked a significant turning point in the ongoing Ming–Vietnamese conflict.
events.name: End of Tran Quy Khoang's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1414, the Yongle Emperor of China departed from Beijing to lead a military campaign against the Oirat Mongols. This campaign was part of his broader efforts to consolidate power and expand the Ming dynasty's influence.
events.name: Yongle Emperor's Campaign against Oirat Mongols

events.enhanced_description: The second English Parliament of King Henry V opened on April 30, 1414, in Westminster, where Walter Hungerford was elected as Speaker of the House of Commons. This session was significant for the legislative developments that occurred during Henry's reign.
events.name: Second English Parliament of Henry V

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1414, Khizr Khan, the governor of Multan under Timur, successfully conquered the Delhi Sultanate from Daulat Khan Lodi, establishing the Sayyid Dynasty. This event marked a significant shift in power within the Indian subcontinent.
events.name: Khizr Khan conquers Delhi Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1414, Yeshaq I succeeded his brother Tewodros I as Emperor of Ethiopia. His ascension marked a continuation of the Solomonic dynasty's influence in the region.
events.name: Yeshaq I becomes Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1414, Iskandar Mirza, who had ruled the Timurid Empire since 1409, was captured as the city of Isfahan surrendered to Shah Rukh. This event marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the Timurid Empire.
events.name: Capture of Iskandar Mirza

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1414, Joanna II ascended to the throne as the reigning Queen of Naples following the death of her brother, King Ladislaus. Her reign would be marked by political intrigue and challenges to her authority.
events.name: Joanna II becomes Queen of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1414, the brotherhood of the Sancta dels Folls Dona Nostra i Desamparats Innocents was founded in Valencia to assist the mentally ill and later expanded its mission to care for homeless and abandoned children. This organization played a significant role in social welfare during its time.
events.name: Foundation of the Sancta dels Folls

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1414, a giraffe was presented to China's Yongle Emperor as a gift from the Sultan of Bengal, Saifuddin Hamza Shah. This event symbolized the diplomatic relations and cultural exchanges between the Ming dynasty and South Asian kingdoms.
events.name: Presentation of a Giraffe to Yongle Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1414, the Bohemian church reformer Jan Hus left his home at the invitation of King Sigismund of Germany to attend the Council of Constance. Unfortunately, upon his arrival, he was imprisoned, leading to his eventual execution.
events.name: Jan Hus departs for the Council of Constance

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1414, Sigismund of Luxembourg was crowned as King of the Romans at Aachen, four years after his election. This event was significant in the context of the Holy Roman Empire and its political dynamics.
events.name: Coronation of Sigismund of Luxembourg

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Constance opened on November 16, 1414, summoned by King Sigismund to resolve the Western Schism, which had seen three different Popes recognized by various factions. This council aimed to restore unity within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Opening of the Council of Constance

events.enhanced_description: The Third Parliament of King Henry V opened on November 19, 1414, in Westminster, where significant laws were passed, including the Suppression of Heresy Act and the Riot Act. This session reflected Henry's efforts to consolidate power and address social issues.
events.name: Third Parliament of Henry V

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1414, the construction of Ahmed Shah's Mosque in Ahmedabad was completed, with the date etched into stone. This mosque is a significant example of Indo-Islamic architecture and reflects the cultural heritage of the region.
events.name: Completion of Ahmed Shah's Mosque

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1414, Casimir officially assumes full power as Duke of Oświęcim upon reaching the age of 18, marking a significant transition in leadership for the region.
events.name: Casimir, Duke of Oświęcim takes full power

events.enhanced_description: In early 1415, Razadarit, the ruler of the Hanthawaddy Kingdom, authorizes a plan to invade the forces of Minkhaung I of the Ava Kingdom, marking a significant escalation in the Forty Years' War.
events.name: Razadarit authorizes invasion plan

events.enhanced_description: In 1415, King Charles VI of France and John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, sign the Treaty of Arras, a pivotal agreement aimed at stabilizing the region amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Treaty of Arras signed

events.enhanced_description: In January 1415, Pope Benedict XIII issued an order for all Talmuds to be delivered to the diocese, where they would be held until further notice. This action reflected the tensions between the Catholic Church and Jewish communities during this period.
events.name: Benedict XIII orders Talmuds to be delivered

events.enhanced_description: In 1415, the Swiss Confederation successfully took control of the territory of Aargau from the House of Habsburg. This event marked a significant expansion of Swiss territory and influence during the early 15th century.
events.name: Swiss Confederation takes Aargau

events.enhanced_description: By 1415, the Grand Canal of China was reinstated after a period of disuse, following restoration efforts that began in 1411. This project, initiated by the Yongle Emperor, aimed to enhance the grain shipment system to support the new capital at Beijing.
events.name: Restoration of the Grand Canal of China

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1415, representatives from England, including the Bishops of Durham and Norwich, meet with King Charles VI of France to extend the truce in the ongoing Burgundian War until May 1.
events.name: Truce extended in the Burgundian War

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1415, the decisive Battle of Dala occurs in Myanmar, where Crown Prince Minye Kyawswa of Ava leads his forces against King Razadarit of Hanthawaddy. Despite his valiant efforts, Minye Kyawswa is killed, but his troops ultimately defeat the invaders.
events.name: Battle of Dala

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1415, Antipope John XXIII escapes from Constance, taking refuge in Schaffhausen, in the Duchy of Austria, despite his earlier promise to resign from his claims to the papacy.
events.name: Antipope John XXIII's escape

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1415, Giorgio Adorno resigns as the Doge of Genoa, despite having been appointed for life, indicating the political instability of the time.
events.name: Giorgio Adorno resigns as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1415, Barnaba Guano is elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa, succeeding Giorgio Adorno amidst a backdrop of political change.
events.name: Barnaba Guano elected as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1415, the Council of Constance approves the decree Haec sancta synodus, establishing the principle that an ecumenical council holds authority over the Pope in matters of faith.
events.name: Haec sancta synodus decree approved

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1415, Frederick I is appointed as the Elector of Brandenburg, a significant position in the Holy Roman Empire that enhances his political influence.
events.name: Frederick I becomes Elector of Brandenburg

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1415, the Council of Constance declares John Wycliffe a heretic, banning his writings and ordering the removal of his remains from consecrated ground, reflecting the church's efforts to suppress dissent.
events.name: Council of Constance condemns John Wycliffe

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1415, Antipope Benedict XIII issues a papal bull from Valencia, imposing eleven prohibitions against Jews, including restrictions on education and public interaction, reflecting the era's pervasive anti-Semitism.
events.name: Antipope Benedict XIII issues prohibitions against Jews

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1415, the Council of Constance formally dismisses Antipope John XXIII from any authority over the Roman Catholic Church, a critical step in resolving the Western Schism.
events.name: Council of Constance dismisses Antipope John XXIII

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1415, Jan Hus is condemned by the Council of Constance for heresy and is subsequently executed by burning at the stake, marking a pivotal moment in the pre-Reformation movement.
events.name: Jan Hus condemned and executed

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1415, Pope Gregory XII officially opens the Council of Constance, where he later abdicates, becoming the last pope to resign until Pope Benedict XVI in 2013.
events.name: Pope Gregory XII opens the Council of Constance

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1415, Jan Hus is executed by burning at the stake in Konstanz, a significant event that highlights the tensions between reformist ideas and the established church.
events.name: Jan Hus burned at the stake

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1415, Sigismund, King of the Romans, departs from the Council of Constance to Perpignan, aiming to secure the resignation of Antipope Benedict XIII and to negotiate peace in ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Sigismund's trip to Perpignan

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1415, King Henry V of England learns of the Southampton Plot against him, leading to the arrest and execution of the conspirators before he launches his invasion of France.
events.name: Henry V informed of Southampton Plot

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1415, Sigismund, King of the Germans, met with Antipope Benedict XIII in Avignon in an effort to persuade him to resign. This meeting was part of Sigismund's broader efforts to resolve the Great Western Schism, which had divided the Catholic Church.
events.name: Sigismund meets with Antipope Benedict XIII

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Agincourt, fought on October 25, 1415, saw the English army, led by King Henry V, achieve a decisive victory against a much larger French force. The battle is particularly noted for the effectiveness of English longbowmen, which played a crucial role in the defeat of the French knights.

image.caption: Memorial to the knights who died at Agincourt, at Centre Azincourt 1415.
image.credit: Patrimoine7vallees — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image dated 2026-03-18; it depicts a later memorial, not the battle itself.
