events.name: Battle of Agincourt

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1415, King Henry V opened the English Parliament for an 8-day session, a significant event in the governance of England during the Hundred Years' War. This session would address various matters of state, including military funding and legislation.
events.name: Opening of the English Parliament by Henry V

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1415, Frederick I, Elector of Brandenburg, pledged his 3-year-old daughter Magdalene to Wartislaw IX, the 15-year-old Duke of Pomerania-Wolgast, in an attempt to resolve ongoing conflicts between their territories. This political maneuver aimed to secure peace through dynastic marriage.
events.name: Marriage pledge between Brandenburg and Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: The English Parliament was closed on November 12, 1415, after successfully passing the Money Act 1415, which increased penalties for the importation of illegal currency. This act was part of Henry V's broader efforts to stabilize the economy during wartime.
events.name: Closure of the English Parliament after passing the Money Act

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1415, the Treaty of Eberswalde was signed between the duchies of Pomerania-Stettin and Brandenburg, temporarily ending the Uckermark War. The treaty involved territorial concessions in exchange for financial compensation, marking a significant diplomatic resolution.
events.name: Treaty of Eberswalde

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1415, Jean de Touraine was named the new Dauphin of France following the death of his older brother, Louis, Duke of Guyenne. This succession was crucial for the French royal lineage during a tumultuous period marked by the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Jean de Touraine becomes Dauphin of France

events.enhanced_description: In 1416, the Trezzo sull'Adda Bridge, which was the longest arch bridge in the world at the time, was destroyed. This event marked a significant loss in architectural heritage during the early 15th century.
events.name: Destruction of Trezzo sull'Adda Bridge

events.enhanced_description: The Hussite Bible was completed in 1416 by translators Tamás Pécsi and Bálint Újlaki. This translation was significant for the Hussite movement, which sought to make the scriptures accessible to the common people.
events.name: Completion of the Hussite Bible

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1416, the Republic of Ragusa became the first state in Europe to officially outlaw slavery. This progressive legislation marked a significant step towards human rights in the region.
events.name: Republic of Ragusa outlaws slavery

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1416, Venetian admiral Pietro Loredan achieved a significant victory at the Battle of Gallipoli, where he destroyed the Ottoman fleet. This battle was pivotal in establishing Venetian naval dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Gallipoli

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1416, Jerome of Prague was burned at the stake as a heretic by the Catholic Church in Konstanz. His execution was part of the broader conflict between the Church and the Hussite movement, which sought reform within the Church.

image.caption: Reproduction of a portrait of Jerome of Prague from Beza’s *Icones*.
image.credit: McCrie, Charles Greig, 1836-1910 Bèze, Théodore de, 1519-1605 — Internet Archive identifier : bezasiconesconte00mccr https://archive.org/download/bezasiconesconte00mccr/bezasiconesconte00mccr.pdf
image.date_qualification: Retrospective portrait reproduction from a 1906 book reproducing portraits published in 1580 and 1581; not a contemporary image of the execution. No image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Burning of Jerome of Prague

events.enhanced_description: In 1417, the earliest extant description of Tynwald Day, the annual meeting of the Isle of Man's parliament, was documented in law. This event is significant in the history of democratic governance in the Isle of Man.
events.name: Earliest description of Tynwald Day

events.enhanced_description: In 1417, the use of street lighting was first recorded in London when Mayor Sir Henry Barton ordered lanterns with lights to be hung out during winter evenings. This initiative marked a significant advancement in urban infrastructure and public safety.
events.name: First recorded use of street lighting in London

events.enhanced_description: In 1417, Mircea cel Bătrân lost the region of Dobruja to the Ottomans, leading to the payment of tribute to prevent Wallachia from becoming an Ottoman province. This event was significant in the context of Ottoman expansion in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Mircea cel Bătrân loses Dobruja to the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In 1417, Chimalpopoca succeeded his father Huitzilihuitl as Tlatoani (monarch) of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire. His reign would be marked by the challenges of maintaining power amidst growing external threats.
events.name: Chimalpopoca succeeds Huitzilihuitl as Tlatoani

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1417, an English fleet led by the Earl of Huntingdon defeated a fleet of Genoese carracks, capturing their admiral, known as the 'Bastard of Bourbon.' This victory underscored the naval prowess of England during this period.
events.name: Defeat of Genoese fleet by English

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1417, Pope Benedict XIII was deposed, effectively ending the Great Western Schism that had divided the Catholic Church for decades. His removal paved the way for the election of Pope Martin V, restoring unity to the Church.
events.name: Deposition of Pope Benedict XIII

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1417, King Henry V of England began using English in his correspondence while on campaign in France. This marked a significant cultural shift, as it was the first time English was used in official documents since the Norman Conquest.
events.name: Henry V begins using English in correspondence

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1417, Henry V of England captured the city of Caen in Normandy, which would remain under English control until 1450. This victory was part of Henry's campaign to reclaim French territories during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Capture of Caen by Henry V

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1417, Pope Martin V was elected as the 206th pope, succeeding Gregory XII, who had abdicated in 1415. His election marked the end of the Great Western Schism and the restoration of papal authority.
events.name: Pope Martin V succeeds Gregory XII

events.enhanced_description: In 1418, João Gonçalves Zarco led one of the first Portuguese expeditions to the Madeira Islands, marking a significant moment in the Age of Discovery. This expedition laid the groundwork for the Portuguese colonization and exploration of the Atlantic.
events.name: João Gonçalves Zarco leads one of the first Portuguese expeditions to the Madeira Islands

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1418, Michael I succeeded Mircea I as the ruler of Wallachia. His ascension came during a period of significant political instability and external threats from the Ottoman Empire.

image.caption: Old iconographic depiction of Mircea I and Mihail I from Cozia Monastery.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Old iconographic depiction from Cozia Monastery
image.date_qualification: An 18th-century depiction of the rulers, not a contemporary image of Michael’s succession; no supported display date is available.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Succession of Michael I of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: The Council of Constance, which began in 1414, concluded on April 22, 1418, resolving significant issues within the Catholic Church, including the election of Pope Martin V and the condemnation of John Hus. This council was pivotal in addressing the Western Schism and reforming church practices.
events.name: The Council of Constance ends

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1418, John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, successfully captured Paris, a critical stronghold during the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years' War. This event significantly shifted the balance of power in France, aligning the Burgundians with the English against the Armagnacs.
events.name: John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, captures Paris

events.enhanced_description: In July 1418, the English forces commenced the Siege of Rouen, a strategic city in Normandy, during the Hundred Years' War. The siege would last until 1419, culminating in the city's surrender and solidifying English control over Normandy.
events.name: The English Siege of Rouen begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1418, King Taejong of the Joseon dynasty abdicated the throne in favor of his son, Sejong the Great. This transition marked the beginning of a reign that would be noted for significant cultural and scientific advancements in Korea.
events.name: King Taejong abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: In November 1419, the Ottoman–Venetian peace treaty was signed, concluding four years of conflict. This treaty recognized Venetian possessions in the Aegean and the Balkans, stabilizing relations between the two powers.
events.name: The Ottoman–Venetian peace treaty is signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1419, Portuguese sea captains João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, discovered the Madeira Islands. This discovery was significant for the expansion of Portuguese maritime exploration.
events.name: Portuguese sea captains discover the Madeira Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1419, the University of Rostock was established, becoming the oldest university in northern Europe. This institution played a crucial role in the development of higher education in the region.
events.name: The University of Rostock is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1419, Mirza Shahrukh, the Timurid ruler of Persia, sent a large embassy to the court of the Yongle Emperor in China. The envoy, Ghiyāth al-dīn Naqqāsh, documented his travels, providing valuable insights into Chinese society and culture.
events.name: Mirza Shahrukh sends an embassy to China

events.enhanced_description: In 1419, Mihail I, the ruler of Wallachia, successfully defended his territory against Ottoman incursions with the assistance of Hungarian forces. This defense was crucial in maintaining Wallachia's autonomy during a period of Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Mihail I defends Wallachia against the Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In 1419, the final 41 treasure ships were constructed in the shipyards of Nanjing, intended for the expeditions of the famed admiral Zheng He. These ships played a key role in establishing maritime trade routes and diplomatic relations across the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Final 41 treasure ships are built in Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1419, Rouen surrendered to Henry V of England, marking a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War. This victory allowed the English to consolidate their control over Normandy, significantly impacting the course of the conflict.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: Rouen surrenders to Henry V of England

events.enhanced_description: The Ōei Invasion of Tsushima Island commenced on June 20, 1419, when Joseon Korea launched an attack on this strategically important island. This invasion was part of broader conflicts between Korea and Japan during this period.
events.name: The Ōei Invasion of Tsushima Island begins

events.enhanced_description: In August 1419, during the Siege of Ceuta, Portuguese forces successfully defended the city against Moroccan attempts to retake it. This victory was crucial for maintaining Portuguese control over the strategic port and marked a significant moment in the Reconquista.
events.name: Siege of Ceuta: The Portuguese successfully defend against Moroccan invaders

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1419, the first Defenestration of Prague took place, where radical Hussites threw several members of the city council out of a window. This event marked the beginning of the Hussite Wars and was a significant moment in Bohemian history.
events.name: The first Defenestration of Prague occurs

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1419, John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, was assassinated by adherents of the Dauphin Charles during a meeting in Montereau. This assassination escalated the conflict between the Burgundians and Armagnacs, further destabilizing France.
events.name: John the Fearless is assassinated

events.enhanced_description: In March 1420, the Çelebi Sultan Mehmed Mosque was inaugurated in Didymoteicho, showcasing the architectural style of the Ottoman Empire. This mosque served as a significant religious site in the region.

image.caption: Çelebi Sultan Mehmed Mosque (Bayezid Mosque) in Didymoteicho, Greece.
image.credit: Ggia — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 2010-03-28 and depicts the mosque site, not its 1420 inauguration.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Didymoteicho, East Macedonia and Thrace, Greece

events.name: The Çelebi Sultan Mehmed Mosque is inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: In 1420, Henry V of England commenced the construction of the ship Grace Dieu, which would become one of the largest and most powerful warships of its time. This vessel represented the advancements in naval technology and the growing importance of maritime power during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Construction of Grace Dieu

events.enhanced_description: In 1420, Tang Saier led a rebellion against the Ming dynasty, successfully capturing two cities before ultimately being defeated. Her uprising highlighted the social unrest and challenges faced by the Ming emperors during this period.
events.name: Tang Saier's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Temple of Heaven in Beijing began in 1420, symbolizing the Ming dynasty's architectural grandeur and religious significance. This site became a central place for imperial ceremonies, reflecting the deep connection between the emperor and the divine.
events.name: Construction of the Temple of Heaven

events.enhanced_description: In 1420, a power struggle for the throne of Wallachia erupted between Radu II Praznaglava, supported by the Ottomans, and Dan II, backed by Hungary. This conflict would last for seven years, resulting in multiple changes of power and significant political instability in the region.
events.name: Struggle for the Throne of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In 1420, Alexandru cel Bun defended Moldavia against the first incursion by Ottoman forces at Cetatea Albă. This battle was significant in establishing Moldavia's resistance against Ottoman expansion in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Defense of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1420, the Treaty of Troyes was signed, recognizing Henry V of England as the heir to the French throne during a period of Burgundian dominance in France. This treaty aimed to solidify English claims and control over French territories.
events.name: Treaty of Troyes is signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1420, Henry the Navigator was appointed Grand Master of the Military Order of Christ, a position that allowed him to further his ambitions in exploration and maritime trade. His leadership significantly influenced the Age of Discovery.

image.caption: Statue of Henry the Navigator on the façade of the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura in Rio de Janeiro.
image.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2018-10-16; not contemporary with the 1420 appointment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Henry the Navigator is appointed Grand Master

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1420, Catherine of Valois married King Henry V of England, a union that strengthened the ties between England and France amidst the ongoing Hundred Years' War. This marriage was politically significant, aiming to secure peace between the two nations.
events.name: Catherine of Valois marries King Henry V of England

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1420, troops of the Republic of Venice captured Udine after a prolonged siege, effectively ending the independence of the Patriarchal State of Friuli. This event marked a significant expansion of Venetian influence in the region.
events.name: Venetian troops capture Udine

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1420, construction began on the dome of the Florence Cathedral, designed by Filippo Brunelleschi. This architectural feat would become a defining symbol of Renaissance architecture and a landmark in Florence.
events.name: Construction of the dome of Florence Cathedral begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1420, a powerful 9.4 magnitude earthquake struck the Atacama Region of Chile, causing widespread devastation and triggering tsunamis that affected coastal areas as far away as Hawaii and Japan.
events.name: A 9.4 magnitude earthquake shakes Chile

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1420, Ghiyāth al-dīn Naqqāsh, an envoy from the Timurid ruler Mirza Shahrukh, documented his crossing of a remarkable floating pontoon bridge over the Yellow River in Lanzhou. His accounts provided valuable insights into the engineering and culture of Ming China.
events.name: Ghiyāth al-dīn Naqqāsh records his travels in China

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1420, Beijing was officially designated as the capital of the Ming Dynasty, coinciding with the completion of the Forbidden City. This decision marked a significant shift in the political landscape of China.
events.name: Beijing designated as the capital of the Ming Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vyšehrad, fought on November 1, 1420, was a significant conflict during the Hussite Wars where Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor, faced a decisive defeat. This battle marked a crucial moment in the Hussite resistance against the imperial forces, leading to Sigismund's ejection from Bohemia.
events.name: Hussite Wars – Battle of Vyšehrad

events.enhanced_description: In 1421, John III of Dampierre, Marquis of Namur, sold his estates to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. This transaction was significant in the context of Burgundian expansion and consolidation of power in the Low Countries.
events.name: Sale of Estates by John III of Dampierre

events.enhanced_description: In 1421, the Republic of Florence issued its first patent, marking a significant development in intellectual property rights during the Renaissance. This initiative reflected the growing importance of innovation and protection of inventions in the burgeoning economy.
events.name: First Patent Issued by Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1421, Portuguese sailors sent by Henry the Navigator successfully crossed Cape Non, reaching as far as Cape Bojador. This expedition was part of the early stages of the Age of Discovery, expanding European knowledge of the African coast.
events.name: Portuguese Exploration under Henry the Navigator

events.enhanced_description: Traditionally dated to 1421, the Larabanga Mosque was founded in northern Ghana, becoming one of the oldest mosques in the country. This site is significant for its architectural style and its role in the spread of Islam in West Africa.
events.name: Foundation of Larabanga Mosque

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1421, the Yongle Emperor officially shifted the Ming dynasty's capital from Nanjing to Beijing. This strategic move was aimed at consolidating power and enhancing the defense against potential invasions.
events.name: Capital Shift to Beijing

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1421, Zheng He received an imperial order from the Yongle Emperor to commence the Ming treasure voyages. These expeditions were significant for establishing Chinese maritime dominance and fostering diplomatic relations across the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Ming Treasure Voyages

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Baugé, fought on March 21, 1421, saw a small French force surprise and defeat a smaller English contingent led by Thomas, Duke of Clarence. This battle was a notable victory for the French during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Baugé

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1421, Mehmed I, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, passed away and was succeeded by his son, Murad II. This transition marked a significant moment in Ottoman history as the empire continued to expand under Murad's leadership.

image.caption: Ottoman miniature depicting Sultan Mehmed I with his dignitaries.
image.credit: Ottoman miniature painter — Badisches Landesmuseum
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1616, nearly two centuries after Mehmed I’s death in 1421.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Mehmed I

events.enhanced_description: In 1422, Ottoman forces overran the last domains of Constantine II of Bulgaria, leading to his death in exile and marking the end of the Bulgarian Empire. This event signified the consolidation of Ottoman power in the Balkans.
events.name: Fall of the Bulgarian Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1422, Venice had a population of approximately 84,000, governed by a small elite of 200 men, while Florence had around 40,000 inhabitants ruled by 600 men. This demographic snapshot illustrates the political structures and social hierarchies of these influential Italian city-states during the Renaissance.
events.name: Population of Venice and Florence

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1422, during the Hussite Wars, the Hussites achieved a significant victory against an army of Royalist Crusaders at the Battle of Německý Brod. This battle further solidified the Hussite movement's resistance against external forces.
events.name: Hussite Wars – Battle of Německý Brod

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1422, during the Hundred Years' War, the Siege of Meaux concluded with the surrender of the city to English forces. This event was a critical moment in the ongoing conflict between England and France.
events.name: Siege of Meaux

events.enhanced_description: In June 1422, the Ottoman Sultan Murad II besieged Constantinople, a pivotal moment in the Ottoman Empire's expansion. However, the siege was ultimately broken off due to the rebellion of Küçük Mustafa, showcasing the internal challenges faced by the Ottomans.
events.name: Ottoman Siege of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1422, the Kingdom of Portugal officially ceased the use of the Spanish era dating system. This change reflected Portugal's growing national identity and independence from Spanish influence.
events.name: End of Spanish Era in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1422, Henry VI ascended to the throne of England at just nine months old, marking the beginning of a tumultuous reign that would see the country embroiled in the Wars of the Roses. His youth and the political instability of the time would shape his rule.
events.name: Henry VI Becomes King of England

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1422, the Teutonic Knights signed the Treaty of Melno with the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, concluding the brief Gollub War. This treaty established the Prussian-Lithuanian border, which remained unchanged until World War I.
events.name: Treaty of Melno

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of King Charles VI of France on October 21, 1422, Henry VI of England was proclaimed King of France in Paris, while his maternal uncle, Charles, was proclaimed King Charles VII in Bourges. This division of claims to the French throne intensified the conflict between England and France.
events.name: Proclamation of Kings in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1423, the Electorate of Saxony merged with the Margravate of Meissen and the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg, creating a more unified political entity. This merger was significant in the context of the Holy Roman Empire's political landscape.
events.name: Merger of Saxon Territories

events.enhanced_description: During the Hundred Years War, English forces captured the strategic island of Tombelaine, located off the coast of Normandy, to establish a base for future attacks on the fortified Mont Saint-Michel. This maneuver was part of the larger conflict between England and France over territorial claims.
events.name: Hundred Years War: The island of Tombelaine is taken by English forces

events.enhanced_description: After a failed siege of Salangpur, Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat was ambushed by Hushang Shah's forces while returning to Ahmedabad. Despite the surprise attack, Ahmad Shah I emerged victorious, allowing him to continue his journey back to the capital.
events.name: Battle of Salangpur

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Amiens was signed during the Hundred Years War, establishing a mutual defense agreement between the Duchy of Burgundy, the Duchy of Brittany, and the Kingdom of England. This treaty aimed to strengthen alliances against French aggression.
events.name: Treaty of Amiens

events.enhanced_description: Francesco Foscari was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Venice following the death of Tommaso Mocenigo. Foscari's tenure would last 34 years, marked by significant political and military events in the Venetian Republic.
events.name: Election of Francesco Foscari as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Hořice, the Taborites, a faction of the Hussite movement, decisively defeated the Utraquists, showcasing the internal divisions within the Hussite forces. This battle was significant in the ongoing Hussite Wars, which were characterized by religious and political strife in Bohemia.

locations.name: Hořice, Hradec Králové Region, Czech Republic

events.name: Battle of Hořice

events.enhanced_description: Ashikaga Yoshimochi abdicated as shogun of Japan, passing the title to his son, Ashikaga Yoshikazu. This transition marked a significant moment in the Ashikaga shogunate, which was characterized by political instability and power struggles.
events.name: Abdication of Ashikaga Yoshimochi

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Melno was ratified, officially ending the Gollub War between the Teutonic Order and the alliance of Poland and Lithuania. This treaty marked a significant step towards stabilizing relations in the region after years of conflict.
events.name: Ratification of the Treaty of Melno

events.enhanced_description: During the Byzantine–Ottoman Wars, Turakhan Beg, the Ottoman governor of Thessaly, successfully breached the Hexamilion wall after a two-day battle. This victory allowed Ottoman forces to ravage the Peloponnese Peninsula, furthering their territorial ambitions in Greece.
events.name: Byzantine–Ottoman Wars: Breakthrough of Hexamilion

events.enhanced_description: After a series of military engagements, Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat successfully returned to his capital, Ahmedabad, to reassume the throne. His return marked a consolidation of power after the challenges he faced during his reign.
events.name: Return of Ahmad Shah I to Gujarat

events.enhanced_description: Gil Sánchez Muñoz y Carbón was elected as Antipope Clement VIII by bishops in Avignon, following the death of Antipope Benedict XIII. This election highlighted the ongoing schism within the Catholic Church, as Clement VIII's legitimacy was contested by the Roman Pope Martin V.

image.caption: Tomb of Antipope Clement VIII at La Seu, Palma de Mallorca.
image.credit: Steffen Löwe — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image date: 2007-03-28; depicts a tomb, not the 1423 election.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Election of Antipope Clement VIII

events.enhanced_description: The Yongle Emperor launched his fourth military campaign against the Northern Yuan, a remnant of the Mongol Empire, in an effort to consolidate Ming control over northern territories. This campaign was part of the broader Ming efforts to secure their borders and assert dominance in the region.
events.name: Yongle Emperor's Campaign Against the Northern Yuan

events.enhanced_description: Pope Martin V officially approved the Treaty of Melno, which ended the Gollub War between the Teutonic Order and the Polish-Lithuanian alliance. This papal endorsement was crucial for legitimizing the treaty and stabilizing the region.
events.name: Papal Approval of the Treaty of Melno

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Cravant, the French army faced a significant defeat against the English and their Burgundian allies. This battle, fought on the banks of the River Yonne, was part of the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years War, showcasing the military prowess of the English forces.
events.name: Battle of Cravant

events.enhanced_description: Ataullah Muhammad Shah I ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Kedah, Malaysia, following the death of his father, Sulaiman Shah I. His reign would last for 50 years, continuing the legacy of his father's rule.
events.name: Ascension of Ataullah Muhammad Shah I

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Sveti Srdj was signed to conclude the Second Scutari War between the Serbian Despotate and the Venetian Republic, resolving territorial disputes over Scutari and other regions previously held by the Venetians.
events.name: Treaty of Sveti Srdj

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of La Brossinière was fought during the Hundred Years War, where an English force led by Sir John De la Pole was decisively defeated by the combined armies of France, Anjou, and Maine. The battle resulted in significant casualties for the English, marking a setback in their campaign.
events.name: Battle of La Brossinière

events.enhanced_description: The Second Parliament of King Henry VI of England convened in London after being summoned on September 1. Under the leadership of John Russell, the House of Commons deliberated on various laws until its adjournment in February of the following year.
events.name: Second Parliament of King Henry VI of England

events.enhanced_description: After a two-year expedition to Byzantium, Giovanni Aurispa returned to Venice with the largest collection of Greek manuscripts ever assembled at that time, including 238 ancient texts. This significant acquisition contributed to the Renaissance's revival of classical knowledge in Europe.
events.name: Giovanni Aurispa's Return to Venice

events.enhanced_description: During the Hussite Wars, General Sigismund Korybut, commander of the Hussite Army, withdrew his troops from Prague following orders from Vytautas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, and Władysław II Jagiełło, King of Poland. This decision reflected the complex alliances and conflicts of the period.

image.caption: Map of the lands of the Bohemian crown during the Hussite Wars, with major towns and cities labelled.
image.credit: Cameron Pauley — Own work
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 2020-06-07; it represents the historical setting, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Withdrawal of Hussite Army from Prague

events.enhanced_description: Aliota Capenna, the lord of Hvar, offered his realm to the Republic of Venice, a significant political maneuver during the period of Venetian expansion in the Adriatic. This offer reflected the complex political landscape of Dalmatia.
events.name: Offer of Hvar to the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: King James I of Scotland was released from captivity in England after 18 years, following a ransom treaty of £40,000 secured by Scottish hostages. His release marked a significant moment in Scottish history, as it allowed him to reclaim his throne and begin his reign.
events.name: Release of King James I of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: King James I returned to Scotland for the first time since his capture in 1406, escorted by nobles from both England and Scotland. This event symbolized the end of his long captivity and the restoration of his rule in Scotland.
events.name: Return of King James I to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of James I as King of Scotland took place at Scone Abbey, where he performed his first knighthood ceremony, honoring 18 prominent nobles. This event marked the formal beginning of his reign and his commitment to restoring order in Scotland.
events.name: Coronation of James I of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of L'Aquila, forces led by Jacopo Caldora and Micheletto Attendolo of the Kingdom of Naples defeated Braccio da Montone, who was fighting for Alfonso V of Aragon. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Italy during the early 15th century.
events.name: Battle of L'Aquila

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Zagonara saw the Duchy of Milan's army, led by Duke Filippo Maria Visconti, defeat the Republic of Florence's forces under Carlo I Malatesta. This victory solidified Milan's power in Northern Italy during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Battle of Zagonara

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Verneuil, an English force led by John, Duke of Bedford, defeated a larger French army commanded by the Duke of Alençon, resulting in the capture of Alençon and the death of Archibald Douglas. This battle was a significant event in the ongoing Hundred Years' War.

image.caption: Illuminated manuscript depicting the Battle of Verneuil.
image.credit: Attributed to Philippe de Mazerolles — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b10023823h/f46
image.date_qualification: Retrospective depiction of the 1424 battle; the image is dated circa 1470–1479.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Verneuil

events.enhanced_description: Prince Zhu Gaochi ascended to the throne as Emperor Renzong of the Ming dynasty following the death of his father, the Yongle Emperor. His reign marked the beginning of the Hongxi era, which aimed to restore stability after years of military campaigns.
events.name: Ascension of Emperor Renzong of Ming

events.enhanced_description: The Bohemian campaign concluded with the signing of a treaty among the factions involved in the Hussite Wars, marking a significant moment in the conflict that had divided the region. This treaty aimed to bring peace and stability to Bohemia.
events.name: Completion of the Bohemian Campaign

events.enhanced_description: Led by Jan Žižka, the Hussites began their march towards North Moravia to suppress a rebellion. This movement was part of the larger Hussite Wars, which were characterized by religious and political strife in Bohemia.
events.name: Hussite March to North Moravia

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Jan Žižka from the plague, Prokop the Great assumed command of the Hussite forces. His leadership was crucial in continuing the Hussite resistance during the ongoing conflicts in Bohemia.

image.caption: Engraved fictional portrayal of Prokop Holý.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.portraitindex.de/documents/obj/33207059 Universitätsbibliothek Leipzig; Bilddatei: ubl0040-0172; Aufn.-Datum: 2009
image.date_qualification: The image dates to 1698/1710, centuries after the event; the supplied date describes the depiction/publication, not the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Prokop the Great Takes Command of the Hussites

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Renzong of the Ming dynasty designated his son, Zhu Zhanji, as Crown Prince. This decision set the stage for Zhu Zhanji's eventual ascension to the throne as Emperor Xuanzong.
events.name: Crown Prince Designation in Ming Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The Bourges astronomical clock, designed by Jean Fusoris, was installed in Bourges Cathedral as a gift from King Charles VII to the town. This clock was a significant advancement in astronomical technology and reflected the growing interest in science during the Renaissance.
events.name: Installation of the Bourges Astronomical Clock

events.enhanced_description: Radu II Chelul ascended to the throne of Wallachia for the third time, taking over from Dan II following an Ottoman invasion. His reign was marked by the challenges of maintaining power amid external threats.
events.name: Radu II Chelul Becomes Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: Kale Kye-Taung Nyo, ruler of the Kingdom of Ava, fled his capital, leading to the succession of Mohnyin Thado. This transition marked a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Fleeing of Kale Kye-Taung Nyo

events.enhanced_description: The Castello Orsini-Odescalchi was constructed in Bracciano by the Orsini family, serving as a significant architectural and cultural landmark in Italy. This castle reflects the feudal power and influence of the Orsini family during the Renaissance.
events.name: Construction of Castello Orsini-Odescalchi

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of St. James near Avranches, an English army led by John, Duke of Bedford, defeated the French forces under Arthur de Richemont. This victory reinforced English control in Normandy during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of St. James

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Usti nad Labem, the Hussites achieved a decisive victory over the crusading armies during the Fourth Anti-Hussite Crusade. This battle was a pivotal moment in the Hussite Wars, showcasing the resilience of the Hussite forces.

locations.name: Ústí nad Labem, Ústí nad Labem Region, Czech Republic

events.name: Battle of Usti nad Labem

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Khirokitia, King Janus of Cyprus was defeated and captured by the Mamluks. He was subsequently taken to Egypt, where he was held for ten months before being ransomed, highlighting the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Battle of Khirokitia

events.enhanced_description: Gabriel V was elected as the Patriarch of the Coptic Church for the second time in 1427. His leadership was significant in the context of the Coptic Christian community in Egypt during a period of political and religious challenges.
events.name: Gabriel V elected Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: Minrekyansa ascended to the throne as the King of Ava in 1427, marking a significant moment in the history of the Burmese monarchy. His reign contributed to the consolidation of power in the region during a time of political fragmentation.
events.name: Minrekyansa becomes King of Ava

events.enhanced_description: The Conflict of Druimnacour took place in Sutherland, Scotland, in 1427. This skirmish was part of the ongoing power struggles among Scottish clans during a tumultuous period in Scottish history.
events.name: Conflict of Druimnacour

events.enhanced_description: The first witch hunts began in Switzerland in 1427, marking the start of a dark chapter in European history characterized by superstition and persecution. These hunts would escalate in intensity over the following decades, leading to widespread fear and injustice.
events.name: First witch hunts begin

events.enhanced_description: The Celestine Order was established in France in 1427, contributing to the monastic landscape of the time. This order emphasized a contemplative lifestyle and played a role in the spiritual revival of the period.
events.name: Celestine Order established

events.enhanced_description: The Celebration of Sant Jordi (Saint George) began in Catalonia in 1427, evolving into a significant cultural event that celebrates love and literature. This tradition continues to be a cherished part of Catalan identity.
events.name: Celebration of Sant Jordi begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1427, Bremen was expelled from the Hanseatic League, a powerful economic alliance of merchant guilds and towns in Northern Europe. This expulsion marked a significant shift in the city's political and economic landscape.
events.name: Bremen expelled from Hanseatic League

events.enhanced_description: In 1427, Portuguese navigator Diogo de Silves discovered seven islands of the Azores archipelago, which would later become an important strategic location for maritime navigation and trade in the Atlantic.
events.name: Diogo de Silves discovers Azores

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Echinades occurred in 1427, where a Byzantine fleet successfully defeated the forces of Carlo I Tocco. This victory was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region during the decline of Byzantine power.
events.name: Battle of the Echinades

events.enhanced_description: In 1427, Itzcoatl became the 4th Tlatoani of Tenochtitlan following the assassination of his nephew Chimalpopoca. His reign marked the beginning of the expansion of the Aztec Empire and the consolidation of power in the Valley of Mexico.
events.name: Itzcoatl becomes Tlatoani of Tenochtitlan

events.enhanced_description: The Bhaktapur Royal Palace was built by King Yaksa Malla in 1427, showcasing the architectural grandeur of the Malla dynasty. This palace remains a significant historical site, reflecting the rich cultural heritage of Nepal.
events.name: Bhaktapur Royal Palace built

events.enhanced_description: Lincoln College, a constituent college of the University of Oxford, was founded by the Bishop of Lincoln in 1427. It has since become one of the prominent colleges within the university, known for its rich history and academic excellence.
events.name: Lincoln College founded

events.enhanced_description: In May 1428, Joan of Arc made her first attempt to reach the Armagnac court at Chinon to support Charles VII of France, but she was rebuffed. This marked the beginning of her significant involvement in the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Joan of Arc's first attempt

events.enhanced_description: In 1428, the Aztec Empire was formed through the alliance of the city-states Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan, defeating Azcapotzalco. Itzcoatl became the first emperor, establishing a powerful political entity in the Valley of Mexico.
events.name: Aztec Empire formed

events.enhanced_description: In 1428, a serious fire occurred at Baynard's Castle in the City of London, causing significant damage to this historic structure. The castle, which had been a royal residence, played a key role in the political history of England.
events.name: Fire at Baynard's Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Lam Sơn uprising, led by Lê Lợi, began in 1428, resulting in the liberation of Annam from Ming dynasty China. This uprising was pivotal in restoring Vietnamese independence and led to the establishment of the Lê dynasty.
events.name: Lam Sơn uprising

events.enhanced_description: The Catalonia earthquake struck on February 2, 1428, with its epicenter near Camprodon. It was part of a series of seismic events that affected the region, causing significant damage and impacting the local population.

image.caption: Relief location map of Catalonia, Spain.
image.credit: Sémhur ( talk ) — Sources: Shorelines, lakes, rivers, borders : NGDC GSHHS Topography and relief: NASA ASTER GDEM V001 ( data acces & policies ). ASTER GDEM is a product of METI and NASA Bathymetry and relief: National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC) ETOPO1
image.date_qualification: A geographic reference map, not an image of the 1428 earthquake; the saved image date is 2017-04-08.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Catalonia earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1428, Dan II led an army against the Ottomans at Golubac Fortress, securing a treaty that allowed him semi-peaceful rule in Wallachia until 1432. This event was crucial in the ongoing struggle against Ottoman expansion in the region.
events.name: Dan II leads army against Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: The Valais witch trials began in Swiss Savoy on August 7, 1428, marking a significant escalation in the witch hunts across Europe. This event led to numerous accusations and executions, reflecting the period's social and religious tensions.
events.name: Valais witch trials begin

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Go-Hanazono ascended to the throne of Japan on August 30, 1428. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Japanese imperial line, characterized by political intrigue and cultural developments.
events.name: Emperor Go-Hanazono accedes to the throne

events.enhanced_description: In October 1428, English forces under Thomas Montacute, 4th Earl of Salisbury, besieged Orléans, a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War. The siege would lead to significant military engagements and the eventual rise of Joan of Arc.
events.name: Siege of Orléans begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1428, Thomas Montacute, 4th Earl of Salisbury, was mortally wounded during an assault on Orléans. His death marked a significant turning point in the siege, leading to William de la Pole taking command of the English forces.
events.name: Thomas Montacute mortally wounded

events.enhanced_description: In September 1429, the Hafsid Saracens launched an unsuccessful attempt to capture Malta, facing fierce resistance from the island's defenders. This event highlighted the strategic importance of Malta in the Mediterranean during the period.
events.name: Hafsid Saracens attempt to capture Malta

events.enhanced_description: In 1429, a devastating fire swept through Turku, causing significant destruction to the city. This event marked a turning point in the city's history, leading to extensive rebuilding efforts.
events.name: Fire destroys Turku

events.enhanced_description: During the reign of the Yongle Emperor in 1429, a series of seven customs offices and barriers were established along the Grand Canal of China. This development was aimed at enhancing trade regulation and control over the vital waterway.
events.name: Customs offices along the Grand Canal

events.enhanced_description: In 1429, Andreyas ascended to the throne as Emperor of Ethiopia, succeeding Yeshaq I. His reign marked a continuation of the Solomonic dynasty's influence in the region.
events.name: Andreyas succeeds Yeshaq I as Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1429, the Battle of Rouvray, also known as the Battle of the Herrings, took place where English forces under Sir John Fastolf defended a supply convoy against the French. This battle was crucial in maintaining supply lines during the Siege of Orléans.
events.name: Battle of Rouvray

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1429, Joan of Arc entered Orléans with a relief expedition, marking a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War. Her arrival inspired the French troops and shifted the momentum of the siege in favor of the French.
events.name: Siege of Orléans relief

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1429, the Tourelles, the last English siege fortification at Orléans, fell to the French forces. Joan of Arc played a crucial role in this victory, leading the final charge despite being wounded, solidifying her status as a national hero.
events.name: Fall of the Tourelles

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1429, weakened by disease and a lack of supplies, the English forces withdrew from Orléans, marking a significant turning point in the Hundred Years' War. This retreat was a direct result of the French resurgence led by Joan of Arc and her allies.
events.name: The English depart Orléans

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1429, the French forces, led by Joan of Arc, decisively defeated the English army at the Battle of Patay. This victory not only boosted French morale but also forced the English to retreat from the Loire Valley, significantly altering the course of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Patay

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1429, Charles VII was crowned King of France in Reims, a pivotal moment that solidified his claim to the throne and marked a significant victory for the French during the Hundred Years' War. The event was heavily influenced by Joan of Arc, who played a crucial role in his ascension.
events.name: Charles VII crowned in Rheims

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1429, Joan of Arc led an attack on Paris in an effort to liberate the city from English control. The assault was ultimately unsuccessful, and Joan was wounded during the confrontation, marking a setback in her campaign.
events.name: Joan of Arc's attack on Paris

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1429, during the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War, Joan of Arc successfully liberated Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier from Burgundian forces. This victory was part of her broader campaign to strengthen Charles VII's position in France.

image.caption: Map showing the approximate areas controlled by French, Burgundian, and English forces in France.
image.credit: Wtfiv — Own work based on: Treaty of Troyes.svg by Aliesin References: Information on the map was simplified, boundaries, and other map images modified according to the map in Barker, Juliet (2009) Conquest: The English Kingdom of France, 1417-1450 , Little, Brown, p. xvii ISBN : 9781408702468 . OCLC : 903613803 . , which shows the situation in 1429. Added County of Rethel to Burgundian holdings based on France 1429 map from Poole's Historical Atlas , 1902.
image.date_qualification: The map represents territorial control in 1429; the supplied image date is 2025-02-26, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Liberation of Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1429, Joan of Arc besieged La Charité, aiming to reclaim the town from English control. This military action was part of her ongoing efforts to strengthen the French position during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Siege of La Charité

events.enhanced_description: In 1430, with the surrender of Chalandritsa and the citadel of Patras to the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, the Principality of Achaea came to an end. This marked a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: End of the Principality of Achaea

events.enhanced_description: In 1430, under the rule of Sigismund of Luxembourg, Bratislava Castle was converted into a fortress. This transformation was part of broader defensive measures in the region.
events.name: Bratislava Castle converted to a fortress

events.enhanced_description: In 1430, the use of optical methods in the creation of art began to emerge, marking a significant development in artistic techniques. This innovation would influence future generations of artists.
events.name: Optical methods in art

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1430, Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, married Isabella of Portugal in Bruges. This union was politically significant, strengthening ties between Burgundy and Portugal.
events.name: Philip the Good marries Isabella of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1430, Philip the Good founded the Order of the Golden Fleece in Bruges, establishing a prestigious chivalric order that would play a significant role in the politics of Europe.
events.name: Order of the Golden Fleece founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1430, the Ottoman Empire, under the command of Sultan Murad II, captured Thessalonica after an eight-year siege. This event marked a significant expansion of Ottoman territory in the Balkans.
events.name: Ottoman Empire captures Thessalonica

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1430, the French forces made their first attempt to relieve the Siege of Compiègne, which was under threat from Burgundian forces. This effort was part of the broader conflict during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: First attempt to relieve the Siege of Compiègne

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1430, while leading an army to relieve the Siege of Compiègne, Joan of Arc was captured by Burgundian forces. This event marked a critical turning point in her life and the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Joan of Arc captured by Burgundians

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1430, William Waynflete was appointed vicar of Skendleby in Lincolnshire. He would later become a notable figure in the church and education.
events.name: William Waynflete becomes vicar of Skendleby

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1430, the Hussites achieved a significant victory over a combined Hungarian-Moravian-Serbian army at the Battle of Trnava. This battle was part of the larger Hussite Wars, which were characterized by religious and political conflict.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration by Věnceslav Černý depicting the death of Velek Koudelník in the Battle of Trnava.
image.credit: Věnceslav Černý — Public Domain - Kramerius Digital Libraryː https://kramerius5.nkp.cz/view/uuid:0952f110-938a-11e7-ab16-005056827e52?page=uuid:4f63c180-caf7-11e7-9c14-005056827e51
image.date_qualification: The image description associates the illustration with a 1926 publication; the supplied image_date is 1926-01-01 and is not the date of the 1430 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Trnava

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1430, Švitrigaila succeeded his cousin Vytautas as the Grand Duke of Lithuania. His ascension marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Švitrigaila succeeds Vytautas as ruler of Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: In March 1431, Alexander I Aldea ascended to the throne of Wallachia with the support of Alexander I of Moldavia. His reign was marked by political maneuvering and alliances in the region.
events.name: Alexander I Aldea takes the throne of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: The University of Poitiers was founded in 1431, becoming one of the oldest universities in France. It played a significant role in the development of higher education in the region.

image.caption: Hôtel Pinet in Poitiers, now the presidency of the University of Poitiers.
image.credit: Danielclauzier — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2012-04-17; depicts a later university site, not the university's 1431 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: University of Poitiers founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1431, the Ayutthaya Kingdom besieged Angkor, leading to the sacking of the Khmer capital and effectively ending the Khmer Empire. This event marked a significant shift in power in Southeast Asia.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom besieges Angkor

events.enhanced_description: Nezahualcoyotl was crowned Tlatoani of the Kingdom of Texcoco in 1431. He is remembered as a philosopher and poet, significantly influencing the culture and politics of the region.
events.name: Nezahualcoyotl crowned Tlatoani

events.enhanced_description: During the Byzantine–Ottoman Wars in 1431, the Ottoman governor of Thessaly, Turahan Bey, broke through the Hexamilion wall for the second time, ravaging the Peloponnese Peninsula. This event highlighted the growing power of the Ottoman Empire in the region.
events.name: Ottoman governor breaks through Hexamilion wall

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1431, pretrial investigations for Joan of Arc began in Rouen, which was under English occupation at the time. This marked the beginning of a controversial trial that would lead to her execution.
events.name: Pretrial investigations for Joan of Arc

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1431, the trial of Joan of Arc for heresy commenced in Rouen. This trial was politically motivated and would ultimately lead to her execution, marking a tragic chapter in her story.
events.name: Trial of Joan of Arc for heresy

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1431, Pope Eugene IV succeeded Pope Martin V as the 207th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy would be marked by significant challenges, including issues of church reform and political conflicts.
events.name: Pope Eugene IV succeeds Pope Martin V

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1431, Joan of Arc, a peasant girl who claimed to have received divine guidance, was executed by burning at the stake in Rouen. Her trial was politically motivated, aimed at discrediting her role in the Hundred Years' War, and she was later canonized as a saint.
events.name: Joan of Arc is burned at the stake

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1431, the Treaty of Christmemel was signed between the Teutonic Knights and Švitrigaila, establishing an anti-Polish alliance. This treaty was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts in Eastern Europe during the period.
events.name: Treaty of Christmemel

events.enhanced_description: In September 1431, the Battle of Inverlochy took place where Donald Balloch led his forces to a decisive victory against the Royalists. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Scotland during the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Battle of Inverlochy

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1431, the Treaty of Medina del Campo was signed, consolidating peace between Portugal and Castile. This treaty marked a significant diplomatic achievement in the Iberian Peninsula during the late Middle Ages.

locations.name: Medina del Campo, Castile and León, Spain

events.name: Treaty of Medina del Campo

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1431, the Battle of Ilava occurred, where Hungarian forces achieved victory over the Hussite army. This battle was part of the broader conflicts involving the Hussites during the Hussite Wars.
events.name: Battle of Ilava

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1431, a treaty was concluded in Suceava, ending an attack on Poland launched by Alexander I of Moldavia during the Lithuanian Civil War. This treaty was significant in the context of regional power struggles.
events.name: Treaty in Suceava

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1431, Vlad II Dracul was inducted into the Order of the Dragon, a chivalric order aimed at defending Christianity. This membership would later influence the legacy of his son, Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler.
events.name: Vlad II Dracul joins the Order of the Dragon

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1431, Henry VI of England was crowned King of France at Notre-Dame de Paris. This event symbolized the height of English claims to the French throne during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Henry VI crowned King of France

events.enhanced_description: In 1432, Iliaș succeeded his father as Prince of Moldavia. His reign was marked by internal strife and external pressures from neighboring powers.
events.name: Iliaș succeeds as Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: The Université de Caen was founded in 1432, contributing to the educational landscape of France. It became a center for learning and scholarship in the region.
events.name: Université de Caen founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1432, the first baccalaureate service is believed to have originated at the University of Oxford, marking a significant development in academic traditions in Europe.
events.name: First baccalaureate service at University of Oxford

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1432, an Albanian revolt led by Gjergj Arianit Komneni broke out against the Ottoman Empire, spreading through most of Albania. This revolt was part of the larger resistance against Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: Albanian revolt against the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In April 1432, Jacqueline, Countess of Hainaut and Countess of Holland and Zeeland, was forced by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, to abdicate all her estates in his favor, marking the end of Hainaut and Holland as independent counties.
events.name: Jacqueline abdicates her estates

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1432, Jan van Eyck's Ghent Altarpiece was first presented to the public. This masterpiece of Early Netherlandish painting is renowned for its intricate details and use of oil paint.
events.name: Jan van Eyck's Ghent Altarpiece presented

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1432, the Battle of San Romano took place, where the forces of Florence defeated those of Siena. This battle was part of the larger conflict known as the Wars in Lombardy.

locations.name: San Romano in Garfagnana, Tuscany, Italy

events.name: Battle of San Romano

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1432, Sigismund Kęstutaitis attempted to capture or murder his rival Švitrigaila, who managed to escape. This event was part of the power struggles during the Lithuanian Civil War.
events.name: Sigismund Kęstutaitis attempts to capture Švitrigaila

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1432, the first battle of the Lithuanian Civil War was fought near Oszmiana between the forces of Švitrigaila and Sigismund Kęstutaitis. This conflict marked the beginning of a tumultuous period in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

image.caption: Monument at the site of the Battle of Pabaiskas.
image.credit: en:User:Orionus — en:File:Pabaiskas monument.JPG
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the battle monument, not a contemporary image of the 1432 opening battle; original image date: 2007-06-14.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Lithuanian Civil War begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1433, the Ming Dynasty of China concluded its last significant maritime expedition, led by the famed Admiral Zheng He. This expedition marked a pivotal moment in maritime history, as the dispersal of Zheng He's fleet significantly altered the balance of power in the Indian Ocean, facilitating the rise of European naval dominance.
events.name: The Ming Dynasty's Last Maritime Expedition

events.enhanced_description: In 1433, cotton was officially recognized as a permanent item of trade in the tax registers of Songjiang prefecture during the Ming Dynasty in China. This development underscored the growing importance of cotton in the Chinese economy and its role in trade.
events.name: Cotton Listed as Trade Item in Ming China

events.enhanced_description: In 1433, Kalantiaw, a figure in early Philippine history, is said to have promulgated a legal code that would later be referred to as the Code of Kalantiaw. However, modern historians express skepticism regarding the authenticity of this code and its historical significance.
events.name: Promulgation of the Code of Kalantiaw

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1433, Sigismund was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome, marking the restoration of the imperial title after a long vacancy since the death of his father, Charles IV, in 1378.
events.name: Sigismund crowned Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1433, Edward I ascended to the throne as King of Portugal. His reign would be marked by significant developments in exploration and trade.
events.name: Edward I becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In September 1433, Cosimo de' Medici was exiled by the Albizzi/Strozzi faction, marking a significant moment in the power struggles of Florence. He would return a year later, solidifying his influence in the city.
events.name: Cosimo de' Medici exiled

events.enhanced_description: In October 1433, Iliaș of Moldavia was deposed by his half-brother Stephen II, marking a shift in the leadership of Moldavia during a turbulent period of internal conflict.
events.name: Iliaș of Moldavia deposed

events.enhanced_description: In late June 1434, miner Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson initiated a rebellion against King Eric of Pomerania in Sweden. This uprising, known as the Engelbrekt Rebellion, would ultimately lead to the king's deposition and significant political changes in Sweden.
events.name: Engelbrekt Rebellion Begins

events.enhanced_description: In September 1434, Cosimo de' Medici returned to Florence after a year of exile imposed by the rival Albizzi and Strozzi factions. His return marked the resurgence of Medici power and influence in the city.
events.name: Cosimo de' Medici Returns to Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1434, the renowned painter Jan van Eyck created the Arnolfini Portrait, a masterpiece of Northern Renaissance art. This painting is celebrated for its intricate detail and use of oil paint, showcasing the artist's innovative techniques.
events.name: Jan van Eyck Paints the Arnolfini Portrait

events.enhanced_description: In 1434, explorer Gil Eanes successfully rounded Cape Bojador, a significant milestone in maritime exploration. This achievement dispelled the myths surrounding the 'Dark Sea' and opened new routes for Portuguese exploration along the African coast.
events.name: Gil Eanes Rounds Cape Bojador

events.enhanced_description: In 1434, a prolonged episode of drought, floods, locust infestations, and famine began to severely impact agriculture and commerce across China, lasting until 1448. This environmental crisis had significant social and economic repercussions for the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: Drought and Famine in Ming China

events.enhanced_description: The Puke Feud, a series of conflicts in Sweden, began in 1434. This feud involved various noble families and was characterized by violent confrontations and political intrigue during a tumultuous period in Swedish history.
events.name: The Puke Feud in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1434, the foundation stone of Nantes Cathedral was laid in Nantes, France. This event marked the beginning of the construction of a significant Gothic architectural masterpiece that would become a central landmark in the city.
events.name: Foundation Stone of Nantes Cathedral Laid

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1434, the Battle of Lipany took place, marking a decisive conflict in the Hussite Wars. The Catholic forces, allied with the Utraquists, defeated the Taborites, effectively ending the Hussite Wars and reshaping the religious landscape of Bohemia.

image.caption: Scene from Luděk Marold’s panorama of the Battle of Lipany, depicting Hussite war leaders.
image.credit: Luděk Marold — Publikace: Maroldovo panorama bitvy u Lipan
image.date_qualification: Created in 1898; a retrospective depiction of the 1434 battle, not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Lipany, Ústí nad Labem Region, Czech Republic

events.name: Battle of Lipany

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1434, Zara Yaqob ascended to the throne as Emperor of Ethiopia. His reign would be marked by significant religious and administrative reforms, strengthening the Ethiopian Orthodox Church and centralizing power.
events.name: Zara Yaqob Becomes Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1434, Suero de Quiñones and his companions staged the Passo Honroso at the Órbigo River in León, Spain. This event was a chivalric tournament that showcased the ideals of knighthood and honor during the late medieval period.
events.name: Passo Honroso

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1434, King Eric of Pomerania was deposed from the Swedish throne during a meeting in Vadstena. Although he retained power in Denmark and Norway, this event marked a significant shift in Swedish governance.
events.name: Deposition of King Eric of Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1434, the University of Catania was founded in Sicily, Italy. This institution would become one of the oldest universities in Italy, contributing to the educational and cultural development of the region.

image.caption: Photograph of Palazzo dell'Università in Catania.
image.credit: Berthold Werner — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2012-10-06; it shows the university site, not the 1434 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of the University of Catania

events.enhanced_description: In August 1435, the Battle of Podraga took place between brothers Iliaș and Stephen II over the throne of Moldavia. The battle ended in a draw, leading to a joint rule facilitated by the intervention of the Polish king.
events.name: Battle of Podraga

events.enhanced_description: In 1435, Francis of Paola founded the Order of the Minims in Italy. This religious order emphasized a life of humility and simplicity, contributing to the spiritual landscape of the Renaissance.
events.name: Foundation of the Order of the Minims

events.enhanced_description: In 1435, China shifted back to a policy of isolation following the expansive maritime expeditions of the Ming Dynasty. This decision significantly impacted China's foreign relations and trade dynamics for centuries to come.
events.name: China Returns to Policy of Isolation

events.enhanced_description: In 1435, Gil Eanes and Afonso Gonçalves Baldaia embarked on a significant exploration of the African coast, reaching as far as Angra dos Ruivos in modern-day Western Sahara. This expedition marked a pivotal moment in the Age of Discovery, expanding European knowledge of the African coastline.
events.name: Gil Eanes and Afonso Gonçalves Baldaia explore the coast of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 1435, Enea Piccolomini, who would later become Pope Pius II, was dispatched by Cardinal Albergati on a covert diplomatic mission to Scotland and Northern England. This mission aimed to strengthen alliances and address political tensions in the region during a time of instability.
events.name: Enea Piccolomini's secret mission to Scotland and Northern England

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1435, Sweden's first Riksdag of the Estates was convened under the leadership of rebel Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson. This assembly marked a significant step towards the establishment of parliamentary governance in Sweden during a period of political upheaval.
events.name: First Riksdag of the Estates in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1435, Pope Eugene IV issued the papal bull Sicut Dudum, which prohibited the enslavement of the Guanche natives in the Canary Islands by the Spanish. This decree was a significant step in the recognition of indigenous rights during the Age of Exploration.

image.caption: Vector coat of arms of Pope Eugenius IV.
image.credit: Odejea — Own work
image.date_qualification: Coat of arms associated with Pope Eugenius IV; not a depiction of the 1435 papal bull. Image date: 2008-08-02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Sicut Dudum Papal Bull

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1435, René of Anjou was recognized as the King of Naples. His reign would be marked by political intrigue and conflict as he navigated the complex power dynamics of Italy during the late medieval period.

image.caption: Medieval manuscript miniature depicting René I of Anjou with his army.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b105380390/f349
image.date_qualification: A fifteenth-century manuscript illustration, not a contemporary depiction of René becoming King of Naples in 1435. The supplied image date is approximate and does not support a display date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: René of Anjou Becomes King of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1435, the Battle of Ponza occurred, where the Duchy of Milan decisively defeated Alfonso V of Aragon in a naval confrontation. This victory solidified Milan's naval power and influence in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Ponza

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1435, the Battle of Wiłkomierz was fought between Sigismund Kęstutaitis and Grand Duke Švitrigaila during the civil war in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Sigismund's decisive victory established his dominance in Lithuanian politics.
events.name: Battle of Wiłkomierz

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1435, the Treaty of Arras was signed between Charles VII of France and Philip III of Burgundy, effectively ending the English-Burgundian alliance. This treaty was a crucial step in the ongoing conflicts of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Treaty of Arras

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1435, Eric of Pomerania was briefly reinstated as king of Sweden, although he was deposed again in January of the following year. This short-lived return highlighted the instability of the Swedish monarchy during this period.
events.name: Reinstatement of Eric of Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, the Incorporated Guild of Smiths was founded in Newcastle upon Tyne, England. This establishment marked an important development in the organization of trades and crafts during the medieval period.

locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, Tyne and Wear

events.name: The Incorporated Guild of Smiths founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, Vlad II Dracul seized the recently vacated throne of Wallachia with the support of Hungary. This event marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the region, setting the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Vlad II Dracul seizes the throne of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, the Bosnian language was first mentioned in a document, marking an important milestone in the recognition and development of the language and its cultural identity.
events.name: First mention of the Bosnian language

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, the Visokom papers were dated, representing the last direct sources on the old town of Visoki. These documents provide valuable insights into the historical context of the region.

image.caption: View from Visočica toward Visoko, showing the setting of the medieval town of Visoki.
image.credit: CJ — Bosnia and Herzegovina Apr-29-2012 022 Uploaded by Smooth_O
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2012-04-29; this is a later site view, not a depiction of the 1436 document dating.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Visokom papers dated

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, the Zhengtong Emperor was inaugurated in Ming dynasty China, marking the beginning of his reign. His ascension to the throne was significant in the context of the Ming dynasty's political landscape.
events.name: Inauguration of the Zhengtong Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, a significant portion of the southern grain tax in Ming dynasty China was commuted to payments in silver, known as the Gold Floral Silver (jinhuayin). This change was driven by the increasing demand for silver in commercial transactions and the challenges of transporting grain.
events.name: Southern grain tax commuted to silver payments

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, the Florentine polymath Leon Battista Alberti began writing his influential treatise On Painting, in which he emphasized the importance of mathematical perspective in creating three-dimensional vision on a two-dimensional plane. This work built upon the ideas of earlier artists like Masaccio.
events.name: Leon Battista Alberti begins writing On Painting

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, Afonso Gonçalves Baldaia became the first European to explore the western coast of Africa beyond the Tropic of Cancer. His explorations contributed to the European understanding of African geography and trade routes.
events.name: Afonso Gonçalves Baldaia explores the western coast of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 1436, Johannes Gutenberg began his groundbreaking work on the printing press, which would revolutionize the dissemination of knowledge and information in Europe. This invention laid the foundation for the spread of literature and ideas during the Renaissance.

image.caption: Gutenbergdenkmal monument in Mainz, Germany.
image.credit: Kenneth C. Zirkel — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2016-07-08; this is a later commemorative monument, not a contemporary image of the 1436 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Johannes Gutenberg begins work on the printing press

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1436, Eric of Pomerania was deposed from the Swedish throne for the second time, just three months after his reinstatement. Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson, a prominent military leader, played a crucial role in the political turmoil of the time, asserting his influence over the realm.

image.caption: Statue of King Eric the Pomeranian at Darłowo Castle, Poland.
