events.name: Eric of Pomerania is declared deposed in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1439, Plymouth was officially incorporated by the English Parliament, marking a significant development in the governance of towns in England. This incorporation set a precedent for local governance and the relationship between towns and the central government.
events.name: Plymouth becomes the first town incorporated by the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: From February to June 1440, the Praguerie was a revolt by the French nobility against King Charles VII, driven by dissatisfaction with royal authority and taxation. This uprising highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and the nobility during a tumultuous period in French history.
events.name: Praguerie: The French nobility rises up against King Charles VII

events.enhanced_description: In April 1440, Murad II laid siege to Belgrade, a strategic city in the Balkans. Despite heavy damage to the city, the defenders' effective use of artillery prevented the Ottomans from capturing it, showcasing the evolving nature of warfare during this period.
events.name: Murad II lays siege to Belgrade

events.enhanced_description: In September 1440, the term of Regent of Sweden Karl Knutsson Bonde ended as Christopher of Bavaria, newly elected king of Denmark, was also elected king of Sweden. This transition marked a significant moment in the political landscape of the Kalmar Union.
events.name: The term of Regent of Sweden Karl Knutsson Bonde ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, Itzcóatl, the ruler of Tenochtitlan, died and was succeeded by Moctezuma I (Moctezuma Ilhuicamina). This transition marked a significant period in the expansion and consolidation of the Aztec Empire under Moctezuma's leadership.
events.name: Itzcóatl dies and is succeeded by Moctezuma I

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, Lorenzo Valla published his work 'De falso credita et ementita Constantini Donatione declamatio,' which effectively demonstrated that the Donation of Constantine was a forgery. This work was pivotal in the field of textual criticism and had lasting implications for the authority of the papacy.
events.name: Lorenzo Valla demonstrates that the Donation of Constantine is a forgery

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, Sir Richard Molyneux was appointed constable of Liverpool Castle, a position that underscored the importance of Liverpool in the defense and administration of the region during a time of political instability.
events.name: Sir Richard Molyneux is appointed constable of Liverpool Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, the Ming dynasty government of China began a decade-long series of harsh edicts targeting illegal silver mining, known as 'miner bandits' (kuangzei). These measures aimed to control the silver market and curb illegal activities, reflecting the economic challenges faced by the dynasty.
events.name: Ming dynasty issues harsh edicts against illegal silver mining

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, Uwaifiokun, the Oba of Benin, was killed by his brother Ogun, who then succeeded him as Ewuare I. This event marked a significant shift in the leadership of the Benin Kingdom, which would go on to become one of the most powerful states in West Africa.
events.name: Uwaifiokun is killed and succeeded by Ogun as Ewuare I

events.enhanced_description: In 1440, Zhu Quan authored the 'Cha Pu' ("Tea Manual"), which is one of the earliest texts on tea culture in China. This work contributed significantly to the understanding and appreciation of tea, which has become an integral part of Chinese culture.
events.name: Zhu Quan writes the Cha Pu ("Tea Manual") in China

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1440, the Prussian Confederation was formed, a coalition of Prussian towns and nobility aimed at opposing the Teutonic Knights' rule. This alliance played a crucial role in the subsequent conflicts that led to the Thirteen Years' War.
events.name: The Prussian Confederation is formed

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1440, Christopher of Bavaria was elected King of Denmark, consolidating his rule over the Kalmar Union, which included Sweden and Norway. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the union amidst internal and external challenges.
events.name: Christopher of Bavaria is elected King of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1440, Eton College was founded by King Henry VI of England, establishing one of the most prestigious educational institutions in the world. The college has since played a significant role in the education of many British leaders and influential figures.

image.caption: Photograph of Eton College.
image.credit: Kazimierz Mendlik — https://web.archive.org/web/20161101175912/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/114546128
image.date_qualification: Photograph taken on 23 August 2014; it does not depict the 1440 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Eton College is founded by Henry VI of England

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1440, Gilles de Rais, a Breton knight and former companion of Joan of Arc, was taken into custody following accusations of murdering children brought against him by the Bishop of Nantes. This marked the beginning of a notorious trial that would reveal the dark side of his legacy.
events.name: Gilles de Rais is taken into custody

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1440, Gilles de Rais confessed to the charges against him and was subsequently sentenced to death. His trial and execution highlighted the moral and legal complexities of the time, as well as the dark aspects of his legacy.
events.name: Gilles de Rais confesses and is sentenced to death

events.enhanced_description: In February 1441, the Republic of Venice annexed the seigniory of Ravenna, effectively ending the da Polenta Dynasty's rule. This annexation was part of Venice's broader expansionist policies during the Renaissance period.
events.name: Venice annexes the seigniory of Ravenna

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, Ouagadougou was established as the capital of the Mossi Kingdoms, a significant political development in the region of West Africa. This move solidified Ouagadougou's status as a central hub for governance and trade among the Mossi people.
events.name: Ouagadougou becomes capital

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, two representatives from the Ethiopian Empire attended a Christian ecclesiastical council in Florence, marking the first recorded contact between the Ethiopian Coptic Church and Europe. This event was pivotal in discussions regarding a potential union between the Coptic and Latin Churches.

image.caption: Woodcut depicting the Synod of Florence, from the Nuremberg Chronicle.
image.credit: Michel Wolgemut, Wilhelm Pleydenwurff ( Hartmann Schedel , editor) — http://www.obrasraras.usp.br/obras/000192/ → File:Liber Chronicarum f 244v.jpg
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1493; it is a retrospective depiction, not a contemporary event photograph or eyewitness image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ecclesiastical Council at Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, a revolt in the Mayan nation of Mayapan led to the fragmentation of the Maya civilization into warring city-states. This internal conflict significantly altered the political landscape of the region and marked the decline of centralized power in the Maya area.

image.caption: Panoramic view of the Mayapan archaeological site from the Kukulcan temple.
image.credit: SiMeCaIS — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image date is given as 07/06/2008; it depicts the site, not the historical revolt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Mayan Revolt in Mayapan

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, Hacı I Giray declared the independence of his province from the Golden Horde, establishing the Crimean Khanate with the support of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. This marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Eastern Europe and the Black Sea region.
events.name: Establishment of the Crimean Khanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, Portuguese explorer Nuno Tristão reached Ras Nouadhibou on the western coast of Africa, marking a significant moment in maritime exploration. This voyage is notable for being one of the first instances where a caravel was used for long-distance sea travel.
events.name: Nuno Tristão reaches Ras Nouadhibou

events.enhanced_description: In 1441, the first enslaved black Africans were brought to Europe at Lagos in the Kingdom of Portugal. This event marked the beginning of a tragic chapter in European colonial history and the transatlantic slave trade.
events.name: First enslaved Africans brought to Europe

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1441, King's College, Cambridge was founded by King Henry VI of England, establishing one of the most prestigious educational institutions in the world. The college has since been renowned for its academic excellence and historical significance.
events.name: King's College, Cambridge, is founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1441, the Battle of Samobor took place, where the army of Ulrich II, Count of Celje, defeated the forces of Stjepan Banić in a conflict that involved the Kingdom of Hungary. This battle was significant in the context of regional power struggles during the period.
events.name: Battle of Samobor

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Cremona, signed on November 20, 1441, ended the conflict between the Republic of Venice and the Duchy of Milan. This treaty restored peace and allowed for the re-establishment of trade and political relations in Northern Italy.
events.name: Peace of Cremona

events.enhanced_description: In September 1442, John Hunyadi achieved another victory against a 70,000-strong Ottoman army led by Hadım Şehabeddin near the Ialomița River. This battle further established Hunyadi's reputation as a formidable opponent of the Ottomans.
events.name: Battle near the Ialomița River

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, the community of Rauma in Finland was granted town rights, marking an important development in its administrative status. This recognition helped to facilitate trade and governance in the region.
events.name: Town rights granted to Rauma

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, the municipality of Juva was founded in Finland, contributing to the administrative organization of the region. This establishment played a role in the local governance and community development.
events.name: Foundation of Juva

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, the national law known as Kristofers landslag was introduced in Sweden, marking a significant development in the legal framework of the country. This law aimed to standardize legal practices and governance across the realm.
events.name: Introduction of Kristofers landslag

events.enhanced_description: Before September 1442, Vlad II Dracul was imprisoned by the Sultan, leading to his temporary replacement by his son Mircea II as ruler of Wallachia. This power shift was indicative of the turbulent political landscape in the region during this period.
events.name: Mircea II replaces Vlad II Dracul

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, a fourth tower was added to Liverpool Castle in England, enhancing its fortifications. This architectural development reflected the ongoing military and political significance of the castle in the region.
events.name: Addition of a tower to Liverpool Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, Jelena Balšić completed the writing of the Gorički zbornik manuscripts at her church of St. Mary on the island of Beška in the Serbian Despotate. This work is significant for its cultural and historical contributions to Serbian literature.
events.name: Completion of Gorički zbornik manuscripts

events.enhanced_description: In 1442, Portuguese sailors first arrived at the Senegal River, marking a significant moment in the Age of Exploration. This event opened new avenues for trade and interaction between Europe and West Africa.
events.name: Portuguese arrival at Senegal River

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1442, John Hunyadi led his forces to a decisive victory against an 80,000-strong army of the Ottoman Empire, commanded by Mesid Bey, near Sibiu in Transylvania. This battle was a crucial moment in the struggle against Ottoman expansion in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Hermannstadt

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1442, Alfonso of Aragon proclaimed himself King of Naples, solidifying his rule over the kingdom. This proclamation was part of his broader campaign to unify southern Italy under Aragonese control.
events.name: Alfonso of Aragon proclaims himself King of Naples

events.enhanced_description: In 1443, the conflict between the co-rulers Iliaș and Stephen II reignited in Moldavia, culminating in Stephen capturing Iliaș and blinding him. This brutal act ensured Stephen's position as the sole ruler of Moldavia.
events.name: Conflict in Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1443, Portuguese explorer Nuno Tristão penetrated the Arguin Gulf off the west coast of Africa, furthering European exploration and trade interests in the region. His voyages contributed to the mapping and understanding of the African coastline.
events.name: Nuno Tristão in the Arguin Gulf

events.enhanced_description: In 1443, King Sejong the Great began the creation of Hangul, the native alphabet of the Korean language, with his scholars. This initiative aimed to improve literacy among common people and is considered one of the most significant cultural achievements in Korean history.
events.name: Creation of Hangul

events.enhanced_description: In January 1443, Vlad II Dracul began his second term as the ruler of Wallachia, following the reign of Basarab II. His rule was marked by efforts to strengthen the principality against external threats, particularly from the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Vlad II Dracul begins his second term as ruler of Wallachia, succeeding Basarab II

events.enhanced_description: In 1443, the Zhihua Temple was constructed in Beijing under the orders of Wang Zhen, the chief eunuch of the Ming Dynasty. This temple became a significant site for Buddhist worship and reflects the cultural and religious dynamics of the period.
events.name: The Buddhist Zhihua Temple is built in Beijing

events.enhanced_description: In 1443, a devastating earthquake struck the Timișoara Fortress, causing significant destruction. This event highlighted the vulnerability of fortifications during natural disasters in the region.
events.name: A powerful earthquake destroys the Timișoara Fortress

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1443, the Battle of St. Jakob an der Sihl took place, where the forces of the city of Zürich were defeated. Despite their loss, the Swiss Confederacy lacked the strength to besiege and capture the city, highlighting the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of St. Jakob an der Sihl

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1443, Skanderbeg and his forces liberated the city of Krujë from Ottoman control, raising the Albanian flag. This event marked a significant moment in the Albanian resistance against Ottoman rule.
events.name: Liberation of Krujë

events.enhanced_description: In August 1444, after negotiating peace with the Karamanids, Ottoman Sultan Murad II abdicated the throne in favor of his son Mehmed II. This transition marked a significant moment in Ottoman history as Mehmed II would later conquer Constantinople.
events.name: Murad II abdicates in favor of Mehmed II

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, Constantine XI Palaiologos, ruler of the Despotate of the Morea, invaded the Duchy of Athens, which was under Florentine control. He successfully forced the Florentines to pay tribute and return Thebes to the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos invades the Duchy of Athens

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, the forces of the Sultan of Egypt attempted to capture the island of Rhodes from the Knights of Rhodes but were unsuccessful. This failure underscored the resilience of the Knights and their strategic importance in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Forces of the Sultan of Egypt fail to take Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, Portuguese explorers reached the mouth of the Senegal and Gambia rivers, marking a significant step in the exploration of West Africa. This exploration laid the groundwork for future trade and colonial endeavors in the region.
events.name: Portuguese explorers reach the mouth of the rivers Senegal and Gambia

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, the Mercado de Escravos, the first European slave market for the sale of African slaves, opened in Lagos, Portugal. This marked a pivotal moment in the history of the transatlantic slave trade and European colonialism.
events.name: The Mercado de Escravos opens in Lagos

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, a serious fire broke out at Old St Paul's Cathedral in London, causing significant damage to the structure. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of medieval architecture to fire hazards.
events.name: A serious fire occurs at Old St Paul's Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, the Iguvine Tablets were discovered in Gubbio, Italy. These ancient inscriptions are significant for their insights into the language and rituals of the ancient Umbrian civilization.

image.caption: The Iguvine Tablets, bronze inscriptions written in Umbrian and Latin.
image.credit: Sailko — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the ancient tablets, not their discovery; the saved image date is 2015-07-12.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Iguvine Tablets are discovered

events.enhanced_description: In 1444, Stephen II of Moldavia appointed his stepbrother Petru as co-ruler, strengthening their political alliance. This partnership was significant in the context of Moldavia's struggles against external threats.
events.name: Stephen II of Moldavia takes Petru as co-ruler

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1444, the League of Lezhë was formed as an alliance of Albanian principalities, with George Kastrioti Skanderbeg proclaimed as its commander. This coalition aimed to resist Ottoman expansion in the region.
events.name: The League of Lezhë is established

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1444, the Treaty of Tours was signed between England and France, establishing a five-year truce in the ongoing Hundred Years' War. This agreement aimed to bring temporary peace between the two nations amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: The Treaty of Tours is signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1444, Cosimo de' Medici established a public library at San Marco in Florence, marking a significant contribution to the cultural and intellectual life of the Renaissance. This library became a center for learning and scholarship.
events.name: Cosimo de' Medici founds a public library at San Marco

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1444, the Battle of Torvioll took place, where Skanderbeg led Albanian forces to a decisive victory against the Ottoman army. This battle solidified Skanderbeg's reputation as a national hero and a formidable opponent of Ottoman expansion.

image.caption: Map illustrating the Battle of Torvioll.
image.credit: NY onja Christian — Own work
image.date_qualification: Map created 2017-11-26; it depicts the 1444 battle retrospectively.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Torvioll

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1444, a Portuguese fleet led by Lançarote de Freitas arrived at Algarve, bringing 235 enslaved individuals from Africa. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the transatlantic slave trade.
events.name: A Portuguese fleet lands slaves at Algarve

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1444, the Peace of Szeged was signed between the Ottoman Empire and Hungary, concluding hostilities and establishing a temporary peace. This treaty was crucial in the ongoing struggle between the two powers.
events.name: The Peace of Szeged is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1444, the Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs occurred during the Old Zürich War, where the Swiss forces faced a larger French army led by Louis, the Dauphin. Despite being outnumbered, the Swiss inflicted heavy casualties, forcing the French to withdraw.
events.name: Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1444, the Battle of Varna took place, where the crusading forces led by King Władysław III of Poland faced defeat against the Ottoman army commanded by Sultan Murad II. The battle resulted in the death of Władysław, significantly impacting the Jagiellonian Union.
events.name: Battle of Varna

events.enhanced_description: In April 1445, Henry VI of England married Margaret of Anjou, a union that aimed to solidify political alliances and strengthen the Lancastrian claim to the English throne. This marriage would have lasting implications for the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Henry VI of England marries Margaret of Anjou

events.enhanced_description: In 1445, the Portuguese established their first trading post, known as a Feitoria, on the island of Arguin off the coast of Africa. This marked the beginning of a significant Portuguese presence in West Africa, facilitating trade and exploration.
events.name: The Portuguese set up their first trading post in Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 1445, Portuguese explorer Dinis Dias discovered the Cap-Vert peninsula on the western coast of Africa. This discovery was part of Portugal's broader efforts to explore and map the African coastline.
events.name: Portuguese explorer Dinis Dias discovers Cap-Vert

events.enhanced_description: In 1445, the Battle of Gomit occurred, where Emperor Zara Yaqob of Ethiopia defeated and killed Sultan Arwe Badlay of Adal. This victory was significant in the ongoing conflicts between the Ethiopian Empire and the Sultanate of Adal.
events.name: Battle of Gomit

events.enhanced_description: In 1445, Vlad II Dracul, with the support of a crusaders' fleet from Burgundy, launched an attack on Giurgiu, where he massacred the Ottoman garrison after their surrender. This event underscored his fierce resistance against Ottoman encroachment.
events.name: Vlad II Dracul attacks Giurgiu

events.enhanced_description: In 1445, Stephen II solidified his power as the sole ruler of Moldavia, navigating the complex political landscape of Eastern Europe during a time of regional instability. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the principality against external threats, particularly from the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Stephen II remains sole ruler of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1445, the Battle of Mokra took place, where Albanian forces under Skanderbeg achieved a significant victory against the Ottomans. This battle was celebrated by Pope Eugene IV, who recognized Skanderbeg as a defender of Christendom.
events.name: Battle of Mokra

events.enhanced_description: The Hunminjeongeum, a document explaining the principles of the Hangul alphabet, was discovered in Korea. This significant finding highlighted the importance of the Korean writing system, which was created to promote literacy among the Korean people.
events.name: Discovery of Hunminjeongeum

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, Sultan Mehmed II was forced to abdicate the throne of the Ottoman Empire in favor of his father, Murad II, due to pressure from the Janissaries. This political upheaval reflected the internal strife within the Ottoman leadership during a period of military challenges.
events.name: Sultan Mehmed II abdicates

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, Nuno Tristão, a Portuguese explorer, was killed by natives on the coast of Senegal. His death highlighted the dangers faced by early European explorers in Africa and the complex interactions between European powers and indigenous populations.

locations.name: Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of Dakar

events.name: Nuno Tristão is killed

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, Portuguese navigator Álvaro Fernandes reached the mouth of the Casamance River in Senegal, marking an important moment in the Age of Exploration. His journey contributed to the European understanding of West African geography and trade routes.
events.name: Álvaro Fernandes reaches the mouth of the Casamance River

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, the Precious Belt Bridge in China was fully reconstructed, showcasing the architectural advancements of the period. This bridge played a significant role in facilitating trade and transportation in the region.
events.name: Precious Belt Bridge reconstruction

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, the Blarney Stone was set into a tower of Blarney Castle in County Cork, Ireland. This stone has since become a symbol of eloquence and is a popular tourist attraction, steeped in legend and folklore.

locations.name: Blarney Castle, Blarney, County Cork, Ireland

events.name: Setting of the Blarney Stone

events.enhanced_description: In 1446, a coalition was formed to counter the growing power of the House of Sforza in Milan. This league represented the ongoing struggles for power among the Italian city-states during the Renaissance, as various factions sought to maintain their autonomy.
events.name: Formation of a league against the House of Sforza

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ragaz, fought on March 6, 1446, marked the conclusion of the Old Zurich War, where the Swiss Confederacy achieved a decisive victory against the Habsburg forces. This battle not only showcased the military prowess of the Confederates but also significantly weakened Habsburg influence in the region.
events.name: The Battle of Ragaz

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1446, John Hunyadi was proclaimed regent of Hungary, a title that granted him significant authority during a tumultuous period marked by Ottoman incursions. Hunyadi's leadership was pivotal in organizing resistance against the Ottomans, leveraging his wealth and influence to finance military campaigns.
events.name: John Hunyadi is proclaimed regent

events.enhanced_description: An armistice was established on June 12, 1446, between the Duchy of Austria and the Swiss Confederation, effectively halting hostilities that had characterized the Old Zurich War. This agreement marked a significant step towards stabilizing relations in the region, allowing both parties to focus on internal matters.
events.name: Armistice between Duchy of Austria and the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1446, Lidköping was granted its charter, officially recognizing it as a city. This event marked an important development in the urbanization of Sweden, contributing to the growth of trade and governance in the region.
events.name: Lidköping gets its charter

events.enhanced_description: In August 1446, Christopher of Bavaria launched a military campaign against Gotland in an attempt to quell piracy led by Eric of Pomerania. Despite his efforts, the campaign proved fruitless, highlighting the challenges faced by the Scandinavian monarchs in maintaining control over their territories.
events.name: Christopher of Bavaria's military campaign against Gotland

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1446, Skanderbeg achieved a significant victory against the Ottoman forces at the Battle of Otonetë. This battle was crucial in establishing Skanderbeg's reputation as a formidable leader in the resistance against Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: Battle of Otonetë

events.enhanced_description: In October 1446, Sultan Murad II invaded Attica, compelling Constantine XI to return Thebes to the Duchy of Athens and imposing a new tribute. This invasion underscored the ongoing Ottoman pressure on the Byzantine territories during this period.
events.name: Murad II invades Attica

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1446, King Sejong the Great proclaimed the hangul alphabet, a significant advancement in Korean literacy and culture. The publication of the Hunmin Jeongeum marked the beginning of a new era in written communication for the Korean people.

image.caption: Graphic showing “Joseongeul” and “Hangeul” written in Hangul.
image.credit: metalslick — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2017-11-10; this is not a depiction of the 1446 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Proclamation of the hangul alphabet in Korea

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1446, Sultan Murad II ordered the destruction of the Hexamilion wall, a significant fortification in the Peloponnese. This act was part of a broader campaign to consolidate Ottoman control over the region, demonstrating the military might of the empire.
events.name: Destruction of the Hexamilion wall

events.enhanced_description: In December 1447, Vlad II Dracul, the ruler of Wallachia, and his eldest son Mircea were assassinated, leading to the ascension of Vladislav II. This event was pivotal in the power dynamics of Wallachia, with John Hunyadi playing a crucial role in the transition.
events.name: Assassination of Vlad II Dracul and his son

events.enhanced_description: The Albanian–Venetian War commenced in 1447, marking a significant conflict between the Albanian principalities and the Venetian Republic. This war was characterized by territorial disputes and the struggle for control over trade routes in the Adriatic Sea.
events.name: The Albanian–Venetian War of 1447–48 begins

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Soest occurred in 1447 during the Soest Feud, a conflict involving various factions in the region. This siege exemplified the political and military struggles of the time, as local powers vied for control.
events.name: Siege of Soest

events.enhanced_description: Tashi Lhunpo Monastery, founded by the 1st Dalai Lama in 1447, became one of the most important monasteries in Tibetan Buddhism, serving as the seat of the Panchen Lama. The monastery is renowned for its impressive architecture and rich history, symbolizing the spread of Buddhism in Tibet.

image.caption: Entrance to Tashilhunpo Monastery in Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China.
image.credit: B_cool from SIN, Singapore — Entrance to Tashillunpo Monastery
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2007-06-14 01:43; the event is dated 1447 in the supplied article excerpt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Tashi Lhunpo Monastery is founded by the 1st Dalai Lama

events.enhanced_description: In 1447, Iizasa Ienao established Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū, recognized as the oldest surviving koryū martial art in Japan. This school of martial arts emphasizes traditional techniques and philosophies, influencing many modern Japanese martial arts.
events.name: Iizasa Ienao founds Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1447, Pope Nicholas V was elected as the 208th pope, succeeding Pope Eugene IV. His papacy would be marked by efforts to promote the Renaissance and reform the Church.
events.name: Pope Nicholas V succeeds Pope Eugene IV

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1447, a devastating fire swept through the center of Valencia, causing significant destruction. This disaster had lasting impacts on the city's architecture and urban planning.
events.name: Major fire destroys the centre of Valencia

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1447, Roman II seized the throne of Moldavia after assassinating his uncle, Stephen II. This violent power shift marked a turbulent period in Moldavian history, with Roman II appointing his other uncle, Petru, as co-ruler.
events.name: Roman II seizes the throne of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In October 1448, Vlad III the Impaler briefly ascended to the throne of Wallachia, only to be deposed by Vladislav II shortly thereafter. His tumultuous reign would later become infamous for its brutality and the legends surrounding his figure.
events.name: Vlad III the Impaler becomes Prince of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In December 1448, Jonas was installed as Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus in Moscow, marking a pivotal moment in the establishment of an independent church structure in the Grand Duchy of Moscow, separate from the Patriarch of Constantinople.
events.name: Jonas installed as Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus

events.enhanced_description: In 1448, Roman II fled to Poland as John Hunyadi's forces advanced to install Petru on the throne of Moldavia. Following Petru's sudden death, Csupor de Monoszló briefly took the throne, illustrating the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Roman II flees to Poland

events.enhanced_description: After enduring a prolonged period of drought, floods, locust infestations, and famine since 1434, the natural disasters in Ming dynasty China began to subside in 1448, allowing agriculture and commerce to return to normalcy, which was crucial for the stability of the empire.
events.name: Natural disasters wane in Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: In 1448, Pope Nicholas V founded the Vatican Library, which became one of the most important libraries in the world, housing a vast collection of texts and manuscripts that contributed to the preservation and dissemination of knowledge during the Renaissance.
events.name: The Vatican Library is founded

events.enhanced_description: Christopher of Bavaria died on January 6, 1448, leaving the thrones of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden vacant. His death led to a power vacuum and the subsequent appointment of co-regents in Sweden, significantly impacting the political landscape of Scandinavia.

image.caption: Portrait of King Christopher the Bavarian of Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
image.credit: Unknown artist for book — From book Taschenbuch für die vaterländische Geschichte , Munich 1853
image.date_qualification: Image dated no later than 1853; scanned in 2014. The event is dated 1448-01-06 in the supplied event record.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Christopher of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: Founded on April 15, 1448, by Margaret of Anjou, Queens' College is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Cambridge. It is notable for its distinctive architecture and has played a significant role in the educational landscape of England.
events.name: Queens' College, Cambridge is founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1448, Karl Knutsson Bonde was elected as King Charles VIII of Sweden, marking the end of the Regency period. His reign was significant in restoring stability and asserting royal authority in Sweden after years of political turmoil.
events.name: Election of Karl Knutsson Bonde as King Charles VIII of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1448, Charles VIII of Sweden was publicly hailed as king at Mora Stones, a significant event that solidified his claim to the throne. He was crowned the following day in Uppsala Cathedral, marking the beginning of his reign.
events.name: Charles VIII of Sweden is publicly hailed as king

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Oronichea on August 14, 1448, saw Albanian forces achieve a decisive victory over the Venetian army. This battle was part of the larger struggle for independence led by Skanderbeg against Venetian control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Oronichea

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1448, Christian of Oldenburg was crowned King Christian I of Denmark, following his betrothal to Queen Dowager Dorothea of Brandenburg. His reign marked the beginning of the Oldenburg dynasty in Denmark.
events.name: Christian I becomes King of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1448, a peace treaty was established between Albania and Venice, concluding hostilities that had persisted for years. This agreement allowed for a temporary respite in the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Peace between Albania and Venice

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1448, Pope Nicholas V appointed Rudolf of Diepholt as cardinal, a significant move that reflected the Pope's efforts to strengthen the Catholic Church's hierarchy during a time of political and religious upheaval.
events.name: Pope Nicholas V appoints Rudolf of Diepholt as cardinal

events.enhanced_description: In February 1449, Alexăndrel seized the throne of Moldavia with the support of local boyars, reflecting the ongoing power struggles within the region. His ascension marked a significant shift in Moldavian politics during a turbulent period.
events.name: Alexăndrel seizes the throne of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In May 1449, an English privateering fleet led by Robert Wennington challenged ships of the Hanseatic League, reflecting the ongoing maritime conflicts and competition for trade dominance in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
events.name: English privateering fleet challenges Hanseatic League

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1449, Constantine XI Palaiologos was crowned Byzantine Emperor in Mistra, marking the last coronation of a Byzantine ruler. His reign would be characterized by the struggle to defend the empire against the advancing Ottoman forces.
events.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos crowned Byzantine Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1449, during the Hundred Years' War, English forces captured the town of Fougères in Brittany. This event was part of the ongoing conflict between England and France, which had significant implications for territorial control in the region.
events.name: Hundred Years' War: English forces capture Fougères

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1449, Felix V, the last Antipope, abdicated, marking the end of a significant chapter in the history of the Catholic Church. His resignation was part of the broader efforts to resolve the Western Schism and restore unity within the Church.

image.caption: Portrait of Amadeus VIII of Savoy from a French edition of Albertanus of Brescia’s works.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Bibliothèque Royale, Bruxelles
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Amadeus VIII, who later claimed the papacy as Antipope Felix V; it is not a depiction of his abdication. Image date: circa 1430/5.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Abdication of Felix V, the last Antipope

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1449, Pope Nicholas V was elected by the Council of Basel, a pivotal moment in the Church's history as it sought to address the issues stemming from the Western Schism. His papacy would later focus on the revival of classical learning and the arts.
events.name: Pope Nicholas V elected by the Council of Basel

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1449, the Council of Basel dissolved itself, concluding a significant ecclesiastical assembly that aimed to address various issues within the Church. This dissolution marked a turning point in the Church's governance and authority.
events.name: Council of Basel dissolves itself

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1449, during the Second Siege of Sfetigrad, the Albanian garrison surrendered to Ottoman forces, resulting in the capture of this strategic fortress. This event underscored the Ottoman Empire's expanding influence in the Balkans.
events.name: Second Siege of Sfetigrad

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1449, the Battle of Alfarrobeira took place, where King Afonso V of Portugal defeated the forces of Peter, Duke of Coimbra. This battle was significant in consolidating Afonso's power and influence in Portugal during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Battle of Alfarrobeira

events.enhanced_description: In July 1449, during the Hundred Years' War, French forces launched an invasion of Normandy, aiming to reclaim territory previously held by the English. This marked a significant turning point in the conflict, as the French sought to consolidate their power in the region.
events.name: French invasion of Normandy

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1449, during the First Margrave War, Margrave Albrecht successfully captured Lichtenau Fortress from the city of Nuremberg. This victory was part of a larger conflict over territorial control in the region.
events.name: Capture of Lichtenau Fortress

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1449, the Oirat Mongols defeated the Ming dynasty army at the Battle of Tumu Fortress, capturing the Zhengtong Emperor of China. This event led to a significant political shift, as the emperor was deposed and his brother ascended to the throne as the Jingtai Emperor.
events.name: Battle of Tumu Fortress

events.enhanced_description: In October 1449, Bogdan II of Moldavia entered the country with troops from John Hunyadi, successfully taking the throne after the previous ruler, Alexandrel, fled. This event marked a significant change in leadership for Moldavia.
events.name: Bogdan II of Moldavia's ascension

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1449, the French forces recaptured Rouen from the English, marking a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War. This victory helped to solidify French control over Normandy.
events.name: Recapture of Rouen

events.enhanced_description: In March 1450, French troops under Guy de Richemont besieged the English commander Edmund Beaufort, 1st Duke of Somerset, in Caen. This siege was part of the larger conflict of the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Caen

events.enhanced_description: Around 1450, construction of Machu Picchu, a pre-Columbian Inca site located high in the Andes, is believed to have begun. This iconic site remains a testament to the architectural and cultural achievements of the Inca civilization.
events.name: Construction of Machu Picchu

events.enhanced_description: Around 1450, a religious sacrifice involving over a hundred children was performed outside the ancient city of Chan Chan, near modern Trujillo, Peru. This event highlights the ritual practices of the societies in pre-Columbian South America.
events.name: Child sacrifice near Chan Chan

events.enhanced_description: By 1450, Johannes Gutenberg had established his movable type printing press in Mainz, Germany, marking a revolutionary advancement in the production of books and the dissemination of knowledge in Europe.
events.name: Gutenberg's printing press

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1450, John de la Pole, 2nd Duke of Suffolk, married Lady Margaret Beaufort, a union that would have significant implications for the political landscape of England, particularly in relation to the Wars of the Roses.
figures: John de la Pole, 2nd Duke of Suffolk
events.name: Marriage of John de la Pole and Lady Margaret Beaufort

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1450, Francesco Sforza entered Milan after a successful siege, becoming the Duke of the city-state. His rule established a dynasty that would govern Milan for the next century.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of Francesco Sforza and Bianca Maria Visconti, with Sforza heraldry.
image.credit: Various — http://www.artivisive.sns.it/stampeditraduzione/
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 2015-06-29; this is not the depicted event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francesco Sforza enters Milan

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1450, the Battle of Formigny took place, where French troops under the Comte de Clermont defeated an English army led by Sir Thomas Kyriel and Sir Matthew Gough, who were attempting to relieve the siege of Caen.

image.caption: Anonymous medieval manuscript illumination depicting the Battle of Formigny.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b10023823h/f405
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration dated circa 1470–1480, later than the 1450 battle; the supported display date is null.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Formigny

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1450, Jack Cade led a rebellion in Kent against King Henry VI of England. This uprising was fueled by discontent over the king's rule and the socio-economic conditions of the time.
events.name: Jack Cade's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1450, Abdal-Latif Mirza, a monarch of the Timurid dynasty, was assassinated. His death marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Central Asia.
events.name: Assassination of Abdal-Latif Mirza

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1457, Charles VIII of Sweden was declared deposed, leading to the appointment of co-regents Jöns Bengtsson Oxenstierna and Erik Axelsson Tott, and the throne being offered to Christian I of Denmark and Norway.
events.name: Deposition of Charles VIII of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1450, the Battle of Solefields occurred, where Jack Cade's rebels were driven from London by loyal troops. This battle was a significant moment in the struggle against Cade's rebellion.
events.name: Battle of Solefields

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1450, Caen surrendered to the French forces, marking a significant victory in the Hundred Years' War. This event further solidified French control over Normandy.
events.name: Surrender of Caen

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1450, Jack Cade was slain in a skirmish, effectively ending his rebellion against King Henry VI. His death marked a turning point in the conflict and the restoration of royal authority.
events.name: Death of Jack Cade

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1450, Cherbourg, the last English territory in Normandy, surrendered to the French forces. This event marked the culmination of the French campaign to reclaim Normandy from English control.
events.name: Surrender of Cherbourg

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1450, Duke Ludwig IX ordered the expulsion of Jews from Lower Bavaria. This act reflected the growing anti-Semitic sentiments in Europe during this period.
events.name: Expulsion of Jews from Lower Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1450, the University of Barcelona was founded, marking a significant development in the educational landscape of Spain. This institution would become a center of learning and culture in the region.
events.name: Founding of the University of Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1450, during the First Siege of Krujë, Albanian troops led by Skanderbeg achieved a decisive victory against the Ottoman Empire, forcing an army of approximately 100,000 men to retreat. This battle was crucial in the struggle for Albanian independence.
events.name: First Siege of Krujë

events.enhanced_description: In 1451, The Great Peacemaker, along with Jigonhsasee and Hiawatha, founded the Haudenosaunee, commonly known as the Iroquois Confederacy, establishing a sophisticated political and social structure among the Native American tribes.
events.name: Founding of the Iroquois Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1451, Pope Nicholas V issued a Papal Bull to establish the University of Glasgow, with classes initially held in Glasgow Cathedral. This institution would become a key center of learning in Scotland.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Glasgow

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1451, Murad II, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, died and was succeeded by his son, Mehmed II, on February 18. This transition marked a significant moment in Ottoman history as Mehmed II would later conquer Constantinople.
events.name: Death of Murad II

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1451, Louis XI of France married Charlotte of Savoy, a union that would strengthen political ties between France and Savoy, impacting the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Marriage of Louis XI and Charlotte of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1451, Celje was granted market town status and town rights by Count Frederic II of Celje, marking a significant step in its development and autonomy within the region.
events.name: Celje acquires market town status and town rights

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1451, the Afghan Lodi Dynasty succeeded the Turkish Sayyid Dynasty in the Delhi Sultanate, marking a significant shift in power and the beginning of a new era in Indian history.

image.caption: Photograph of Sikandar Lodi’s tomb at sunset.
image.credit: AKS.9955 — Own work
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of a Lodi-era monument, not a depiction of the 1451 dynastic succession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Lodi Dynasty succeeds Sayyid Dynasty in Delhi Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1451, French troops under Jean de Dunois invaded Guyenne and successfully captured Bordeaux, a key strategic city during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: French troops capture Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1451, the French forces captured Bayonne, the last English stronghold in Guyenne, effectively ending English territorial claims in the region.
events.name: French capture Bayonne

events.enhanced_description: In October 1451, after assassinating Bogdan II of Moldavia, Petru Aron ascended to the throne, marking a turbulent period in Moldavian politics.
events.name: Petru Aron takes the throne of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1451, the citizens of Ghent revolted against Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, leading to significant political tensions in the region.
events.name: Revolt of Ghent against Philip the Good

events.enhanced_description: In February 1452, Alexăndrel successfully retook the throne of Moldavia after a prolonged struggle against Petru Aron, reinstating his rule over the region.
events.name: Alexăndrel retakes the throne of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1452, William Douglas, the 8th Earl of Douglas, was killed by James II of Scotland at Stirling Castle, an event that escalated the power struggles among Scottish nobility.
events.name: William Douglas killed by James II of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1452, during the Reconquista, the Battle of Los Alporchones took place near Lorca, where the combined forces of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of Murcia defeated the Emirate of Granada.
events.name: Battle of Los Alporchones

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1452, Frederick III became the last Holy Roman Emperor to be crowned in Rome, a significant event in the history of the Holy Roman Empire.

image.caption: A symbolic device used by the Habsburg emperors and created by Frederick III.
image.credit: Friedrich III. — Scan aus: Peter Diem –- Die Symbole Österreichs , Wien: Kremayr & Scheriau, 1995 S. 192 ISBN 3-218-00594-9
image.date_qualification: A symbolic device associated with Frederick III, not a depiction of his coronation. The original date is given as 15th century; no supported display date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Frederick III crowned in Rome

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1452, Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, officially declared war on Ghent, intensifying the conflict during the Revolt of Ghent.
events.name: Philip the Good declares war on Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1452, Pope Nicholas V issued the papal bull Dum Diversas, which legitimized the colonial slave trade, significantly impacting European colonial policies.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Pope Nicholas V by Peter Paul Rubens.
image.credit: Peter Paul Rubens — Museum Plantin-Moretus / Prentenkabinet
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the bull’s issuer, not a depiction of the 1452 issuance; the image is dated between 1612 and 1616.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pope Nicholas V issues Dum Diversas

events.enhanced_description: In January 1453, Ottoman forces began mobilizing in preparation for war against the Byzantine Empire, setting the stage for the Siege of Constantinople.
events.name: Ottoman forces mobilize against Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: In March 1453, a large cohort of English troops departed to reinforce Gascony, reflecting the ongoing conflict in the region during the Hundred Years' War.
events.name: English troops reinforce Gascony

events.enhanced_description: In April 1453, Sayf al-Din Inal deposed the young sultan Al-Mansur Uthman, who had only recently ascended to power, indicating the instability within the Mamluk Sultanate.
events.name: Sayf al-Din Inal deposes Al-Mansur Uthman

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Constantinople commenced in 717, led by Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, who aimed to capture the strategically vital city. The siege faced significant challenges, including disease among the besieging forces and the formidable defenses of the city.
events.name: Siege of Constantinople begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1453, Ottoman forces, led by Sultan Mehmed II, launched their first assault against Constantinople, marking the beginning of the end for the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: First assault on Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1453, Ottoman forces led by Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, marking the end of the Byzantine Empire. This pivotal event not only transformed the city into the new Ottoman capital but also significantly shifted the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Ottoman forces capture Constantinople, destroying the Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1453, Ludovico Gonzaga defended the city of Mantua against an assault by Venetian forces commanded by his brother Carlo. This conflict highlighted the intense rivalries within Italian city-states during the Renaissance period.
events.name: Ludovico Gonzaga of Mantua defends the city against Venetian forces led by his brother Carlo

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1453, the Giant Bible of Mainz was completed, showcasing the advancements in printing technology by Johannes Gutenberg. This monumental work played a crucial role in the spread of literacy and the Reformation in Europe.
events.name: The Giant Bible of Mainz is completed

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1453, the French forces decisively defeated the English army at the Battle of Castillon, effectively ending the Hundred Years' War. This battle marked a significant turning point in the struggle for control over France.
events.name: The French destroy the English army at the Battle of Castillon

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1453, Duke Philip the Good's Burgundian army defeated the rebel forces of Ghent at the Battle of Gavere. This victory solidified Burgundian control over the region and suppressed the Ghent rebellion.
events.name: The Burgundian army led by Duke Philip the Good defeats the rebel forces of Ghent at the Battle of Gavere

events.enhanced_description: In August 1453, French forces under René of Anjou arrived in the Piedmont region to assist Milan and Florence against Venetian aggression. This intervention was part of the broader conflicts involving Italian city-states during this period.
events.name: French forces led by René of Anjou arrive in the Piedmont

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1453, Pope Nicholas V issued a crusading bull against the Ottoman Empire, calling for a united Christian response to the Ottoman threat following the fall of Constantinople. This document reflected the growing concern among European powers regarding Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Pope Nicholas V issues a crusading bull against the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1453, the last English holdouts in Gascony, including Bordeaux, surrendered to French forces, effectively ending the Hundred Years' War. This marked a significant shift in territorial control and national identity in France.
events.name: The last English holdouts in Gascony surrender to France, ending the Hundred Years' War

events.enhanced_description: In December 1453, an exceptionally cold winter caused heavy snowfall across the Huai River valley in China, leading to numerous deaths. This climatic event had significant social and economic impacts on the region.
events.name: An exceptionally cold winter leads to heavy snows across China

events.enhanced_description: In 1454, Johannes Gutenberg's printing press in Mainz produced the first printed documents that bore a date, marking a significant milestone in the history of printing. This innovation revolutionized the dissemination of information and literature across Europe.
events.name: The press of Johannes Gutenberg produces the first printed documents bearing a date

events.enhanced_description: In 1454, Isaac Zarfati sent a circular letter to Jewish communities in Rhineland, Swabia, Moravia, and Hungary, praising the favorable conditions for Jews under Ottoman rule compared to their experiences in Christian territories. This letter encouraged Jewish migration to the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Isaac Zarfati sends a circular letter praising conditions for Jews under the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1454, the Statutes of Nieszawa were enacted in Poland, establishing important legal reforms and regulations. These statutes played a significant role in shaping the governance and legal framework of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: The Statutes of Nieszawa are enacted in Poland

events.enhanced_description: In 1454, the Drought of One Rabbit was recorded in Aztec history, marking a significant climatic event that affected agriculture and society in the Aztec Empire. This drought had lasting implications for the population and their resources.
events.name: The Drought of One Rabbit is recorded in Aztec history

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1454, the Secret Council of the Prussian Confederation sent a formal act of disobedience to the Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, marking the beginning of the Thirteen Years' War. This rebellion was a response to the oppressive rule of the Teutonic Order.
events.name: Thirteen Years' War: The Secret Council of the Prussian Confederation sends a formal act of disobedience

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1454, Casimir IV of Poland formally renounced his allegiance to the Teutonic Knights, further escalating tensions that would lead to the Thirteen Years' War. This act was pivotal in rallying support for the Prussian Confederation against the Knights.
events.name: Casimir IV of Poland renounces allegiance to the Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1454, Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, was appointed Protector for the mentally unstable King Henry VI of England. This power shift marked the beginning of the political turmoil that would lead to the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, becomes Protector for King Henry VI of England

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1454, Francesco Sforza established a triple alliance between the Duchy of Milan, the Republic of Florence, and the Kingdom of Naples through the Treaty of Lodi. This alliance aimed to stabilize the power dynamics in Italy and prevent further conflicts.
events.name: Treaty of Lodi: Francesco Sforza forms a triple alliance

events.enhanced_description: In August 1454, Petru Aron successfully retook the throne of Moldavia from Alexăndrel. This political maneuvering was part of the ongoing power struggles within the region during the 15th century.
events.name: In Moldavia, Petru Aron retakes the throne from Alexăndrel

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1454, during the Thirteen Years' War, the Polish army faced defeat against a smaller but more professional Teutonic army at the Battle of Chojnice. This battle underscored the military challenges faced by the Polish forces during the conflict.
events.name: Thirteen Years' War – Battle of Chojnice

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1454, the Malbork treaty was signed between the authorities of the Teutonic Order and the mercenary forces fighting for them. This agreement aimed to stabilize the situation during the ongoing Thirteen Years' War.
events.name: Thirteen Years' War: Malbork treaty

events.enhanced_description: In December 1454, King Henry VI of England, having regained his sanity, dismissed Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, from his position as Protector. This decision intensified the political rivalry that would eventually lead to the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: King Henry VI of England dismisses the Duke of York as Protector

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1455, Pope Nicholas V published the encyclical Romanus Pontifex, which sanctioned the conquest of non-Christian lands and the enslavement of non-Christian populations. This document had profound implications for European colonialism and the treatment of indigenous peoples.
events.name: Pope Nicholas V publishes Romanus Pontifex

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1455, the Gutenberg Bible became the first major book printed using movable type. This groundbreaking achievement by Johannes Gutenberg revolutionized the production of books and the spread of knowledge throughout Europe.
events.name: The Gutenberg Bible is the first book printed with movable type

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1455, the Wars of the Roses began in England, a series of civil wars for control of the English throne between the houses of Lancaster and York. This conflict would shape English history for decades to come.
events.name: The Wars of the Roses begin in England

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1455, Pope Calixtus III succeeded Pope Nicholas V as the 209th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy would be marked by efforts to address the Ottoman threat and promote the Crusades.

image.caption: Portrait of Pope Callixtus III, attributed to Sano di Pietro.
image.credit: Sano di Pietro — http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image:Calixtusiii.jpg
image.date_qualification: Image metadata dates the work to 1455; this is not established as the date of the succession event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pope Calixtus III succeeds Pope Nicholas V

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Arkinholm, fought on May 1, 1455, was a significant conflict in which the forces loyal to King James II of Scotland defeated the supporters of the powerful Earl of Douglas. This battle marked a pivotal moment in the ongoing power struggles within Scotland, consolidating the king's authority.
events.name: Battle of Arkinholm

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of St Albans, fought on May 22, 1455, was the opening battle of the Wars of the Roses, where Richard, Duke of York, defeated and captured King Henry VI of England. This battle set the stage for a prolonged conflict over the English throne between the houses of York and Lancaster.
events.name: First Battle of St Albans

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1455, during the Thirteen Years' War, the Teutonic Order achieved a decisive victory at the Battle for Kneiphof. Despite this victory, the war ultimately ended unfavorably for the Order with the signing of the Treaty of Thorn in 1466.
events.name: Battle for Kneiphof

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1455, tensions escalated between Vladislav II of Wallachia and John Hunyadi, leading Hunyadi to support Vlad the Impaler for the Wallachian throne. This conflict was part of a larger power struggle in Eastern Europe during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Conflict between Vladislav II and John Hunyadi

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, Lazar Branković was appointed as the despot of Serbia, marking a significant moment in Serbian history as he took on leadership during a period of political instability and external threats.
events.name: Lazar Branković becomes despot of Serbia

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, the Venetian explorer Alvise Cadamosto discovered several of the Cape Verde Islands, contributing to the European exploration and colonization of the Atlantic islands.
events.name: Alvise Cadamosto discovers Cape Verde Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, the Portuguese explorer Diogo Gomes reached the Geba River in Guinea-Bissau and explored the Gambia River, expanding European knowledge of West African geography and trade routes.
events.name: Diogo Gomes explores Geba and Gambia Rivers

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, Emperor Zara Yaqob of Ethiopia founded the city of Debre Berhan, which became an important center for trade and culture in the region.
events.name: Zara Yaqob founds Debre Berhan

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, Muscovy and the Novgorod Republic concluded the Treaty of Yazhelbitsy, which marked a significant step in the consolidation of power by the Grand Duchy of Moscow over the Novgorod region.
events.name: Treaty of Yazhelbitsy

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, Petru Aron became the first ruler of Moldavia to pay tribute to the Ottomans, signaling a shift in the region's political dynamics and the influence of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Petru Aron pays tribute to Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In 1456, the fifth Mersenne prime, 8191, was discovered, contributing to the field of number theory and the study of prime numbers.
events.name: Discovery of the fifth Mersenne prime

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Oronichea, fought on May 18, 1456, saw the Ottoman forces of 15,000 swiftly defeated by the smaller forces of Skanderbeg in Albania. This victory was significant in the ongoing resistance against Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: Second Battle of Oronichea

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1456, Halley's Comet made a notable appearance, which was documented by the humanist scholar Platina. This event contributed to the growing interest in astronomy during the Renaissance period.
events.name: Halley's Comet appearance

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1456, a retrial acquitted Joan of Arc of heresy, 25 years after her execution. This posthumous vindication highlighted the political and religious tensions of the time and contributed to her eventual canonization.
events.name: Retrial of Joan of Arc

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1456, the Battle of Nándorfehérvár saw Hungarian forces under John Hunyadi decisively defeat the Ottoman army led by Sultan Mehmed II. This victory was celebrated throughout Christendom, with the noon bell ordered by Pope Callixtus III commemorating the event.
events.name: Battle of Nándorfehérvár

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1456, Vladislav II of Wallachia was killed in hand-to-hand combat by Vlad the Impaler, who then succeeded him. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within Wallachia and the region.
events.name: Death of Vladislav II

events.enhanced_description: The University of Greifswald was established on October 17, 1456, making it the second oldest university in Northern Europe. Its founding marked a significant development in higher education in the region.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Greifswald

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1456, two devastating earthquakes struck central Italy, resulting in the deaths of an estimated 12,000 to 70,000 people. This catastrophe had a profound impact on the region's population and infrastructure.
events.name: Earthquakes in central Italy

events.enhanced_description: Albrechts University, founded in 1457 in Freiburg im Breisgau, became one of the prominent centers of learning in Germany. Its establishment marked a significant development in the educational landscape of the time, contributing to the Renaissance humanist movement.

image.caption: Seal of the University of Freiburg.
image.credit: Original: University of Freiburg Vector: Calestyo — Own work based on: Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg Wappen.gif
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2009-08-18, not the 1457 founding date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: trademarked|insignia

events.name: Foundation of Albrechts University

events.enhanced_description: Edo Castle, constructed by Ōta Dōkan in 1457, served as the seat of power for the Tokugawa shogunate and played a crucial role in Japanese history. Its strategic location and impressive fortifications made it a symbol of political authority in Japan.
events.name: Construction of Edo Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1457, the Zhengtong Emperor of China was reinstated as the Tianshun Emperor after years of captivity, marking a significant event in the Ming Dynasty's history.
events.name: Reinstatement of the Zhengtong Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1457, King James II of Scotland issued a decree banning the games of futebawe and golf, marking the first historical mention of golf. This decree reflected the king's concerns over the distractions from military training.
events.name: King James II's decree on golf

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1457, Ștefan cel Mare secured the throne of Moldavia, a position he would hold for the next 47 years, during which he became known for his military prowess and resistance against foreign powers.

image.caption: Coat of arms of Stephen III of Moldavia.
image.credit: Madboy74 — Own work https://cimerek.hu/cimer/iii-istvan-moldvai-fejedelem-cimere/
image.date_qualification: A modern depiction of a historical coat of arms, not an image of the 1457 accession event. Image date: 2012-01-02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ștefan cel Mare secures Moldavian throne

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1457, Christian I was elected king of Sweden, effectively ending the war between Sweden and Denmark and restoring the Kalmar Union, which sought to unify the Nordic countries under a single monarch.
events.name: Christian I elected king of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1457, the Dutch city of Dordrecht was devastated by a catastrophic fire that destroyed a significant portion of the city. This disaster had lasting effects on the community and its economy.
events.name: Fire in Dordrecht

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1457, the Mainz Psalter was printed, marking it as the second major book printed with movable type in the West and the first to carry a printed date. This event was a significant milestone in the history of printing and the spread of literature.
events.name: Printing of the Mainz Psalter

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ujbardha, fought on September 2, 1457, was a significant victory for Skanderbeg against the Ottoman forces. This battle showcased Skanderbeg's military prowess and his ongoing resistance against Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
events.name: Battle of Ujbardha

events.enhanced_description: In 1458, the Jewish community of Erfurt was expelled, leading to the sale of their homes and the conversion of their synagogue into an arsenal. This event reflects the growing anti-Semitic sentiments in Europe during this period.
events.name: Expulsion of the Jewish community from Erfurt

events.enhanced_description: Moctezuma I, the Tlatoani of Tenochtitlán, led an expedition to the Mixtec city-state of Coixtlahuaca in 1458 but faced defeat. This event highlights the challenges faced by the Aztec Empire in consolidating its power over diverse territories.
events.name: Moctezuma I's expedition to Coixtlahuaca

events.enhanced_description: A major volcanic eruption occurred in 531, contributing to climatic changes that would have significant effects on agriculture and society in the years that followed. The specific location of this eruption remains unidentified, but its impact was felt globally.

image.caption: Diagram of a Peléan eruption, showing an ash plume, lava dome, pyroclastic flow, and underlying volcanic structures.
