image.date_qualification: Diagram dated 2007-10-07; it does not establish the date or location of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Major volcanic eruption

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1458, Matthias Corvinus ascended to the throne of Hungary at the young age of 14. His reign would later be marked by significant cultural and military achievements, establishing Hungary as a major power in Central Europe.
events.name: Matthias Corvinus becomes King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: George of Poděbrady was elected King of Bohemia on February 27, 1458. His reign was characterized by efforts to maintain peace and stability in a region marked by religious and political strife.
events.name: George of Poděbrady elected King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1458, The Loveday was staged in London, an event orchestrated by Henry VI to reconcile the warring factions of the Wars of the Roses. This public display aimed to foster unity among the nobles and reduce tensions in the kingdom.
events.name: The Loveday staged in London

events.enhanced_description: In June 1458, Francesco II Acciaioli, the last Duke of Athens, surrendered the city to the Ottoman Empire, leading to Mehmed II's peaceful entry in August. This event marked a significant shift in control over Athens, with the Ottomans issuing decrees to protect its historical sites.
events.name: Surrender of Athens to the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Magdalen College, one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford, was founded on July 15, 1458. It has since become renowned for its academic excellence and beautiful architecture, contributing significantly to the cultural heritage of Oxford.
events.name: Foundation of Magdalen College, Oxford

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1458, Pope Pius II succeeded Callixtus III as the 210th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy was marked by efforts to reform the church and address the challenges posed by the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Pope Pius II succeeds Callixtus III

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1458, King Afonso V of Portugal successfully conquered Ksar es-Seghir in North Africa. This victory was part of Portugal's broader efforts to expand its influence and control in the region during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Afonso V of Portugal conquers Ksar es-Seghir

events.enhanced_description: The Wallachian town of Bucharest was first mentioned in historical records in 1459. This event marks the beginning of Bucharest's significance as a cultural and political center in Romania.
events.name: First mention of Bucharest

events.enhanced_description: In 1459, Rao Jodha founded the city of Jodhpur in western India, which would later become a significant center of trade and culture in the region. The city's establishment marked the rise of the Rathore dynasty in Marwar.
events.name: Foundation of Jodhpur

events.enhanced_description: Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, returned to Ireland in 1459, where the Irish Parliament in Drogheda upheld his authority against King Henry VI. This visit was pivotal in solidifying his political influence in Ireland.
events.name: Richard, Duke of York's second visit to Ireland

events.enhanced_description: In 1459, Richard Hygons began fifty years of service as a composer at Wells Cathedral, contributing to the rich musical heritage of the institution. His long tenure reflects the importance of church music during this period.
events.name: Richard Hygons begins service at Wells Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In 1459, King Thomas of Bosnia forced the clergy of the Bosnian Church into exile, reflecting the ongoing religious tensions and political struggles within the region. This event had lasting implications for the religious landscape of Bosnia.
events.name: King Thomas of Bosnia forces clergy into exile

events.enhanced_description: According to legend, the wedding of Christian Rosenkreuz took place in 1459, symbolizing the union of spiritual and temporal knowledge. This event is often associated with the mystical and esoteric traditions of the time.
events.name: Legendary wedding of Christian Rosenkreuz

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1459, Pope Pius II founded the Order of Our Lady of Bethlehem, aimed at defending the island of Lemnos. This religious order was part of the broader efforts to strengthen Christian presence in the region.
events.name: Foundation of the Order of Our Lady of Bethlehem

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Blore Heath, fought on September 23, 1459, was a decisive engagement in the Wars of the Roses, where the Yorkists, led by Richard Neville, defeated a Lancastrian force. This battle underscored the intense power struggles of the period.
events.name: Battle of Blore Heath

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1459, Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, fled to Ireland as royal forces advanced on his fortress at Ludlow. His ally, Richard Neville, the 16th Earl of Warwick, sought refuge in Calais, highlighting the precarious nature of noble alliances during the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Duke of York flees to Ireland

events.enhanced_description: In 1460, Ali Bey Mihaloğlu successfully captured Michael Szilágyi, a significant event reflecting the ongoing conflicts in the region during this period. The capture underscored the shifting power dynamics in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Ali Bey Mihaloğlu captures Michael Szilágyi

events.enhanced_description: In 1460, Portuguese navigator Pedro de Sintra reached the coast of modern-day Sierra Leone, marking an important moment in the Age of Exploration. This expedition contributed to European knowledge of West Africa and the expansion of trade routes.
events.name: Pedro de Sintra reaches Sierra Leone

events.enhanced_description: In 1460, a severe famine broke out in the Deccan Plateau of India, affecting the agricultural productivity and livelihoods of the local population. This event highlighted the vulnerability of the region to climatic changes and socio-political factors.
events.name: Famine in the Deccan Plateau

events.enhanced_description: In 1460, a monk named Leonardo da Pistoia arrived in Florence from Macedonia, bringing with him the Corpus Hermeticum. This text played a significant role in the Renaissance, influencing philosophical and theological thought in Europe.
events.name: Leonardo da Pistoia arrives in Florence

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1460, King Christian I of Denmark issued the Treaty of Ribe, which allowed him to regain control of the Duchy of Schleswig and solidify his power in the region. This treaty was a significant step in the consolidation of Danish authority.
events.name: Treaty of Ribe issued by King Christian I of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: The University of Basel was founded on April 4, 1460, becoming one of the oldest universities in Switzerland. Its establishment marked a significant advancement in higher education and intellectual discourse in the region.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Basel

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1460, Richard Neville, the Earl of Warwick, and Edward, Earl of March, landed in England with a formidable army, marking a significant moment in the Wars of the Roses. Their march towards London aimed to challenge the Lancastrian rule and assert Yorkist claims to the throne.
events.name: Wars of the Roses: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick and Edward, Earl of March land in England

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1460, the cannons of the Tower of London, still under Lancastrian control, were fired upon the city, which was predominantly held by Yorkists. This act escalated tensions in the ongoing conflict of the Wars of the Roses, leading to the eventual surrender of the Tower on July 19.
events.name: Cannons of the Tower of London fired on the city

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1460, the Battle of Northampton saw Warwick and March decisively defeat a Lancastrian army, capturing King Henry VI of England. This battle was pivotal as it led to the agreement that Richard, Duke of York, would be Henry's heir, sidelining the King's son.
events.name: Battle of Northampton

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1460, King James II of Scotland was killed during a siege of Roxburgh Castle when one of his own cannons exploded. His death marked a significant turning point in Scottish history, leading to a power struggle for the throne.

locations.name: Roxburgh Castle, Kelso, Scottish Borders, Scotland

events.name: Death of King James II of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1460, the Battle of Wakefield resulted in a decisive victory for the Lancastrians, led by Henry Beaufort and Henry Percy, against the Yorkist forces commanded by Richard of York and his son, Edmund. Both York and Edmund were killed, leading to Edward, York's son, rising as the new leader of the Yorkist faction.
events.name: Battle of Wakefield

events.enhanced_description: In July 1461, Byzantine general Graitzas Palaiologos surrendered Salmeniko Castle, the last garrison of the Despotate of the Morea, to Ottoman forces after a year-long siege. This event marked the end of Byzantine resistance in the region.
events.name: Surrender of Salmeniko Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1461, Cirencester Grammar School was founded in southwest England by the Bishop of Durham, marking an important development in the educational landscape of the period.
events.name: Cirencester Grammar School founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1461, renowned artists Leonardo da Vinci and Sandro Botticelli became students of Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence. This mentorship played a crucial role in shaping their artistic careers and the development of Renaissance art.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci and Sandro Botticelli become students of Verrocchio

events.enhanced_description: In 1461, Sarajevo was founded by the Ottomans, laying the groundwork for what would become the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This establishment marked a significant moment in the region's history and Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Foundation of Sarajevo

events.enhanced_description: In 1461, the French poet François Villon wrote Le Grand Testament, a significant work that reflects the social and political issues of his time. This poem is considered one of the masterpieces of French literature.
events.name: François Villon writes Le Grand Testament

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1461, the Battle of Mortimer's Cross took place, where Yorkist troops led by Edward, Duke of York, defeated Lancastrians under Owen Tudor and his son Jasper Tudor. This victory was crucial in solidifying Yorkist power in the ongoing Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Battle of Mortimer's Cross

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1461, the Second Battle of St Albans occurred, where the Earl of Warwick's forces were defeated by a Lancastrian army led by Queen Margaret. This battle allowed Margaret to regain control for her husband, King Henry VI.

image.caption: Map for the Second Battle of St Albans by James Henry Ramsay.

image.date_qualification: 1889; retrospective map of the 1461 battle
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Second Battle of St Albans

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1461, the Duke of York seized London and proclaimed himself King Edward IV of England. This bold move was a critical step in the Yorkist claim to the throne during the tumultuous Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Duke of York proclaims himself King Edward IV

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1461, Henry VI of England was deposed by Edward, Duke of York, marking a pivotal moment in the Wars of the Roses. This event solidified Edward's claim to the throne and shifted the balance of power in England.

image.caption: Illuminated miniature depicting Henry VI of England.

events.name: Henry VI of England is deposed

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1461, the Battle of Towton was fought, where Edward IV's forces defeated Queen Margaret's Lancastrians. This battle is considered one of the bloodiest in English history and was crucial in securing Edward's claim to the throne.
events.name: Battle of Towton

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1461, Edward IV, son of Richard of York, was crowned King of England. His ascension marked a significant shift in the power dynamics of the Wars of the Roses, as he established Yorkist rule.
events.name: Edward IV crowned King of England

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1461, Stephen Tomašević was crowned as the last King of Bosnia in Saint Mary's Church, Jajce, following the death of his father, Stephen Thomas. His reign marked the end of the Bosnian kingdom as it faced increasing pressure from the Ottoman Empire.

locations.name: Jajce, Central Bosnia, Bosnia and Herzegovina

events.name: Stephen Tomašević becomes the last King of Bosnia

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1461, Louis XI succeeded Charles VII as King of France, beginning a reign that would last until 1483. His rule was marked by efforts to strengthen the monarchy and centralize power in France.
events.name: Louis XI of France succeeds Charles VII

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1461, military general Cao Qin staged a coup against the Tianshun Emperor in the Imperial City of Beijing. The uprising ended in failure, leading to Cao's suicide, marking a turbulent period in the Ming Dynasty.
events.name: Coup against the Tianshun Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1461, the Empire of Trebizond fell to the Ottoman Empire under Mehmed II after a 21-day siege. This event marked the end of the last major Romano-Greek outpost and expanded Ottoman control in the region.

image.caption: Banner of the Empire of Trebizond.

image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fall of the Empire of Trebizond

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1461, a severe earthquake struck L'Aquila, causing significant destruction and loss of life. This natural disaster highlighted the geological vulnerabilities of the region.
events.name: 1461 L'Aquila earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In 1462, the Jewish community was expelled from Mainz, Germany, a significant event reflecting the growing anti-Semitic sentiments in Europe during this period. This expulsion was part of a broader trend of persecution against Jews in various regions.
events.name: Expulsion of Jews from Mainz

events.enhanced_description: In 1462, Portugal began settling the Cape Verde Islands, utilizing enslaved individuals from the coast of Guinea. This marked a significant step in the Portuguese exploration and colonization efforts in the Atlantic.
events.name: Settlement of Cape Verde Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1462, during the War of the Roses, the Yorkists defeated the Lancastrians at the Battle of Piltown in Ireland. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the two factions vying for control of the English throne.
events.name: Battle of Piltown

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1462, Ivan III ascended to the throne of Russia following the death of his father, Vasili II. His reign marked the beginning of the centralization of power in Russia and the expansion of its territories.
events.name: Ivan III of Russia becomes the ruler of Russia

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1462, Vlad III Dracula launched a surprise night attack against the Ottoman forces led by Mehmed II, forcing them to retreat from Wallachia. This bold maneuver showcased Vlad's tactical prowess and his fierce resistance against Ottoman expansion.
events.name: The Night Attack

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1462, Frederick I, Elector Palatine, achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Seckenheim against four opposing factions. This battle solidified his power in the region and demonstrated the ongoing conflicts of the time.
events.name: Battle of Seckenheim

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1462, Stephen the Great's first siege of Chilia ended in failure, resulting in serious injuries for the Moldavian ruler. This event highlighted the ongoing struggles for control in the region during the conflicts with the Ottomans.
events.name: First siege of Chilia

events.enhanced_description: In September 1462, Mehmed II successfully captured the town of Mytilene, thus conquering the island of Lesbos. This event was part of the Ottoman Empire's broader campaign to expand its territory in the Aegean Sea.

image.caption: Fortress of Mytilini, the Gattilusi palace.
image.credit: Katsiaryna Naliuka — Own work
image.date_qualification: Site photograph dated 2012-04-25; the conquest took place in September 1462.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Siege of Mytilene

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1462, during the Thirteen Years' War, the Kingdom of Poland achieved a significant victory over the Teutonic Order at the Battle of Świecino. This battle was pivotal in shifting the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Świecino

events.enhanced_description: In December 1462, after Radu III the Fair took the throne in Wallachia, Vlad III Dracula sought assistance in Transylvania but was captured by Mathias Corvinus. He was imprisoned for twelve years on false charges of treason, marking a significant turn in his tumultuous reign.
events.name: Vlad III Dracula seeks help in Transylvania

events.enhanced_description: In May 1463, the Kingdom of Bosnia fell to the Ottoman Empire, marking a significant expansion of Ottoman control in the Balkans. This event was part of the broader Ottoman conquests during this period.
events.name: Fall of the Kingdom of Bosnia

events.enhanced_description: In 1463, Muhammad Rumfa began his rule in Kano, a significant city in the Hausa Kingdoms of Nigeria. His reign is noted for its contributions to trade and Islamic scholarship in the region.
events.name: Muhammad Rumfa starts to rule in Kano

events.enhanced_description: In 1463, Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin, making this important work of Hermetic philosophy accessible to a wider audience in Renaissance Europe. This translation played a crucial role in the revival of interest in ancient philosophical texts.

image.caption: Title page of the first Latin edition of the Corpus Hermeticum, translated by Marsilio Ficino.
image.credit: Marsilio Ficino — https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6179873
image.date_qualification: The title page documents the Latin edition, not the 1463 translation event itself; the saved image date is 1471-12-18.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Translation of Corpus Hermeticum

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1463, the French poet François Villon received a reprieve from death by hanging and was subsequently banished from Paris. His life after this event remains undocumented, adding to the mystery surrounding his legacy.
events.name: François Villon receives a reprieve

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1463, the navy of the Prussian Confederation achieved a decisive victory over the Teutonic Order at the Battle of Vistula Lagoon. This battle was crucial in the ongoing conflict between these two powers.
events.name: Battle of Vistula Lagoon

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1463, the Truce of Hesdin marked the end of French support for the House of Lancaster in England. This political shift had significant implications for the ongoing War of the Roses.
events.name: Truce of Hesdin

events.enhanced_description: In 1464, a small rebellion occurred in Huguang during the Ming Dynasty, followed by a larger uprising in Guangxi involving the Miao and Yao peoples. The Ming throne responded by dispatching 30,000 troops to quell the unrest, which would continue until 1466.
events.name: Rebellion in Huguang and Guangxi, China

events.enhanced_description: Jehan Lagadeuc authored the 'Catholicon', a pioneering dictionary that served as the first comprehensive reference for the Breton language, alongside French and Latin. This work marked a significant milestone in the preservation and promotion of the Breton language and culture.
events.name: Jehan Lagadeuc writes a Breton-French-Latin dictionary called the Catholicon

events.enhanced_description: Tenguella, a prominent leader, ascended to the position of chief of the Fula people, laying the groundwork for the establishment of the Empire of Great Fulo. His leadership was pivotal in unifying various Fula clans and initiating a period of expansion and influence.
events.name: Tenguella becomes chief of the Fula people

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1464, the Yorkist forces under John Neville defeated the Lancastrians led by Sir Ralph Percy at the Battle of Hedgeley Moor. This battle was significant in the ongoing conflict of the War of the Roses.
events.name: Battle of Hedgeley Moor

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1464, Edward IV of England secretly married Elizabeth Woodville, a union that would have significant political implications during the War of the Roses. The marriage was kept secret for five months, reflecting the tumultuous nature of the period.
events.name: Edward IV secretly marries Elizabeth Woodville

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1464, the Battle of Hexham saw John Neville defeat a Lancastrian army led by King Henry VI and Queen Margaret. This battle marked a significant decline in organized Lancastrian resistance during the War of the Roses.
events.name: Battle of Hexham

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1464, Pope Pius II took up the cross for the Crusades and departed for Ancona, appointing Skanderbeg as general captain of the Holy See. This marked a significant moment in the papacy's involvement in military campaigns against the Ottomans.
events.name: Pope Pius II shoulders the cross of the Crusades

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1464, Christian I of Denmark and Norway was declared deposed from the throne of Sweden, leading to the re-election of his predecessor Charles VIII. This political shift was part of the ongoing power struggles in the Nordic region.
events.name: Christian I of Denmark and Norway is deposed as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1464, Emperor Go-Hanazono of Japan abdicated the throne, passing the imperial authority to his son, Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Japanese imperial line.
events.name: Emperor Go-Hanazono abdicates

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1464, Pope Paul II succeeded Pope Pius II as the 211th pope of the Roman Catholic Church. His papacy would be marked by various political and religious challenges.
events.name: Pope Paul II succeeds Pope Pius II

events.enhanced_description: In 1465, central and southern China experienced massive flooding that prompted the initial construction of hundreds of new bridges. This disaster highlighted the need for improved infrastructure and disaster management in the region.
events.name: Massive flooding in central and southern China

events.enhanced_description: In 1465, the main altar of St Martin's Church in Colmar was completed by painter Caspar Isenmann. This work is notable for its artistic significance and reflects the rich cultural heritage of the region during the late Gothic period.
events.name: The main altar of St Martin's Church, Colmar is finished

events.enhanced_description: In 1465, Kerei Khan and Janibek Khan founded the Kazakh Khanate, establishing a significant political entity in Central Asia. This khanate played a crucial role in the history of the region, influencing trade and cultural exchanges.
events.name: The Kazakh Khanate is founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1465, Stephen the Great of Moldavia successfully captured Chilia after a second siege, reinforcing Moldavia's strategic position along the Black Sea. This victory was part of Stephen's broader campaign to secure and expand his territory against external threats.
events.name: Chilia is conquered by Stephen the Great of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: Amadeus IX ascended to the title of Duke of Savoy on January 29, 1465, marking a significant moment in the history of the region. His reign would be characterized by efforts to strengthen the duchy's political and economic standing in Northern Italy.

image.caption: Fresco portrait of Amadeus IX, Duke of Savoy, attributed to Antoine de Lonhy, at San Domenico church in Turin.
image.credit: Laurom — Own work
image.date_qualification: Fresco dated after 1474; image_date records 2005-01 and is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Amadeus IX becomes Duke of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1465, Charles VIII of Sweden was deposed, leading to Kettil Karlsson Vasa assuming the regency. This political upheaval was part of the ongoing power struggles in Sweden during the Kalmar Union period.

image.caption: Photograph of Karl Knutsson Bonde’s grave effigy at Riddarholm Church, sculpted by Lucas van der Werdt.

events.name: Charles VIII of Sweden is deposed

events.enhanced_description: In March 1465, Elizabeth Woodville played a crucial role in the refounding of Queens' College, Cambridge, which had significant implications for women's education in England. This act symbolized the growing importance of education and the role of women in the academic sphere.
events.name: Queens' College, Cambridge is refounded by Elizabeth Woodville

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1465, the Moroccan Revolt erupted in Fez, resulting in the ousting of the Maranid rulers and leading to widespread violence, including the tragic killing of many Jews. This revolt marked a significant turning point in Moroccan history, leading to changes in governance and social dynamics.
events.name: The Moroccan Revolt in Fez

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1465, Elizabeth Woodville was crowned Queen consort of Edward IV in a grand ceremony at Westminster Abbey. This event solidified her position in the English court and marked a significant moment in the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Elizabeth Woodville is crowned Queen consort of Edward IV

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1465, the Battle of Montlhéry took place, where troops loyal to King Louis XI of France clashed with a coalition of nobles organized as the League of the Public Weal. The battle ended inconclusively, reflecting the ongoing tensions between the monarchy and the nobility.
events.name: Battle of Montlhéry

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1465, former King Henry VI of England was captured by Yorkist forces, marking a pivotal moment in the Wars of the Roses. Following his capture, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London, while his queen consort and son fled to France.
events.name: Former King Henry VI of England is captured

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1465, Kettil Karlsson Vasa was succeeded as Regent of Sweden by Jöns Bengtsson Oxenstierna. This transition marked a significant shift in the governance of Sweden during a tumultuous period of political instability.
events.name: Kettil Karlsson Vasa succeeded by Jöns Bengtsson Oxenstierna

events.enhanced_description: In 1466, the Kingdom of Georgia began to fragment into rival states, including Kartli, Kakheti, and Imereti, leading to a period of anarchy. This disintegration was finalized in 1490 when the monarch recognized the independence of these rival principalities.
events.name: The Kingdom of Georgia collapses into anarchy

events.enhanced_description: In 1466, the Mentelin Bible was produced, marking the first printed Bible in the German language. This significant work contributed to the spread of literacy and the Reformation in the German-speaking regions.
events.name: The Mentelin Bible is produced

events.enhanced_description: In 1466, Louis XI of France introduced silk weaving to Lyon, transforming the city into a major center for silk production. This initiative not only boosted the local economy but also enhanced Lyon's reputation in the textile industry.
events.name: Louis XI of France introduces silk weaving to Lyon

events.enhanced_description: In 1466, the first known shop specializing in eyeglasses opened in Strasbourg, marking a significant advancement in optical science and accessibility. This development reflected the growing importance of vision correction in society.
events.name: The first known shop specialising in eyeglasses opens in Strasbourg

events.enhanced_description: In 1466, Meister Goswin aus Fritzlar cast the second largest bell for Saint Peter's Church in Fritzlar. This bell became an important symbol of the church and showcased the craftsmanship of the period.
events.name: The second largest bell of Saint Peter's Church is cast

events.enhanced_description: In 1467, the Third Siege of Krujë was launched by Mehmed II, marking another unsuccessful attempt by the Ottomans to conquer Albania. This siege was part of the larger conflict between the Ottoman Empire and Albanian resistance led by Skanderbeg.
events.name: Third Siege of Krujë

events.enhanced_description: The Ōnin War, which marks the beginning of the Sengoku period in Japan, starts in Kyoto. This conflict arises from a power struggle between rival factions of the Ashikaga shogunate, leading to widespread civil war and social upheaval across the country.
events.name: The Ōnin War begins

events.enhanced_description: While Hassan III of the Maldives is on Hajj, Sayyidh Muhammad seizes the opportunity to depose his son, who is acting as regent. Upon Hassan's return, he successfully regains the throne, highlighting the political instability of the time.
events.name: Sayyidh Muhammad deposes Hassan III

events.enhanced_description: In Rome, Pope Paul II orders the arrest and torture of several papal abbreviators, including Filippo Buonaccorsi. This event reflects the tense atmosphere of the papacy during this period, marked by political intrigue and power struggles.
events.name: Arrests of papal abbreviators

events.enhanced_description: King Matthias Corvinus establishes the Universitas Istropolitana in Bratislava, marking the first university in Slovakia. This institution becomes a significant center for education and culture in the region.
events.name: Foundation of Universitas Istropolitana

events.enhanced_description: Leon Battista Alberti invents the first European polyalphabetic cipher, a significant advancement in cryptography. This invention allows for more secure communication, influencing the development of secret writing.
events.name: Invention of the polyalphabetic cipher

events.enhanced_description: Juan de Torquemada publishes his influential work, Meditationes, seu Contemplationes devotissimae. This book contributes to the spiritual and philosophical discourse of the time.
events.name: Publication of Meditationes

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1467, Philip the Good passed away and was succeeded by his son Charles the Bold as Duke of Burgundy. This transition marked a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region, as Charles sought to expand his territories.
events.name: Philip the Good is succeeded as Duke of Burgundy by Charles the Bold

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1467, the Battle of Brustem occurred, where Charles the Bold led his forces to a decisive victory against the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Burgundian state and the local principalities.
events.name: Battle of Brustem

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1467, the Battle of Chapakchur took place, where Uzun Hasan defeated Jahan Shah. This battle was significant in the context of the power struggles in Persia and the rise of the Aq Qoyunlu dynasty.
events.name: Battle of Chapakchur

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1467, Regent Erik Axelsson Tott publicly supported the re-election of the deposed Charles VIII of Sweden. This act was part of the ongoing political turmoil and factional struggles within Sweden during the Kalmar Union.
events.name: Regent Erik Axelsson Tott supports Charles VIII's re-election

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1467, the Battle of Baia saw Stephen III of Moldavia decisively defeat the forces of Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary. This battle marked the end of Hungarian attempts to dominate Moldavia and solidified Stephen's reputation as a formidable leader.

image.caption: Relief map of Romania.
image.credit: Nzeemin — ETOPO for Relief and bathymetry GSHHS dataset for rivers and coastline File:Romania location map.svg for borders Own work This PNG graphic was created with Inkscape .
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2012-09-16; not contemporary to the 1467 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Baia

events.enhanced_description: After a seven-year siege, the Lancastrians surrender Harlech Castle to King Edward IV of England. This event marks a significant victory for the Yorkists in the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Surrender of Harlech Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Great Council of the Republic of Venice enacts legislation aimed at curbing the power of the Council of Ten, restricting their authority to emergency matters. This reflects ongoing tensions within the Venetian government.
events.name: Great Council of Venice legislation

events.enhanced_description: Christian I of Norway pledges Orkney as security for the dowry of his daughter Margaret, who is betrothed to James III of Scotland. The failure to pay the dowry leads to a lasting connection between Orkney and the Scottish crown.
events.name: Pledge of Orkney

events.enhanced_description: A fire breaks out at Metz Cathedral in France, causing significant damage to this historic structure. The incident highlights the vulnerabilities of medieval architecture to disasters.
events.name: Fire at Metz Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: Sonni Ali, the king of the Songhai Empire, takes control of Timbuktu, a vital center of trade and culture in West Africa. His reign marks a significant expansion of the empire's influence and power.
events.name: Sonni Ali takes power over Timbuktu

events.enhanced_description: Catherine Cornaro is married by proxy to James II of Cyprus in Venice, initiating the Venetian conquest of Cyprus. This marriage strengthens Venetian influence in the region and sets the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Marriage by proxy of Catherine Cornaro

events.enhanced_description: Baeda Maryam ascends to the throne of Ethiopia, succeeding his father Zara Yaqob. His reign continues the legacy of his father's efforts to strengthen the Ethiopian Empire.
events.name: Baeda Maryam succeeds Zara Yaqob

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Péronne is signed between Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and Louis XI of France. This treaty aims to resolve ongoing conflicts and territorial disputes between the two powers.
events.name: Treaty of Péronne signed

events.enhanced_description: Troops of Charles the Bold conduct the Sack of Liège, a brutal attack that devastates the city. This event exemplifies the violent power struggles of the time and the harsh realities of medieval warfare.
events.name: Sack of Liège

events.enhanced_description: Sigismund of Austria sells Upper-Elsass to Charles the Bold in exchange for military support against the Swiss. This transaction illustrates the complex political alliances and conflicts of the time.
events.name: Sale of Upper-Elsass to Charles the Bold

events.enhanced_description: Moctezuma I, the ruler of the Aztec Empire, dies and is succeeded by his son Axayacatl. This transition of power marks a significant moment in the history of the Aztec civilization.
events.name: Death of Moctezuma I

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Hanseatic War erupts, marking a significant conflict between England and the Hanseatic League. This war reflects the growing tensions over trade and maritime dominance in Northern Europe.
events.name: Anglo-Hanseatic War breaks out

events.enhanced_description: Marsilio Ficino completes his translation of Plato's works and writes a commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love, while also beginning his work on Platonic Theology. His contributions significantly influence Renaissance thought.
events.name: Marsilio Ficino's works

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Qarabagh, Uzun Hasan decisively defeats the Timurids led by Abu Sa'id Mirza. This victory solidifies Uzun Hasan's power and influence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Qarabagh

events.enhanced_description: Caister Castle is besieged by John de Mowbray, 4th Duke of Norfolk, during the summer months. This siege reflects the ongoing conflicts and power struggles among the nobility in England.
figures: John de Mowbray, 4th Duke of Norfolk
events.name: Siege of Caister Castle

events.enhanced_description: During the Battle of Edgcote, the Yorkists are defeated, and King Edward IV of England is taken prisoner. This battle represents a critical moment in the Wars of the Roses, shifting the balance of power.
events.name: Battle of Edgcote

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand II of Aragon marries Isabella I of Castile in Valladolid, creating a powerful dynastic union that lays the groundwork for the unification of Spain. This marriage significantly impacts the political landscape of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Marriage of Ferdinand II and Isabella I

events.enhanced_description: In 1470, the Pahang Sultanate was established in Pahang Darul Makmur, modern-day Malaysia. This marked the rise of a significant Malay sultanate that would play a crucial role in regional trade and politics.
events.name: Establishment of the Pahang Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1470, the first contact occurred between Europeans and the Fante nation of the Gold Coast when a party of Portuguese navigators met with the King of Elmina. This meeting marked the beginning of significant European involvement in West African trade.
events.name: First contact between Europeans and the Fante nation

events.enhanced_description: In 1470, Johann Heynlin introduced the printing press into France, marking a pivotal moment in the spread of knowledge and literature in the region. His first book printed this year contributed to the burgeoning Renaissance culture.
events.name: Johann Heynlin introduces the printing press into France

events.enhanced_description: In or around 1470, the Tuʻi Tonga Dynasty ceded its temporal powers to the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua Dynasty in Tonga. This transition marked a significant change in the political landscape of the islands, influencing governance for the next century.
events.name: Tuʻi Tonga Dynasty cedes powers

events.enhanced_description: Between 1470 and 1700, a total of 8,888 witches were tried in the Swiss Confederation, with 5,417 executions recorded. This period highlights the intense fear and superstition surrounding witchcraft in Europe during the late medieval period.
events.name: Witch trials in the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: In 1470, Sir George Ripley dedicated his book, The Compound of Alchemy, to King Edward IV of England. This dedication reflects the intersection of alchemical studies and royal patronage during the Renaissance.
events.name: Sir George Ripley dedicates his book

events.enhanced_description: In 1470, the Chimor–Inca War concluded with an Inca victory, resulting in the absorption of the Chimor Empire into the Inca Empire. This victory significantly expanded Inca territory and influence in South America.
events.name: Chimor–Inca War ends

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Losecoat Field, the House of York defeats the House of Lancaster, continuing the violent struggle for the English throne during the Wars of the Roses. This battle further shifts the balance of power in favor of the Yorkists.
events.name: Battle of Losecoat Field

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Nibley Green is fought, marking the last engagement between the private armies of feudal magnates in England. This battle signifies the decline of feudal warfare as centralized power begins to rise.

image.caption: View toward Nibley Green from the Tyndale Monument on Nibley Knoll.
image.credit: Dr Duncan Pepper ; cropped by Lobsterthermidor at en.wikipedia — From geograph.org.uk
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2010-06-18; this is a later view of the battle site, not an image of the 1470 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Nibley Green

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1470, privateers from the Hanseatic League set sail during the Anglo-Hanseatic War, a conflict primarily driven by trade disputes and territorial control in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. This marked a significant escalation in hostilities between England and the Hanseatic merchants.
events.name: Spring: Anglo-Hanseatic War: Hanseatic League privateers set sail

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1470, Charles VIII of Sweden died after serving three terms as king. His death led to Sten Sture the Elder proclaiming himself Regent of Sweden the following day, marking a significant shift in Swedish governance.

image.caption: Grave effigy of Charles VIII of Sweden, sculpted by Lucas van der Werdt, at Riddarholm Church in Stockholm.

events.name: Death of Charles VIII of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1470, Sten Sture the Elder was officially recognized as the ruler of Sweden by the estates, solidifying his power following the death of Charles VIII. This recognition marked the beginning of a new political era in Sweden.
events.name: Sten Sture recognized as Swedish ruler

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1470, the Ottoman Empire successfully captured the island of Euboea, a strategic location in the Aegean Sea. This event was part of the Ottomans' broader campaign to expand their influence in the region.
events.name: Ottomans capture Euboea

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1470, Stephen the Great of Moldavia achieved a significant victory against the Volga Tatars of the Golden Horde, led by Ahmed Khan, at the Battle of Lipnic. This battle reinforced Stephen's reputation as a formidable leader in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Lipnic

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1470, a rebellion led by Richard Neville, the 16th Earl of Warwick, forced King Edward IV of England to flee the country. This rebellion was a pivotal moment in the Wars of the Roses, showcasing the shifting allegiances among the English nobility.
events.name: Richard Neville's rebellion against Edward IV

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1470, Richard Neville released Henry VI of England from the Tower of London, restoring him to the throne. This act marked a significant turn in the ongoing power struggles of the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Henry VI restored to the throne

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1470, Emperor Lê Thánh Tông of Đại Việt launched a naval expedition against the Champa kingdom, marking the beginning of the Cham–Annamese War. This conflict would significantly alter the political landscape of Southeast Asia.
events.name: Cham–Annamese War begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1470, Lê Thánh Tông led the Đại Việt army into Champa, conquering the territory in less than three months. This rapid conquest expanded the influence of Đại Việt and diminished the Champa kingdom.
events.name: Lê Thánh Tông conquers Champa

events.enhanced_description: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, a transformative ruler of the Inca Empire, died in 1471 and was succeeded by his son Topa Inca Yupanqui. Pachacuti is credited with expanding the empire significantly and establishing its administrative structure.

image.caption: Map showing the expansion of the Inca Empire with present-day borders.
image.credit: QQuantum — Own work
image.date_qualification: The map covers 1438–1533 CE; the supplied image date is 2018-03-12, not the date of the depicted historical events.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui

events.enhanced_description: In 1471, Moorish exiles from Spain, led by Moulay Ali Ben Moussa Ben Rached El Alami, founded the city of Chefchaouen in northern Morocco. The city became a refuge for those fleeing the Reconquista and is known for its distinctive blue-washed buildings.
figures: Moulay Ali Ben Moussa Ben Rached El Alami
events.name: Founding of Chefchaouen

events.enhanced_description: In 1471, Marsilio Ficino published his Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, a collection of writings that would significantly influence Renaissance thought and the revival of interest in ancient philosophies.
events.name: Publication of Corpus Hermeticum

events.enhanced_description: In 1471, the world population is estimated to have reached 500 million, marking a significant milestone in human demographic history. This population growth was influenced by various factors, including agricultural advancements and the expansion of trade.
events.name: World population reaches 500 million

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1471, Portuguese forces occupied Tangier after the city's population fled, marking a significant moment in the Portuguese expansion along the North African coast. This occupation was part of a broader strategy to control trade routes and establish a foothold in the region.
events.name: The Portuguese occupy Tangier

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1471, the Battle of Brunkeberg took place in Stockholm, where the forces of Regent Sten Sture the Elder, supported by local farmers and miners, successfully repelled an attack by Christian I, King of Denmark. This battle was pivotal in asserting Swedish independence from Danish rule.
events.name: Battle of Brunkeberg

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1471, Portuguese navigators João de Santarém and Pedro Escobar discovered the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, which would later become significant for the Portuguese sugar trade and colonial expansion in Africa.

locations.name: São Tomé, São Tomé and Príncipe

events.name: Discovery of São Tomé and Príncipe

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, 20-year-old Leonardo da Vinci was admitted as a master in his own right to the artists' Guild of Saint Luke in Florence. This recognition marked the beginning of his formal career as an artist and contributed to his later success.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci admitted to Guild of Saint Luke

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, the Wattasid dynasty founded the Kingdom of Fez, with Sultan Abu Abd Allah al-Sheikh Muhammad ibn Yahya as its first ruler. This kingdom played a crucial role in the political landscape of Morocco during the late 15th century.
figures: Abu Abd Allah al-Sheikh Muhammad ibn Yahya
events.name: Founding of the Kingdom of Fez

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, an extensive slave trade began in modern Cameroon as Portuguese sailors navigated up the Wouri River. This marked the beginning of a dark chapter in the region's history, contributing to the transatlantic slave trade.
events.name: Slave trade begins in Cameroon

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, Fernão do Pó claimed the central-African islands of Bioko and Annobón for Portugal. This claim was part of Portugal's broader efforts to explore and colonize territories along the African coast.
events.name: Claim of Bioko and Annobón for Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, João Vaz Corte-Real possibly discovered the island of Bacalao, which is believed to be Newfoundland off the coast of North America. This event is significant in the context of early European exploration of the Americas.
events.name: Possible discovery of Bacalao

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, the first printing of Thomas à Kempis' The Imitation of Christ was likely completed posthumously in Augsburg. This work became one of the most widely read Christian texts, reaching 100 editions and translations by the end of the century.
events.name: First printing of The Imitation of Christ

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, Johannes de Sacrobosco's De sphaera mundi, the first printed astronomical book, was published in Ferrara. This work played a crucial role in the education of astronomy during the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication of De sphaera mundi

events.enhanced_description: In 1472, Pietro d'Abano's medical texts Conciliator differentiarum quae inter philosophos et medicos versantur and De venenis eorumque remediis were first published. These texts contributed to the understanding of medicine and philosophy in the medieval period.
events.name: Publication of Pietro d'Abano's medical texts

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1472, the islands of Orkney and Shetland were returned to Scotland from Norway due to a defaulted dowry payment. This event marked a significant shift in territorial control in the North Sea region.
events.name: Return of Orkney and Shetland to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1472, a mount of piety was established in Siena, which later evolved into Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, recognized as the world's oldest surviving retail bank. This institution played a crucial role in the development of banking in Europe.

image.caption: Photograph of Palazzo Salimbeni, which houses the main offices of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena.
image.credit: . Ray in Manila — https://www.flickr.com/photos/rayinmanila/51707894733/
image.date_qualification: Photograph uploaded 26 November 2021; this is an upload date, not a verified date the photograph was taken.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Mount of Piety in Siena

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1472, the first printed edition of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy was published in Foligno, marking a significant moment in the history of literature and the dissemination of classical texts during the Renaissance.

image.caption: Title page of the first printed edition of Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy.
image.credit: Alighieri, Dante — Available in the BEIC digital library and uploaded in partnership with BEIC Foundation .
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies this as the first edition; the article excerpt dates that edition to 1472. No specific depicted day is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First printed edition of Divine Comedy

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1472, the Cathedral and Metropolitical Church of Saint Peter in York, commonly known as York Minster, was declared complete and consecrated. This Gothic cathedral is one of the largest in Northern Europe and a significant religious site.
events.name: Completion of York Minster

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1472, the city council of Amsterdam enacted a prohibition against snowball fights, reflecting the social norms and regulations of the time. This unusual law highlights the city's governance and community standards.
events.name: Amsterdam prohibits snowball fights

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, Stephen the Great of Moldavia refused to pay tribute to the Ottomans, a defiance that would lead to an Ottoman invasion in 1475. This act of resistance is celebrated in Moldavian history as a symbol of national pride.
events.name: Stephen the Great refuses tribute to Ottomans

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, Axayacatl, the ruler of Tenochtitlan, launched a military campaign against the neighboring city-state of Tlatelolco. The invasion resulted in the death of Tlatelolco's ruler and the loss of its independence, marking a significant expansion of Aztec power in the region.

image.caption: Map showing the expansions undertaken by various Aztec rulers.
image.credit: enwiki/Maunus — en wiki http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image:Aztecexpansion.png
image.date_qualification: Map image dated 2006-08-26; it is a modern map, not a contemporary image of the 1473 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Axayacatl invades Tlatelolco

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, explorers Didrik Pining and João Vaz Corte-Real are believed to have discovered the island of Bacalao, which is thought to be present-day Newfoundland. This event is significant as it represents early European exploration of North America.

locations.name: 50 miles off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada

events.name: Discovery of Bacalao

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, the city walls and defensive moat were constructed in Celje, Slovenia, enhancing the city's fortifications. This development reflects the growing importance of urban defense during the late Middle Ages.
events.name: Construction of city walls in Celje

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, the Almanach cracoviense ad annum 1474 was published in Kraków, marking the oldest known printing in Poland. This astronomical wall calendar reflects the advancements in printing technology and the dissemination of knowledge during the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication of Almanach cracoviense

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, the influential Florentine physician and philosopher Marsilio Ficino was ordained as a Catholic priest. His work in philosophy and the revival of Platonic thought significantly impacted the Renaissance intellectual landscape.
events.name: Marsilio Ficino becomes a priest

events.enhanced_description: In 1473, William Caxton printed the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye in Bruges, marking it as the first book printed in English. This event is pivotal in the history of English literature and the spread of printed works.
events.name: First book printed in English

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1473, the first complete edition of Avicenna's The Canon of Medicine, translated into Latin, was published in Milan. This work became a cornerstone of medical education in Europe for centuries.
events.name: Publication of Avicenna's The Canon of Medicine

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1473, the Battle of Otlukbeli occurred, where Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II defeated the White Sheep Turkmens led by Uzun Hasan. This victory solidified Ottoman control over eastern Anatolia.
events.name: Battle of Otlukbeli

events.enhanced_description: In 1474, Marsilio Ficino completed his influential work, Theologia Platonica (Platonic Theology). This text played a crucial role in the revival of Platonic thought during the Renaissance and influenced many subsequent philosophers.
events.name: Marsilio Ficino completes Theologia Platonica

events.enhanced_description: In 1474, Axayacatl led a successful military campaign against the Matlatzinca people of the Toluca Valley. This victory further solidified the Aztec Empire's dominance in central Mexico.
events.name: Axayacatl defeats Matlatzinca

events.enhanced_description: In February 1474, the Treaty of Utrecht was signed, bringing an end to the Anglo-Hanseatic War. This treaty marked a significant diplomatic resolution between England and the Hanseatic League.
events.name: Treaty of Utrecht ends Anglo-Hanseatic War

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1474, the Senate of the Republic of Venice enacted the Venetian Patent Statute, establishing one of the earliest patent systems in the world. This legislation laid the groundwork for modern intellectual property rights.
events.name: Venetian Patent Statute enacted

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Henry IV of Castile on December 12, 1474, a civil war erupted between his designated successor, Isabella I of Castile, and her niece Juana, who was supported by Afonso V of Portugal. Isabella ultimately triumphed, solidifying her power and paving the way for the unification of Spain.
events.name: Civil War in Castile

events.enhanced_description: In 1475, Rashi's commentary on the Torah became the first dated book to be printed in Hebrew, in Reggio di Calabria. This publication marked a significant milestone in Jewish literature and the history of printing.
events.name: First book printed in Hebrew

events.enhanced_description: In 1475, Conrad of Megenberg published his book, Buch der Natur, in Augsburg. This work is notable for its early contributions to natural history and reflects the growing interest in scientific inquiry during the Renaissance.
events.name: Publication of Buch der Natur

events.enhanced_description: In 1475, Radu cel Frumos lost the throne of Wallachia for the last time, being replaced by Basarab Laiotă. This political shift was part of the ongoing power struggles in the region during the late 15th century.
events.name: Radu cel Frumos loses throne

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1475, the Battle of Vaslui took place, where Stephen III of Moldavia achieved a significant victory against the Ottoman Empire, led by Mehmed II. This battle is noted for its strategic importance in the Moldavian resistance against Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Battle of Vaslui

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1475, Edward IV of England landed in Calais, France, to support the Duchy of Burgundy against France during the Burgundian Wars. This military action was part of the broader conflict between England and France.

image.caption: Posthumous portrait of Edward IV.
image.credit: Lucas Horenbout — Scanned from Hearn, Karen, ed. Dynasties: Painting in Tudor and Jacobean England 1530-1630 . New York: Rizzoli, 1995. ISBN 0-8478-1940-X .
image.date_qualification: Posthumous portrait, circa 1520; source notes an original circa 1470–1475. Not an event-date image.
image.image_date: circa 1520 date QS:P,+1520-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902 , posthumous portrait from original circa 1470-1475
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Edward IV lands in Calais

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1475, the Treaty of Picquigny was signed, officially ending the brief war between France and England. This treaty marked a significant moment in Anglo-French relations during the late 15th century.
events.name: Treaty of Picquigny

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1475, during the Burgundian Wars, the forces of the Old Swiss Confederacy achieved a decisive victory against the Duchy of Savoy near Sion, Switzerland. This battle underscored the military prowess of the Swiss and their resistance against Burgundian expansion.
events.name: Battle on the Planta

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1475, the original Landshut Wedding took place between George, Duke of Bavaria, and Hedwig Jagiellon. This event was not only a significant political alliance but also a grand cultural celebration that showcased the opulence of the time.
events.name: Landshut Wedding

events.enhanced_description: In December 1475, the Principality of Theodoro fell to the Ottoman Empire, marking the end of a significant remnant of Roman civilization after nearly 2,228 years. This event symbolized the decline of Christian states in the region and the rise of Ottoman power.
events.name: Fall of the Principality of Theodoro

events.enhanced_description: In 1476, Leonardo da Vinci was acquitted of charges of sodomy, a serious accusation in Renaissance Florence. Following his acquittal, he vanished from the historical record for two years, a period that remains largely mysterious and has led to much speculation about his activities during that time.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci acquitted of sodomy charges

events.enhanced_description: In 1476, Axayacatl, the sixth Tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, faced a significant defeat against the Tarascans of Michoacán. This battle highlighted the challenges faced by the Aztec Empire in maintaining control over its territories and the rising power of the Tarascan state.
events.name: Defeat of Axayacatl by the Tarascans

events.enhanced_description: In 1476, the Goyghor Mosque was constructed by Musa ibn Haji Amir and his son, Majlis Alam. This mosque is a notable example of Islamic architecture in the region and reflects the cultural and religious influences present during that period.
events.name: Construction of Goyghor Mosque

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1476, the Battle of Toro was fought during the War of the Castilian Succession. Although the battle was militarily inconclusive, it secured the Catholic Monarchs' claim to the Crown of Castile, laying the foundation for the modern Spanish state.
events.name: Battle of Toro

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1476, the Battle of Grandson occurred during the Burgundian Wars, where Swiss forces defeated the Burgundians. This victory was a significant moment in the struggle against Burgundian dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Grandson

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1476, the Battle of Morat took place during the Burgundian Wars, resulting in a crushing defeat for the Burgundians at the hands of the Swiss. This battle further weakened Burgundian power in the region and showcased the effectiveness of Swiss military tactics.
events.name: Battle of Morat

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Valea Albă, fought on July 26, 1476, was a significant conflict during the Moldavian–Ottoman Wars, where the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II defeated Stephen III of Moldavia. This battle marked a crucial moment in the struggle for control over Moldavia, showcasing the military prowess of the Ottomans and the resilience of Moldavian forces.
events.name: Battle of Valea Albă

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1476, Vlad the Impaler declared himself the reigning Voivode of Wallachia for the third and final time. His reign was marked by conflict with the Ottomans, and he was ultimately killed on the march to Bucharest, with his head sent to his enemy, Sultan Mehmed II, symbolizing the end of his tumultuous rule.
events.name: Vlad the Impaler declares himself reigning Voivode of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: In February 1477, the Bardarbunga volcano in Iceland erupted with a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 6. This significant eruption had lasting effects on the local environment and contributed to the geological understanding of volcanic activity in the region.
events.name: Eruption of Bardarbunga

events.enhanced_description: In 1477, Ivan III of Russia initiated military actions against the Novgorod Republic, marking the beginning of Russian colonialism. This campaign was part of Ivan's broader efforts to consolidate power and expand the territories of the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
events.name: Ivan III marches against Novgorod Republic

events.enhanced_description: In 1477, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola began his studies in canon law at the University of Bologna. Pico was a pivotal figure of the Renaissance, known for his philosophical works and his advocacy for the synthesis of various philosophical traditions.
events.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola studies canon law

events.enhanced_description: In 1477, Thomas Norton authored the 'Ordinall of Alchemy,' a significant work in the field of alchemy. This text contributed to the understanding and practice of alchemy during the late medieval period.
events.name: Thomas Norton writes Ordinall of Alchemy

events.enhanced_description: In 1477, the first edition of 'The Travels of Marco Polo' was printed, bringing the accounts of Polo's journeys to a wider audience. This work played a crucial role in shaping European perceptions of Asia and its cultures.
events.name: First edition of The Travels of Marco Polo printed

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Nancy, fought on January 5, 1477, resulted in the defeat and death of Charles the Bold, the Duke of Burgundy. This battle marked a decisive end to the Burgundian Wars and significantly altered the political landscape of France and the Low Countries.
events.name: Battle of Nancy

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1477, Mary of Burgundy was compelled by her subjects to sign the Great Privilege, restoring local and communal rights to the Flemish cities that had been suppressed by the Burgundian dukes. This event was pivotal in the struggle for autonomy within the Low Countries.
events.name: Mary of Burgundy signs the Great Privilege

events.enhanced_description: Uppsala University was founded on February 27, 1477, becoming the first university in Sweden and all of Scandinavia. This institution has played a crucial role in the development of higher education in the region and continues to be a leading university today.
events.name: Founding of Uppsala University

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1477, Mary of Burgundy married Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, in Ghent. This marriage was significant as it brought her Flemish and Burgundian lands into the Holy Roman Empire, effectively detaching them from French influence.
events.name: Marriage of Mary of Burgundy and Maximilian I

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1477, William Caxton produced the first full-length book printed in England, translating Earl Rivers' work into English. This marked a significant milestone in the history of printing and literature in England, paving the way for the spread of knowledge.
events.name: William Caxton produces first full-length book printed in England

events.enhanced_description: In November 1478, Eskender succeeded his father, Baeda Maryam, as Emperor of Ethiopia at the tender age of six. His ascension marked a significant moment in Ethiopian history, although his reign would be heavily influenced by regents due to his young age.
events.name: Eskender succeeds as Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: In 1478, the Grand Duchy of Moscow began to assert its independence from the Golden Horde, marking a significant shift in the power dynamics of Eastern Europe. This event laid the groundwork for the future expansion of Russian territory and influence.
events.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow devolves from the Golden Horde

events.enhanced_description: In 1478, Lorenzo de' Medici became the sole ruler of Florence, consolidating power after the tumultuous events surrounding the Pazzi conspiracy. His leadership would significantly influence the cultural and political landscape of Florence during the Renaissance.
events.name: Lorenzo de' Medici becomes sole ruler of Florence

events.enhanced_description: The Demak Sultanate, under the leadership of Raden Patah, successfully gained independence from the Majapahit Empire following a civil war that weakened Majapahit's control over Java. This event marked the rise of Islam in Java and the establishment of one of the first Islamic sultanates in Indonesia.
events.name: The Demak Sultanate gains independence from Majapahit, after a civil war

events.enhanced_description: The Fourth Siege of Krujë concluded with the Ottoman Empire capturing the town after three previous unsuccessful attempts. This siege was part of the larger conflict between the Ottomans and the Albanian resistance led by Skanderbeg, which significantly impacted the region's history.

image.caption: Engraving depicting the siege of Krujë.
image.credit: Johann Andreas Thelot — Rycaut, Paul; Sagredo, Giovanni Die Neu-eröffnete Ottomannische Pforte: Bestehend: Erstlichen, In einer ... Beschreibung Deß gantzen Türckischen Staats- und Gottesdiensts (Band 1) — Augsburg, 1694. Online: https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/en/view/bsb00073812?page=11
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration created in 1694, depicting the 1477–1478 siege; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Fourth Siege of Krujë, Albania by the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: Vladislav II of Bohemia negotiated a peace treaty with Hungary, which helped stabilize relations between the two kingdoms during a period of political tension in Central Europe. This agreement was crucial for maintaining regional stability.
events.name: Vladislav II of Bohemia makes peace with Hungary

events.enhanced_description: The earliest known reference to cricket, termed "criquet," was discovered in France, although its authenticity has been debated by historians. This mention is significant as it marks the potential origins of cricket as a sport in Europe.
events.name: First reference to cricket in France

events.enhanced_description: Mondino de Liuzzi's 'Anathomia corporis humani' was the first complete published anatomical text, marking a significant advancement in the field of medicine and anatomy. This work laid the foundation for future anatomical studies and education.
events.name: Mondino de Liuzzi's Anathomia corporis humani is first printed

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1478, Novgorod surrendered to Ivan III, Grand Prince of Moscow, effectively ending the independence of the Novgorod Republic. This event marked a significant step in the centralization of power in Russia and the expansion of the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
events.name: Novgorod surrenders to Ivan III

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1478, Richard of Shrewsbury, Duke of York, married Anne de Mowbray, 8th Countess of Norfolk. This marriage was politically significant, linking two prominent noble families in England during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Marriage of Richard of Shrewsbury and Anne de Mowbray

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1478, George Plantagenet, 1st Duke of Clarence, was executed in the Tower of London after being convicted of treason against his brother, King Edward IV. His death marked a significant moment in the power struggles of the English nobility during the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Execution of George Plantagenet

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1478, the Pazzi Family launched an attack on Lorenzo de' Medici during High Mass in Florence Cathedral, resulting in the assassination of his brother, Giuliano. This event was a pivotal moment in the power struggles of Florence and led to a violent backlash against the Pazzi.

locations.name: Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore

events.name: Pazzi Family attack Lorenzo de' Medici

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Shkodra began on May 14, 1478, as Ottoman forces sought to capture this strategic city in Albania. The siege was part of the larger conflict between the Ottomans and the Albanian resistance, led by figures such as Skanderbeg.
events.name: Siege of Shkodra begins

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish Inquisition officially began on November 1, 1478, under the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. This institution aimed to maintain Catholic orthodoxy in their kingdoms and led to widespread persecution of Jews and Muslims.
events.name: Spanish Inquisition begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1478, the Battle of Giornico took place, where Swiss troops defeated the Milanese forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict involving the Swiss Confederation and the Duchy of Milan, showcasing the military strength of the Swiss.
events.name: Battle of Giornico

events.enhanced_description: A devastating outbreak of plague struck Florence, contributing to the city's historical narrative of suffering and resilience. This epidemic had significant social and economic impacts on the population.
events.name: The plague breaks out in Florence

events.enhanced_description: Johann Neumeister published a new edition of Juan de Torquemada's 'Meditations', reflecting the growing interest in devotional literature during the Renaissance. This work contributed to the spiritual and cultural landscape of the time.
events.name: Johann Neumeister prints a new edition of Juan de Torquemada's Meditations

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand II ascended to the throne of Aragon, ruling alongside his wife Isabella I of Castile. Their union marked the beginning of a powerful dynastic partnership that would lead to the unification of Spain and significant territorial expansion.
events.name: Ferdinand II ascends the throne of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: The ratification of the Treaty of Constantinople in Venice marked the end of the Siege of Shkodra and solidified Ottoman control over Albania. This event was pivotal in the expansion of Ottoman influence in the Balkans.
events.name: Ratification of the Treaty of Constantinople in Venice

events.enhanced_description: Christopher Columbus married Felipa Perestrelo Moniz in Lisbon, receiving her father's maps and navigational papers as part of her dowry. This marriage significantly influenced Columbus's future voyages and explorations.
events.name: Christopher Columbus marries Felipa Perestrelo Moniz

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Guinegate saw a French army, sent to invade the Netherlands, decisively defeated by the forces of Maximilian of Austria. This battle was part of the larger conflicts involving France and the Habsburgs during this period.
events.name: Battle of Guinegate

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Alcáçovas was signed between the Catholic Monarchs of Spain and King Afonso V of Portugal, concluding the War of the Castilian Succession. This treaty established territorial claims and marked a significant moment in Iberian history.
events.name: The Treaty of Alcáçovas is signed

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Breadfield, the Kingdom of Hungary's forces, led by Pál Kinizsi and István Báthory, achieved a significant victory over the Ottoman Empire, resulting in heavy casualties for the Turks. This battle was a crucial moment in the ongoing struggle between Hungary and the Ottomans.

image.caption: Eduard Gurk’s painting depicting the Battle of Kenyérmező (Breadfield).
image.credit: Eduard Gurk — https://www.bildarchivaustria.at/Pages/ImageDetail.aspx?p_iBildID=13767312
image.date_qualification: 19th-century retrospective battle illustration; it does not depict the battle contemporaneously. The saved image date identifies the period only as the 19th century.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Breadfield

events.enhanced_description: The Great Stand on the Ugra River marked a pivotal moment in Russian history, as Muscovy successfully resisted the Golden Horde's advances, leading to its independence. This event is often seen as a significant step towards the emergence of a unified Russian state.

image.caption: A miniature from the Russian chronicle depicts the Stand on the Ugra River.
image.credit: Anonymous Russian manuscript illuminators, 1560-1570s Facial Chronicle (Illustrated Chronicle of Ivan the Terrible) (in 10 volumes: pdf , pdf with translation ) Public domain image — Scanned from russian book "Энциклопедия для детей - История России". Аванта+, 2000.

image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Great Stand on the Ugra River

events.enhanced_description: An Ottoman army landed near Otranto, prompting Pope Sixtus IV to call for a crusade to repel the invasion. This event highlighted the ongoing conflict between Christian Europe and the expanding Ottoman Empire.
events.name: An Ottoman army lands near Otranto, Italy

events.enhanced_description: The final remains of the Lighthouse of Alexandria disappeared when Sultan Qaitbay constructed the Citadel of Qaitbay on its site. This marked the end of one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, symbolizing the transition from ancient to medieval architecture.

locations.name: Monastery of St. Macarius, Wadi El Natrun

events.name: The Lighthouse of Alexandria's final remains disappear

events.enhanced_description: Magdalen College School was established by William Waynflete in Oxford, contributing to the educational landscape of England. The school has a long history of academic excellence and remains one of the leading independent schools in the country.
events.name: Magdalen College School, Oxford, is established

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Toledo recognized the African conquests of Afonso V of Portugal and formalized the cession of the Canary Islands to Spain. This treaty was part of the broader negotiations following the Treaty of Alcáçovas.
events.name: Treaty of Toledo is signed

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Mehmed II's attempt to capture the strategically important island of Rhodes from the Knights of Rhodes ended in failure, marking a significant setback for Ottoman expansion in the Mediterranean. The defense of Rhodes became a symbol of resistance against Ottoman power.
events.name: Mehmed II fails in his attempt to capture Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish Inquisition was initiated by Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, aiming to identify and punish heretics, particularly among converted Jews. This marked the beginning of a dark chapter in Spanish history characterized by religious intolerance.
events.name: Spanish Inquisition is initiated

events.enhanced_description: In 1481, a series of earthquakes struck the island of Rhodes, with the largest causing an estimated 30,000 casualties. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the local population and infrastructure, leading to significant rebuilding efforts.
events.name: Rhodes earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Mehmed II, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, died in 1481 and was succeeded by his son, Bayezid II. His reign was marked by significant territorial expansion and cultural achievements, and his death marked a transition in the empire's leadership.
events.name: Death of Mehmed II

events.enhanced_description: In 1481, the Catalan Courts approved the Constitució de l'Observança, which established the submission of royal power to the laws of the Principality of Catalonia. This document was significant in the context of Catalan autonomy and governance.
events.name: Constitució de l'Observança

events.enhanced_description: In 1481, Ludovico Sforza emerged as the Regent of Milan, a position he would hold until 1499. His regency was marked by political maneuvering and cultural patronage, contributing to the Renaissance in Milan.
events.name: Ludovico Sforza emerges as Regent of Milan
