events.enhanced_description: Axayacatl, the Aztec ruler of Tenochtitlan, died in 1481 and was succeeded by his brother Tízoc. His reign was marked by military conquests and the expansion of the Aztec Empire.
events.name: Death of Axayacatl

events.enhanced_description: In 1481, the Aztec Calendar Stone, also known as the Sun Stone, was carved. This monumental sculpture is one of the most iconic representations of Aztec cosmology and artistry, symbolizing the importance of time and the sun in Aztec culture.
events.name: Carving of the Aztec Calendar Stone

events.enhanced_description: In 1481, Fribourg and Solothurn were recognized as cantons of Switzerland, marking their formal inclusion in the Swiss Confederation. This development was significant in the political landscape of Switzerland, contributing to its federal structure.
events.name: Fribourg and Solothurn become Cantons of Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: The 1481 Rhodes earthquake was the largest in a series of seismic events that struck the island, resulting in an estimated 30,000 casualties. This disaster had a profound impact on the local population and architecture.
events.name: The 1481 Rhodes earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Christian I, the King of Denmark and Norway, died and was succeeded by his son John. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the monarchy and navigate the complexities of Scandinavian politics.
events.name: Christian I, King of Denmark and Norway, dies

events.enhanced_description: The papal bull Aeterni Regis granted Portugal dominion over all lands south of the Canary Islands, reinforcing the country's colonial ambitions and maritime exploration during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: The papal bull Aeterni Regis is issued

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1481, a devastating fire broke out at Reims Cathedral, causing significant damage to its roof and spires. This Gothic masterpiece, known for its historical significance and architectural beauty, underwent extensive restoration following the incident.
events.name: Fire destroys the roof and the spires of Reims Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1481, John II ascended to the throne of Portugal, marking the beginning of his reign characterized by significant exploration and consolidation of royal power. His rule is often noted for its efforts to strengthen the monarchy and expand Portuguese influence overseas.
events.name: John II of Portugal starts to rule in his own right

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1481, Alphonso II of Naples successfully recaptured the city of Otranto, which had been under foreign control. This event was part of the broader conflicts in Italy during the late 15th century, reflecting the ongoing power struggles in the region.
events.name: Alphonso II of Naples recaptures the city of Otranto

events.enhanced_description: The death of Duke Charles IV of Anjou on December 10, 1481, led to the reversion of Anjou and Provence to the French crown under Louis XI. This transition was significant in the consolidation of royal power in France and the diminishing influence of the nobility.
events.name: Death of Duke Charles IV of Anjou

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1481, the Battle of Westbroek took place, where the forces of Holland defeated the troops of Utrecht. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the provinces in the Netherlands during the late 15th century.
events.name: Battle of Westbroek

events.enhanced_description: In February 1482, Johann Reuchlin left Stuttgart to visit Florence, where he met the influential philosopher Marsilio Ficino. This meeting was significant in the context of the Renaissance, as it facilitated the exchange of ideas between German and Italian humanists.
events.name: Johann Reuchlin visits Florence

events.enhanced_description: In August 1482, Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão became the first European to enter the Congo River, marking a significant moment in the Age of Exploration. His journey opened new avenues for trade and interaction between Europe and Africa.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Diogo Cão enters the Congo

events.enhanced_description: In 1482, Ivan III of Russia formally renounced the rule of the Mongol Khanate, marking a significant step towards Russian independence and the consolidation of power in Moscow. This act symbolized the end of Mongol dominance in Russia.
events.name: Ivan III renounces Mongol rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1482, Johannes Trithemius became a novice at the Abbey of St. Martin at Sponheim, in the Diocese of Mainz. His time at the abbey would influence his later works in history and cryptography.
events.name: Johannes Trithemius becomes a novice

events.enhanced_description: In 1482, the first Latin translation of Euclid's Elements was printed by the German printer Erhard Ratdolt in Venice. This edition was notable for its incorporation of geometric diagrams, significantly contributing to the dissemination of mathematical knowledge in Europe.
events.name: The first edition of Euclid's Elements (Latin translation) is printed

events.enhanced_description: The Schreierstoren, a historic tower in Amsterdam, was erected in the late 15th century. It later became significant as the departure point for Henry Hudson's voyage on April 4, 1609, aboard the Halve Maen, which led to the exploration of New York and the Hudson River.
events.name: Schreierstoren is erected in Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1482, a Portuguese fleet commanded by Diogo de Azambuja arrived at the mouth of the River Benya on the Gold Coast, where they erected the fort of São Jorge da Mina, known today as Elmina Castle. This marked a significant moment in the European exploration and colonization of West Africa.
events.name: Portuguese fleet arrives at the mouth of the River Benya

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1482, the probable first printing of the Torah occurred in Bologna, marking a significant development in the dissemination of Jewish texts and culture during the Renaissance. This event reflects the growing importance of printing technology in Europe.
events.name: Probable first printing of the Torah in Bologna

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1482, Christian forces captured the village of Alhama de Granada, initiating the Granada War aimed at expelling the Moors from the Iberian Peninsula. This marked a significant step in the Reconquista, the centuries-long effort to reclaim territory in Spain.
events.name: Capture of Alhama de Granada

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1482, Pope Sixtus IV issued a papal bull granting self-government rights to the Italian town of Ascoli Piceno. This act was significant in the context of the political landscape of Italy, reflecting the Pope's influence over local governance.
events.name: Papal bull grants self-government to Ascoli Piceno

events.enhanced_description: The death of Mary of Burgundy on March 27, 1482, triggered the first of the Flemish revolts against Maximilian of Austria. Her passing created a power vacuum that led to significant political unrest in the region.
events.name: Death of Mary of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1482, Symeon I succeeded Maximus III as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. His leadership was significant for the Orthodox Church during a period of political and religious challenges.
events.name: Symeon I succeeds Maximus III

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1482, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, invaded Scotland and captured Edinburgh during the Anglo-Scottish Wars. This military campaign was part of the ongoing conflict between England and Scotland during this period.
events.name: Richard, Duke of Gloucester invades Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1482, the Scots surrendered the border town of Berwick-upon-Tweed to Richard, Duke of Gloucester, effectively ending his campaign in Scotland. This event was significant in the context of the Anglo-Scottish Wars.
events.name: Capture of Berwick-upon-Tweed

events.enhanced_description: In 1483, the expulsion of Jews from Andalusia marked a significant event in the history of the Spanish Inquisition and the broader context of religious intolerance in Spain. This expulsion was part of a larger trend of forced conversions and expulsions of Jews across the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: The Jews are expelled from Andalusia

events.enhanced_description: In 1483, Isaac Abravanel, a prominent Jewish financier and philosopher, fled Portugal after being implicated in a plot against the king. His departure was emblematic of the increasing persecution faced by Jews in Iberia during this period.
events.name: Isaac Abravanel flees Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In 1483, the Prince of Moscow constructed the fortress of Ivangorod, strategically located facing Narva. This fortress played a significant role in the defense and expansion of Russian territories.
events.name: The Prince of Moscow builds the fortress of Ivangorod

events.enhanced_description: In 1483, Giovanni Bellini was appointed as the official painter of the Republic of Venice, a position that recognized his significant contributions to Venetian art. His works would go on to influence the development of Renaissance painting.
events.name: Giovanni Bellini is named official painter of the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1483, Flavio Biondo published his work Historiarum ab inclinatione romanorum imperii, which provided a historical account of Rome's decline. This publication is considered an important contribution to Renaissance historiography.

image.caption: Portrait of Flavius Blondus (Flavio Biondo).
image.credit: Theodor de Bry — J. J. Boissard and T. de Bry, Icones quinquaginta virorum illustrium doctrina et eruditione præstantium ad vivum effictae , part 1 (Frankfurt 1597), p. 92, no. VIII ( digitized by the Getty Research Institute ).
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1597. This is a portrait made after Biondo’s lifetime and does not depict the 1483 publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Flavio Biondo publishes his Historiarum ab inclinatione romanorum imperii

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1483, the General Council of the Inquisition was established in Spain, centralizing the authority of the Inquisition and intensifying efforts against heresy. This institution played a crucial role in the enforcement of Catholic orthodoxy during the Spanish Renaissance.
events.name: The General Council of the Inquisition is created in Spain

events.enhanced_description: In April 1483, King Edward V and his younger brother Richard, Duke of York, were placed in the Tower of London, where they would remain until their mysterious disappearance later that year. This event initiated one of the most enduring mysteries in English history regarding the fate of the Princes in the Tower.
events.name: King Edward V of England and Richard, Duke of York reside in the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: Edward V was proclaimed King of England on April 9, 1483, but his reign was short-lived as he was deposed shortly thereafter. His ascension marked a tumultuous period in English history, leading to the rise of his uncle Richard III.
events.name: Edward V becomes King of England

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1483, Gran Canaria was conquered by the Kingdom of Castile, marking a significant step in the Spanish expansion into the Canary Islands. This conquest facilitated further Spanish exploration and colonization efforts in the Atlantic.
events.name: Gran Canaria is conquered by the Kingdom of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1483, William Hastings, 1st Baron Hastings, was executed in the Tower of London, marking the first recorded execution at this infamous site. His death was part of the power struggles during the early reign of Richard III.
events.name: William Hastings, 1st Baron Hastings, is executed

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1483, Fernando II, Duke of Braganza, was executed in Portugal along with over 80 other noblemen for conspiring against the royal crown. This event exemplified the intense political intrigue and instability of the period.
events.name: Fernando II, Duke of Braganza is executed in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1483, Edward V was deposed by his uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, who subsequently ascended the throne as Richard III. This event marked a pivotal moment in the Wars of the Roses and the tumultuous history of the English monarchy.
events.name: Edward V of England is deposed by Richard, Duke of Gloucester

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1483, Richard III and Anne Neville were crowned King and Queen of England at Westminster Abbey. This coronation solidified Richard's claim to the throne amidst the ongoing conflicts of the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Richard III and Anne Neville are crowned King and Queen of England

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1483, John of Denmark was crowned King of Norway, marking a significant moment in the history of the Kalmar Union, which sought to unify the crowns of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden.
events.name: John of Denmark is crowned King of Norway

events.enhanced_description: The Sistine Chapel was opened in the Apostolic Palace in Rome on August 15, 1483. This iconic chapel would later become famous for its stunning frescoes, including Michelangelo's ceiling, and serve as the site of papal conclaves.
events.name: The Sistine Chapel opens in the Apostolic Palace in Rome

events.enhanced_description: On the night of September 3, 1483, the uncrowned Edward V and his brother Richard, Duke of York, were possibly murdered in the Tower of London. This event has fueled speculation and mystery surrounding the fate of the Princes in the Tower for centuries.
events.name: The Princes in the Tower are perhaps murdered

events.enhanced_description: In October 1483, Richard III successfully crushed a rebellion led by the Duke of Buckingham, solidifying his control over the throne. This conflict was part of the ongoing power struggles during the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: A rebellion by the Duke of Buckingham is crushed by Richard III

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1483, the forces of the Kingdom of Croatia achieved a significant victory against the Ottoman Empire at the Battle of Una. This battle was part of the broader conflict between the Ottomans and the Christian states in the region.
events.name: Battle of Una: Forces of the Kingdom of Croatia defeat the army of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1484, the first sugar mill became operational in Gran Canaria, marking a significant development in the sugar industry. This event contributed to the rise of sugar as a valuable commodity in Europe and the Atlantic trade.
events.name: First sugar mill operational

events.enhanced_description: In 1484, the first cuirassier units, known as kyrissers, were formed in Austria. This development marked a significant evolution in cavalry tactics and military organization in Europe.

locations.historical_name: Bavaria (historically relevant region during the 8th century)
locations.name: Salzburg

events.name: Formation of cuirassier units

events.enhanced_description: In 1484, King John II of Portugal appointed a commission of mathematicians to refine navigational tables, aiding seamen in determining their latitude. This initiative was crucial for the Age of Exploration, enhancing maritime navigation.
events.name: Commission of mathematicians in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In 1484, Maximilian I, Duke of Burgundy, ordered foreign merchants to vacate Bruges, leading many to relocate to Antwerp. This decision significantly contributed to Antwerp's rise as a major international trading hub.
events.name: Maximilian I orders foreign merchants to leave Bruges

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Leitzersdorf took place in 1484, where the Imperial Army led by Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor, faced defeat against Hungarian forces. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Central Europe during this period.
events.name: Battle of Leitzersdorf

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1484, William Caxton, the first printer of books in English, printed his translation of Aesop's Fables in London. This work played a crucial role in popularizing fables and moral stories in English literature.
events.name: William Caxton prints his translation of Aesop's Fables

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1484, Charles VIII of France was crowned, marking the beginning of his reign. His rule would be characterized by efforts to strengthen the French monarchy and expand its territories.
events.name: Charles VIII of France is crowned

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1484, Anna Rügerin produced the first known book printed by a woman, an edition of Eike of Repgow's Sachsenspiegel, in Augsburg. This landmark achievement highlighted the role of women in the early printing industry.
events.name: The first known book printed by a woman is produced in Augsburg

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1484, Portuguese sea captain Diogo Cão discovered the mouth of the Congo River during his explorations along the west coast of Africa. This discovery was significant for the expansion of Portuguese trade and influence in the region.

locations.name: Congo River, Republic of the Congo

events.name: Diogo Cão finds the mouth of the Congo River

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lochmaben Fair occurred on July 22, 1484, where a raiding party of 500 men led by Alexander Stewart, Duke of Albany, and James Douglas, 9th Earl of Douglas, was defeated by forces loyal to James III of Scotland. This battle was significant in the ongoing power struggles within Scotland, leading to the capture of Douglas.
events.name: Battle of Lochmaben Fair

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1484, Pope Innocent VIII was elected as the 213th pope, succeeding Pope Sixtus IV. His papacy would be marked by significant events, including the initiation of the witch hunts in Europe.
events.name: Pope Innocent VIII succeeds Pope Sixtus IV

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Nottingham, signed on September 21, 1484, established a three-year truce between the kingdoms of England and Scotland. This treaty was part of the ongoing efforts to stabilize relations between the two nations during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Treaty of Nottingham

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1484, Pope Innocent VIII issued the Papal bull Summis desiderantes affectibus, which authorized the Inquisition to hunt down heretics and witches in Germany. This document significantly contributed to the witch hunts that would sweep through Europe in the following decades.
events.name: Papal bull Summis desiderantes affectibus

events.enhanced_description: Leon Battista Alberti's treatise De Re Aedificatoria, written between 1443 and 1452 and published posthumously, became the first printed work on architecture. This influential text laid the groundwork for Renaissance architectural theory.
events.name: Leon Battista Alberti's De Re Aedificatoria

events.enhanced_description: Around 1485, Leonardo da Vinci began producing designs for various flying machines, including the aerial screw, which is often considered an early concept of the helicopter. While these designs were not practical at the time, they showcased da Vinci's visionary thinking.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci's designs for flying machines

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1485, a solar eclipse crossed northern South America and Central Europe, an astronomical event that would have been observed and recorded by various cultures.
events.name: Solar eclipse crosses northern South America and Central Europe

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1485, multiple earthquakes struck near Taishan, China. This seismic activity was part of a series of natural disasters that affected the region during this period.

locations.name: Mount Tai, Taishan District, Shandong, China

events.name: Multiple earthquakes near Taishan

events.enhanced_description: In June 1485, Matthias of Hungary successfully captured Vienna from Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor, establishing the city as his capital. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Central Europe.
events.name: Matthias of Hungary takes Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1485, the first outbreak of sweating sickness was recorded in England. This mysterious illness would cause widespread panic and numerous fatalities in subsequent years.
events.name: First outbreak of sweating sickness in England

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Bosworth, fought on August 22, 1485, was a decisive conflict in which King Richard III of England was defeated by Henry Tudor, leading to Richard's death and the rise of Henry as King Henry VII. This battle effectively ended the Wars of the Roses.

locations.name: Bosworth Field, Market Bosworth, Leicestershire, England

events.name: Battle of Bosworth

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1485, Muscovian forces successfully conquered Tver, a significant event in the consolidation of power by the Grand Duchy of Moscow. This conquest was part of the broader expansion of Muscovite territory.
events.name: Muscovian forces conquer Tver

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1485, Peter Arbues, an Inquisitor of Aragon, was assaulted while praying in the cathedral at Zaragoza, Spain, and died two days later. His assassination highlighted the tensions surrounding the Inquisition's campaign against heresy.

image.caption: Francesco Cecchini’s etching depicting the martyrdom of Saint Pedro de Arbués.
image.credit: Francesco Cecchini — http://www.enciclopedia-aragonesa.com/recurso.asp?recurso_id=796
image.date_qualification: Etching dated “finales del siglo XVII” (late 17th century); the assault occurred in 1485.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Peter Arbues is assaulted

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1485, Henry VII of England was crowned at Westminster Abbey, marking the official beginning of his reign. His ascension to the throne represented the end of the Wars of the Roses and the start of the Tudor dynasty.
events.name: King Henry VII of England is crowned

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1485, the Peace of Bourges was established, effectively ending the Mad War in France. This agreement marked a significant step towards stabilizing the political landscape in the region.
events.name: Peace of Bourges

events.enhanced_description: Tízoc, the Aztec ruler of Tenochtitlan, died in 1486 under mysterious circumstances, with some sources suggesting poisoning or sorcery. He was succeeded by his brother Āhuitzotl, who would lead the empire to greater heights.
events.name: Death of Tízoc, Aztec ruler

events.enhanced_description: In 1486, Sigismund, Archduke of Tyrol, introduced the guldengroschen, a large silver coin that would later influence the development of the thaler, a significant currency in Europe. This coinage reform was part of broader economic changes in the region, facilitating trade and commerce.
events.name: Sigismund, Archduke of Tyrol, issues Europe's first large silver coin, the guldengroschen, which will later become the thaler

events.enhanced_description: In 1486, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola returned to Florence, where he composed his seminal work, 'Oration on the Dignity of Man.' This text is often regarded as a manifesto of Renaissance humanism, emphasizing the potential and worth of the individual.
events.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola returns to Florence, and writes Oration on the Dignity of Man

events.enhanced_description: In 1486, the Medici giraffe, a gift from the Sultan of Egypt to Lorenzo de' Medici, arrived in Florence, captivating the city's inhabitants. This exotic animal symbolized the Medici's wealth and influence, as well as the broader European fascination with the natural world and exploration.
events.name: The Medici giraffe arrives in Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1486, Johann Reuchlin, a German humanist and scholar, began his studies of the Hebrew language, which would later influence the Renaissance's approach to biblical texts and Jewish scholarship. His work contributed to the revival of interest in Hebrew among Christian scholars.
events.name: Johann Reuchlin begins studying the Hebrew language

events.enhanced_description: In 1486, the term 'football' was first documented in writing to refer to the ball used in the game, marking an important moment in the history of sports terminology. This usage reflects the growing popularity of the game in England during the late Middle Ages.
events.name: The first written use of the word football to describe the ball

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1486, King Henry VII of England married Elizabeth of York, uniting the rival houses of Lancaster and York. This marriage symbolized the end of the Wars of the Roses and the establishment of the Tudor dynasty.
events.name: Marriage of Henry VII and Elizabeth of York

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1486, Archduke Maximilian I of Habsburg was elected King of the Romans in Frankfurt, a significant step in his rise to power within the Holy Roman Empire. He would later be crowned Emperor in 1493.
events.name: Maximilian I elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was born on February 18, 1486, in Nadia, West Bengal, India. He is revered as an incarnation of Lord Krishna and is known for initiating the sankirtana movement, emphasizing the chanting of the Holy Names.
events.name: Birth of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1486, the Sentència Arbitral de Guadalupe was adopted, effectively ending the War of the Remences in the Principality of Catalonia. This agreement marked a significant resolution to the conflict between the peasantry and the nobility.
events.name: Sentència Arbitral de Guadalupe ends the War of the Remences

events.enhanced_description: In March 1487, Sigismund, Archduke of Austria, declared war on Venice, driven by poor counsel and the desire to seize control of silver mines in the Sugana Valley. This conflict marked a significant moment in the ongoing power struggles in Northern Italy.
events.name: Sigismund, Archduke of Austria, declares war on Venice

events.enhanced_description: In August 1487, Bartolomeu Dias set sail from Lisbon on a historic voyage to the Cape of Good Hope, marking a significant milestone in the Age of Exploration. His journey would pave the way for future maritime routes to India and beyond.
events.name: Bartolomeu Dias leaves Lisbon, on his voyage to the Cape of Good Hope

events.enhanced_description: In 1487, explorers Afonso de Paiva and Pêro da Covilhã embarked on an overland journey from Lisbon in search of the fabled Kingdom of Prester John in Ethiopia. Their expedition was part of the larger Portuguese efforts to explore and establish trade routes in Africa.
events.name: Afonso de Paiva and Pêro da Covilhã travel overland from Lisbon, in search of the Kingdom of Prester John (Ethiopia)

events.enhanced_description: In 1487, the infamous witch-hunters' manual 'Malleus Maleficarum' was published in Speyer, written by Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger. This book played a significant role in the witch hunts that swept through Europe in the following decades.
events.name: The witch-hunters' manual Malleus Maleficarum is published at Speyer

events.enhanced_description: In 1487, Aztec emperor Ahuitzotl dedicated the Great Temple Pyramid of Tenochtitlán, an event marked by thousands of human sacrifices. This dedication underscored the religious fervor and the importance of the temple in Aztec society.
events.name: Aztec emperor Ahuitzotl dedicates the Great Temple Pyramid of Tenochtitlán

events.enhanced_description: In 1487, Italian architects were commissioned to work on the Moscow Kremlin, contributing to its architectural evolution. This collaboration marked a significant cultural exchange between Italy and Russia during the Renaissance.
events.name: Italian architects work on the Moscow Kremlin

events.enhanced_description: Around 1487, Leonardo da Vinci created his iconic drawing, the Vitruvian Man, which exemplifies the blend of art and science during the Renaissance. This work reflects da Vinci's fascination with proportion and the human form.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci creates his Vitruvian Man drawing (approximate date)

events.enhanced_description: In 1487, Stockport Grammar School was founded in the north of England, establishing a significant educational institution that would serve the community for centuries. The school played a vital role in the development of education in the region.
events.name: Stockport Grammar School is founded, in the north of England

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1487, Richard Foxe was appointed Bishop of Exeter, a significant position within the Church of England. His tenure would later see him play a crucial role in the politics of the Tudor court.
events.name: Richard Foxe becomes Bishop of Exeter

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1487, Lambert Simnel was crowned as King 'Edward VI of England' in Christ Church Cathedral, Dublin, claiming to be the rightful heir to the English throne. This act was part of a rebellion against King Henry VII, which would lead to significant conflict.
events.name: Lambert Simnel is crowned King "Edward VI of England" in Christ Church Cathedral, Dublin, Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1487, the Battle of Stoke Field took place, where forces loyal to King Henry VII defeated the rebellion led by Lambert Simnel and his supporters, including John de la Pole and Francis Lovell. This battle effectively ended the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Battle of Stoke Field: The rebellion of pretender Lambert Simnel is crushed

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1487, the Siege of Málaga concluded with the capture of the city by Spanish forces, marking a pivotal moment in the Reconquista. This victory was part of the broader campaign to reclaim Muslim-held territories in Spain.
events.name: The Siege of Málaga (1487) ends, when the Spanish take the city

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1487, Hongzhi ascended to the throne as the Emperor of China during the Ming Dynasty. His reign is noted for its emphasis on Confucian values and administrative reforms, which aimed to strengthen the central government.
events.name: Hongzhi becomes Emperor of China (Ming Dynasty)

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1487, Albert IV, Duke of Bavaria, enacted the Reinheitsgebot, a beer purity law that specified the only ingredients allowed in beer production were water, malt, and hops. This regulation laid the foundation for Germany's brewing tradition.
events.name: Albert IV, Duke of Bavaria promulgates the Reinheitsgebot

events.enhanced_description: Jasper Tudor, a prominent figure in the Wars of the Roses, took possession of Cardiff Castle, solidifying his influence in Wales. This event marked a significant moment in the Tudor family's consolidation of power in the region.
events.name: Jasper Tudor, 1st Duke of Bedford, takes possession of Cardiff Castle

events.enhanced_description: Michelangelo Buonarroti began his artistic journey as an apprentice to Domenico Ghirlandaio in Florence, where he honed his skills in painting and sculpture. This apprenticeship laid the foundation for Michelangelo's later masterpieces and his pivotal role in the Renaissance.
events.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti becomes apprentice to Domenico Ghirlandaio

events.enhanced_description: Rao Bika established the city of Bikaner in western India, which would become a significant center of trade and culture. The city is known for its rich history and architectural heritage, including the famous Junagarh Fort.
events.name: The city of Bikaner in western India is founded by Rao Bika

events.enhanced_description: Rathbornes Candles was established in Dublin, becoming one of the oldest candle-making companies in the world. The company has continued to thrive into the 21st century, reflecting the enduring tradition of craftsmanship in Ireland.
events.name: Rathbornes Candles is established in Dublin

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1488, the Royal Netherlands Navy was established by decree of Maximilian of Austria, marking the beginning of organized naval forces in the region. This development was crucial for the protection of trade routes and maritime interests.
events.name: The Royal Netherlands Navy is formed, by the decree of Maximillian of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1488, Bartolomeu Dias became the first known European to land at Mossel Bay after rounding the Cape of Good Hope, entering the Indian Ocean. This landmark achievement opened new maritime routes for exploration and trade.

locations.name: Mossel Bay, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Bartolomeu Dias of Portugal lands in Mossel Bay

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1488, Choe Bu, a Korean official, shipwrecked on the southeast coast of China in Taizhou, Zhejiang. His experiences during this ordeal were later documented, providing insights into the maritime challenges of the period.
events.name: Choe Bu shipwrecks on the south east coast of China

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1488, the Battle of Sauchieburn occurred, resulting in the death of King James III of Scotland and the ascension of his son, James IV, to the throne. This battle marked a significant shift in Scottish politics and royal power.
events.name: Battle of Sauchieburn: James IV of Scotland becomes king

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1488, Choe Bu returned to Korea after enduring months of shipwrecked travel in China. His accounts of the journey provided valuable information about the region and its cultures.
events.name: Joseon Dynasty official Choe Bu returns to Korea

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1488, the Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier took place, where troops loyal to King Charles VIII of France defeated rebel forces led by the Dukes of Orleans and Brittany. This battle was a critical engagement in the Mad War, consolidating royal power.
events.name: Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier: Troops loyal to King Charles VIII defeat rebel forces

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 11, Anne of Brittany was declared Duchess of Brittany, a title that would play a crucial role in the political landscape of France. Her subsequent marriage to King Charles VIII in 1491 marked the end of Breton independence, integrating Brittany into the French crown.

image.caption: Illuminated miniature depicting Anne of Brittany, by Jean Bourdichon.
image.credit: Jean Bourdichon — http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b52500984v/f14.item
image.date_qualification: Portrait miniature from 1503–1508, after Anne became Duchess of Brittany in 1488; it is not a contemporary depiction of that event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Anne of Brittany becomes Duchess of Brittany at the age of 11

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded appearance of typhus in Europe occurred during the Siege of Baza, a significant military engagement in the Granada War. This outbreak highlighted the health challenges faced by armies during prolonged sieges.
events.name: Typhus first appears in Europe during the Siege of Baza

events.enhanced_description: The sovereign, a gold coin valued at one pound sterling, was issued during the reign of Henry VII of England. This coin became a symbol of the Tudor dynasty's economic policies and the growing importance of currency in medieval England.
events.name: A gold coin equal to one pound sterling, called a sovereign, is issued for Henry VII of England

events.enhanced_description: King Henry VII granted a town charter to the port of Southwold, enhancing its status and allowing for greater local governance. This charter was part of the Tudor efforts to promote trade and strengthen local economies.
events.name: King Henry VII of England gives a town charter to the port of Southwold

events.enhanced_description: Lucas Watzenrode was appointed as the bishop of Warmia, a significant ecclesiastical position that influenced the religious landscape of the region. His tenure contributed to the development of the Catholic Church in Poland during the late 15th century.
events.name: Lucas Watzenrode becomes bishop of Warmia

events.enhanced_description: Johannes Widmann published his work 'Behende und hüpsche Rechenung auff allen Kauffmanschafft' in Leipzig, which included the first printed use of plus and minus signs. This publication was a significant advancement in the field of arithmetic and commerce.
events.name: Johannes Widmann publishes mercantile arithmetic

events.enhanced_description: Catherine Cornaro, the last queen of Cyprus, sold her kingdom to the Republic of Venice, marking a significant shift in the control of the island. This transaction ended the independent rule of Cyprus and initiated a period of Venetian governance.
events.name: Catherine Cornaro sells her kingdom to the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Medina del Campo was a pivotal agreement between England and Spain that included provisions for a marriage alliance between Arthur, the son of King Henry VII, and Infanta Catherine of Aragon. This treaty strengthened ties between the two kingdoms and set the stage for future political developments.

locations.name: Medina del Campo, Castile and León, Spain

events.name: The Treaty of Medina del Campo between England and Spain

events.enhanced_description: King James IV of Scotland granted Andrew, Lord Gray, the lands and Barony of Lundie, a significant act that reinforced the feudal system in Scotland. This grant exemplified the king's role in land distribution and noble patronage during his reign.
events.name: King James IV grants Andrew, Lord Gray, the lands and Barony of Lundie in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Sikandar Lodi ascended to the throne as the sultan of the Delhi Sultanate, succeeding his father Bahlul Khan Lodi. His reign is noted for administrative reforms and the expansion of the sultanate's territory.
events.name: Sikandar Lodi succeeds Bahlul Khan Lodi as sultan of the Delhi Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: Arthur Tudor was officially named Prince of Wales, a title that conferred significant status and responsibility within the English monarchy. This designation was part of the Tudor dynasty's efforts to solidify their rule and establish a strong royal lineage.
events.name: Arthur Tudor is named Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: Jeannetto de Tassis was appointed as Chief Master of Postal Services in Innsbruck, a role that would lead to the establishment of a comprehensive postal system across Europe by his descendants. This appointment marked a significant development in communication and administration during the Renaissance.
events.name: Jeannetto de Tassis is appointed Chief Master of Postal Services

events.enhanced_description: The Qingyang event, presumed to be a meteor shower or air burst, occurred over Qingyang in Ming dynasty China, reportedly causing casualties. This event is significant in the study of historical meteorological phenomena.
events.name: Qingyang event, a presumed meteor shower

events.enhanced_description: Perkin Warbeck made a bold claim at the court of Burgundy, asserting that he was the son of King Henry VII of England. This claim sparked significant political intrigue and conflict, as Warbeck sought to challenge the legitimacy of Henry's rule.
events.name: Perkin Warbeck claims to be the son of King Henry VII

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Glendale was a conflict between the Scottish clans MacDonald and MacLeod, reflecting the clan rivalries that characterized the Highlands during this period. The battle is traditionally dated to 1490, although specific details about its outcome and significance remain scarce.
events.name: Battle of Glendale

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, Catholic missionaries arrived in the Kingdom of Kongo, marking the beginning of significant European influence in Central Africa. This event initiated a long-term relationship between the Kongo kingdom and Portugal, leading to the eventual conversion of its king and many subjects to Christianity.

image.caption: Illustration of the King of Kongo giving an audience to Portuguese visitors and his subjects.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.antislavery.org/breakingthesilence/images/slave_routes/pictures/portugalkingofkongo2.jpg ; http://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/files/fullsize/dc7ced980c13daa29f4e2aaa64f8a4e6.jpg via http://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/exhibits/show/africanpassageslowcountryadapt/introductionatlanticworld/trans_atlantic_slave_trade
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration dated before 1850; it depicts a Kongo-Portuguese audience, not the 1490 arrival itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Arrival of Catholic missionaries in Kongo

events.enhanced_description: Pêro da Covilhã, a Portuguese explorer, arrived in Ethiopia around 1490, contributing to the European understanding of the region. His travels were significant for establishing early diplomatic and trade relations between Portugal and Ethiopia.
events.name: Pêro da Covilhã arrives in Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, a regular postal service was established connecting the Habsburg residences of Mechelen and Innsbruck, marking a significant advancement in communication and administration within the Habsburg territories. This service facilitated the swift exchange of information and governance across the empire.
events.name: Establishment of postal service between Mechelen and Innsbruck

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, Leonardo da Vinci made observations on capillary action in small-bore tubes, contributing to the early understanding of fluid dynamics. His scientific inquiries laid the groundwork for future studies in hydraulics and fluid mechanics.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci observes capillary action

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, Leonardo da Vinci developed an innovative oil lamp design, featuring a flame enclosed in a glass tube placed inside a water-filled glass globe. This invention demonstrated his ingenuity in combining art and science, and it reflected the technological advancements of the Renaissance.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci develops an oil lamp

events.enhanced_description: The construction of All Saints' Church, also known as the Schlosskirche, began in 1490 in Wittenberg, Germany. This church would later become famous as the site where Martin Luther famously nailed his Ninety-Five Theses, marking the start of the Protestant Reformation.

image.caption: All Saints' Church (Schlosskirche) in Wittenberg.
image.credit: Horst Pomplun — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2025-09-20; it depicts the church site, not its construction in 1490.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Construction of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, the chivalric novel 'Tirant lo Blanch' was published by Joanot Martorell and Martí Joan de Galba in Valencia, Spain. This work is considered one of the most important pieces of Catalan literature and had a significant influence on the development of the novel as a literary form.
events.name: Publication of Tirant lo Blanch

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, Aldus Manutius, a prominent Venetian printer and publisher, moved to Venice, where he would establish his printing house. His innovations in typography and book design significantly influenced the spread of humanist literature during the Renaissance.
events.name: Aldus Manutius moves to Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, John Colet received his Master of Arts degree from Magdalen College, Oxford. Colet would later become a prominent theologian and educator, known for his reformist ideas and contributions to the development of humanist education in England.
events.name: John Colet receives M.A. from Magdalen College

events.enhanced_description: In 1490, Johann Reuchlin, a German humanist and scholar, met Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in Florence. This meeting was significant in the context of Renaissance humanism, as both figures were influential in the revival of classical philosophy and the study of Hebrew texts.
events.name: Johann Reuchlin meets Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

events.enhanced_description: Around 1490, merchants began transporting coffee from Yemen to Mecca, marking the beginning of coffee's spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula. This trade would eventually lead to coffee becoming a popular beverage across the Middle East and Europe.
events.name: Merchants carry coffee from Yemen to Mecca

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Chocontá occurred in 1490 between the northern (zaque) and southern (zipa) tribes of the Muisca Confederation in present-day Colombia. This conflict exemplified the internal divisions within the Muisca society and their struggles for power.
events.name: Battle of Chocontá

events.enhanced_description: Anne of Brittany declared that any individuals who allied themselves with the king of France would be guilty of the crime of Lèse-majesté. This announcement reflected her determination to maintain Breton autonomy in the face of French expansion.
events.name: Anne of Brittany announces Lèse-majesté law

events.enhanced_description: At just one year old, Charles II was proclaimed Duke of Savoy, with his mother Blanche of Montferrato serving as regent. This early ascension to power highlighted the dynastic politics of the region during the late 15th century.
events.name: Charles II becomes Duke of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Bonefield, John Corvinus faced defeat against the Kingdom of Hungary. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Central Europe during the late 15th century.
events.name: Battle of Bonefield

events.enhanced_description: John of Kastav completed a cycle of frescoes in the Holy Trinity Church located in Hrastovlje, Slovenia. This work is celebrated for its artistic significance and reflects the cultural heritage of the region.
events.name: John of Kastav finishes frescoes in Holy Trinity Church

events.enhanced_description: Ashikaga Yoshitane was appointed as the 10th Muromachi shōgun of Japan, a position that held significant power during the Muromachi period. His leadership was marked by political challenges and cultural developments.
events.name: Ashikaga Yoshitane becomes 10th Muromachi shōgun of Japan

events.enhanced_description: The first edition of the chivalric romance 'Tirant lo Blanch' by Joanot Martorell was printed in Valencia. This work is considered one of the most important pieces of Catalan literature and reflects the cultural richness of the period.
events.name: First edition of Tirant lo Blanch is printed

events.enhanced_description: Anne of Brittany was married by proxy to Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, in a political maneuver aimed at strengthening alliances in Europe. This marriage was part of the complex dynastic politics of the time.
events.name: Anne of Brittany is married to Maximilian I by proxy

events.enhanced_description: Santa Fe, Argentina, was founded on November 15, 1573, by Spanish explorer Juan de Garay. This establishment was part of the Spanish colonial expansion in South America, aimed at consolidating their control over the region and facilitating trade.

locations.name: Santa Fe, Santa Fe Province, Argentina

events.name: Foundation of Santa Fe

events.enhanced_description: In March 1491, the French–Breton War resumed, a conflict that had significant implications for the political landscape of France and Brittany. This war was characterized by a series of battles and shifting alliances as both sides sought to assert control over Brittany.
events.name: French–Breton War resumes

events.enhanced_description: From March 19 to 20, 1491, Alain I of Albret captured the Château des ducs de Bretagne for the French, a pivotal moment in the French–Breton War. This victory helped to solidify French control over Brittany and marked a turning point in the conflict.

image.caption: Aerial photograph of the Château des ducs de Bretagne in Nantes.
image.credit: Jibi44 , avec l'aimable autorisation de LP de Nantes — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2008 aerial view of the castle, not a photograph of its capture in 1491.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Nantes, Pays de la Loire, France

events.name: Capture of Château des ducs de Bretagne

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1517, the Ottoman–Mamluk War officially concluded as the Ottoman Empire annexed the territories of the Mamluk Sultanate, including Egypt and the Hejaz. This annexation marked a significant expansion of Ottoman influence in the Middle East.
events.name: End of the Ottoman–Mamluk War

events.enhanced_description: In September 1491, the Battle of Vrpile Gulch took place in southern Croatia, where forces of the Ottoman Empire were defeated by those of the Kingdom of Croatia. This battle was part of the broader conflicts between the Ottomans and various European states.
events.name: Battle of Vrpile Gulch

events.enhanced_description: In November 1491, the pretender Perkin Warbeck began a campaign to claim the English throne, landing in Ireland. His efforts were part of a larger series of challenges to the Tudor monarchy, reflecting the political instability of the time.

image.caption: 15th-century drawing of Perkin Warbeck, attributed to Jacques Le Boucq.
image.credit: Jacques Le Boucq — Original drawing from the Recueil d’Arras (Arras, Bibliothèque municipale, Ms. 266)
image.date_qualification: The source dates the drawing to the 15th century; this is not a date for the campaign or a specific event scene.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Perkin Warbeck's campaign

events.enhanced_description: The reign of Ramathibodi II began in 1491 in the Ayutthaya Kingdom, marking a significant period in Thai history characterized by cultural and political developments. His leadership would influence the kingdom's expansion and prosperity.

locations.name: Ayutthaya, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Thailand

events.name: Beginning of Ramathibodi II's reign

events.enhanced_description: In 1491, the population of China reached approximately 56.238 million, reflecting the vast demographic scale of one of the world's oldest civilizations. This population growth had significant implications for the economy and society of China.
events.name: Population of China

events.enhanced_description: The Bread and Cheese Revolt erupted in 1491 in West Frisia, driven by famine among peasants due to adverse weather conditions. This revolt highlighted the social tensions and economic struggles faced by the rural population during this period.
events.name: Bread and Cheese Revolt

events.enhanced_description: In 1491, a major fire broke out in Dresden, causing significant damage to the city. This event underscored the vulnerabilities of urban centers during this period, particularly in terms of fire safety and urban planning.
events.name: Major fire in Dresden

events.enhanced_description: In 1491, copper and silver ores were discovered in the Komi Republic, which had been annexed by Russia in 1478. This discovery marked the region's emergence as an important mining and metallurgical center, contributing to Russia's economic development.
events.name: Discovery of ores in Komi

events.enhanced_description: In 1491, Nicolaus Copernicus enrolled at the University of Kraków, where he began his studies in mathematics and astronomy. This pivotal moment set the stage for his later revolutionary contributions to the field of astronomy.
events.name: Nicolaus Copernicus enters University of Kraków

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1491, Alain I of Albret signed the Treaty of Moulins with Charles VIII of France, solidifying French claims in Brittany. This treaty was a significant step in the consolidation of French power during the late 15th century.
events.name: Treaty of Moulins

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1491, the Catholic Monarchs of Spain besieged Granada, the last Muslim stronghold in Spain. This siege was a crucial event in the Reconquista, culminating in the fall of Granada in 1492 and the unification of Spain under Christian rule.
events.name: Siege of Granada

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1491, Nkuwu Nzinga, the ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo, was baptized by Portuguese missionaries, adopting the name João I. This event marked a significant moment in the Christianization of the Kongo and the establishment of ties with Portugal.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Manikongo João I of Kongo, also known as Nzinga a Nkuwu.
image.credit: Pierre Duflos — Histoire des Voyages NYPL
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the baptized ruler, not a contemporary depiction of the baptism; dated before 1816.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Baptism of Nkuwu Nzinga

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1491, a solar eclipse occurred over Metz, France. Such celestial events were often interpreted as omens and had significant cultural and scientific implications during the Renaissance.
events.name: Solar eclipse over Metz

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1491, Louis of Orléans was released by Charles VIII of France after three years of imprisonment. This event was significant in the context of French politics, as it reflected the ongoing power struggles within the French nobility.
events.name: Release of Louis of Orléans

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1491, an auto-da-fé was held in Brasero de la Dehesa, outside Ávila, concluding the case of the Holy Child of La Guardia. This event involved the execution of several Jewish and converso suspects, reflecting the intense religious persecution of the time.

image.caption: Pedro Berruguete’s painting of an auto-da-fé presided over by Saint Dominic, from the sacristy of Santo Tomás church in Ávila.
image.credit: Pedro Berruguete — [2]
image.date_qualification: The image date is circa 1493–1499; it is not the date of the event depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Auto-da-fé in Ávila

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Granada, signed on November 25, 1491, effectively ended the Granada War, extending the Siege of Granada for two additional months. This treaty marked a significant moment in the Reconquista, solidifying the Catholic Monarchs' control over the last Muslim stronghold in Spain.
events.name: Treaty of Granada

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1491, King Charles VIII of France married Anne of Brittany, a union that forced her to break her marriage contract with Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor. This marriage was pivotal in incorporating Brittany into the French crown, altering the political landscape of France.
events.name: Marriage of Charles VIII and Anne of Brittany

events.enhanced_description: The Truce of Coldstream, signed on December 21, 1491, established a five-year peace between Scotland and England. This agreement was crucial in maintaining stability in the border regions during a time of political tension.
events.name: Truce of Coldstream

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, the Alhambra Decree led to the expulsion of Jews from Spain, with estimates of 40,000 to 200,000 leaving the country. This event significantly impacted Jewish communities in Europe and the Ottoman Empire, where many sought refuge.
events.name: The Jews are expelled from Spain

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, Martin Behaim created the Erdapfel, the first surviving globe of the Earth. This globe, however, did not include the New World, as Columbus had not yet returned from his voyage.
events.name: Martin Behaim constructs the Erdapfel

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, the Arboretum Trsteno was designed and planted near Dubrovnik, Croatia. It is recognized as the first arboretum in the world, showcasing a variety of plant species and reflecting the Renaissance's growing interest in botany.
events.name: The first arboretum is designed

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, the Ivangorod Fortress was constructed on the eastern banks of the Narva River by Russian forces. This fortress played a strategic role in the defense against invasions and the expansion of Russian territories.
events.name: Ivangorod Fortress is built

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, during the Ming dynasty, the commercial transportation of grain to the northern border was monetized in exchange for salt certificates. This development marked a significant step in the monetization of trade and the economy in China.
events.name: Commercial transportation of grain is monetized in Ming China

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, Ermysted's Grammar School was founded in Skipton, North Yorkshire. This institution has played a significant role in the education of young men in the region for centuries.
events.name: Ermysted's Grammar School is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, Marsilio Ficino published his translation and commentary of Plotinus, a significant figure in Neoplatonism. This work contributed to the Renaissance's intellectual revival and the study of classical philosophy.
events.name: Marsilio Ficino publishes his translation of Plotinus

events.enhanced_description: In 1492, the Stiegl brewery was first recorded in Salzburg, Austria. This brewery has since become one of the most recognized and traditional breweries in the region.
events.name: Stiegl brewery first recorded

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1492, Muhammad XII, the last Emir of Granada, surrendered the city to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II and Isabella I, after a lengthy siege. This event marked the end of the Granada War and the Reconquista, concluding nearly 800 years of Muslim rule in Spain.
events.name: Fall of Granada

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella made their triumphant entry into Granada, celebrating the culmination of the Reconquista. This event symbolized the unification of Spain under Christian rule and the end of centuries of Muslim governance.
events.name: Ferdinand and Isabella enter Granada

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1492, Christopher Columbus met with Ferdinand and Isabella at the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos in Córdoba, persuading them to support his ambitious voyage across the Atlantic. This meeting was pivotal in launching Columbus's expedition that would lead to the discovery of the Americas.
events.name: Columbus meets Ferdinand and Isabella

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1492, Antonio de Nebrija published the 'Gramática de la lengua castellana,' the first grammar text for the Castilian Spanish language. This work was presented to Ferdinand and Isabella as a vital tool for the administration of their empire.
events.name: Publication of Gramática de la lengua castellana

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1492, the Pentateuch was first printed, marking a significant moment in the history of Jewish literature and the dissemination of religious texts. This event reflects the growing importance of printing technology in the late 15th century.
events.name: First printing of the Pentateuch

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree, expelling all Jews from Spain unless they converted to Roman Catholicism. This decree marked a significant moment in Spanish history, leading to the forced conversion and expulsion of thousands.
events.name: Signing of the Alhambra Decree

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1492, the Capitulations of Santa Fe were signed between Christopher Columbus and the Crown of Castile, outlining the terms of his upcoming voyage across the Atlantic. This agreement was crucial in facilitating Columbus's expedition that would lead to the discovery of the New World.
events.name: Capitulations of Santa Fe

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1492, Casimir IV Jagiellon died, ending his reign over Poland and Lithuania. His death marked a significant transition in the political landscape of Eastern Europe, leading to the ascension of his son, John I Albert.
events.name: Death of Casimir IV Jagiellon

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1492, Elizabeth Woodville, the last living Yorkist queen consort, died in England. Her death marked the end of an era in English history, as she was a key figure in the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Death of Elizabeth Woodville

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1492, the expulsion of Jews from Spain was enacted, leading to the departure of between 40,000 and 200,000 individuals. Sultan Bayezid II of the Ottoman Empire responded by sending the Ottoman Navy to rescue the expelled Jews, facilitating their relocation to Ottoman territories.
events.name: Expulsion of Jews from Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail from Palos de la Frontera with three ships, the Niña, the Pinta, and the Santa María, aiming to find a westward route to Asia. This voyage would lead to the European discovery of the Americas.
events.name: Christopher Columbus sails from Palos de la Frontera

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1492, Pope Alexander VI succeeded Pope Innocent VIII after the first papal conclave held in the Sistine Chapel. This conclave was significant as it marked a shift in papal leadership during a time of political and religious upheaval in Europe.
events.name: Papal Conclave of 1492

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed from La Gomera, his final port of call before embarking on his historic voyage across the Atlantic Ocean. This journey would lead to the European discovery of the Americas.
events.name: Columbus sails from La Gomera

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Boulogne was a significant military engagement during the Italian War of 1542–46, where King Henry VIII of England laid siege to the French city of Boulogne. The siege lasted for almost two months, culminating in the city's surrender on September 14, 1544, marking a pivotal moment in the conflict between England and France.
events.name: Siege of Boulogne

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus's expedition made landfall in the Caribbean, landing on Guanahani, which he named San Salvador. Believing he had reached the East Indies, this event marked the beginning of European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

image.caption: Portrait of Christopher Columbus in Alejo Fernández’s painting *Virgen de los Navegantes*.
image.credit: Alejo Fernández (1475-1545) — Photo by historian Manuel Rosa.
image.date_qualification: Painting dated 1531–36; not a contemporary image of the 1492 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Columbus lands in the Caribbean

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on the northern coast of Cuba during his first voyage across the Atlantic. He believed he had reached the outskirts of Asia, marking a significant moment in European exploration and the eventual colonization of the Americas.

locations.name: Off the coast of Havana, Cuba

events.name: Christopher Columbus lands in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1492, the Peace of Étaples was signed between England and France, effectively ending the conflict over Perkin Warbeck's claim to the English throne. This treaty marked a significant diplomatic achievement for Henry VII, restoring peace and returning English-held territories in France.
events.name: The Peace of Étaples is signed

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1492, the Ensisheim meteorite, weighing 127 kg (280 lb), fell in a wheat field near the village of Ensisheim in Alsace. This event is notable as one of the earliest recorded meteorite falls in Europe, sparking interest in meteorites and their origins.
events.name: The Ensisheim meteorite lands

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1492, Christopher Columbus became the first European to set foot on the island of Hispaniola during his first voyage. This event marked the beginning of European colonization in the Caribbean, leading to significant cultural and demographic changes in the region.
events.name: Christopher Columbus lands on Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1492, Columbus' flagship, the Santa María, ran aground off the coast of Cap-Haïtien, leading to its loss. This incident forced Columbus to leave a contingent of men on the island and return to Spain, marking a pivotal moment in his first voyage.
events.name: Santa María runs aground

events.enhanced_description: In 1493, England, under King Henry VII, imposed sanctions on the Duchy of Burgundy due to its support for Perkin Warbeck, a pretender to the English throne. This political maneuver was part of the broader conflict between England and those who challenged the legitimacy of Henry's rule.
events.name: England imposes sanctions on Burgundy for supporting Perkin Warbeck

events.enhanced_description: In 1493, King James IV of Scotland seized the lands of John MacDonald II, effectively ending the Lordship of the Isles. This act consolidated royal power in Scotland and marked the decline of the MacDonald clan's influence in the region.
events.name: James IV of Scotland seizes lands of John MacDonald II

events.enhanced_description: In 1493, Huayna Capac ascended to the throne as the emperor of the Inca Empire, a significant period that saw the expansion and consolidation of Inca territory. His reign would be marked by both internal challenges and external threats, particularly from Spanish conquistadors in the following decades.
events.name: Huayna Capac becomes emperor of the Inca Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1493, Leonardo da Vinci conceptualized the first known design for a helicopter, showcasing his innovative spirit and understanding of aerodynamics. This design, although never built in his lifetime, laid the groundwork for future advancements in aviation.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci creates the first known design for a helicopter

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1493, the Treaty of Barcelona was signed, whereby Charles VIII of France returned the territories of Cerdagne and Roussillon to Ferdinand II of Aragon. This treaty marked a significant step in stabilizing relations between France and Spain.
events.name: Treaty of Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1493, Martín Alonso Pinzón returned to Bayona, France, from Columbus's voyage of discovery, bringing the first news of the New World to the Catholic Monarchs. His return was pivotal in confirming the success of Columbus's expedition.
events.name: Martín Alonso Pinzón returns to Bayona

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1493, Christopher Columbus anchored in Lisbon, Portugal, where he completed his letter detailing the discoveries made during his first voyage. This letter was crucial in informing European powers about the New World.
events.name: Christopher Columbus anchors in Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1493, Christopher Columbus and Martín Alonso Pinzón returned to Palos de la Frontera, Spain, marking the end of Columbus's first voyage. Their return was celebrated as a monumental achievement in the Age of Exploration.
events.name: Columbus and Pinzón return to Palos de la Frontera

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1493, the Battle of Anfao took place, where Askia Mohammad I defeated Sonni Baru, usurping the throne of the Songhai Empire. This battle marked a significant shift in power within one of West Africa's largest empires.
events.name: Battle of Anfao

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued the papal bull Inter caetera, declaring that all lands discovered 100 leagues west of the Azores were to be considered Spanish territory. This decree played a crucial role in the territorial disputes between Spain and Portugal.
events.name: Papal bull Inter caetera

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1493, Maximilian I succeeded his father, Frederick III, as Holy Roman Emperor. His reign marked significant political changes and the strengthening of the Habsburg dynasty in European politics.
events.name: Maximilian I succeeds Frederick III

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1493, the Battle of Krbava Field occurred in southern Croatia, where forces of the Ottoman Empire defeated those of the Kingdom of Croatia. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Ottomans and the Croatian nobility.
events.name: Battle of Krbava Field

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1493, Christopher Columbus departed from Cádiz on his second voyage of exploration to the New World. This voyage aimed to establish a permanent Spanish presence in the Americas.
events.name: Christopher Columbus leaves Cádiz

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued the bull Dudum siquidem to the Catholic Monarchs, extending the grant of newly discovered lands made in the previous bull Inter caetera. This reaffirmed Spain's claims to territories in the New World.
events.name: Pope Alexander VI issues the bull Dudum siquidem

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1493, Christopher Columbus landed on the coast of the island of Borinquen, which he renamed San Juan, during his second voyage. This event marked the European discovery of Puerto Rico and the beginning of Spanish colonization in the Caribbean.
events.name: Christopher Columbus lands on Borinquen

events.enhanced_description: In December 1493, Christopher Columbus returned to La Navidad, only to find the settlement destroyed and its inhabitants killed. This event underscored the challenges of European colonization in the Americas and the violent encounters that ensued.
events.name: Columbus return to La Navidad 1493

events.enhanced_description: In May 1494, Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, recognized Perkin Warbeck as the rightful King of England, further complicating the political landscape of Europe. This recognition was a significant endorsement for Warbeck's claim against Henry VII.
events.name: Maximilian I recognizes Perkin Warbeck

events.enhanced_description: In 1494, Aztec forces conquered and sacked the city of Mitla, a significant event in the consolidation of Aztec power in the region. This conquest demonstrated the military strength of the Aztecs and their expansionist ambitions.
events.name: Aztec forces conquer and sack Mitla

events.enhanced_description: In 1494, Johann Reuchlin published De verbo mirifico, a significant work that contributed to the study of Hebrew and Jewish mysticism in Europe. This publication played a crucial role in the Renaissance humanist movement.
events.name: Johann Reuchlin publishes De verbo mirifico

events.enhanced_description: In 1494, Charles VIII of France purchased the right to the Byzantine Empire from the exiled pretender Andreas Palaiologos. This transaction reflected the ongoing interest of European powers in the remnants of the Byzantine Empire and its historical significance.
events.name: Charles VIII purchases the right to the Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1494, the Cetinje Octoechos was completed in Cetinje, marking a significant achievement in Eastern Orthodox liturgical literature. It was the first book printed in Cyrillic in Southeast Europe, reflecting the cultural and religious heritage of the region.

image.caption: A copy of the Cetinje Octoechos of the Fifth Tone (Oktoih petoglasnik) in the Educational Museum in Belgrade.
image.credit: Mickey Mystique — Own work
image.date_qualification: The book dates to 1494; the image was photographed on 2017-12-24.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Completion of the Cetinje Octoechos

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1494, Alfonso II ascended to the throne of Naples, a position that would soon be challenged by external forces during the Italian Wars. His reign was marked by political instability and the shifting allegiances of Italian city-states.
events.name: Alfonso II becomes King of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1494, Christopher Columbus first sighted Jamaica during his second voyage to the New World. This discovery would later lead to the island becoming a significant site for Spanish colonization and trade.
events.name: Christopher Columbus first sights Jamaica

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1494, the infant Amda Seyon II succeeded his father Eskender as Emperor of Ethiopia. His reign began during a tumultuous period marked by internal strife and external threats.
events.name: The infant Amda Seyon II succeeds his father Eskender as Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1494, the First Battle of Acentejo took place, where the native Guanches of Tenerife defeated the invading Spanish forces. This battle marked a significant resistance against Spanish colonization in the Canary Islands.

image.caption: Location map of the Canary Islands.
image.credit: Miguillen — Own work based on: EspañaLoc.svg by HansenBCN
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2010-11-18; it does not depict the 1494 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: First Battle of Acentejo

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1494, the Treaty of Tordesillas was signed, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal. This agreement, sanctioned by Pope Alexander VI, aimed to resolve conflicts over newly discovered lands and set the stage for future colonial expansion.
events.name: Treaty of Tordesillas

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1494, the first hurricane ever observed by Europeans struck the Spanish settlement of La Isabela on Hispaniola. This event highlighted the challenges faced by early European settlers in the Caribbean.
events.name: First hurricane observed by Europeans strikes Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1494, Ludovico Sforza became Duke of Milan and invited Charles VIII of France to invade Italy, marking the beginning of the Italian War of 1494–98. This invitation set off a series of conflicts that would reshape the political landscape of Italy.
events.name: Ludovico Sforza invites Charles VIII to invade Italy

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1494, Amda Seyon II was deposed and killed, leading to his uncle Na'od succeeding him as Emperor of Ethiopia. This event marked a significant shift in the Ethiopian monarchy during a period of political instability.
events.name: Amda Seyon II is deposed and killed

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1494, the Medici Bank declared insolvency, leading to the expulsion of the House of Medici from Florence. This event marked a significant turning point in Florentine politics and the decline of Medici influence in the region.
events.name: The Medici Bank becomes insolvent

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1494, Fra Luca Pacioli published his influential work, Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità, in Venice. This book is notable for being the first printed account of algebra in the vernacular and for its description of the double-entry accounting system.
events.name: Fra Luca Pacioli's Summa de arithmetica is published

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1494, during the Italian War of 1494–98, the armies of Charles VIII of France entered Florence. This event marked a significant moment in the conflict, as Florence was a key city-state in Italy's political landscape.
events.name: Italian War of 1494–98: Charles VIII enters Florence

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1494, the Second Battle of Acentejo occurred, where Spanish forces defeated the native Guanches of Tenerife. This battle led to the subjugation of the last bastion of resistance in the Canary Islands.
events.name: Second Battle of Acentejo

events.enhanced_description: In February 1495, King's College, Aberdeen, was founded on the petition of William Elphinstone, Bishop of Aberdeen. It became the first English-speaking university to teach medicine, marking a significant development in higher education in Scotland.
events.name: King's College, Aberdeen is founded

events.enhanced_description: The Reisszug, a private cable railway providing goods access to Hohensalzburg Fortress in Salzburg, Austria, is considered the oldest extant cable railway, dating back to 1495. This innovative transport system exemplifies early engineering advancements in the region.
events.name: Reisszug cable railway

events.enhanced_description: In 1495, Poynings' Law was enacted, placing the Parliament of Ireland under the authority of the Parliament of England. This legislation marked a significant step in the consolidation of English control over Irish governance.
events.name: Poynings' Law

events.enhanced_description: The Reichskammergericht, or Imperial Chamber Court, was founded in Frankfurt in 1495 as a court of the Holy Roman Empire. It played a crucial role in the administration of justice within the empire.
events.name: Foundation of the Reichskammergericht

events.enhanced_description: In 1495, Henry VII of England commissioned the world's first dry dock at Portsmouth, revolutionizing shipbuilding and maintenance. This innovation significantly enhanced naval capabilities and set a precedent for future maritime infrastructure.
events.name: Commissioning of the world's first dry dock

events.enhanced_description: In 1495, Piero Pacini da Pescia published 'Epistles, Gospels, and Popular Readings' in the Tuscan language, contributing to the literary and cultural landscape of the Renaissance. This work reflects the growing importance of vernacular literature during this period.
events.name: Publication of Epistles, Gospels, and Popular Readings
