events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1495, during the Italian War of 1494–98, King Charles VIII of France entered Naples to claim the city's throne. This invasion would lead to significant political upheaval and military conflict in Italy.
events.name: Italian War of 1494–98: Charles VIII enters Naples

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1495, a Spanish army led by Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba landed in Calabria with the intent of ousting the French and restoring Ferdinand II of Naples to the throne. This military action was part of the larger conflict of the Italian Wars.

image.caption: Portrait of Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, known as El Gran Capitán, painted by Eduardo Carrió.
image.credit: Eduardo Carrió — [2]
image.date_qualification: Retrospective portrait, not a depiction of the 1495 landing; the saved image date is approximate.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Spanish army under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba lands in Calabria

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1495, Brother John Cor of Lindores Abbey paid duty on malt to the Exchequer in Scotland to make aqua vitae for King James IV. This record is recognized as the first written reference to Scotch whisky, highlighting the early beginnings of whisky production in Scotland.
events.name: First written reference to Scotch whisky

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Seminara, fought on June 28, 1495, marked a significant defeat for the Spanish forces led by Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba against the French army commanded by Bernard Stewart, Lord of Aubigny. This battle was part of the larger conflict during the Italian Wars, showcasing the shifting power dynamics in Renaissance Italy.
events.name: Battle of Seminara

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1495, John, King of Denmark, set sail for Kalmar, Sweden, to negotiate with Sten Sture the Elder in an attempt to restore the Kalmar Union. Unfortunately, his flagship, Gribshunden, caught fire and sank, leading to the abandonment of his diplomatic mission.
events.name: John, King of Denmark's mission to Kalmar

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1495, the Battle of Deal occurred when Perkin Warbeck's forces landed in Kent to support his claim to the English crown. However, the troops were quickly routed before Warbeck could disembark, forcing him to retreat to Ireland and then Scotland, marking a significant setback in his rebellion.
events.name: Battle of Deal

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Fornovo, fought on July 6, 1495, saw the French army under King Charles VIII successfully defeat a combined Milanese-Venetian force led by Giovanni Francesco Gonzaga. This battle was crucial for securing the French retreat from Italy during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Battle of Fornovo

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1495, Manuel I ascended to the throne of Portugal, succeeding his cousin, King John II. His reign would be marked by the continuation of the Age of Discoveries, expanding Portugal's influence overseas.
events.name: King Manuel I of Portugal begins his reign

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1495, an explosion at Vyborg Castle played a crucial role in deterring Russian forces that had invaded Sweden through Karelia. This incident highlighted the ongoing conflicts in the region during the late 15th century.
events.name: Explosion at Vyborg Castle

events.enhanced_description: In July 1496, Spanish forces under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba successfully captured Atella after a siege, restoring Ferdinand II of Naples to his throne. This event was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Capture of Atella

events.enhanced_description: In 1496, Jan de Groote, a Dutchman, obtained a grant from King James IV of Scotland for the north ferry from the mainland of Scotland to Orkney. This grant facilitated transportation and trade between the mainland and the islands.
events.name: Jan de Groote's ferry grant

events.enhanced_description: In February 1496, Pietro Bembo's 'Petri Bembi de Aetna' was published in Venice by Aldus Manutius, notable for being the first book printed in the humanist typeface cut by Francesco Griffo. This publication represents a significant moment in the history of printing and literature.
events.name: Publication of Petri Bembi de Aetna

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1496, King Henry VII of England signed the Intercursus Magnus, a commercial treaty with Venice, Florence, and the cities of the Hanseatic League and the Netherlands. This treaty aimed to enhance trade relations and economic cooperation.

image.caption: Flag of Florence, featuring a lily.
image.credit: Kanchelskis — This vector image includes elements that have been taken or adapted from this file:
image.date_qualification: A contemporary vector depiction of a Florence flag, not an image of the treaty signing; image date is 2008-04-04.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Intercursus Magnus treaty

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1496, Henry VII of England issued letters patent to John Cabot and his sons, authorizing them to discover unknown lands. This act marked a significant moment in the Age of Exploration, paving the way for future voyages to the New World.
events.name: John Cabot's letters patent

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1496, Christopher Columbus departed from Hispaniola for Spain, concluding his second visit to the Western Hemisphere. His time on the island was marked by the subjugation of the Taíno people and the establishment of a colonial system.
events.name: Christopher Columbus leaves Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1496, Jesus College, Cambridge, was founded, contributing to the rich academic tradition of one of the world's leading universities. The college has since played a significant role in the education of many notable figures.
events.name: Founding of Jesus College, Cambridge

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1496, Bartholomew Columbus, brother of Christopher Columbus, formally founded the city of Santo Domingo on Hispaniola, making it the oldest permanent European settlement in the New World. This city would become a crucial center for Spanish colonial administration.
events.name: Founding of Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1496, James IV of Scotland invaded Northumberland in support of the pretender Perkin Warbeck's claim to the English throne. This military action was part of the broader conflict between England and Scotland during this period.
events.name: James IV of Scotland invades Northumberland

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1496, Joanna of Castile married Philip, archduke of the Burgundian Netherlands and heir to the Holy Roman Empire. This marriage was significant in strengthening ties between Spain and the Habsburgs, influencing European politics for generations.
events.name: Marriage of Joanna of Castile and Philip

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1496, King Manuel I of Portugal issued a decree ordering the expulsion of 'heretics' from the country. This action was part of the broader context of the Inquisition and religious intolerance prevalent in Europe during this period.
events.name: Expulsion of heretics from Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In March 1497, the Russo-Swedish War concluded with a six-year truce, as Swedish leader Sten Sture the Elder sought peace with Ivan III of Moscow due to growing unrest at home. This truce marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between the two nations.
events.name: End of the Russo-Swedish War

events.enhanced_description: In May 1497, the Cornish Rebellion broke out in England, incited by discontent over war taxes imposed by King Henry VII. This uprising highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and the local populace, ultimately leading to significant political consequences.
events.name: Cornish Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 1497, Ivan the Great issued the Sudebnik, a comprehensive law code that aimed to standardize legal practices across Russia. This code was significant in the development of Russian law and governance.
events.name: Ivan the Great issues his law code, the Sudebnik

events.enhanced_description: In 1497, the Ottoman Empire granted Russian merchants freedom of trade within its territories, fostering economic relations between the two powers. This agreement was crucial for the development of trade routes and commerce in the region.
events.name: The Ottomans give Russian merchants freedom of trade

events.enhanced_description: In 1497, the work 'De mysteriis Aegyptorum' by Iamblichus, edited by Marsilio Ficino, was published in Florence. This publication contributed to the Renaissance's revival of interest in Neoplatonism and ancient philosophies.
events.name: Iamblichus De mysteriis Aegyptorum edited by Marsilio Ficino is published

events.enhanced_description: In 1497, the Annals of the Four Masters documented a famine that 'prevailed through all Ireland.' This historical record provides insight into the social and agricultural challenges faced by the Irish population during this period.
events.name: The Annals of the Four Masters refer to a famine in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1497, followers of Girolamo Savonarola conducted the Bonfire of the Vanities in Florence, burning thousands of 'immoral' objects. This event was emblematic of the religious fervor and cultural upheaval of the time, reflecting Savonarola's influence.
events.name: Bonfire of the Vanities

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1497, Amerigo Vespucci set sail from Cádiz, Spain, embarking on a voyage that would lead him to the shores of the New World. His explorations contributed significantly to the understanding of the Americas and ultimately led to the continent being named after him.

image.caption: Woodcut depicting Amerigo Vespucci’s first voyage, reproduced as a photographic facsimile.
image.credit: Amerigo Vespucci — 1893 First Four Voyages of Amerigo Vespucci , London: B. Quaritch
image.date_qualification: The woodcut is described as probably dating to circa 1505; the supplied image is an 1893 facsimile. Neither date establishes the event’s exact departure date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Amerigo Vespucci allegedly leaves Cádiz for his first voyage to the New World

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1497, Pope Alexander VI excommunicated the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola, who had gained significant influence in Florence by denouncing corruption and immorality in the Church. This act marked a pivotal moment in the conflict between Savonarola and the papacy.
events.name: Pope Alexander VI excommunicates Girolamo Savonarola

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1497, John Cabot departed from Bristol aboard the ship Matthew, seeking new lands to the west. His voyage is credited with the European discovery of parts of North America, paving the way for future exploration and colonization.

image.caption: Painting of John Cabot in traditional Venetian garb.
image.credit: Giustino Menescardi — John Cabot in traditional Venetian garb by Giustino Menescardi (1762). A mural painting in the 'Sala dello Scudo' in the Palazzo Ducale. Taken from a reproduction in "History of Maritime maps", Donald Wigal
image.date_qualification: Portrait painting by Giustino Menescardi, dated 1762; a later depiction, not an image of Cabot's 1497 voyage.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: John Cabot sets sail from Bristol on the ship Matthew

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1497, the Catholic Monarchs of Spain issued the ordinance of Medina del Campo, establishing a monetary system based on the copper maravedí, which would later evolve into the peso. This system significantly influenced trade and currency in the Americas and beyond.

locations.name: Medina del Campo, Castile and León, Spain

events.name: The Catholic Monarchs issue the ordinance of Medina del Campo

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1497, the Battle of Deptford Bridge took place, where Cornish rebels led by Michael An Gof were decisively defeated by the forces of King Henry VII. This battle was a significant event in the Cornish Rebellion against taxation and royal authority.
events.name: Battle of Deptford Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1497, John Cabot made landfall in North America, specifically near present-day Bonavista, Newfoundland. This event marked one of the earliest European explorations of the continent, leading to further expeditions and eventual colonization.
events.name: John Cabot lands in North America

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1497, Vasco da Gama's fleet set sail from Lisbon, Portugal, embarking on an expedition that would ultimately lead to the discovery of the maritime route to India. This journey was crucial in establishing Portugal's dominance in the spice trade.
events.name: Vasco da Gama's fleet departs from Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1497, Perkin Warbeck landed near Land's End, Cornwall, as part of the Second Cornish Uprising against King Henry VII. He was proclaimed King in Bodmin on September 10, highlighting the discontent with the monarchy during this period.

locations.name: Land's End, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Second Cornish Uprising in England

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1497, the Battle of Rotebro occurred, where John, King of Denmark, defeated Sten Sture the Elder. This battle was significant in the ongoing power struggles in Scandinavia during the late 15th century.
events.name: Battle of Rotebro

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1497, the Treaty of Ayton was established, creating a seven-year peace between England and Scotland. This treaty was a crucial step in stabilizing relations between the two kingdoms during a tumultuous period.
events.name: The Treaty of Ayton

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1497, the leaders of the Second Cornish Uprising surrendered to King Henry VII at Taunton. The following day, Perkin Warbeck was captured at Beaulieu Abbey after abandoning his forces, marking the end of the rebellion.
events.name: Leaders of the Second Cornish Uprising surrender

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1497, Sten Sture the Elder was forced to resign after a prolonged conflict with King John of Denmark. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within Sweden, restoring the Kalmar Union.

image.caption: Grave of Swedish regent Sten Sture the Elder in Strängnäs Cathedral.

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1497, King Manuel I of Portugal issued an edict demanding that Jews convert to Christianity or leave the country. This decree was part of a broader trend of religious intolerance in Europe during this period.
events.name: King Manuel I of Portugal's edict against Jews

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1497, Sheen Palace was destroyed by fire, prompting King Henry VII to rebuild it as Richmond Palace. This event marked a significant transformation in royal residences in England.
events.name: Sheen Palace is destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: The discovery of the sea route to India by the Portuguese in 1498, led by Vasco da Gama, marked a significant milestone in the Age of Exploration. This route opened direct trade between Europe and Asia, transforming global commerce and geopolitics.
events.name: The Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India

events.enhanced_description: In May 1498, John Cabot set out from Bristol on an expedition, never to be seen again. His disappearance remains a mystery, but his earlier voyages had already laid the groundwork for future exploration of North America.
events.name: John Cabot leaves Bristol on an expedition

events.enhanced_description: In June 1498, Niccolò Machiavelli was elected by the Great Council as the second chancellor of the Republic of Florence. His political writings during this period would later influence modern political theory.
events.name: Niccolò Machiavelli is elected as chancellor of Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, John Cabot departed from Bristol on an expedition to North America, but he was never seen again. His disappearance remains a mystery in the history of exploration.
events.name: John Cabot's expedition

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, the English Merchant Adventurers were granted a trade monopoly with the Netherlands, significantly impacting trade relations between England and the Low Countries.
events.name: Trade monopoly granted

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, explorers João Fernandes Lavrador and Pedro de Barcelos journeyed to Greenland and discovered the land they named Labrador, contributing to European knowledge of North America.
events.name: Discovery of Labrador

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, founded the Wiener Hofmusikkapelle, which later evolved into the famous Vienna Boys' Choir, marking a significant development in the musical culture of Austria.
events.name: Foundation of Wiener Hofmusikkapelle

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, the technique of gun barrel rifling was invented in Augsburg, Bavaria, marking a significant advancement in firearms technology that would enhance accuracy and range.
events.name: Invention of gun barrel rifling

events.enhanced_description: In 1498, Leonardo da Vinci completed his iconic mural, The Last Supper, on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. This masterpiece remains one of the most celebrated works of art in history.
events.name: Completion of The Last Supper

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1498, Vasco da Gama visited Quelimane and Mozambique during his expedition to India. This visit was part of his broader journey to establish trade routes along the eastern coast of Africa.
events.name: Vasco da Gama visits Quelimane and Mozambique

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1498, Vasco da Gama reached Malindi, Kenya, during his voyage to India. This stop was significant for establishing relations with local rulers and facilitating trade in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Vasco da Gama reaches Malindi

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1498, Vasco da Gama arrived at Calicut (modern-day Kozhikode), India, becoming the first European to reach India by sailing around Africa. This monumental achievement opened up new trade routes and marked the beginning of European colonialism in Asia.
events.name: Vasco da Gama arrives at Calicut, India

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1498, Girolamo Savonarola, a prominent critic of the papacy and a reformer in Florence, was executed. His death marked the end of his influence and the return of Medici power in the city.
events.name: Girolamo Savonarola is executed

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1498, Christopher Columbus embarked on his third voyage to the Western Hemisphere from Sanlúcar, Spain. This journey aimed to explore the coasts of South America and establish further Spanish claims in the New World.
events.name: Christopher Columbus sets out on his third voyage

events.enhanced_description: The final Welsh revolt of the medieval era erupted in Meirionnydd, North Wales, where rebels captured Harlech Castle. This uprising was part of the ongoing struggle for Welsh independence, ultimately suppressed by English forces.
events.name: Final Welsh Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1498, Christopher Columbus became the first European to visit the island of Trinidad during his third voyage to the Americas. This marked a significant moment in the European exploration of the Caribbean.
events.name: Columbus visits Trinidad

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1498, Columbus discovered the mouth of the Orinoco River, a significant geographical feature in South America. This discovery expanded European knowledge of the continent's geography.
events.name: Columbus discovers the Orinoco

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1498, Columbus explored the Gulf of Paria, landing on the Paria Peninsula, marking the first recorded landing of Europeans on the mainland of the Americas.
events.name: Columbus explores the Gulf of Paria

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1498, a significant earthquake struck off the coast of Japan, known as the Nankai earthquake. This seismic event is part of the complex tectonic activity in the region.
events.name: Nankai earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In August 1499, Polydore Vergil completed De inventoribus rerum, the first modern history of inventions, which would influence the study of technology and innovation in Europe.
events.name: Polydore Vergil completes De inventoribus rerum

events.enhanced_description: In 1499, the French under Louis XII seized Milan, driving out Duke Ludovico Sforza, prompting Leonardo da Vinci to flee to Venice. This event marked a significant shift in power in Northern Italy.
events.name: French seize Milan

events.enhanced_description: In 1499, Montenegro, the last free monarchy in the Balkans, was annexed by the Ottoman Empire, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in the region. The ruling monarch, Stefan II Crnojević, was removed from office as Montenegro became part of the sanjak of Shkodër.
events.name: Annexation of Montenegro by the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 1499, Johannes Trithemius, a German Benedictine abbot and scholar, inadvertently revealed his interests in magic and cryptography through a letter to a Carmelite friar. This correspondence discussed a treatise he was writing on steganography, the art of hidden writing, which would later influence the fields of cryptography and magic.
events.name: Johannes Trithemius' Letter on Steganography

events.enhanced_description: In 1499, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a notable German polymath, philosopher, and occult writer, matriculated at the University of Cologne. His studies and writings would later contribute significantly to the fields of magic, philosophy, and science during the Renaissance.
events.name: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa Matriculates at Cologne University

events.enhanced_description: In 1499, Reverend James Carr founded Giggleswick School in England, establishing an institution that would become one of the oldest schools in the country. The school has a rich history of academic excellence and has contributed to the education of many notable figures over the centuries.
events.name: Foundation of Giggleswick School

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1499, Louis XII of France married Anne of Brittany, fulfilling a political alliance that had been established by his predecessor, Charles VIII. This marriage was significant for the unification of Brittany with the French crown.
events.name: Marriage of Louis XII and Anne of Brittany

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1499, 18-year-old Catherine of Aragon was married by proxy to 12-year-old Arthur, Prince of Wales, marking an important political alliance for the English crown.
events.name: Marriage of Catherine of Aragon and Arthur

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1499, the Swiss decisively defeated the army of Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, at the Battle of Dornach, a pivotal moment in the Swabian War that led to Swiss independence.
events.name: Battle of Dornach

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1499, the Turkish navy won a decisive victory over the Venetians at the First Battle of Lepanto, marking a significant moment in the struggle for control of the Mediterranean.
events.name: First Battle of Lepanto

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1499, Alonso de Ojeda and Amerigo Vespucci discovered Lake Maracaibo, one of the largest lakes in Latin America, contributing to the European understanding of the region's geography.
events.name: Discovery of Lake Maracaibo

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1499, Vasco da Gama returned to Lisbon after his successful voyage to India, where he was received by King Manuel of Portugal, marking a significant achievement in the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Vasco da Gama returns to Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1499, the Treaty of Basel was signed, forcing Maximilian I to grant the Swiss de facto independence, a pivotal moment in Swiss history.
events.name: Treaty of Basel

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1499, the Pont Notre-Dame in Paris, constructed under Charles VI of France, collapsed into the Seine River, highlighting the challenges of medieval engineering.
events.name: Collapse of the Pont Notre-Dame

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1499, the Catholicon, a Breton–Greek–Latin dictionary written by Jehan Lagadeuc, was published in Tréguiers, marking a significant contribution to the linguistic heritage of Brittany.
events.name: Publication of the Catholicon

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1499, Perkin Warbeck, a pretender to the English throne, was hanged after attempting to escape from the Tower of London, marking the end of his claim to the crown.
events.name: Execution of Perkin Warbeck

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1499, Edward Plantagenet, the last male member of the House of York, was executed for allegedly attempting to escape from the Tower of London, a significant event in the Wars of the Roses.
events.name: Execution of Edward Plantagenet

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1499, the Rebellion of the Alpujarras began in the Kingdom of Granada against the forced conversions of Muslims in Spain, marking a significant conflict in the history of religious tolerance.
events.name: Rebellion of the Alpujarras begins

events.enhanced_description: In the year 1500, Europe's population was estimated to be around 56.7 million people, reflecting the demographic changes and growth of the continent during this period. This estimate is part of broader historical studies on population dynamics.
events.name: Europe's population estimated

events.enhanced_description: In 1500, the mint at Annaberg in Saxony began producing guldengroschens, also known as guldiners, marking a significant development in the currency system of the region. This coinage would play an important role in trade and commerce.
events.name: Saxony's mint begins producing guldengroschens

events.enhanced_description: In 1500, it is believed that the last wolf in England was killed, marking the extinction of the species in the country. This event occurred in Allithwaite, Cumbria, and reflects the broader environmental changes and human impact on wildlife.
events.name: Last wolf in England killed

events.enhanced_description: Around the year 1500, a group of Māori migrated from the New Zealand mainland to the Chatham Islands, where they developed a distinct pacifist culture known as the Moriori. This migration reflects the broader patterns of Polynesian exploration and settlement.
events.name: Māori migration to Chatham Islands

events.enhanced_description: The iconic She-wolf statue, depicting the legendary she-wolf that nursed the twins Romulus and Remus, is believed to have been created in the late 15th or early 16th century. This sculpture has become a symbol of Rome and is currently housed in the Museo Capitolino, showcasing the city's rich artistic heritage.
events.name: Creation of the She-wolf Statue

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1500, Duke Ludovico Sforza successfully recaptured Milan from the French forces, marking a brief resurgence of his power. However, this victory was short-lived as he was soon driven out again by the French, leading to further instability in the region.
events.name: Duke Ludovico Sforza recaptures Milan

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1500, Spanish navigator Vicente Yáñez Pinzón became one of the first Europeans to reach the northern coast of Brazil. This event marked a significant moment in the Age of Discovery, as it opened up new territories for exploration and potential colonization.

locations.historical_name: Part of the regions inhabited by indigenous populations in southern South America
locations.name: Buenos Aires

events.name: Vicente Yáñez Pinzón reaches Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1500, Ludovico Sforza's Swiss mercenary army successfully retook the city of Milan from the French during the ongoing conflicts of the Second Italian War. This event illustrated the shifting allegiances and power struggles characteristic of Italian city-states during this period.
events.name: Ludovico Sforza's Swiss mercenary army retakes Milan

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1500, the Battle of Hemmingstedt took place, where the Danish army attempted to conquer the peasants' republic of Dithmarschen. The battle ended in a surprising defeat for the Danish forces, showcasing the resilience of the local populace.

image.caption: Colour lithograph depicting the Danish attack on Dithmarschen, by Rasmus Christiansen.
image.credit: Rasmus Christiansen (1863-1940) — AU Library, Campus Emdrup
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration published in 1898, depicting the 1500 Battle of Hemmingstedt; it is not a contemporary image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Hemmingstedt

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1500, Pedro Álvares Cabral departed from Lisbon with a fleet of 13 ships on a voyage to the New World. This expedition would lead to the discovery of Brazil and significantly impact the course of Portuguese exploration and colonization.
events.name: Pedro Álvares Cabral departs Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1500, the Parliament of Bohemia adopted a new constitution that limited the power of King Vladislav II and subsequent monarchs. This significant political reform aimed to establish a more balanced governance structure in the Kingdom of Bohemia.
events.name: Parliament of Bohemia adopts new constitution

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1500, Vasco de Ataíde and his crew of 150 met a tragic fate when their ship sank in a storm shortly after departing the Cape Verde Islands. This incident highlighted the perils faced by explorers during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Vasco de Ataíde's shipwreck

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1500, Portuguese navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral and his fleet became the first Europeans to discover Brazil, anchoring at Monte Pascoal. Cabral claimed the land for Portugal, naming it Vera Cruz, which marked the beginning of Portuguese colonization in South America.
events.name: Cabral discovers Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1500, Pêro Vaz de Caminha completed his chronicle of the Portuguese discovery of Brazil while accompanying Cabral. This document is considered one of the earliest accounts of Brazil and provides valuable insights into the land and its indigenous peoples.

locations.historical_name: Part of the regions inhabited by indigenous populations in southern South America
locations.name: Buenos Aires

events.name: Pêro Vaz de Caminha finishes chronicle

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1500, after a brief stay, Pedro Álvares Cabral and his fleet departed from Brazil, sailing eastward toward Africa to resume their journey to India. This marked the continuation of Cabral's significant voyage that would reshape European understanding of the world.

locations.historical_name: Part of the regions inhabited by indigenous populations in southern South America
locations.name: Buenos Aires

events.name: Cabral departs Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1500, representatives of the English and Spanish royal families signed a treaty in Canterbury for the marriage of 13-year-old Arthur, Prince of Wales, to 14-year-old Princess Catherine of Aragon. This alliance was significant for both kingdoms, although Arthur's untimely death would alter the course of history.
events.name: Treaty for Arthur and Catherine's marriage

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1500, Hieronymus Brunschwig published 'Liber de arte distillandi de simplicibus', the first guide to distilling liquor. This work laid the foundation for the science of distillation and had a lasting impact on the production of alcoholic beverages.
events.name: First guide to distilling published

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1500, while traveling eastward from Brazil, Cabral's fleet encountered a storm near the Cape of Good Hope, resulting in the loss of four ships. Among those lost was navigator Bartolomeu Dias, highlighting the dangers faced by explorers during this era.
events.name: Cabral's fleet loses ships in storm

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1500, Pope Alexander VI issued the papal bull 'Quamvis ad amplianda', calling for a Roman Catholic crusade against the Ottoman Empire. This declaration reflected the ongoing tensions between Christian Europe and the Muslim Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Papal bull Quamvis ad amplianda

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1500, a combined force of troops from the Kingdom of France and the Republic of Florence laid siege to the city of Pisa. This siege was part of the broader conflicts in Italy during the Renaissance, reflecting the intense power struggles of the time.
events.name: Siege of Pisa

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1500, Sultan Abu Sa'id Qansuh of Egypt was overthrown and sent into exile. Al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasir Janbalat was crowned as the new Mamluk sultan, although his reign would last less than six months, indicating the instability of the Mamluk Sultanate during this period.
events.name: Overthrow of Sultan Abu Sa'id Qansuh

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1500, the Muscovites achieved a significant victory over the Lithuanians and Poles in the Battle of Vedrosha. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Grand Duchy of Moscow and its neighbors, contributing to the rise of Moscow as a powerful state.
events.name: Battle of Vedrosha

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1500, during the Ottoman–Venetian War, the Turkish fleet under Kemal Reis defeated the Venetians in the Second Battle of Lepanto. This battle was part of the larger struggle for control of the Mediterranean and showcased the naval prowess of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Second Battle of Lepanto

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1500, the Ottoman Empire captured the Venetian strongholds of Modon and Coron, referred to as the 'two eyes of the Republic'. This event marked a significant territorial gain for the Ottomans in their ongoing conflict with Venice.
events.name: Capture of Modon and Coron

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1500, Diogo Dias discovered an island he named São Lourenço, in honor of Saint Lawrence. This island is now known as Madagascar, and its discovery contributed to the European understanding of the Indian Ocean region.
events.name: Diogo Dias discovers São Lourenço

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1500, Francisco de Bobadilla arrived in Santo Domingo as the newly appointed Spanish Governor-General of the New World. He quickly took action against Christopher Columbus, who had been accused of mismanagement and tyranny.

image.caption: Engraving depicting Francisco de Bobadilla arresting Christopher Columbus on Hispaniola.
image.credit: Benson John Lossing according to the source, but there is the signature of William Z., that may be William Barritt, who made engravings with him. — http://etc.usf.edu/clipart/55200/55281/55281_bobadilla_co.htm Benson John Lossing, ed. Harper's Encyclopedia of United States History (vol. 2) (New York, NY: Harper and Brothers, 1912)
image.date_qualification: A retrospective 19th-century engraving of the arrest, not a contemporary depiction of Bobadilla’s arrival; the supplied image date is approximate and does not support a display date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francisco de Bobadilla arrives in Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1500, George the Bearded ascended to the dukedom of Saxony in Emden, following the death of his father, Albert III. His reign would last over 38 years, significantly impacting the political landscape of the region.
events.name: George the Bearded begins reign

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1500, Pedro Cabral's fleet arrived in India, landing at the port of Calicut. This marked a significant moment in the Age of Discovery, as it established a direct sea route from Europe to India.

locations.name: Calicut International Airport (CCJ), Kozhikode, Kerala, India

events.name: Cabral arrives in India

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1500, Christopher Columbus was placed under arrest along with his brothers by Francisco de Bobadilla, who had replaced him as the Spanish Governor of the New World. This marked a dramatic fall from grace for Columbus, who had previously been celebrated for his discoveries.
events.name: Columbus placed under arrest

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1500, Bobadilla concluded his investigation into Columbus's governance, hearing testimony from 22 witnesses. He determined that Columbus and his brothers intended to overthrow him, leading to their manacling and deportation to Spain.
events.name: Bobadilla's investigation of Columbus

events.enhanced_description: In October 1500, Christopher Columbus and his brothers were arrested in Santo Domingo due to allegations of mismanagement and tyranny during their governorship. They were deported back to Spain, marking a significant downfall for Columbus, who had once been celebrated for his discoveries.
events.name: Christopher Columbus and his brothers deported from Santo Domingo to Spain

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1500, Nasir-ud-Din Shah staged a coup against his father, Ghiyath Shah, who had ruled the Malwa Sultanate for over three decades. Following his ascension, Nasir executed his brother and solidified his power through ruthless measures.
events.name: Nasir-ud-Din Shah overthrows Ghiyath Shah

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1500, Emperor Go-Kashiwabara ascended to the throne of Japan during the Meiō era. His reign would be marked by the ongoing political struggles of the time, including the influence of powerful shoguns.
events.name: Emperor Go-Kashiwabara accedes to the throne

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1500, Christopher Columbus and his brothers arrived in Seville, Spain, after a grueling six-week journey across the Atlantic. They were released on their own recognizance, marking a pivotal moment in Columbus's controversial legacy.
events.name: Columbus arrives in Spain after deportation

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1500, King Ferdinand II and Queen Isabella I dismissed all charges against Christopher Columbus and his brothers regarding their governance of Hispaniola. This decision reflected the complex political landscape and the monarchs' reliance on Columbus's navigational skills.
events.name: Charges against Columbus brothers dismissed

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1500, the Siege of the Castle of St. George concluded with the capture of Cephalonia by a joint Venetian-Spanish fleet. This event was part of the broader conflict between the Venetian Republic and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Siege of the Castle of St. George ends

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1500, the last incunable, or book printed before 1501, was produced in Venice. This marked the end of an era in the history of printing, as the transition to the printed book became more widespread.
events.name: Last incunable printed in Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, the cantons of Basel and Schaffhausen formally joined the Old Swiss Confederacy, a defensive alliance of Swiss cantons that had been established to provide mutual protection against external threats. This expansion marked a significant step in the consolidation of Swiss independence and political unity.

image.caption: Locator map of the Swiss Confederacy.
image.credit: myself — File:Blank map of Europe 1714.svg
image.date_qualification: The map represents 1714, not the 1501 accession; the supplied image date is 2022-02-04.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Swiss cantons of Basel and Schaffhausen join the Old Swiss Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Portuguese navigator Gaspar Corte-Real made the first documented European landing in North America since the Norse expeditions around 1000 A.D. His exploration contributed to the European understanding of the North American coastline and its resources.

image.caption: Portrait of Portuguese explorer Gaspar Corte-Real.
image.credit: Lorraine Boissoneault — JSTOR Daily
image.date_qualification: Portrait associated with Gaspar Corte-Real; the saved image date is 2016-01-28, not the date of his landing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Gaspar Corte-Real's landing in North America

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Rodrigo de Bastidas became the first European to explore the Isthmus of Panama while searching for gold. His expedition laid the groundwork for future Spanish exploration and colonization in Central America.
events.name: Rodrigo de Bastidas explores the Isthmus of Panama

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Amerigo Vespucci mapped the stars Alpha Centauri and Beta Centauri, along with the constellation Crux, which are not visible from Europe. This work contributed significantly to the understanding of the southern hemisphere's celestial navigation.
events.name: Amerigo Vespucci maps southern stars

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Sikandar Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi, captured the strategic town of Dhaulpur, consolidating his power in northern India. This event was part of his broader campaign to expand the influence of the Lodi dynasty.
events.name: Sikandar Lodi takes Dhaulpur

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Michelangelo returned to Florence to begin work on his iconic statue of David, which would become a symbol of Renaissance art. The statue, carved from a single block of marble, showcases Michelangelo's mastery of form and human anatomy.
events.name: Michelangelo begins work on the statue David

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Aldus Manutius introduced Italic type in an edition of Virgil at his Aldine Press in Venice, marking a significant advancement in typography. This innovation allowed for more elegant and readable printed texts, influencing the future of publishing.
events.name: First use of Italic type by Aldus Manutius

events.enhanced_description: In 1501, Martin Luther enrolled at the University of Erfurt, where he would later become a pivotal figure in the Protestant Reformation. His education here laid the foundation for his theological studies and eventual challenges to the Catholic Church.
events.name: Martin Luther enters the University of Erfurt

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1501, Cesar Borgia returned triumphantly to Rome after his campaigns in Romagna. His return was marked by political maneuvering and consolidation of power within the Italian states.
events.name: Cesar Borgia returns to Rome

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1501, the Duchy of Bavaria-Dachau reverted to the control of Bavaria-Munich upon the death of Sigismund, Duke of Bavaria. This transition marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Bavaria.
events.name: Duchy of Bavaria-Dachau reverts to Bavaria-Munich

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1501, Minkhaung II became the sole King of Burma following the death of his son, Thihathura II, with whom he had co-ruled for 15 years. His reign would be short-lived, ending just five weeks later.
events.name: Minkhaung II becomes sole King of Burma

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1501, Portuguese navigator João da Nova discovered Ascension Island, which would later be officially named by Afonso de Albuquerque on May 20, 1503. This discovery was part of the broader Age of Discovery.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Ascension Island, Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha

events.name: João da Nova discovers Ascension Island

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1501, Shwenankyawshin Narapati ascended to the throne as the King of Burma following the death of his father, Minkhaung II. His reign would last nearly 26 years.
events.name: Shwenankyawshin Narapati becomes King of Burma

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1501, the Rebellion in the Alpujarras concluded with a treaty that forced the last Muslim insurgents in the region to either convert to Christianity or face expulsion. This marked the end of significant Muslim resistance in southern Spain.
events.name: Rebellion in the Alpujarras ends

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1501, the formal coronation of King Shwenankyawshin took place in Inwa, marking the beginning of his nearly 26-year reign over Burma.
events.name: Coronation of King Shwenankyawshin

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1501, the Venetian Republic signed a treaty with the Kingdom of Hungary and Pope Alexander VI to secure military support for Venetian Dalmatia during the ongoing Ottoman-Venetian War. This alliance was crucial for the defense of Venetian territories.
events.name: Venetian Republic signs treaty with Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1501, Ottaviano Petrucci published Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first printed collection of polyphonic music. This work was a significant milestone in the history of music publishing and the dissemination of musical knowledge.

image.caption: Soprano and tenor parts of Josquin des Prez’s “Adieu mes amours” in the anthology *Harmonice Musices Odhecaton*.
image.credit: Ottaviano Petrucci/Josquin des Prez — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b55007217d/f32
image.date_qualification: Third edition, printed 1504; this is not an image of the 1501 publication event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Harmonice Musices Odhecaton published

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1501, the semi-independent city of Basel officially joined the Swiss Confederation as its eleventh canton. This integration marked an important expansion of the Confederation's influence and unity.
events.name: Basel joins the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1501, Alexander Jagiellon, who had been Grand Duke of Lithuania since 1492, ascended to the throne of Poland following the sudden death of his brother, Jan I Olbracht. His reign would be marked by efforts to strengthen the Polish-Lithuanian union.
events.name: Alexander Jagiellon becomes King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1501, Nicolau Coelho returned to Portugal after being part of Pedro Cabral's expedition to India. His journey contributed to the growing knowledge and trade routes established between Europe and Asia.
events.name: Nicolau Coelho returns from India

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1501, Cesare Borgia's French troops stormed and captured the fortress at Capua in the Kingdom of Naples, defeating the defenses led by Fabrizio Colonna. This victory was part of Borgia's campaign to consolidate power in southern Italy.
events.name: Cesare Borgia's troops storm Capua

events.enhanced_description: Pedro Álvares Cabral and his crew returned to Lisbon after a 15-month expedition to India, having lost six of their original thirteen ships. Despite the losses, the expedition was financially successful, yielding a profit of nine times the initial investment for the Portuguese crown.

image.caption: Detail of Aurélio de Figueiredo’s painting depicting Pedro Álvares Cabral with the letter of Pero Vaz de Caminha.
image.credit: Aurélio de Figueiredo — História do Brasil (v.1), Rio de Janeiro: Bloch, 1980.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting dated 1900; it depicts the reading of a letter, not Cabral’s return to Lisbon in 1501.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Return of Pedro Álvares Cabral to Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: The Kingdom of Naples, under King Federico I, capitulated to the forces of Cesare Borgia, which included French and Aragonese troops. This surrender marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Italy during the early 16th century.
events.name: Surrender of the Kingdom of Naples

events.enhanced_description: Nicolaus Copernicus was formally installed as a canon at Frauenberg Cathedral, a position that allowed him to pursue his astronomical studies while serving the Church. This role would later influence his groundbreaking work on heliocentrism.
events.name: Installation of Copernicus as Canon

events.enhanced_description: King Hans of Denmark was deposed from the Swedish throne after fleeing following a defeat at the hands of Swedish rebels in Örebro. His wife, Christina of Saxony, remained in Stockholm as regent, while Hans sought to reclaim his throne.
events.name: Deposition of King Hans of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: King Federico of Naples abdicated following the conquest of his kingdom by French forces, leading to Louis XII of France assuming the title of nominal monarch. This event solidified French influence in southern Italy.
events.name: Abdication of King Federico of Naples

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of the Siritsa River, the Livonian Order, allied with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, achieved a decisive victory over the forces of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. This battle was a key engagement in the Second Muscovite–Lithuanian War.
events.name: Battle of the Siritsa River

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella of Spain ordered the recall of Francisco de Bobadilla from Santo Domingo following complaints from Christopher Columbus, who had been arrested and replaced as Viceroy. This decision marked a significant shift in colonial governance in the New World.
events.name: Recall of Bobadilla by Queen Isabella

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian I, Archduke of Austria, issued a decree mandating safety tests for firearms, reflecting the growing importance of gunpowder technology in warfare and governance during this period.
events.name: Maximilian I's Firearms Safety Decree

events.enhanced_description: Grand Duke Aleksandras Jogailaitis issued a decree requiring all Roman Catholic priests in the Duchy of Lithuania to become fluent in the Lithuanian language, promoting cultural integration and the use of the local language in religious practices.
events.name: Decree on Lithuanian Language by Aleksandras Jogailaitis

events.enhanced_description: Queen Isabella ordered the return of assets confiscated from Christopher Columbus and his brothers, signaling a shift in the Spanish Crown's approach to Columbus's governance in the New World.
events.name: Return of Confiscated Assets to Columbus

events.enhanced_description: Leonardo Loredan was elected as the 75th doge of the Venetian Republic, a position he would hold for nearly two decades, during which Venice would navigate significant political and military challenges.
events.name: Election of Leonardo Loredan as Doge

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian I of Austria and Louis XII of France signed the Treaty of Trente, which recognized French territorial conquests in northern Italy, further entrenching French influence in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Trente

events.enhanced_description: The Banquet of Chestnuts is said to have been held by Cesare Borgia in the Papal Palace of Rome, although historical accuracy is disputed and may be exaggerated by Borgia's enemies.
events.name: Banquet of Chestnuts

events.enhanced_description: Amerigo Vespucci discovered and named Baía de Todos os Santos in Brazil on All Saints' Day, marking a significant moment in the European exploration of South America.

locations.name: Baía de Todos os Santos, Salvador, Bahia, Brazil

events.name: Discovery of Baía de Todos os Santos

events.enhanced_description: During the Second Muscovite–Lithuanian War, Grand Prince Ivan's Southern Muscovite army defeated the forces of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at the Battle of Mstislavl, showcasing the military strength of Moscow.
events.name: Battle of Mstislavl

events.enhanced_description: Sten Sture the Elder was elected Regent of Sweden for the second time after the deposition of King Hans of Denmark. His leadership marked a period of increased autonomy for Sweden.
events.name: Election of Sten Sture the Elder as Regent of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Arthur, Prince of Wales, married the Spanish princess Catherine of Aragon, a union that would later have significant implications for English history, particularly with her later marriage to Henry VIII.
events.name: Marriage of Arthur and Catherine of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: A large army from the Grand Duchy of Moscow overran Livonia during the Second Muscovite–Lithuanian War, demonstrating the aggressive expansionist policies of Ivan III.
events.name: Moscow's Overrun of Livonia

events.enhanced_description: Grand Duke Aleksandras Jogailaitis ascended to the throne as King of Poland, adopting the name Aleksander I Jagiellończyk. His reign marked a significant period in the union of the Polish-Lithuanian state.
events.name: Aleksandras Jogailaitis becomes King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: Ismail I was enthroned as the first Shah of Iran, establishing the Safavid dynasty and declaring Shi'ism the state religion, which would shape the religious landscape of Iran for centuries.
events.name: Enthronement of Ismail I as Shah of Iran

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Cannanore marked the first Portuguese naval engagement in the Indian Ocean, where João da Nova's fleet clashed with the forces of the Zamorin outside the harbor of Cannanore.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the First Battle of Cannanore by Roque Gameiro.
image.credit: Roque Gameiro — [1]
image.date_qualification: The image is described as an illustration of the 1501–1502 battle and dated circa 1900; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Battle of Cannanore

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Portuguese explorers led by Gonçalo Coelho mistakenly entered Guanabara Bay, believing it to be the mouth of a river. This event marked the European discovery of what would later become the city of Rio de Janeiro.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Portuguese explorers sail into Guanabara Bay

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, the first African slaves were brought to the New World, arriving on the island of Hispaniola. This marked the beginning of a tragic chapter in history, as the transatlantic slave trade expanded significantly in the following decades.
events.name: First African slaves arrive in the New World

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Bristol merchants returned from Newfoundland, carrying three native people and cod from the Grand Banks. This journey marked an early instance of English exploration and trade in North America.
events.name: Bristol merchants return from Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Moctezuma II was elected as the emperor of the Aztecs following the death of his predecessor, Ahuitzotl. His reign would be marked by significant events, including the arrival of Spanish conquistadors.
events.name: Moctezuma II elected emperor of the Aztecs

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Meñli I Giray defeated the Golden Horde and sacked their capital, Sarai. This victory was significant in the power dynamics of the region, contributing to the decline of the Golden Horde's influence.
events.name: Meñli I Giray defeats the Golden Horde

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Wittenberg University was founded, becoming a significant center of learning and thought in Germany. It would later play a crucial role in the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Wittenberg University founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Peter Henlein of Nuremberg created a portable timepiece using iron parts and coiled springs. This innovation marked a significant advancement in horology and the development of timekeeping devices.
events.name: Peter Henlein builds portable timepiece

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Asher Lämlein, a Jewish mystic in Italy, proclaimed that the Messiah would arrive within six months, leading to a year of penance among his followers. This declaration reflected the religious fervor and messianic expectations of the time.
events.name: Asher Lämlein declares Jewish Messiah arrival

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Sir John Percyvale founded The King's School in Macclesfield, England. This institution became an important center for education in the region.
events.name: The King's School, Macclesfield founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa received the degree of magister artium from the University of Cologne. Agrippa would later become known for his writings on magic and the occult.
events.name: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa receives degree

events.enhanced_description: In 1502, Wilhelm Bombast, known as Paracelsus, moved to Villach with his son. Paracelsus would later become a prominent figure in the history of medicine and alchemy.
events.name: Wilhelm Bombast moves to Villach

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1502, commissioners from Scotland and England met at Richmond Palace to finalize the marriage agreement between King James IV of Scotland and Princess Margaret Tudor, daughter of King Henry VII of England. This union was intended to solidify peace between the two nations.

locations.name: Richmond Palace, Richmond upon Thames, London, England

events.name: Marriage agreement between Scotland and England

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1502, Isabella I of Castile issued an edict outlawing Islam in her realm, compelling her Muslim subjects to convert to Christianity. This decree was part of the broader efforts of the Spanish monarchy to enforce religious uniformity following the Reconquista.
events.name: Isabella I issues edict outlawing Islam

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1502, Nicolás de Ovando departed Spain with a fleet of 30 ships to replace Francisco de Bobadilla as Viceroy of the New World. His arrival in Santo Domingo marked a new chapter in the Spanish administration of the Caribbean.
events.name: Nicolás de Ovando departs Spain for Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1502, Christopher Columbus began preparations for his fourth and final voyage to the New World, aiming to find a westward passage linking the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. This expedition would ultimately lead to further exploration of Central America.
events.name: Christopher Columbus prepares for fourth voyage

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1502, the first recorded earthquake struck Medvednica, Croatia, with an estimated intensity of VIII on the Mercalli scale. This event marked a significant geological occurrence in the region's history.
events.name: First recorded earthquake in Croatia

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1502, Arthur, Prince of Wales, heir to the English throne, died after a prolonged illness, just months after marrying Catherine of Aragon. His death shifted the line of succession, making his younger brother, Henry, the new heir.
events.name: Arthur, Prince of Wales, dies

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1502, Dmitry Ivanovich Vnuk, co-ruler of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, was arrested along with his mother on suspicion of conspiracy. This event led to a significant shift in the power dynamics of the Russian nobility.
events.name: Dmitry Ivanovich Vnuk arrested

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1502, Ivan the Great was formally crowned as Grand Prince of Moscow, solidifying his role as the sole ruler of the Russian territories. This coronation was a pivotal moment in the establishment of centralized Russian authority.
events.name: Coronation of Ivan the Great

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1502, Portuguese navigator João da Nova discovered the uninhabited island of Saint Helena during his voyages in the South Atlantic. This island would later become a crucial stopover point for ships traveling to and from Asia.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Saint Helena

events.name: João da Nova discovers Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1502, Christopher Columbus set sail from Cadiz for his fourth and final voyage to the New World, aiming to explore Central America and find a passage to the Indian Ocean. This voyage would lead to significant discoveries and encounters.
events.name: Columbus leaves for fourth voyage

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1502, Christopher Columbus and his crew completed the rescue of stranded Portuguese soldiers in Asilah, Morocco, before embarking on their transatlantic journey. This operation showcased Columbus's ongoing involvement in maritime affairs beyond exploration.
events.name: Columbus rescues Portuguese soldiers in Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1502, Columbus and his crew landed on the island of Martinique, marking another significant stop during his fourth voyage. This encounter further expanded European knowledge of the Caribbean islands.
events.name: Columbus lands on Martinique

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1502, Columbus attempted to land at Santo Domingo to avoid an impending hurricane, despite being ordered not to return. Viceroy Nicolás de Ovando refused him entry, which led to a dramatic turn of events as the hurricane struck shortly after.
events.name: Columbus attempts to land at Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1502, a powerful hurricane swept through the Caribbean, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. The storm wrecked many ships, including those of the new Viceroy, Nicolás de Ovando, and raised suspicions about Columbus's involvement in invoking the storm.
events.name: Hurricane strikes the Caribbean

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1502, Maximilian I, King of the Romans, signed a treaty in Augsburg with representatives of King Henry VII of England, agreeing not to support English rebels. This treaty was part of the broader political maneuvering in Europe during this period.
events.name: Maximilian I signs treaty with England

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1502, the Columbus brothers anchored at Guanaja, marking the first recorded encounter between Europeans and the Maya people. This event led to the looting of Mayan traders' cargo by Bartolomeo Columbus and his crew, highlighting the tensions of early contact.
events.name: First encounter between Europeans and the Maya

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1502, Christopher Columbus and his crew made landfall at Puerto Castilla, marking the first European visit to the mainland of Honduras. This event was part of Columbus's fourth voyage to the New World, aimed at finding a passage to Asia.
events.name: Christopher Columbus lands at Puerto Castilla

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1502, Christopher Columbus landed on the shores of what is now Costa Rica during his fourth voyage. This marked the first European contact with the region, which would later become a significant part of Spanish colonial territories.
events.name: Christopher Columbus lands in Costa Rica

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1502, Anne of Foix-Candale was crowned Queen of Hungary in a ceremony held in Székesfehérvár, following her marriage to Vladislaus II, King of Hungary and Bohemia. This union strengthened political ties between Hungary and France.
events.name: Anne of Foix-Candale proclaimed Queen of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1502, Christopher Columbus and his crew arrived at Almirante Bay in Panama during his fourth voyage. This landing was part of his exploration of the Central American coast and aimed at finding a passage to the Pacific Ocean.

locations.name: Almirante Bay, Bocas del Toro Province, Panama

events.name: Columbus arrives at Almirante Bay

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1502, Ismail I proclaimed himself Shah of Iran after defeating the Aq Qoyunlu tribes, marking the establishment of the Safavid dynasty. This event laid the foundation for a significant shift in Persian politics and culture, leading to the establishment of Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion.
events.name: Ismail I founds the Safavid dynasty

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1502, the Cantino planisphere, a detailed map of the New World, was acquired by Alberto Cantino, an agent for the Duke of Ferrara. This map was significant as it revealed new territories discovered by the Portuguese, influencing European exploration.

image.caption: The Cantino planisphere, a Portuguese world map by an unknown cartographer.
image.credit: anonymous Portuguese (1502) — Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Italy
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 1502; the article says Cantino smuggled it to Italy in 1502. The evidence does not establish that the map was acquired specifically on November 19.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Acquisition of the Cantino planisphere

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1502, Cesare Borgia executed Ramiro d'Orco, a ruthless governor, to gain favor with the populace of Romagna. This act was later referenced by Machiavelli in 'The Prince' as a demonstration of political strategy and power.
events.name: Cesare Borgia kills Ramiro d'Orco

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1502, Cesare Borgia occupied Urbino, imprisoning and executing two of his allies, Vitellozzo and Oliveretto, who he suspected of treachery. This ruthless act solidified his control over the region and showcased his political machinations.
events.name: Cesare Borgia occupies Urbino

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Cerignola, fought in 1503, marked a significant moment in military history as it is considered the first battle won by gunpowder small arms. Spanish forces under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba defeated the French troops led by Louis d'Armagnac, who was killed in the battle.
events.name: Battle of Cerignola

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1503, Seville was granted exclusive rights to trade with the New World, solidifying its status as a major port and center of commerce in Spain. This decision significantly impacted the flow of goods and wealth from the Americas to Europe.
events.name: Seville awarded exclusive trade rights

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1503, the construction of the Henry VII Chapel at Westminster Abbey began, representing the final stage of English Gothic art. This chapel would later become a significant site for royal burials.
events.name: Construction of Henry VII Chapel begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1503, the Challenge of Barletta took place, where thirteen Italian knights defeated thirteen French knights near Barletta. This event was a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts between France and Italy.
events.name: Challenge of Barletta

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1503, during the French–Spanish Wars in Italy, the Battle of Ruvo occurred, where Spanish forces defeated the French. This battle was part of the larger struggle for control over Italy.
events.name: Battle of Ruvo

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1503, Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama and his crew became the first Europeans to sight the Seychelles islands, noting the discovery of Silhouette Island. This event expanded European knowledge of the Indian Ocean region.
events.name: Vasco da Gama sights the Seychelles

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1503, the Kingdom of Cochin, ruled by a Portuguese-installed raja, was invaded by 50,000 Nair troops of the Zamorin of Calicut. This conflict highlighted the tensions between local rulers and Portuguese interests in India.
events.name: Invasion of the Kingdom of Cochin

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1503, Christopher Columbus discovered the Cayman Islands, which he named Las Tortugas due to the abundance of sea turtles in the area. This discovery was part of his fourth voyage to the New World, aimed at finding a passage to Asia.
events.name: Discovery of the Cayman Islands

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1503, Spanish forces captured the city of Naples, marking a significant event in the Italian Wars. This victory solidified Spanish control over southern Italy and was part of the broader conflict between Spain and France for dominance in the region.
events.name: Capture of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1503, Portuguese admiral Afonso de Albuquerque first definitively sighted Ascension Island during his voyages in the Atlantic. This sighting contributed to European knowledge of the island, which would later serve as a strategic naval base.

image.caption: Map showing the location of Ascension Island on a globe.
image.credit: RaviC — Own work based on: United Kingdom on the globe (Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha special) (Africa centered).svg : by TUBS
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2017-06-23; it does not depict the 1503 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Ascension Island

events.name: Sightings of Ascension Island

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1503, Moctezuma II was crowned as the ruler of the Aztec Empire in Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City. His reign would be marked by significant encounters with Spanish explorers, leading to profound changes in the region.
events.name: Coronation of Moctezuma II

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1503, King James IV of Scotland married Margaret Tudor, daughter of King Henry VII of England, at Holyrood Abbey in Edinburgh. This marriage was a significant political alliance that aimed to secure peace between Scotland and England.

image.caption: Portrait of James IV, King of Scots.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — National Gallery of Scotland
image.date_qualification: Image date supplied as “15 th century date QS:P571,+1450-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”; this is a portrait, not a contemporary image of the wedding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Marriage of James IV of Scotland and Margaret Tudor

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1503, Murad, the last Sultan of the Aq Qoyunlu, engaged in a battle against Ismail I, the Safavid King of Persia, near Hamadan. The battle resulted in significant casualties for Murad's forces, marking a pivotal moment in the power struggle between the two empires.
events.name: Battle near Hamadan

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1503, representatives of King Henry VII of England and Queen Isabella of Spain signed a treaty for the marriage of 12-year-old Henry, Prince of Wales, to Catherine of Aragon, the widow of Henry's son Arthur. This treaty was significant in establishing alliances between England and Spain.
events.name: Marriage Treaty for Henry, Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1503, Christopher Columbus and his crew were forced to beach their ships on the island of Jamaica after a storm damaged them. They remained stranded on the island for six months, facing challenges in securing food and assistance.
events.name: Stranding of Columbus in Jamaica

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1503, the book 'The Imitation of Christ' by Thomas à Kempis was re-published in an English translation. This work has been influential in Christian spirituality and devotion, emphasizing the importance of inner piety.
events.name: Publication of The Imitation of Christ

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1503, orbital calculations indicated that Pluto moved outside Neptune's orbit, a significant event in the study of celestial mechanics. This phenomenon would remain in effect for 233 years.
events.name: Orbital calculations of Pluto

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1503, Saint Helena was first definitively sighted by ships of Portuguese navigator Estêvão da Gama returning from the East. This sighting would later lead to the island's use as a strategic location for maritime navigation.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Saint Helena

events.name: Sightings of Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1503, Pope Alexander VI died after a controversial reign of 11 years. His death led to the largest gathering of cardinals up to that time for a papal conclave to elect his successor.
events.name: Death of Pope Alexander VI

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1503, a treaty finalized on June 11 between Vladislaus II of Hungary and Bayezid II of the Ottoman Empire went into effect. This treaty aimed to suppress warfare along the Hungarian-Ottoman border and included provisions for Stephen III of Moldavia.
events.name: Treaty between Vladislaus II and Bayezid II

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1503, Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini was elected as Pope Pius III after a contentious conclave. His papacy was notably short, lasting only 26 days before his death.
events.name: Election of Pope Pius III

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1503, Fort Emmanuel was christened at Cochin after Afonso de Albuquerque obtained permission to build it. This fort marked the first European fort in India and was crucial for Portuguese trade and military presence in the region.
events.name: Christening of Fort Emmanuel

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1503, Pope Pius III died less than four weeks after his election, prompting the calling of a second papal conclave to elect his successor. His brief papacy was marked by political intrigue and challenges within the Church.
events.name: Death of Pope Pius III

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1503, Queen Isabella I of Spain issued an edict prohibiting violence against indigenous peoples in the New World. This edict reflected the growing awareness of the consequences of colonial expansion and the need for ethical governance.
events.name: Edict by Queen Isabella I

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1503, Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere was elected as Pope Julius II at the end of the year's second papal conclave. His election marked the beginning of a papacy that would be influential in the arts and politics of the Renaissance.
events.name: Election of Pope Julius II

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1503, Bernard Stewart, 4th Lord of Aubigny, was released from Castel Nuovo in Naples after being captured at the Battle of Seminara. His release followed a truce between France and Spain, highlighting the ongoing political negotiations of the time.
events.name: Release of Bernard Stewart

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1503, Pope Julius II added four new members to the College of Cardinals, including two relatives from his own family. This action was part of his broader strategy to consolidate power within the Church.
events.name: Pope Julius II adds Cardinals

events.enhanced_description: In January 1504, French troops under King Louis XII surrendered the strategic port city of Gaeta to Spanish forces led by Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba. This event marked a significant shift in control over southern Italy during the Italian Wars.
events.name: French troops of King Louis XII surrender Gaeta to the Spanish

events.enhanced_description: In the early 16th century, Ahmad ibn Abi Jum'ah, a prominent Islamic scholar, issued the Oran fatwa, which provided guidance to Muslims living in Spain, particularly in the context of the challenges they faced following the Reconquista. This fatwa was significant in addressing the spiritual and legal needs of the Muslim community in a predominantly Christian environment.
events.name: Islamic scholar Ahmad ibn Abi Jum'ah issues the Oran fatwa for Muslims in Spain

events.enhanced_description: Lê Túc Tông, the Emperor of Vietnam, died after a brief reign of only six months in 1504. His untimely death led to a power vacuum and subsequent struggles for the throne, impacting the political landscape of the Lê dynasty.
events.name: Lê Túc Tông dies after a reign of only six months as Emperor of Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In the early 16th century, Amara Dunqas, a leader of the Funj people, founded the Sultanate of Sennar, marking a significant moment in the Islamization of the Sudan region. This sultanate became a center of Islamic culture and governance in the area.
events.name: Islamization of the Sudan region: A Funj leader, Amara Dunqas, founds the Sultanate of Sennar

events.enhanced_description: Sheikh Ahmed, the last leader of the Great Horde, was last recorded as a prisoner in Vilnius, Lithuania, around 1504. His captivity marked the decline of the Great Horde's influence and the shifting power dynamics in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Sheikh Ahmed, the final leader of the Great Horde, is last heard of as a Lithuanian prisoner at Vilnius

events.enhanced_description: In 1504, in Florence, Leonardo da Vinci and Niccolò Machiavelli became involved in a controversial scheme to divert the Arno River to cut off water supply to Pisa, aiming to force its surrender. The project, however, failed due to the foreman's inability to follow da Vinci's design, highlighting the challenges of engineering and military strategy of the time.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci and Niccolò Machiavelli's failed scheme to divert the Arno River

events.enhanced_description: In 1504, the Venetian Council of Ten deliberated on a proposal to construct a Suez Canal, aiming to enhance trade routes. However, the discussion was ultimately abandoned, reflecting the complexities and challenges of such ambitious engineering projects during the Renaissance.
events.name: The Council of Ten discusses the Suez Canal proposal

events.enhanced_description: In 1504, Aldus Manutius, a prominent Venetian printer and humanist, published his edition of Demosthenes, contributing significantly to the Renaissance revival of classical literature.
