His work helped disseminate Greek texts and fostered a greater appreciation for classical rhetoric in Europe.
events.name: Aldus Manutius publishes his edition of Demosthenes in Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1504, the Signoria of Florence commissioned both Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo to paint the walls of the Grand Council Chamber in the Palazzo Vecchio. This collaboration between two of the Renaissance's greatest artists underscored Florence's cultural prominence during this period.
events.name: The Signoria of Florence commissions Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo

events.enhanced_description: In 1504, Raphael completed The Marriage of the Virgin, a masterpiece that exemplifies the principles of High Renaissance art, including balance, harmony, and perspective. This painting is celebrated for its composition and the emotional depth of its figures.
events.name: Raphael paints The Marriage of the Virgin

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Sten Sture the Elder in December 1503, Svante Nilsson was elected as the new Regent of Sweden on January 21, 1504. His leadership would play a crucial role in the political landscape of Sweden during a time of internal strife and external threats.
events.name: Svante Nilsson is elected the new Regent of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1504, the Treaty of Lyon was signed, resulting in France ceding the Kingdom of Naples to Ferdinand II of Aragon, who subsequently became King Ferdinand III of Naples. This treaty solidified Spanish dominance in southern Italy.
events.name: Treaty of Lyon: France cedes Naples to Ferdinand II of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1504, King Ferdinand V of Castile contracted with the navigator Juan de la Cosa to finance an independent expedition to the Pearl Islands and the Gulf of Urabá. This expedition aimed to expand Spanish influence in the New World.
events.name: King Ferdinand V of Castile contracts with Juan de la Cosa

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1504, the investiture of Prince Henry of England as Prince of Wales and Earl of Chester took place, marking a significant step in his eventual ascension to the throne as Henry VIII. This event was part of the Tudor dynasty's consolidation of power.
events.name: Investiture of Prince Henry of England as Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On February 29, 1504, Christopher Columbus leveraged his knowledge of an impending lunar eclipse to persuade the indigenous people of Jamaica to provide him and his crew with supplies. This clever tactic showcased his navigational skills and understanding of astronomy.
events.name: Christopher Columbus uses lunar eclipse to gain supplies

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1504, King James IV of Scotland opened the Scottish Parliament for the first time since 1496, signaling a renewed commitment to governance and law-making in Scotland. This event was pivotal in the development of Scottish political institutions.
events.name: King James IV of Scotland opens the Scottish Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1504, the Zamorin of Calicut launched a second invasion of the Portuguese-supported Kingdom of Cochin, initiating a conflict that would last until July 3. This invasion was part of the broader struggle for control over trade routes in the region.
events.name: Second invasion of the Kingdom of Cochin by the Zamorin of Calicut

events.enhanced_description: The Eisho era began on March 30, 1504, during the reign of Emperor Go-Kashiwabara, marking a new period in Japanese history. This era would be characterized by significant cultural and political developments in Japan.
events.name: Eisho era begins in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1504, English guilds were placed under state control, marking a significant shift in the relationship between the government and trade organizations. This change aimed to regulate commerce and maintain order in the burgeoning economy.
events.name: English guilds become subject to state control

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1504, Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, granted the Landshut inheritance to Albert IV during the War of the Succession of Landshut. This decision was crucial in determining the territorial disputes within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Maximilian I grants the Landshut inheritance to Albert IV

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1504, Le Hien Tong, Emperor of Vietnam, died after a six-year reign and was succeeded by his 15-year-old son, Le Tuc Tong. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Le dynasty.
events.name: Le Hien Tong dies and is succeeded by Le Tuc Tong

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1504, Rao Bika Rathore, the ruler of the Kingdom of Bikaner, died after a 32-year reign. His death led to a brief succession crisis as his elder son Nara succeeded him but died shortly thereafter, leading to his brother Lunkaran taking the throne.
events.name: Rao Bika Rathore dies after a reign of 32 years

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1504, after being marooned in Jamaica for six months, Christopher Columbus and his crew were rescued by a Spanish ship. This event marked the end of a challenging period for Columbus during his fourth voyage.
events.name: Christopher Columbus is rescued after being marooned

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1504, Bogdan III the One-Eyed ascended to the throne as the new Prince of Moldavia following the death of his father, Stephen the Great. His reign would continue the legacy of his father's leadership in the region.
events.name: Bogdan III becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1504, the siege of Cochin concluded with a decisive victory for the Portuguese and Cochin defenders against the invading forces of Calicut. The battle resulted in heavy casualties for Calicut, significantly weakening their military presence in the region.
events.name: Siege of Cochin ends with Portuguese victory

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1504, at the age of 16, Le Tuc Tong became the new Emperor of Vietnam following the death of his father, Le Hien Tong. His reign was short-lived, lasting only six months before his own death.
events.name: Le Tuc Tong becomes Emperor of Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1504, Pope Julius II issued an order reforming the official coinage of the Papal States, increasing the silver content of the carlino coin. This reform was significant for the economy of the Papal States and reflected the Pope's influence over monetary policy.
events.name: Pope Julius II reforms Papal coinage

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1504, the Battle of Knockdoe took place in County Galway, where English Lord Deputy Gerald FitzGerald, 8th Earl of Kildare, led 6,000 troops to assist Maelsechlainn mac Tadhg Ó Cellaigh against Ulick Fionn Burke's forces. The battle resulted in a victory for Kildare's forces.
events.name: Battle of Knockdoe is fought

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1504, Michelangelo's iconic sculpture of David was unveiled in Florence, marking a significant moment in Renaissance art. The statue, representing the biblical hero, became a symbol of Florentine freedom and artistic achievement.

image.caption: Marble sculpture of David by Michelangelo at the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence.
image.credit: Jörg Bittner Unna — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies the sculpture at the Galleria dell'Accademia, where it was moved in 1873; this is a later site depiction, not a photograph of the 1504 unveiling. Image date: 2016-07-28.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Michelangelo's sculpture of David is unveiled

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1504, Queen Isabella I of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon issued a Royal Warrant for the construction of the Capilla Real, a Royal Chapel in Granada. This chapel would later become the burial site for the Catholic Monarchs.
events.name: Royal Warrant for Capilla Real issued

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1504, the Treaty of Blois was agreed upon by Philip I of Castile, Maximilian I, and Louis XII, establishing terms for their respective territories and alliances. This treaty was a key diplomatic effort during the complex political landscape of early 16th-century Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Blois is agreed upon

events.enhanced_description: In October 1504, Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, besieged and captured Kabul, marking a significant expansion of his territory. This conquest laid the groundwork for his future campaigns in India and the establishment of Mughal rule.
events.name: Babur besieges and captures Kabul

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1504, Isabella I of Castile signed her will and testament, outlining the succession of her crown and the future of her kingdoms. This document would have lasting implications for the Spanish monarchy and its territories.
events.name: Isabella I of Castile signs her will

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1504, Christopher Columbus returned to Spain from his fourth voyage, during which he explored the coast of Central America from Belize to Panama. His return marked the end of a significant chapter in his explorations of the New World.

locations.name: Palos de la Frontera, Andalusia, Spain

events.name: Christopher Columbus returns to Spain from his fourth voyage

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1504, Isabella I of Castile, the Catholic Queen of Castile and Aragon, passed away. Her death marked a pivotal moment in Spanish history as the crown of Castile passed to her daughter Joanna, leading to significant political changes.
events.name: Death of Isabella I of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1504, Nils Ravaldsson, the leader of a rebellion following the death of Knut Alvsson, faced a decisive defeat at Olsborg Castle in Bohuslän. This event marked a significant moment in the power struggles of Sweden during the early 16th century, as it effectively crushed the resistance against the ruling authorities.
events.name: Nils Ravaldsson's resistance crushed at Olsborg Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, the Spanish Army under Ramón de Cardona captured Mers-el-Kébir, a strategic port in the Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen. This event was part of Spain's efforts to expand its influence in North Africa.
events.name: Capture of Mers-el-Kébir

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Peter Henlein crafted the Pomander Watch in Nuremberg, recognized as the earliest known pocket watch. This innovative timepiece would later be rediscovered in London, highlighting the craftsmanship and technological advancements of the period.
events.name: Pomander Watch of 1505

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Portuguese merchants established factories and fortresses along the east coast of Africa, including Kilwa, Sofala, and Malindi. This expansion was crucial for the Portuguese in securing trade routes and resources in the region.
events.name: Portuguese Establishment in East Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Spanish explorer Juan de Bermúdez discovered Bermuda, marking the island's first recorded sighting by Europeans. This discovery would later lead to further exploration and eventual colonization.
events.name: Discovery of Bermuda

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Judah Abravanel became the personal physician to the viceroy of Naples. His role was significant in the context of the medical practices and Jewish contributions to medicine during the Renaissance.
events.name: Judah Abravanel Becomes Physician

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, the Battle of Achnashellach took place in Scotland, where Clan Cameron emerged victorious over Clan Munro and Clan MacKay. This battle was part of the ongoing clan conflicts that characterized Scottish history during this period.
events.name: Battle of Achnashellach

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Portuguese explorer Gonçalo Álvares became the first to sight what would later be known as Gough Island in the South Atlantic. This discovery contributed to the European understanding of the South Atlantic region.

image.caption: Map of Gough Island.
image.credit: User:Apcbg — http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Image:Tristan_Map.png
image.date_qualification: Map of the island, not a depiction of its discovery. The image date is 2007-10-04.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Gough Island, Tristan da Cunha, Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha

events.name: Discovery of Gough Island

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, St Catherine's Monastery on the Sinai Peninsula was captured and sacked by Bedouins. Despite attempts by the Mamluk sultan to restore order, the raid highlighted the ongoing instability in the region.
events.name: Sacking of St Catherine's Monastery

events.enhanced_description: In 1505, Pope Julius II ordered the demolition of Old St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, paving the way for the construction of the new basilica that would become a masterpiece of Renaissance architecture.
events.name: Demolition of Old St. Peter's Basilica

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1505, Pope Julius II issued the papal bull Cum tam divino, which aimed to reform the Roman Catholic Church by prohibiting simony, the practice of buying and selling church offices. This decree was part of Julius II's broader efforts to address corruption within the Church.
events.name: Pope Julius II issues the papal bull Cum tam divino

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1505, Lunkaran ascended to the throne as the Rao of Bikaner, in present-day Rajasthan, India. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Bikaner state, contributing to its political and cultural development.
events.name: Lunkaran begins his reign as the Rao of Bikaner

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1505, Pope Julius II established the line of demarcation in the New World under the Treaty of Tordesillas, delineating territories between Spain and Portugal. This decision had lasting implications for colonial expansion and territorial claims in the Americas.
events.name: Pope Julius II sets the line of demarcation under the Treaty of Tordesillas

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1505, Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, played a game of tennis against Thomas Grey, 2nd Marquess of Dorset, at Windsor Castle. This event is notable for being the first recorded use of tennis rackets, marking a significant moment in the history of the sport.
events.name: Philip the Handsome plays tennis at Windsor Castle

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1505, Dom Francisco de Almeida, appointed as the Viceroy of Portuguese India, departed from Lisbon with an armada of 22 ships and approximately 1,500 men. His expedition aimed to establish and strengthen Portuguese influence in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Dom Francisco de Almeida departs for Portuguese India

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1505, King Alexander Jagiellon of Poland agreed to support the Act of Nihil novi, which prohibited the king from issuing laws without the consent of the nobles represented by their parliament, the Sejm. This act marked a significant step towards the establishment of a Nobles' Democracy in Poland.
events.name: King Alexander Jagiellon supports the Act of Nihil novi

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1505, Italian explorer Sebastiano Caboto was granted a lifetime annuity of £10 per year by King Henry VII of England for his services in exploring North America. This recognition underscored the growing interest in transatlantic exploration during the Age of Discovery.
events.name: Sebastiano Caboto granted annuity by King Henry VII

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1505, David X ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Kartli in present-day Georgia following the death of his father, Constantine II. His reign was marked by efforts to consolidate power and navigate the complex political landscape of the region.
events.name: David X becomes ruler of the Kingdom of Kartli

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1505, Christ's College in Cambridge, England, was re-founded with a charter granted by Lady Margaret Beaufort. This event marked a significant development in the history of higher education in England, contributing to the establishment of one of the country's leading universities.
events.name: Christ's College, Cambridge is re-founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1505, King Alexander I Jagiellon granted the Act of Nihil novi, which was passed by the Sejm, establishing a legal framework that required the king to seek the consent of the nobility for new laws. This act marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of Poland's political system towards a more democratic structure.
events.name: Poland's Act of Nihil novi is granted

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1505, the M8.2–8.8 Lo Mustang earthquake struck Nepal, causing severe damage in Kathmandu and surrounding areas. This natural disaster had significant repercussions for the region, affecting infrastructure and the local population.
events.name: The M8.2–8.8 Lo Mustang earthquake strikes Nepal

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1505, Zhu Houzhao, the 13-year-old son of the late Hongzhi Emperor, was enthroned as the Zhengde Emperor of the Ming Dynasty in China. His ascension marked the beginning of a reign characterized by significant cultural and political developments.
events.name: Zhu Houzhao enthroned as the Zhengde Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1505, the future King Henry VIII of England repudiated his engagement to Catherine of Aragon at the command of his father, King Henry VII. This decision would have far-reaching implications for English history, particularly regarding the future marriage and the English Reformation.
events.name: Henry VIII repudiates engagement to Catherine of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: The Kalmar Bloodbath occurred on July 2, 1505, when King Hans of Denmark ordered the execution of several leaders involved in the Swedish Uprising against his rule. This brutal act was a response to the perceived treason of the mayor and city officials of Kalmar, marking a significant moment in the struggle for Swedish independence.
events.name: The Kalmar Bloodbath

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1505, Martin Luther entered the Augustinian monastery in Erfurt, marking the beginning of his monastic life. This decision was influenced by a life-altering experience during a thunderstorm, which led him to vow to become a monk, setting the stage for his later role in the Protestant Reformation.
events.name: Martin Luther Enters Monastic Life

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1505, Portuguese explorers led by Francisco de Almeida attacked the city-state of Kilwa, killing Emir Abraham for failing to pay tribute. This event marked a significant escalation in Portuguese colonial ambitions along the East African coast.

image.caption: Bird’s-eye view of Kilwa from Georg Braun and Franz Hogenberg’s *Civitates orbis terrarum*.
image.credit: Georg Braun and Franz Hogenberg — Civitates orbis terrarum
image.date_qualification: Depicted in 1572, 67 years after the 1505 event; not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sack of Kilwa

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1505, the Portuguese established the State of India in what is now Kerala, following their conquest of territories from the Bijapur Sultanate in Calicut. This marked the beginning of a significant Portuguese colonial presence in India.
events.name: Foundation of the Portuguese State of India

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1505, Francisco de Almeida's fleet destroyed the East African city of Mombasa. This attack was part of Almeida's broader campaign to establish Portuguese dominance along the East African coast.
events.name: Destruction of Mombasa

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1505, Francisco de Almeida arrived at Anjediva Island to begin constructing fortresses as part of his duties as the first Viceroy of India. This strategic move was essential for securing Portuguese interests in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Construction of Fortresses in Anjediva Islands

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1505, Lucien Grimaldi took over as the Lord of Monaco after murdering his brother, Jean II. This violent act marked a significant shift in the leadership of the Grimaldi family and the governance of Monaco.
events.name: Lucien Grimaldi Becomes Lord of Monaco

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1505, the King of Cannanore granted Francisco de Almeida permission to build the Fortaleza de Santo Ângelo in Kannur. This fortress was crucial for the Portuguese to secure their trade routes along the Indian coast.
events.name: Construction of Fortaleza de Santo Ângelo

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1505, Vasili III succeeded his father, Ivan III, as Grand Prince of Muscovy. His reign would further consolidate the power of the Russian state and expand its territories.
events.name: Vasili III Succeeds Ivan III

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1505, Portuguese explorer Lourenço de Almeida and his fleet were driven to the island of Sri Lanka by a storm, where they were granted permission by King Dharma Parakramabahu IX to establish a trade station and a Roman Catholic chapel in Colombo.
events.name: Lourenço de Almeida in Sri Lanka

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1505, the Treaty of Salamanca was signed between King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Philip, Duke of Burgundy, establishing them as co-regents for Joanna the Mad, Queen of Castile. This agreement was pivotal in the political landscape of Spain during this period.
events.name: Treaty of Salamanca

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1505, Érard de La Marck was elected as the prince-bishop of Liège. His election was significant in the context of the political and religious dynamics of the region during the early 16th century.
events.name: Érard de La Marck Elected Prince-Bishop of Liège

events.enhanced_description: In 1506, the Portuguese mariner Tristão da Cunha sighted the remote islands of Tristan da Cunha, naming them after himself. This discovery was part of the broader age of exploration that expanded European knowledge of the world's geography.

locations.country: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
locations.name: Tristan da Cunha

events.name: Tristão da Cunha sights Tristan da Cunha

events.enhanced_description: In 1506, during the Ming dynasty in China, the costs of the courier system were shifted from corvée labor service to a tax in silver on land. This reform reflected the changing economic policies of the Ming government.
events.name: Ming dynasty courier system tax reform

events.enhanced_description: In 1506, Duarte Barbosa, a notable Portuguese explorer and chronicler, returned to Lisbon after his voyages. His accounts contributed to the understanding of the newly discovered lands and trade routes.
events.name: Duarte Barbosa returns to Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: Johannes Trithemius, a noted scholar and abbot, became the abbot of the monastery of St. Jacob in Würzburg, a significant center of learning during the Renaissance period.
events.name: Johannes Trithemius becomes abbot of the monastery of St. Jacob

events.enhanced_description: Leonardo da Vinci completed most of his work on the Mona Lisa, a masterpiece of Renaissance art, which would later become one of the most famous paintings in the world.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci completes most of his work on the Mona Lisa

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1506, the classical statue of Laocoön and His Sons was unearthed in Rome. Following its discovery, Pope Julius II purchased the statue and placed it on public display in the Vatican, showcasing the Renaissance's revival of classical art.
events.name: Unearthing of Laocoön and His Sons

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1506, the Swiss Guard, a group of elite soldiers, arrived at the Vatican to serve as the personal bodyguards of Pope Julius II. This event marked the beginning of a longstanding tradition of Swiss mercenaries serving the papacy, known for their distinctive uniforms and loyalty.
events.name: The Swiss Guard arrives at the Vatican

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1506, Henry, Prince of Wales, was inducted into the prestigious Order of the Golden Fleece by Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor. This honor reflected the close ties between the English and Habsburg royal families during this period.
events.name: Henry, Prince of Wales is made a Knight of the Golden Fleece

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1506, Iye Roy Mackay, the Chief of Clan Mackay in Scotland, documented a grant of six lands in what is now Sutherland County. This act initiated a feud with Euphemia II, Countess of Ross, highlighting the turbulent clan dynamics of the time.
events.name: Iye Roy Mackay records his grant of lands

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1506, the Portuguese fleet, commanded by Lourenço de Almeida, achieved a decisive victory against the fleet of the Zamorin of Calicut at the Battle of Cannanore. This battle was significant in establishing Portuguese dominance in the Indian Ocean and marked a turning point in the region's maritime conflicts.
events.name: Battle of Cannanore

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1506, King Vladislaus II of Hungary and Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, signed a treaty to arrange the marriage of Vladislaus's daughter to Maximilian's son. This alliance aimed to strengthen political ties between Hungary and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Treaty between Vladislaus II and Maximilian I

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1506, Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone for the new St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, marking the beginning of a monumental architectural project that would take over a century to complete. This basilica would become one of the most significant symbols of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Foundation stone of St. Peter's Basilica laid

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on April 19, 1506, the Lisbon Massacre was a tragic event marked by three days of violence against the Jewish community in Lisbon, Portugal, where thousands were tortured and killed by Catholic mobs. This event reflected the intense religious intolerance of the period.
events.name: The Lisbon Massacre begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1506, the Malus Intercursus treaty was signed between King Henry VII of England and Duke Philip IV of Burgundy. This treaty aimed to improve trade relations and resolve ongoing disputes between the two powers.
events.name: Malus Intercursus treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1506, Badi' al-Zaman Mirza ascended to the position of Emir of the Timurid Empire following the death of his father, Sultan Husayn Bayqara. His reign marked a continuation of the Timurid legacy in Central Asia.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of Prince Badi al-Zaman at his father Sultan Husayn Bayqara’s coronation in Herat.
image.credit: 1469 artist, Herat — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: Depicted scene: 1469; the associated event is dated 1506-05-04.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Badi' al-Zaman Mirza becomes Emir

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1506, Emperor Moctezuma II of the Aztec Empire quelled a rebellion in Zozollan, east of Achiutia. Following the victory, he executed the captured prisoners as sacrifices to the gods, reflecting the religious practices of the Aztec civilization.
events.name: Moctezuma II subdues rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1506, Mahmud Shah II ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Kedah, a significant Muslim kingdom on the Malay Peninsula, following the death of his father, Adilin I. His reign would last for 41 years, shaping the region's political landscape.
events.name: Mahmud Shah II begins reign

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1506, the Treaty of Villafáfila was signed between Austria and Spain, solidifying political alliances and addressing territorial disputes. This treaty was part of the broader Habsburg strategy to strengthen their influence in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Villafáfila signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1506, Philip the Fair, Duke of Burgundy, became the ruler of the Spanish Kingdom of Castile alongside his wife, Joanna of Castile. His reign was short-lived, lasting only two months before he succumbed to typhoid fever.
events.name: Philip the Fair becomes ruler of Castile

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1506, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania achieved a significant victory over the Tatars of the Crimean Khanate at the Battle of Kletsk. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Lithuanian state and the Tatar incursions into its territory.
events.name: Battle of Kletsk

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1506, Sigismund I the Old succeeded his brother as King of Poland. His reign would last for over 40 years, during which he would significantly influence Polish politics and culture.
events.name: Sigismund I the Old becomes King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1506, Emperor Yonsangun of the Joseon Dynasty was deposed in a coup led by his younger brother, who became King Jungjong. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Korea, as Yonsangun was known for his tyrannical rule.
events.name: Emperor Yonsangun deposed

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1506, Philip I, the first Spanish Habsburg King of Castile, died suddenly from typhoid fever. His death had significant implications for the Spanish crown and the future of the Habsburg dynasty.

image.caption: Illustration from Johannes de Vico’s world chronicle, *Chronicon*.
image.credit: Unknown illustrator (illustration); Johannes de Vico (book author) — Nagy, Eszter (1 January 2021). "A World Chronicle for Philip the Fair". Codices manuscripti & impressi: 43–64. Link: https://www.academia.edu/50719472/A_World_Chronicle_for_Philip_the_Fair
image.date_qualification: A manuscript illustration made around 1495–1498, before Philip I’s death; it is contextual rather than a depiction of the death event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Philip I dies

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1506, a revolt erupted in Córdoba, Spain, where members of the nobility and the general public rose against the Spanish inquisitor Diego Rodriguez de Lucero and General Inquisitor Diego de Deza. The mob successfully liberated prisoners from the Córdoba prison, reflecting widespread discontent with the Inquisition.
events.name: Córdoba revolt against Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1506, Pope Julius II issued a papal bull excommunicating Giovanni II Bentivoglio, the ruler of Bologna. This act was part of Julius II's efforts to reclaim control over the city-state and assert papal authority.
events.name: Pope Julius II excommunicates Giovanni II Bentivoglio

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1506, Charles II, the six-year-old son of King Philip of Castile, was proclaimed Duke of Burgundy and 'Lord of the Netherlands.' This proclamation marked the beginning of his future role in European politics as a member of the Habsburg dynasty.
events.name: Charles II proclaimed Lord of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1506, Pope Julius II personally led his troops into Bologna to reclaim the city from Giovanni II Bentivoglio, who had been excommunicated. This military action underscored the pope's determination to restore papal authority in the region.
events.name: Pope Julius II retakes Bologna

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1506, Sigismund I the Old, the younger brother of the late Alexander Jagiellon, was crowned King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. His reign would last over 40 years, significantly impacting the political landscape of both nations.
events.name: Sigismund I the Old becomes King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: The Timurid Dynasty came to an end in 1507 when Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani captured the capital city of Herat. Emir Badi' al-Zaman Mirza fled, marking a significant shift in power in Central Asia.
events.name: End of the Timurid Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1507, the Portuguese expanded their territorial claims by occupying Mozambique and the islands of Socotra and Lamu. This expansion was part of their broader strategy to control trade routes along the eastern coast of Africa and the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Portuguese occupation of Mozambique and islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1507, the Portuguese founded the town of Stone Town in Mozambique, which would later become a significant center for trade and cultural exchange in the region. The town's architecture reflects a blend of African, Arab, and European influences.
events.name: Founding of Stone Town in Mozambique

events.enhanced_description: In 1507, Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros was appointed as the inquisitor general of Castile, a position that allowed him to enforce religious orthodoxy and combat heresy during a time of significant religious upheaval in Spain.
events.name: Cardinal Cisneros appointed inquisitor general of Castile

events.enhanced_description: In 1507, King Henry VII of England took decisive action against lords who maintained private armies, fearing they posed a threat to his regime. This move was part of his broader efforts to consolidate power and stabilize the monarchy.
events.name: King Henry VII prosecutes lords for private armies

events.enhanced_description: In 1507, the renowned artist Raphael completed 'The Deposition', a significant work that exemplifies the High Renaissance style. This painting reflects his mastery of composition and emotional expression.
events.name: Raphael paints The Deposition

events.enhanced_description: According to Bernardino de Sahagún, the Aztec New Fire ceremony was held for the last time in 1507. This ritual was crucial in Aztec cosmology, symbolizing renewal and the cyclical nature of time.
events.name: Last Aztec New Fire ceremony

events.enhanced_description: Sigismund I the Old was formally crowned King of Poland in a grand ceremony in Kraków, marking the beginning of his reign which would significantly influence Polish history.
events.name: Sigismund I the Old is formally crowned King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: The crew of the Portuguese ship Cirne, commanded by Diogo Fernandes Pereira, became the first Europeans to sight the island of Réunion, naming it Santa Apolonia, marking an important moment in the Age of Discovery.
events.name: First Europeans sight the island of Réunion

events.enhanced_description: In response to the Lisbon Massacre, King Manuel I of Portugal issued an edict allowing the cristãos-novos, or New Christians, to emigrate freely from Portugal, reflecting the complex dynamics of religious tolerance and persecution during this period.
events.name: King Manuel I of Portugal issues an edict for New Christians

events.enhanced_description: Cesare Borgia, an Italian mercenary leader, completed his conquest of the Spanish city of Viana, but his pursuit of fleeing defenders led to his capture and subsequent death, illustrating the perils of ambition in warfare.
events.name: Cesare Borgia completes conquest of Viana

events.enhanced_description: The revolutionary council of the Republic of Genoa declared war against French invaders, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflicts over control of Italian territories during the Renaissance.
events.name: Republic of Genoa declares war against French invaders

events.enhanced_description: Martin Luther, a pivotal figure in the Protestant Reformation, was ordained as a priest in Erfurt by Bishop Johann Bonemilch, marking the beginning of his religious career that would challenge the Catholic Church.
events.name: Martin Luther is ordained as a priest

events.enhanced_description: Paolo da Novi was installed as the first Doge of the Republic of Genoa in nearly two decades, but his reign was short-lived as he fled from French occupation forces shortly thereafter.
events.name: Paolo da Novi becomes Doge of the Republic of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: Martin Waldseemüller published his work Cosmographiae Introductio, which included the first map to depict the Americas as a separate continent, significantly influencing cartography and the understanding of the New World.
events.name: Martin Waldseemüller publishes Cosmographiae Introductio

events.enhanced_description: Troops from the Kingdom of Cannanore began a four-month siege of the Portuguese garrison at Fort Saint Angelo in Kerala, India, where a small number of defenders held out against a vastly larger force until relief arrived.

locations.name: Fort Saint Angelo, Kannur, Kerala, India

events.name: Siege of Fort Saint Angelo begins

events.enhanced_description: After a seven-day siege, French troops successfully retook the city of Genoa from rebel forces, restoring control over a key Italian city during the turbulent conflicts of the period.
events.name: French troops retake Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The unveiling of Lorenzo Lotto's Santa Cristina al Tiverone Altarpiece at the Church of Santa Cristina in Treviso showcased the artist's mastery and contributed to the rich tapestry of Renaissance art.
events.name: Lorenzo Lotto unveils Santa Cristina al Tiverone Altarpiece

events.enhanced_description: King Ferdinand II of Aragon left Naples after being denied recognition by Pope Julius II, a significant political event that underscored the tensions between the Spanish crown and the Papacy.
events.name: King Ferdinand II of Aragon departs from Naples

events.enhanced_description: In a spectacular ceremony, King Ferdinand II of Aragon was welcomed by King Louis XII of France in Savona, where they began discussions on the division of the Italian kingdoms, reflecting the geopolitical complexities of the time.
events.name: King Ferdinand II of Aragon meets King Louis XII of France

events.enhanced_description: After a series of political maneuvers, King Ferdinand II of Aragon returned to Valencia to resume his rule, a move that solidified his control over his Spanish kingdom.
events.name: King Ferdinand II of Aragon returns to Valencia

events.enhanced_description: Afonso de Albuquerque set sail from the Yemeni island of Socotra with six ships, embarking on a campaign to conquer the Persian Gulf port of Hormuz, a strategic location for trade and military dominance.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque departs from Socotra

events.enhanced_description: A fleet of 11 ships from the Portuguese Navy's 8th Armada arrived in India to rescue the defenders of Fort Saint Angelo, who had been under siege by the Kingdom of Cannanore for four months.

locations.name: Fort Saint Angelo, Kannur, Kerala, India

events.name: Portuguese Navy rescues defenders of Fort Saint Angelo

events.enhanced_description: King James IV of Scotland granted a patent for the first printing press in Scotland, allowing for the production of books and literature, which would significantly impact Scottish culture and education.
events.name: King James IV grants patent for first printing press in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Afonso de Albuquerque's fleet arrived at the port of Hormuz on the Persian Gulf, initiating a campaign to conquer this vital trading hub, which was crucial for controlling maritime routes.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque arrives at Hormuz

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move to control trade routes in the Persian Gulf, the Kingdom of Portugal, led by Afonso de Albuquerque, successfully conquers Hormuz Island. This victory solidified Portuguese dominance in the region and facilitated their trade interests in Asia.
events.name: The Kingdom of Portugal conquers the island of Ormuz in the Persian Gulf

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1507, Portuguese Admiral Tristão da Cunha led a fleet of 12 ships to engage a Muslim merchant fleet of 13 ships off the coast of Ponnani. The Portuguese emerged victorious, further establishing their naval power in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Battle of Ponnani

events.enhanced_description: Pope Julius II issued a damnatio memoriae against the House of Borgia on November 26, 1507, effectively erasing their legacy and influence from the Papal States. This act was part of Julius II's broader efforts to reform the Church and diminish the power of corrupt families.
events.name: Damnatio Memoriae of the House of Borgia

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1507, Princess Mary of England, the daughter of King Henry VII, was betrothed to the 7-year-old Duke of Burgundy. This political alliance aimed to strengthen ties between England and the powerful Burgundian court.
events.name: Betrothal of Princess Mary of England

events.enhanced_description: In 1508, Ferdinand II of Aragon appointed Florentine merchant Amerigo Vespucci as Chief Navigator of Spain. This position was pivotal in the Age of Exploration, as Vespucci's voyages contributed to the understanding of the New World.
events.name: Amerigo Vespucci appointed Chief Navigator

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1508, Maximilian I, King of the Romans, sought permission from the Republic of Venice to march through their territory to Rome. His request was denied, prompting him to initiate his Italienzug, a military campaign in Italy.
events.name: Maximilian requests passage through Venetian territory

events.enhanced_description: During the Glinski rebellion on February 2, 1508, Lithuanian noble Mykolas Glinskis launched an attack on Grodno, decapitating Jan Zabrzeziński, a key ally of Grand Duke Alexander. This act intensified the conflict between the Lithuanian nobles and the ruling powers.
events.name: Mykolas Glinskis attacks Grodno

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1508, Maximilian I proclaimed himself Holy Roman Emperor in Trento after being blocked by Venice from reaching Rome for his coronation by Pope Julius II. This self-proclamation marked a significant assertion of his authority.
events.name: Maximilian proclaims himself Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1508, Maximilian I launched an attack against the Republic of Venice, resulting in the sacking of Ampezzo. This conflict was part of the larger struggle for power in Northern Italy.
events.name: Maximilian I attacks the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his father Philip on February 28, 1508, Louis V ascended as the new prince elector of the Palatinate. His election was significant in the context of the Holy Roman Empire's political landscape.
events.name: Louis V becomes prince elector of the Palatinate

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1508, the Republic of Venice achieved a decisive victory over Maximilian I in the Battle of Cadore. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between Venice and the Holy Roman Empire.

image.caption: Peter Paul Rubens’s drawing after Titian’s painting of the Battle of Cadore.
image.credit: Peter Paul Rubens — https://dams.antwerpen.be/asset/kfXajO3klTdEAMgO8db5yQOx
image.date_qualification: Retrospective drawing made between 1600 and 1650 after a Titian painting; it is not a contemporary depiction made at the 1508 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Cadore

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1508, Ludovico Ariosto premiered 'La Cassaria', recognized as the first Italian language comedy. This work marked a significant development in Italian literature and theater.
events.name: Premiere of La Cassaria

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1508, the first Red Hose Race was held in Carnwath, Scotland, marking the beginning of what would become the oldest annual foot race in Europe. This event reflects the cultural traditions of Scottish communities.
events.name: First Red Hose Race

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his father Albrecht IV on March 18, 1508, Wilhelm IV ascended to the title of Duke of Bavaria. His reign would be marked by significant political and cultural developments in the region.
events.name: Wilhelm IV becomes Duke of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: In March 1508, Leonardo da Vinci began compiling his 'collection without order', a series of scientific discoveries and observations, while working from the house of Piero di Braccio Martelli in Florence. This work would contribute significantly to the fields of art and science.
events.name: Leonardo da Vinci begins scientific writings

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1508, Mihnea cel Rău, son of Vlad the Impaler, ascended to the position of Voivode of Wallachia following the death of his cousin Radu IV the Great. His rule would be characterized by political intrigue and conflict.
events.name: Mihnea cel Rău becomes Voivode of Wallachia

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1508, Michelangelo signed a contract with the Vatican to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, agreeing to a fee of 3,000 gold ducats. This monumental project would become one of the most celebrated works of art in history.
events.name: Michelangelo signs contract for Sistine Chapel

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1508, Prince Lajos was crowned as the designated successor to his father, King Vladislaus II of Hungary, in Székesfehérvár, a city with a rich royal history. This event marked a significant moment in the Hungarian monarchy, as it established Lajos's future role in the governance of the kingdom.
events.name: The coronation of Prince Lajos

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1508, Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I signed an armistice with the Republic of Venice, temporarily halting his ambitions in Italy. This agreement reflected the complex political landscape of the Italian Wars, where shifting alliances and territorial disputes were common.
events.name: Armistice signed by Maximilian I and the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1508, Hun-Iq' ascended to the throne as one of the two kings of the Kaqchikel Maya civilization following the death of his father, King Oxlahuh-Tz'i. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Kaqchikel, a prominent Maya group in the region.

locations.name: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Guatemala City

events.name: Hun-Iq' becomes king of Kaqchikel Maya

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1508, the process of removing previous layers of paint from the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was completed, allowing Michelangelo to begin marking the surface for his iconic frescoes. This project would later become one of the most celebrated works of art in Western history.
events.name: Completion of paint removal in the Sistine Chapel

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1508, Emperor Na'od of Ethiopia died in battle, leading to the ascension of his son, Lebna Dengel, who would take the regnal name Dawit II. This transition marked a pivotal moment in Ethiopian history as it set the stage for future conflicts and reforms.
events.name: Death of Emperor Na'od of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1508, Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León landed on the island of Puerto Rico, marking the beginning of Spanish settlement. He was welcomed by Agüeybaná I, the Taíno leader, and soon established the settlement of Caparra, which would become a significant site in the Spanish colonization of the Caribbean.

locations.name: Caparra Archaeological Site, Guaynabo, Puerto Rico

events.name: Spanish settlement of Puerto Rico begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1508, Cardinal Galeotto Franciotti della Rovere died unexpectedly, leaving England without a Roman Catholic Cardinal protector. This event set the stage for a power vacuum that would be further complicated by the subsequent death of King Henry VII and the rise of Henry VIII.
events.name: Death of Cardinal Galeotto Franciotti della Rovere

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1508, an inconclusive peace treaty was signed to end the third of the Muscovite–Lithuanian Wars. This treaty highlighted the ongoing tensions and territorial disputes between the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
events.name: Inconclusive peace treaty in the Muscovite–Lithuanian Wars

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1508, King Louis XII of France convened a court at the Parlement de Normandie in Rouen. This event was part of his efforts to consolidate power and administer justice in his realm during a time of political strife.
events.name: King Louis XII convenes court in Rouen

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1508, at the age of 16, Prince Wolfgang of the House of Ascania became the ruler of the principality of Anhalt-Köthen, succeeding his father Waldemar VI. Wolfgang would later play a significant role in the Protestant Reformation within his territory.
events.name: Prince Wolfgang becomes ruler of Anhalt-Köthen

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1508, the astronomer Mikołaj Kopernik was granted benefits by Pope Julius II, enabling him to pursue his astronomical studies. This support would later prove crucial in the development of his heliocentric theory, which revolutionized the understanding of the cosmos.
events.name: Mikołaj Kopernik granted benefits by Pope Julius II

events.enhanced_description: In December 1508, Michelangelo began painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City, following a commission from Pope Julius II. This monumental work would become one of the most renowned masterpieces of Renaissance art.
events.name: Michelangelo begins painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1508, the League of Cambrai was formed as an alliance against the Republic of Venice, involving key figures such as Pope Julius II, Louis XII of France, Maximilian I, and Ferdinand II of Aragon. This coalition aimed to curb Venetian power in Italy during the Italian Wars.
events.name: Formation of the League of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1508, the Battle of Dabul took place, where Portuguese forces under Francisco de Almeida attacked Khambhat. This battle was part of the Portuguese efforts to establish dominance in the Indian Ocean and secure trade routes.
events.name: Battle of Dabul

events.enhanced_description: Under the command of King Louis XII, the French army crossed the Adda River at Cassano d'Adda, marking a significant maneuver in the Italian Wars. This movement was part of the broader conflict for control over Northern Italy.
events.name: French army crosses the Adda River

events.enhanced_description: The Venetian forces, encamped around Treviglio, strategically moved south towards the Po River in search of better positions during the ongoing conflicts in Northern Italy. This maneuver was part of the larger military engagements of the Italian Wars.
events.name: Venetians move towards the Po River

events.enhanced_description: Henry VIII married Catherine of Aragon, solidifying a political alliance between England and Spain. Their marriage would later become a pivotal point in English history, leading to significant religious and political changes.
events.name: Marriage of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: Luca Pacioli published his influential work 'De divina proportione' in Venice, which explored the mathematical concept of the golden ratio. The book featured illustrations by the renowned artist Leonardo da Vinci, bridging the gap between art and mathematics.
events.name: Publication of De divina proportione

events.enhanced_description: Erasmus composed his most famous work, 'In Praise of Folly', which critiqued societal norms and the Church. This satirical text became a cornerstone of Renaissance humanism and influenced later reformers.
events.name: Erasmus writes In Praise of Folly

events.enhanced_description: St Paul's School was founded by John Colet, Dean of St Paul's Cathedral, as a response to the need for a more rigorous education for boys. The school has since become one of the leading independent schools in the UK.
events.name: St Paul's School founded

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Grammar School in Guildford was founded under the will of Robert Beckingham, aiming to provide quality education to boys. It has a long-standing tradition of academic excellence.
events.name: Royal Grammar School founded

events.enhanced_description: Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School was established as a grammar school for boys in Blackburn, contributing to the educational landscape of England. It has maintained a reputation for academic rigor.
events.name: Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School founded

events.enhanced_description: Georg Tannstetter was appointed by Maximilian I as the Professor of Astronomy at the University of Vienna, reflecting the growing interest in scientific inquiry during the Renaissance period.
events.name: Georg Tannstetter appointed Professor of Astronomy

events.enhanced_description: Johannes Pfefferkorn authored his fourth and fifth pamphlets, 'Das Osterbuch' and 'Der Judenfeind', which condemned the Jewish faith and people. These works contributed to the anti-Semitic discourse of the time.
events.name: Johannes Pfefferkorn writes pamphlets

events.enhanced_description: Basil Solomon was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East, a significant religious leadership position within the Syriac Orthodox Church. His role was crucial in maintaining the church's influence in the region.
events.name: Basil Solomon becomes Maphrian

events.enhanced_description: Brasenose College, one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford, was founded through the efforts of Sir Richard Sutton and Bishop William Smyth. The college has since become known for its rich history and academic excellence.
events.name: Brasenose College, Oxford is founded

events.enhanced_description: Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon were crowned as King and Queen of England in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. This event marked the beginning of their tumultuous reign and significant historical impact on England.
events.name: Coronation of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: Venetian forces successfully retook the city of Padua from French control, marking a significant victory in the ongoing conflicts of the Italian Wars. This event underscored the shifting power dynamics in Northern Italy.
events.name: Venetian forces retake Padua

events.enhanced_description: Krishnadevaraya ascended the throne of the Vijayanagara Empire, becoming one of the most celebrated rulers in Indian history. His reign is noted for significant advancements in art, architecture, and literature.
events.name: Krishnadevaraya ascends the throne

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian I of the Holy Roman Empire, alongside French allies, initiated a siege of Padua that would last for several months. This military action was part of the broader conflict during the Italian Wars.

image.caption: Jacopo Palma il Giovane’s painting “Padova riacquistata da Andrea Gritti e da Giovanni Diedo.”
image.credit: Jacopo Palma il Giovane — Palazzo Ducale (Venezia). Digitalizzata dal sito Web Gallery of Art https://www.wga.hu/html_m/p/palma/giovane/1/4ducale31.html
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting associated with the Venetian recapture of Padua; it is not a contemporary depiction of the siege. Image date: 1584.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Padua begins

events.enhanced_description: Maximilian I issued an order for all Jews within the Holy Roman Empire to destroy books that opposed Christianity, reflecting the religious tensions of the time. This decree was part of a broader pattern of persecution against Jewish communities.
events.name: Maximilian I orders Jewish book purge

events.enhanced_description: A devastating earthquake struck Constantinople, resulting in the destruction of 109 mosques and an estimated death toll of 10,000 people. This disaster had significant social and economic repercussions for the city.
events.name: Constantinople earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Portuguese fidalgo Diogo Lopes de Sequeira became the first European to reach Malacca after crossing the Gulf of Bengal. His arrival marked the beginning of European influence in the region.
events.name: Diogo Lopes de Sequeira reaches Malacca

events.enhanced_description: A violent storm struck the Dutch coast, resulting in potentially thousands of fatalities. This natural disaster highlighted the vulnerability of coastal communities to extreme weather events.
events.name: Storm ravages Dutch coast

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Padua concluded with a Venetian victory, forcing the retreat of Holy Roman Empire and French forces back to Tyrol and Milan. This victory allowed the Venetians to regain control over key territories.
events.name: Siege of Padua ends

events.enhanced_description: Afonso de Albuquerque was appointed as the Viceroy of Portuguese India, succeeding Francisco de Almeida, who tragically lost his life shortly after in a battle against local forces. Albuquerque's leadership would shape Portuguese colonial policy in the region.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque becomes Viceroy

events.enhanced_description: Uriel von Gemmingen was tasked with securing opinions on the continuation of the Jewish book purge initiated by Maximilian I. This reflects the ongoing religious intolerance and persecution faced by Jewish communities in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Uriel von Gemmingen assigned for Jewish book purge

events.enhanced_description: Prince Le Oanh orchestrated a coup d'état against his cousin, Emperor Le Uy Muc, and was enthroned as Emperor Le Tuong Duc at the young age of 14. This political upheaval marked a significant shift in the Vietnamese monarchy.
events.name: Coup d'état in Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In 1510, Grand Prince Vasili III of Moscow conquered Pskov, further expanding his territory and consolidating power in the region. This conquest was part of his broader campaign to unify Russian lands.
events.name: Vasili III conquers Pskov

events.enhanced_description: In 1510, Paolo Cortese published 'De Cardinalatu', a manual for cardinals that included advice on palatial architecture. This work would later inspire Thomas Wolsey in his construction projects at Hampton Court Palace.
events.name: Publication of De Cardinalatu

events.enhanced_description: In 1510, Spaniards brought sunflowers to Europe from the Americas. This introduction marked the beginning of the sunflower's cultivation and popularity in European gardens and agriculture.
events.name: Introduction of sunflowers to Europe

events.enhanced_description: An 18-year-old Henry VIII jousted anonymously at Richmond, drawing applause from spectators before revealing his identity. This event showcased his athletic prowess and charisma, which would define his early reign.
events.name: Henry VIII jousts anonymously

events.enhanced_description: The Mary Rose, a warship of the English Tudor navy, was laid out in Portsmouth in 1510. She would later be launched in 1511 and famously sank during the Battle of the Solent in 1545, marking a significant event in naval history.
events.name: The Mary Rose ship is laid out

events.enhanced_description: Catherine of Aragon, the first wife of King Henry VIII, gave birth to a stillborn daughter on January 31, 1510. This event marked the beginning of a series of personal and political challenges for the couple, as they struggled to produce a male heir.
events.name: Catherine of Aragon gives birth to her first child

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1510, Afonso de Albuquerque began a nine-month campaign to conquer Goa, a strategic coastal city in India. This conquest marked a significant expansion of Portuguese influence in the region, establishing Goa as a key base for trade and military operations.
events.name: Portuguese conquest of Goa begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1510, the indigenous ǃUriǃcaekua people decisively defeated sailors of the Portuguese Empire at the Battle of Salt River. This battle highlighted the resistance of local populations against European colonial forces in South Africa.

locations.name: Salt River, Cape Town, South Africa

events.name: Battle of Salt River

events.enhanced_description: Mihnea cel Rău, the ruling Prince of Wallachia, was assassinated on March 12, 1510, while attending Mass in Sibiu. His death marked a significant political upheaval in Wallachia, leading to a power struggle among local nobility.
events.name: Assassination of Mihnea cel Rău

events.enhanced_description: The 'Disturbance of the Three Ports' began on April 4, 1510, as Japanese merchants revolted against the Korean government in the cities of Dongnae, Changwon, and Ulsan. This uprising reflected the tensions between Japan and Korea during the period of Japanese incursions.

locations.name: Changwon, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea

events.name: Disturbance of the Three Ports

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1510, Park Won-jong resigned as Chief State Councillor of the Korean Empire, paving the way for Kim Su-dong to succeed him. This transition was part of the broader political dynamics within the Korean court during the early 16th century.
events.name: Park Won-jong resigns as Chief State Councillor

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1510, the Korean Emperor Jungjong suppressed a simultaneous Japanese uprising, resulting in a two-year halt of trade between Korea and Japan. This event underscored the fragile relations between the two nations during this period.
events.name: Suppression of Japanese uprising in Korea

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1510, King Min Raza of the Kingdom of Arakan permanently relocated from Mrauk-U to the old capital of Waithali. His lack of interest in governance during this period raised concerns about the stability of his reign.
events.name: Min Raza relocates capital

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1510, Zhu Zhifan, the Prince of Anhua, initiated a rebellion by killing officials at a banquet, aiming to oust the powerful eunuch Liu Jin during the reign of the Zhengde Emperor. This act of defiance marked a significant moment in the Ming dynasty's internal power struggles.
events.name: Prince of Anhua rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1510, the Prince of Anhua rebellion came to an end when rebel leader Zhu Zhifan was defeated and captured by commander Qiu Yue. This event reinforced the authority of the Ming dynasty and highlighted the challenges posed by internal dissent.
events.name: End of the Prince of Anhua rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1510, Sultan Abu Abdallah V of Tlemcen agreed to pay tribute to Ferdinand II of Aragon, which prompted Ferdinand to plot an invasion of Ifriqiya and its capital, Tripoli. This diplomatic maneuvering was part of the broader power struggles in North Africa.
events.name: Sultan of Tlemcen agrees to tribute

events.enhanced_description: In July 1510, the Holy League, formed to defend the Italian States, launched an attack on French-occupied Genoa. This military action was part of the ongoing conflicts in Italy during the Renaissance, reflecting the complex political alliances of the time.
events.name: Holy League attacks French-occupied Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1510, Spanish troops captured Tripoli under the command of Pedro Navarro, following the orders of King Ferdinand II of Aragon. This event marked a significant expansion of Spanish influence in North Africa.
events.name: Spanish capture of Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1510, the Royal Dano-Norwegian Navy was founded when Henrich Krummedige was appointed chief captain of all naval forces. This establishment marked the beginning of organized naval power in Denmark and Norway.
events.name: Foundation of the Royal Dano-Norwegian Navy

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1510, Sir Thomas More was appointed undersheriff of the City of London. This position marked an important step in his political career, leading to his later prominence as a statesman and author.
events.name: Sir Thomas More becomes undersheriff of London

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1510, an estimated 6.7 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Japan near Nanko-Higashi in the Seto Inland Sea. This natural disaster caused significant damage and loss of life in the region.
events.name: Earthquake in the Seto Inland Sea

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1510, an earthquake in the Enshunada Sea off the coast of Hamamatsu produced a devastating tsunami. This event had catastrophic effects on coastal communities in the region.
events.name: Earthquake and tsunami in Enshunada Sea

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1510, Mingyi Nyo declared independence from the Ava Kingdom, establishing the Toungoo dynasty in upper Burma. This declaration marked the beginning of a new era in Burmese history.
events.name: Mingyi Nyo declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1510, Afonso de Albuquerque successfully conquered Goa, establishing it as a colony of Portuguese India. This victory solidified Portuguese control over key trade routes in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque conquers Goa

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1510, the Battle of Marv took place, where Shah Ismail I defeated the Uzbek forces led by Shaybani Khan in Khorasan. This victory was pivotal in consolidating Ismail's power in Persia.
events.name: Battle of Marv

events.enhanced_description: St John's College, Cambridge, was founded by Lady Margaret Beaufort, receiving its charter on January 1, 1511. This college would become a significant institution in higher education.
events.name: Foundation of St John's College, Cambridge

events.enhanced_description: The Şahkulu Rebellion broke out in Anatolia, led by Sakhulu Baba against the Ottoman Empire. This uprising highlighted the tensions within the empire during this period.
events.name: Şahkulu Rebellion in Anatolia

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, Diego Velázquez, appointed by the Spanish crown, led the conquest of Cuba alongside Hernán Cortés. Following the successful subjugation of the island, Velázquez was appointed its first governor, establishing Spanish colonial rule in the region.

image.caption: Portrait of Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — John Carter Brown Library
image.date_qualification: Image date supplied as 1728; it is not contemporary with the 1511 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Diego Velázquez and Hernán Cortés conquer Cuba; Velázquez is appointed Governor

events.enhanced_description: Duarte Barbosa, a Portuguese explorer, arrived in India for the second time in 1511, serving as a clerk in the Portuguese factory at Cananor. His role was crucial as he acted as a liaison with local Indian rulers, facilitating trade and diplomatic relations.
events.name: Duarte Barbosa arrives in India for the second time

events.enhanced_description: After the fall of Malacca in 1511, Afonso de Albuquerque dispatched Duarte Fernandes on a significant diplomatic mission to Burma and Siam. This marked the first recorded visit by a European envoy to these regions, establishing early diplomatic ties.
events.name: Afonso de Albuquerque sends Duarte Fernandes on a diplomatic mission to Burma and Siam

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, Ferdinand II of Aragon made a controversial observation regarding labor in the New World, stating that 'one black can do the work of four Indians.' This remark reflected the growing reliance on African slaves for labor in the Spanish colonies.
events.name: Ferdinand II of Aragon observes that 'one black can do the work of four Indians'

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, Spanish sailor Juan de Agramonte is believed to have traveled to Newfoundland, potentially marking one of the early European contacts with North America. His journey highlights the expanding horizons of European exploration during this period.
events.name: Juan de Agramonte possibly travels to Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, the indigenous Taíno people revolted against Spanish colonial rule in southwestern Puerto Rico, particularly near Guánica. This uprising was a response to the harsh treatment and exploitation they faced under Spanish settlers.
events.name: The indigenous Taíno people revolt against the Spanish in Puerto Rico

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, the first black slaves were brought to Colombia, marking the beginning of a tragic chapter in the country's history. This event signified the start of the transatlantic slave trade's impact on the region and its societies.
events.name: The first black slaves arrive in Colombia

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish conquest of the Yucatán Peninsula began in 1511, as Spanish forces sought to subjugate the indigenous Maya civilization. This marked the start of a prolonged conflict that would lead to significant changes in the region's demographics and culture.
events.name: The Spanish conquest of Yucatán begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1511, the Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus published his seminal work, 'The Praise of Folly' (Laus Stultitiae), which critiqued the social and religious practices of the time. This work became one of the most influential texts of the Renaissance, promoting critical thought and reform.
events.name: Erasmus publishes The Praise of Folly

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1511, the Siege of Mirandola concluded after 18 days of fighting, resulting in the capture of the city by the Papal States with assistance from Spanish and Venetian troops. Pope Julius II personally led the troops, emphasizing the importance of this military campaign.
events.name: Siege of Mirandola

events.enhanced_description: King Henry VIII of England hosted a grand tournament in Westminster to celebrate the birth of his son, Prince Henry. The festivities were later immortalized in the 1511 Westminster Tournament Roll, which depicted the events in a series of painted images.
events.name: Westminster Tournament for Prince Henry

events.enhanced_description: The League of Cambrai, initially formed to counteract Venetian power, was dissolved as Spain and the Holy Roman Empire withdrew, forming an alliance against France. This shift marked a significant change in European political alliances during the early 16th century.
events.name: Dissolution of the League of Cambrai

events.enhanced_description: In what is now Myanmar, King Shwenankyawshin Narapati II dedicated his exquisite golden palace, showcasing the architectural and cultural achievements of the Ava Kingdom during this period.
events.name: Dedication of the Golden Palace by King Shwenankyawshin Narapati II

events.enhanced_description: On 'Fat Thursday', citizens of Friuli revolted against their Venetian occupiers, attacking Udine and committing acts of violence against the nobility. The rebellion was suppressed shortly after by special troops sent from Gradisca d'Isonzo.
events.name: Friuli Revolt against Venetian Rule

events.enhanced_description: Spanish conquistador Juan Ponce de León led an incursion against the local Taino warriors at Yahuecas, confronting Chief Urayoán. This event marked a significant moment in the Spanish colonization of Puerto Rico.

image.caption: Monument to conquistador Juan Ponce de León in Old San Juan, Puerto Rico.
image.credit: Matthew in Boston — https://www.flickr.com/photos/71187350@N08/8267505554/
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2012-12-08; monument dedicated in 1882. Neither date is the date of the 1511 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Juan Ponce de León's Incursion at Yahuecas

events.enhanced_description: A devastating 6.9 magnitude earthquake struck Slovenia and Italy, resulting in the deaths of over 10,000 people. The epicenter was near Idrija, causing widespread destruction across the region.
events.name: Earthquake in Slovenia and Italy

events.enhanced_description: St John's College in Cambridge received its charter, founded by Lady Margaret Beaufort. This institution would become one of the leading colleges in the University of Cambridge.
events.name: Charter of St John's College, Cambridge

events.enhanced_description: Five Roman Catholic cardinals, including Federico di Sanseverino, signed a document urging Pope Julius II to convene a council in Pisa to discuss church reform. The council was intended to address significant issues within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Cardinals Call for Council in Pisa
